docs.text: Lowen fears that he will freeze when it matters, and that his father was right.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could join the Heron's voyage alongside Lowen, help him prove himself to the race crew, or find out what is tearing his father's nets before Lowen meets it on the open sea.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Gwennol: mother
  • Cobb: father
  • Bree: sister
  • Thaddeus: self-appointed coach
  • Caspian: friend

docs.title: Mabyn
docs.text:
Keeper of the Hall Door

Town Bain Harbour Where Harbour Hall Role Service Age Elder In the game Mabyn

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gentle, chatty and endlessly fond of the old stories. She treats every visitor as if they had come all this way just to see her.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Mabyn keeps the door of the Harbour Hall. She opens it at dawn and closes it at dusk, and in between she greets every captain, merchant, fisherman and lost traveller who comes up the steps as if they had come all this way just to see her. She is seventy-four, gentle, chatty and endlessly fond of the old stories, and she knows more tales of Old Bain than anyone alive. She is sure at least half of them are true. She is not always sure which half.

docs.title: The galley years
docs.text:
Mabyn went to sea at fifteen as a cook's girl, peeling potatoes in the galley of a coasting trader, and she was a ship's cook for most of her life after. She cooked on half a dozen ships along the coast of Veligor, and sailors still tell each other which of her stews they would sail through a gale for. She was the cook aboard the Sandpiper, a small coasting ship long since broken up, when a twelve-year-old deck girl called Quenna came aboard, loud, hungry and certain of everything. Mabyn fed her, scolded her, bandaged her rope-burned hands and listened to her plans for owning her own ship one day. Quenna is now Harbour Master, and Mabyn is still the person she talks to when she cannot talk to anyone else.

When Mabyn's knees gave up on galley ladders twenty-one years ago, she came ashore and asked the council for the job of keeping the hall door. She has kept it ever since. She never married and has no children of her own, but half the children in Bain Harbour grew up on her stories, and she counts them all.

docs.title: The boat-hook
docs.text: Every morning, before she unbolts the door, Mabyn climbs a little stool and polishes Old Bain's boat-hook, which hangs above the door of the Harbour Hall. It is a long, dark, battered thing of ash and iron, and its shaft is covered in nicks. Mabyn can tell you which nick came from which legendary fight, and she taught every one of them to Jowan, the Harbour Master's son, when he was a small boy running errands through the hall. He can still recite them, and she is very proud of that.

docs.title: The tales
docs.text:
According to Mabyn, Old Bain was a fisherwoman who built the first ship big enough to sail all the way around Veligor, and then sailed it, with a crew of her own cousins and a goat for luck. According to Mabyn, she rowed out into a winter storm with that boat-hook to haul a capsized boat home by its stern ring, and the deepest nick on the shaft is where the ring bit. According to Mabyn, the summer race around the island began as a dare, when a crew from another harbour said they could do what Old Bain had done faster. Mabyn believes every word of the first two. She thinks the third is probably true, because it sounds like sailors.

She and Hobart, the warehouseman, have a long and happy disagreement about the four ancient crates at the back of his oldest warehouse. Hobart says they have been there since Old Bain's day. Mabyn says that in that case they are full of Old Bain's spare boat-hooks, and that she will polish those too if he ever opens them.

docs.title: The keeper of secrets
docs.text:
Quenna trusts Mabyn with anything at all. When a council meeting has gone badly, the Harbour Master sits on the hall steps after everyone has gone, and Mabyn sits beside her with a pot of tea and listens. What Quenna tells her there, Mabyn has never repeated to a single soul, not even in a story, and for a woman who loves to talk as much as she does, that is the greatest compliment she knows how to pay.

Ottilie, the clerk, works just inside the door, and the two of them are firm friends of opposite kinds: Ottilie tidy and quiet, Mabyn chatty and never quite finished with a sentence. Mabyn brings her a sweet bun every morning and has decided she works too hard.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Mabyn wants the old stories to outlive her. She fears that the new stories the sailors are telling about the deep water will one day turn out to be the true half.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could find the truth behind one of Mabyn's tales of Old Bain, find out whether the deepest nick on the boat-hook really came from a stern ring, or carry a pot of tea and a message from the Harbour Master that she cannot send through the council.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Quenna: friend

docs.title: Maren
docs.text:
Harbour Schoolteacher

Town Bain Harbour Where Merchant Street Role Scholar Age Adult In the game Maren

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Patient, bright and strict about spelling. She can make a lesson out of anything that washes up on the beach.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Maren is the harbour schoolteacher, and she teaches the children of Bain Harbour their letters, their sums and the names of the stars. She is thirty-five, patient, bright and strict about spelling, and she can make a lesson out of anything that washes up on the beach. A crab shell is a lesson in counting legs. A piece of driftwood is a lesson in where the current runs. A message in a bottle, which has happened twice, was a whole week of lessons.

docs.title: The front room
docs.text:
Bain Harbour has no schoolhouse. Maren teaches in the front room of her narrow house on Merchant Street, which holds about twenty children if some of them sit on upturned crates and nobody minds their elbows. There are lessons every morning, and the children come when they can: the fishermen's children before the boats come in, the shipwrights' children when the yard can spare them, and the dock children whenever the docks are quiet. Maren has learned to teach a room in which half the pupils have just arrived and the other half are about to leave.

Among her pupils are Kit, the shipwright's son, who can spell "gunwale" but not "necessary"; Finch, the errand runner, who is the fastest at sums in the room because he has been counting coppers all his life; and Ossie, the lighthouse boy, who walks in all the way from the lighthouse and asks one question at a time, each of which takes the rest of the morning to answer. She loves all three of them and would not say so to any of them.

docs.title: Where she comes from
docs.text: Maren grew up on Merchant Street. Her mother, Elowen, kept the books for the merchants there and taught Maren to read from bills of lading before she could hold a pen properly. At eighteen Maren went to Selsior and spent three years in the Scholars' Quarter, where she learned more than she had known there was to learn and decided she would rather teach it than keep it. She came home at twenty-one, and she has taught the harbour children for thirteen years. Elowen died ten years ago. Maren still teaches from her mother's old desk.

docs.title: The schoolhouse
docs.text: What Maren wants most is a proper schoolhouse, with a roof that does not leak on the slates, a room big enough for every child in the harbour, and windows that look out at the sea, because so many of her lessons begin out there. She has asked the harbour council for one every year. The council is made of captains, shipwrights and merchants, and every one of them agrees the harbour needs a school and then asks whether it might wait until after the race, or after the harvest, or after the second pier Garrow keeps shouting about. Maren has started bringing her pupils' best work to the council meetings to make her case. Last time she brought Kit's spelling, which may have been a mistake.

docs.title: The things on the beach
docs.text: Lately the beach has been teaching lessons Maren does not know how to give. The children bring her things that have washed up: a piece of driftwood scored with long straight grooves, a fish of a kind no one at the Fish Market could name, a shell larger than her hand that none of her books describe. She keeps them on a shelf in the front room with a careful label on each, and she has stopped making lessons out of them. The children have noticed. Ossie has asked her, one question at a time, what they are, and she has had to say she does not know, which is the hardest thing a teacher can say.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text: Maren is afraid that one morning one of her pupils will not come in, and that she will have to find out why from the sea.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could help Maren make the council's case for a schoolhouse in a way they cannot put off, find out what the strange things on her shelf are, or bring back one of her pupils who has gone looking for the answer himself.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Kit: pupil
  • Finch: pupil
  • Ossie: pupil

docs.title: Marisol
docs.text:
Spice Merchant

Town Bain Harbour Where Merchant Street Role Council Age Adult Sells Spices, dyes and teas from all over the island In the game Marisol

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Charming, sharp-eyed and impossible to haggle down. She remembers the name of every customer's child.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Marisol keeps the spice shop on Merchant Street, and you can find it with your eyes shut: cinnamon, pepper, cloves and smoke-dried tea leaves drift out of the door and halfway down the street. She is forty-five, charming, sharp-eyed and impossible to haggle down, and she remembers the name of every customer's child. Sailors who have not been ashore for a season come in to buy a twist of pepper and find themselves telling her how their daughter is getting on with her letters, because Marisol asked, by name, before they reached the counter.

docs.title: The shop
docs.text:
Marisol came to Merchant Street at sixteen to sweep the floor of the spice shop for old Ferrand, a spice merchant who had kept it for most of his life and could tell a cargo's origin from a single sniff. She swept, then weighed, then bargained, and when Ferrand grew too old to climb his own ladder she bought the shop from him. She was twenty-four. That was twenty-one years ago, and Ferrand lived long enough to see her double his trade and to complain that she sold too cheap.

She sells spices, dyes and teas from every corner of Veligor. Everything she sells comes in by sea. Pepper and cloves come on the Bright Morrow, because Captain Seraphine is fastest and spices lose their life in the hold; dyes come on whatever coaster has room; tea comes packed in lead-lined chests that Hobart, the warehouseman, complains about every time he has to count them. Poppy, the baker's daughter, brings Marisol a salt roll every morning, and Marisol always asks after Kit, and always remembers what Kit said last week.

docs.title: Cordelia
docs.text: Marisol's business partner is Cordelia, the cloth merchant along the street, who dresses better than anyone in the harbour and wants everyone to know it. They have kept separate shops and a shared purse for twelve years. Together they hire cargo space by the hold rather than by the crate, which no merchant could afford alone, and split the cost and the risk down the middle. Cordelia brings the gossip and Marisol brings the sums, and they enjoy each other enormously. Cordelia dreams of opening a second shop. Marisol has promised to go halves on it once the cargoes settle down.

docs.title: The council
docs.text: Marisol speaks for the merchants on the harbour council, and has done for ten years. She is the Harbour Master's firmest ally there. When the council chose Quenna eight years ago, it was Marisol who counted the votes in advance and told her she would win, and Quenna has relied on her ever since. They do not always agree. Marisol thinks Quenna decides too fast; Quenna thinks Marisol counts too long. Between them they usually get it right.

docs.title: Late cargoes
docs.text:
Lately some of Marisol's cargoes have arrived late, and some not at all. Three this spring were weeks behind, because the captains bringing them now hug the coast and keep out of deep water. A consignment of blue dye never came: the coaster carrying it turned back halfway and put into another harbour along the coast, and its master will not sail that stretch again until someone tells him what is out there. Last autumn, too, one of Kaldemor's harvest carts never reached the harbour, and Marisol has not forgotten that the empty cart would have gone home with her spices.

She has not let anyone see how much this worries her. She smiles at customers, bargains as hard as ever, and tells Cordelia that delays are part of the trade. Privately she keeps a small book of every late and missing cargo, with the ship, the route and the days lost, and the list is getting longer.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Marisol wants her shelves full and her customers' children growing up on Merchant Street. She fears that one day the sea will simply stop bringing what the harbour needs, and that she will be the first to know and the last to admit it.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could fetch the missing blue dye from the harbour where it was left, ride along with one of Marisol's cargoes to see why it keeps coming late, or help her decide whether to show the council her book of missing cargoes.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Cordelia: business partner
  • Quenna: council ally

docs.title: Merriwether
docs.text:
Ship's Chandler

Town Bain Harbour Where Waterfront Sells Rope, tar, lanterns, hooks and ship's stores In the game Merriwether

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Wilmot: supplier

docs.title: Morwenna
docs.text:
Sailor of the Saltlark

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Worker Age Adult In the game Morwenna

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cheerful, tough and always singing under her breath. She misses home as soon as she leaves and misses the sea as soon as she is home.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Morwenna is a sailor of the Saltlark, and you will usually hear her singing before you see her: a shanty, a lullaby, half a hymn, always under her breath and always slightly out of tune. She is thirty-eight, cheerful and tough, and she has the oldest complaint of every sailor in Bain Harbour. She misses home as soon as she leaves it, and she misses the sea as soon as she is home.

docs.title: The lighthouse girl
docs.text: Morwenna was born in the lighthouse on the headland. Her mother, Ysolde, has kept the light for forty years, and Morwenna grew up climbing its stairs, polishing its great lamp and watching the ships come in from the top of the tower while her mother told her exactly what she thought of every captain aboard them. Her father, Kenver, was a fisherman, and as soon as she was big enough she went out with him in his boat. He taught her to row, to read the weather and to sing at the oars, because, he said, a song keeps time better than counting. He died sixteen years ago, quite suddenly, mending his nets on the fish market steps. Morwenna still sings his songs.

docs.title: The Saltlark
docs.text:
After her father died Morwenna worked the Fish Market for a few restless years, and at twenty-six she went to Captain Annis of the Saltlark and asked to sail with her. Annis looked her up and down, asked her three questions about the weather and one about her boots, and took her on. That was twelve years ago. Morwenna has crewed the Saltlark ever since, and she knows the old ship and its older captain better than anyone. She ties her boots left first, double knot, never on deck, because Annis does, and she does not tease Annis about the pinch of salt over the stern, because she has come to suspect it works. Annis is blunt, superstitious and trusts the sea more than people; Morwenna is the person she trusts most of all, and both of them know it.

Morwenna married Tamar, who worked in the ropewalk on the Waterfront, and their son Ossie was born eight years ago. Tamar died of a lung fever the next winter, when Ossie was barely one. Since then, while Morwenna is at sea, Ossie lives at the lighthouse with his grandmother, and when Morwenna is home she lives there too, back in the little room at the bottom of the tower where she slept as a girl. Ossie has decided to be a lighthouse keeper. Morwenna is secretly relieved that he has not decided to be a sailor.

docs.title: What she has not told them
docs.text:
On the Saltlark's last voyage, in deep water on a still night, something large brushed along the keel from bow to stern and was gone. The whole crew felt it. Morwenna was at the wheel. Annis turned the ship for home at once and took the mark to Ambrose the chartmaker the next morning.

Morwenna has not told her mother or her son. She tells herself she is protecting Ossie, who would ask questions about it one at a time for a month, and her mother, who is seventy and climbs a hundred and seventeen stairs every night. Really, she does not want to hear it said aloud in the lighthouse, where she has always felt safe. Annis has noticed and has not pressed her. What Morwenna does not know is that her mother, from the top of the tower, has been seeing pale lights moving under the water far out past the headland, and has not told her either.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could carry a message between Morwenna and her mother that neither will say in person, sail with the Saltlark back to the place where the keel was brushed, or find Morwenna a song that will get Ossie to sleep on the nights she is away.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ysolde: mother
  • Ossie: son
  • Annis: captain

docs.title: Nerissa
docs.text:
Pearl Diver

Town Bain Harbour Where Fish Market Role Worker Age Young In the game Nerissa

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fearless, quiet and happiest underwater. She speaks in short sentences, as if saving her breath.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Nerissa dives for pearls and shellfish beyond the harbour wall, or she did until a few weeks ago. She is twenty-seven, fearless and quiet, and she is happiest underwater, where nobody expects her to talk. On land she speaks in short sentences, as if saving her breath. Asked how a dive went, she says "Good." Asked what she found, she opens her hand.

docs.title: The diver's granddaughter
docs.text:
Nerissa learned to dive from her grandmother, Demelza, who dived the reef beyond the harbour wall for fifty years and could stay down longer than anyone in Bain Harbour. Nerissa's parents moved inland to Selsior when she was small, to work for a cloth merchant there, and she chose to stay behind with her grandmother and the sea. They still write. They have long since stopped asking her to come.

Demelza taught her everything: how to breathe slowly on the surface before going down, how to clear her ears, how to read the reef's ledges and the colour of the sand, how to open an oyster with a twist of the knife so the pearl does not scratch, and never to dive alone without telling someone on shore. Demelza died six years ago, in her own bed, with a string of her best pearls round her neck. Nerissa has dived alone since, and tells Wenna on the fish market steps when she is going, because Demelza would have wanted someone told.

docs.title: The reef
docs.text: Beyond the harbour wall the bottom falls away to a long reef, and below the reef, in the dark, the shelf drops off into deep water. Nerissa knows every ledge of the reef by touch. She brings up oysters, mussels and scallops, which she sells at the Fish Market, and now and then a pearl, which she sells to traders passing through the harbour. It is not a rich living. She does not want a rich living. She wants the green light and the quiet and the sound of her own heart slowing down.

docs.title: Tristram
docs.text:
Her sweetheart is Tristram, the harpooner. They met four years ago when he was still hunting big fish from his narrow boat, the Patience, and saw her go down off the reef and not come up. He had rowed halfway to the spot to fish her out when she surfaced beside his oar, laughing. He laughed too, completely, and she decided then that she liked him.

They suit each other. Neither says more than they need to, and they can sit on the harbour wall together for a whole evening without a word. He is patient and still. She is fearless and quick. Since the deep water changed, he stands at the bow of the Heron for Captain Corwin, and she waits on the wall for the ship to round the headland.

docs.title: The last dive
docs.text:
Some weeks ago, late this spring, Nerissa went down on an ordinary morning to the edge of the reef, where the shelf drops into the dark. She was reaching for an oyster when something moved below her, down past the edge, in the dark where the light does not go. She saw it only for a moment. She came up faster than Demelza ever allowed, sat on the harbour wall shaking, and has not gone back down since.

She will not say why, not to Wenna, not to anyone, not even to Tristram. He has not pressed her, and she loves him for it. The truth is that she is not frightened for herself. She is frightened that if she tells Tristram what she saw, and where, he will take his father's harpoon and go down there to look, because he has wanted to see what is in the deep water for longer than she has known him.

So she sits on the step below Wenna's, sorting other people's catch, and looks at the water.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Nerissa wants to dive again, and to feel the way she felt before. She fears that she never will, and she fears even more that one day Tristram will find out what she saw without her.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could dive the reef where Nerissa stopped, bring her back a pearl from the ledge she was reaching for, or help her find the words to tell Tristram before he goes looking on his own.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Tristram: sweetheart

docs.title: Ossie
docs.text:
Lighthouse Boy

Town Bain Harbour Where Lighthouse Role Child Age Child In the game Ossie

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Curious, solemn and full of questions he asks one at a time. He climbs the lighthouse stairs faster than anyone.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ossie is eight years old and lives in the lighthouse on the headland with his grandmother, Ysolde, the Keeper of the Light. He is curious and solemn, with a serious face and a great many questions, which he asks one at a time and waits for properly. He climbs the lighthouse stairs faster than anyone, all one hundred and seventeen of them, and he has counted them more often than he has counted anything else.

docs.title: The boy in the tower
docs.text:
Ossie's mother, Morwenna, is a sailor on Captain Annis's Saltlark, and while she is at sea, Ossie lives at the lighthouse with his grandmother. When his mother is home, she lives there too, and sings him to sleep in the little room at the bottom of the tower where she slept as a girl. His father, Tamar, worked in the ropewalk on the Waterfront and died of a fever when Ossie was barely one, so Ossie does not remember him. He has a piece of rope his father made, tied in a knot nobody can name, and he keeps it under his pillow.

Ossie's days have the lighthouse's shape. He helps his grandmother trim the wicks and polish the great lamp in the afternoon, climbs up with her at dusk to light it, and in between he watches the sea. His grandmother counts ships the way other people count sheep, and Ossie has learned to count them with her. She tells him what she thinks of every captain in the harbour, and Ossie writes it all down, though he has been told very firmly not to repeat any of it.

docs.title: The logbook
docs.text:
Ossie has decided he will be a lighthouse keeper too. He made the decision last winter, after reading one of his grandmother's old logbooks from cover to cover, and he has already started his own: a little book with a blue cover that Maren the schoolteacher gave him when he told her his plan. In it he writes down every ship that comes in or goes out, with its name, the time and the weather, and every bird he sees, with a drawing. His spelling is improving. His drawings of birds are very good. His drawings of ships are a little like birds.

He walks the long way down to Merchant Street most mornings for Maren's lessons, and he is her most patient pupil, though not her quickest. He asks her one question at a time and does not move on until she has answered it, and some mornings one question is the whole lesson. Lately he has been asking her about the strange things the other children bring in from the beach, and she has started saying she does not know. Ossie writes that down too.

docs.title: The entry he does not understand
docs.text: One night this spring Ossie could not sleep and climbed to the top of the tower by himself. Far out past the headland, under the water, he saw a pale light moving where there should have been nothing. He wrote it in his logbook, with the time and the weather, the way he writes everything. He did not tell his grandmother, because he thought she would send him back to bed, and he did not tell his mother, because she was at sea. He does not know that his grandmother has seen the same lights from the same window on other nights, or that she has not told anyone either.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Ossie wants to keep the light one day, and to see everything first, the way his grandmother does. He is afraid of only one thing, which he has never asked anybody about, one question at a time or otherwise: that one day his mother's ship will not be in his logbook when it should be.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could read Ossie's logbook and find a pattern in it nobody else has noticed, help him climb the tower on a night when the lights come back, or answer one of his questions properly, which is harder than it sounds.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Morwenna: mother
  • Ysolde: grandmother
  • Maren: teacher

docs.title: Ottilie
docs.text:
Clerk of the Harbour Hall

Town Bain Harbour Where Harbour Hall Role Official Age Adult In the game Ottilie

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Precise, tidy and fond of rules, but kinder than her ledgers suggest. She keeps a jar of sweets for anyone who fills in a form correctly.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ottilie is the Clerk of the Harbour Hall, and if it happened in Bain Harbour, she has written it down. Every ship that comes and goes, every cargo landed or loaded, every harbour due paid or owed and every decision of the harbour council goes into her ledgers, in a small upright hand with no blots. She is thirty-eight, precise, tidy and fond of rules, but kinder than her ledgers suggest. On the corner of her desk stands a glass jar of sweets, and anyone who fills in a form correctly may take one. Sailors have been known to fill in a form twice for the practice.

docs.title: Learning the columns
docs.text:
Ottilie grew up on Merchant Street, and at fourteen she went to learn bookkeeping from Elowen, who kept the books for half the merchants on the street and whose daughter Maren is now the harbour schoolteacher. Elowen taught her that a ledger is a promise: that what is written there must be what happened, no more and no less, or the whole harbour is building on sand. Ottilie believed her completely, and still does. When the clerk's desk at the Harbour Hall fell empty fourteen years ago, Elowen recommended her, and the council took her on at twenty-four.

She served six years under the Harbour Master before Quenna and has served Quenna for eight. She likes Quenna enormously and finds her exhausting. Quenna decides things before the tide turns; Ottilie writes them down as she goes, and occasionally, very politely, reminds the council of what it decided last time.

docs.title: The hall
docs.text:
Ottilie's desk stands just inside the door of the Harbour Hall, under the window, where the light is best for writing. Mabyn, who keeps the door, brings her a sweet bun every morning and has decided she works too hard. They are firm friends of opposite kinds: Mabyn never finishes a sentence and Ottilie never leaves one unfinished.

She is fond of the harbour's children, though she would never say so in those words. She gave Jowan sweets for years when he ran errands through the hall, long before he was old enough to fill in a form. When Bree, the fishmonger's daughter, showed her the slate on which she keeps her crab-shell accounts, Ottilie said it was neater than half the ledgers she receives, and meant it. Now and then she walks down to the warehouses with her ledger to check her figures against Hobart's chalk tallies, because he is the only other person in the harbour who counts as carefully as she does.

docs.title: The small boats
docs.text:
Because she records everything, Ottilie notices things nobody else has added up. A few years ago she began, out of simple tidiness, to keep a tally of the small boats that go out past the headland: fishing boats, rowing boats, pleasure boats, anything without a cargo to declare. The Harbour Watch notes them and she copies the notes into a column of their own. Once she had started, she could not resist going back through the Watch's old notes and filling the column in for ten summers past.

The column is getting shorter. Ten summers ago, a fair week saw forty or more small boats go out past the headland. Last summer, a fair week saw twenty-two. This spring it is fewer still. Nobody has made a rule about it, and nobody has said a word in council. The fishing families have simply, one by one, stopped going out so far.

Ottilie is not sure who she should tell. A clerk records; she does not advise. The council is made of captains, shipwrights and merchants, and the small boats belong to none of them. She could tell Quenna, but Quenna would decide something at once, and Ottilie is not sure yet what there is to decide. And she knows, in the tidy part of her mind that never lies, that once she says it aloud, the column will mean something, and she will have to admit what.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Ottilie wants the ledgers to stay true and the harbour to stay safe, and she has always believed the first would take care of the second. She fears that it will not, and that the numbers she wrote so neatly will be read one day as a warning nobody heard.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could carry Ottilie's column of small boats to the right person, ask the fishing families why they no longer go past the headland, or find the one council decision missing from her ledgers that she has never been able to account for.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Quenna: employer

docs.title: Peregrine
docs.text:
Shipwright's Apprentice

Town Bain Harbour Where Shipyard Role Craftsman Age Young In the game Peregrine

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Clever, clumsy and full of ideas, about one in ten of them good. He talks fast when he is nervous.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Peregrine is Dunstan's apprentice at the Bain Harbour shipyard, now in his second year. He is nineteen, clever, clumsy and full of ideas, about one in ten of them good. He talks fast when he is nervous, which around Dunstan is most of the time, and he has a habit of explaining his newest idea while walking backwards, which is how he went off the end of the slipway into the harbour in his first week.

docs.title: From the city
docs.text:
Peregrine grew up in Selsior, where his parents still live, and at fourteen he was apprenticed to a cabinetmaker there. He was good with wood and bad at furniture: every chair he made came out a little too much like a boat. One summer his master sent him to deliver a writing desk to a merchant in Bain Harbour, and Peregrine stood on the quay with the desk on a handcart and watched a ship being launched from Dunstan's yard. He forgot the desk for most of an afternoon. A little over a year ago, at eighteen, he finished his indenture, walked back to the coast with his tools on his back, and asked Dunstan to take him on. Dunstan said no three times. The fourth time he said Peregrine could sweep the yard and see how long he lasted.

He lasted. He sleeps in the loft above the yard's workshop, among the spare oars and the smell of pitch, and he writes to his parents every month with drawings of whatever he is building. They write back telling him to eat more.

docs.title: The yard
docs.text:
Dunstan treats Peregrine's ideas the way a man treats weather: he lets the boy talk until he runs out of breath, then puts him to work planing. Peregrine has proposed, in his time at the yard, a bucket that empties itself, a mast that folds in half for low bridges, a rudder worked from the bow and a sail with windows in it so the crew can see where they are going. He keeps a notebook of every idea, good and bad, and crosses out the bad ones himself, usually after Alwyn has looked at them. Alwyn, Dunstan's son, listens to all of them kindly and keeps about one in ten. Peregrine likes him very much and is slightly in awe of how much timber he can carry.

Kit, Dunstan's nine-year-old grandson, thinks Peregrine is the most interesting person in the yard after his grandfather, because Peregrine's ideas come even faster than Kit's. The two of them can talk for an hour without either finishing a sentence. Peregrine taught Kit to read a set of lines; Kit taught Peregrine two knots he did not know and laughed at him for not knowing them.

docs.title: The faster hull
docs.text:
Peregrine's one great idea, the one he is sure is in the good tenth, is a faster hull for the summer race around Veligor. It is longer and narrower than the boats Dunstan builds, with a finer entry at the bow and a flatter run under the stern, so that in a good breeze it would lift and skim instead of pushing the sea aside. He has drawn it a dozen times and carved a half-model of it from a single block of pear wood. With Kit's help he has tested it against a model of the old shape in the rock pools under the harbour wall, towing both on strings, and his model won every time but one, when Kit stepped on it.

The half-model sits on the end of Dunstan's workbench under a rag, where Peregrine left it two months ago. Dunstan has not lifted the rag. He is building his own new race boat this summer, the plans for which he keeps rolled in oilcloth under his bed and will not show to anyone. Peregrine has never tried to look at them. He has thought about it. He would like it noted that he has not.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Peregrine wants to see a boat built to his lines cross the finish line first, and he wants Dunstan to be the one who builds it. He fears that the old man will never lift the rag, and that he himself is one of the nine bad ideas and has not noticed yet.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could race Peregrine's model against the old shape in front of witnesses, get Dunstan to lift the rag on his workbench, or help Peregrine fetch a length of pear wood good enough for a full-sized trial hull.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Dunstan: mentor

docs.title: Poppy
docs.text:
Baker's Daughter

Town Bain Harbour Where Merchant Street Role Child Age Child In the game Poppy

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Shy, thoughtful and fond of drawing. She notices things grown-ups miss.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Poppy is eleven, shy and thoughtful, and she notices things grown-ups miss. She is the daughter of Bryony the baker and Alwyn the shipwright, the older sister of Kit, and the granddaughter of Dunstan, the master shipwright. Every morning she delivers bread along Merchant Street, and in every spare moment she draws.

docs.title: The bread round
docs.text:
Poppy's mother is up before the sun, and by the time the first light is on the water Poppy is out of the door with a basket on each arm. She knows every door on Merchant Street and the order to knock on them: salt rolls to Marisol's spice shop, a plain loaf to Cordelia's, hard biscuits for any ship that sails that day, and a warm roll for Ambrose the chartmaker, who always forgets breakfast. She does not talk much on the round, but she sees everything. She knows which shutters are open early, which shops have new stock, which ships came in during the night and which captains look worried.

Her mother hopes she will grow up to like flour more than salt water. Poppy likes both, as long as she can draw them.

docs.title: The drawings
docs.text:
Poppy sketches the ships in the bay from the end of Merchant Street, where the road turns and you can see the whole harbour at once. She draws them carefully and accurately, every mast and stay in its place, and she labels them in small, neat letters. Her father pins every one up in the shipyard's tool shed. Her grandfather keeps them in a box and pretends he does not. Her brother Kit draws ships too, but his have sea monsters in them, and the two of them argue about this constantly.

Lately Poppy's drawings have changed. She has started drawing the bay itself, not just the ships: the line of the harbour wall, the rocks at the headland, the lighthouse, the channel where the ships come in. Without quite meaning to, she has started making maps.

docs.title: Ambrose
docs.text:
Poppy admires Ambrose the chartmaker more than almost anyone. She has watched him at work through his shop window for years, bent over a chart with a pen so fine she can barely see the line it makes. One morning he caught her looking, invited her in, and showed her how he draws a coastline from a captain's sightings. Since then she has stopped in every morning after her round, and he has started teaching her: how to use a compass and dividers, how to write tiny, how to mark a rock so a sailor cannot mistake it. He apologises to his ink when he spills it, and Poppy has started doing the same.

She wants to make maps like Ambrose one day. She has not told her parents yet, because her father would be pleased and her grandfather would want to know why she didn't want to build ships.

Poppy has noticed that Ambrose keeps a drawer in his workroom locked, that captains sometimes come in and speak to him very quietly, and that afterwards he opens the drawer. She has not asked about it. She has, however, noticed that the marks he is given are always out past the headland.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Poppy wants to map the whole coast of Veligor. She is afraid of loud rooms, of being asked to speak in front of people, and of the look on the captains' faces when they come to the locked drawer.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could help Poppy chart a stretch of shore she cannot reach alone, or start with a drawing she made of the bay that shows something in the water no one else noticed.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Alwyn: father
  • Bryony: mother
  • Kit: brother
  • Ambrose: mentor

docs.title: Tegan
docs.text:
Sailmaker

Town Bain Harbour Where Shipyard Role Craftsman Age Adult Sells Sails, canvas and patching In the game Tegan

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brisk, practical and a little sharp, with a needle always tucked behind her ear. She judges a ship by its stitching.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tegan is the sailmaker of Bain Harbour, and she has sewn the sails for half the ships in the harbour. She is forty-one, brisk, practical and a little sharp, and she always has a needle tucked behind her ear, where other people keep a pencil. She does not judge a ship by its lines or its paint or its captain. She judges it by its stitching, and she can tell you from the quay, with one look at a reefed mainsail, whether a ship has been cared for or merely sailed.

docs.title: The loft at the yard
docs.text:
Tegan grew up in the sail loft at the edge of the shipyard, a long, high room with a floor wide enough to spread a whole mainsail. Her mother, Kensa, was the sailmaker before her, and Tegan spent her childhood under the canvas, sorting thread, chasing dropped needles between the floorboards and being told to keep her feet off the cloth. Kensa put a palm and needle in her hands at eight and made her sew practice seams on scraps until they were straight enough to please her, which took about three years. Kensa died fifteen years ago, and Tegan, then twenty-six, has kept the loft ever since. She still sews with her mother's sail palm, a leather strap worn to the shape of a hand that was not quite hers.

Her oldest friend is Alwyn, Dunstan's son. They were both children underfoot in the yard, she in the loft and he among the timbers, and between them they fell off most of the things in the shipyard that could be fallen off. Alwyn's mother painted the names on the hulls in gold, and Tegan's mother made the sails that carried them away, and the two children used to sit on the slipway and argue about which mattered more. They still have that argument, about once a month, though now it is about whether a ship is a hull with sails or sails with a hull. Tegan is fond of Alwyn's children, too. Kit has asked her a great many questions about sails. Poppy draws them better than anyone else in the harbour, and Tegan says so, which is rare praise from her.

Tegan never married, and she says she never had the time. She lets the little room above her loft to Brisa of the Harbour Watch, who came to her at sixteen with nowhere else to go and very little money. Tegan has sewn the buttons back on Brisa's coat more times than she can count, and Brisa has never once buttoned it.

docs.title: A day in the loft
docs.text:
Tegan's days begin with the light, because sailmaking needs it. She cuts new canvas, sews new sails, and patches the old ones the captains bring in, spread out across the loft floor, and she buys her bolt rope, the rope that edges every sail, from Wilmot the ropemaker, because she says nobody else's rope sits as true along a seam. She made the tall new suit of sails for Captain Seraphine's Bright Morrow when Seraphine rebuilt the ship's rig nine years ago, and she has told Seraphine every summer since that she carries too much of them. She thinks Captain Corwin's sails are the best kept in the harbour and Captain Annis's are the oldest. She patches both without comment, which for Tegan is a compliment.

Since the deep water turned strange, the work has changed. Captains want heavier storm canvas, doubled seams and spare sails folded in the hold, and some of them want to talk about what tore the old ones, which Tegan does not encourage. She sews what she is asked and keeps her opinions for the stitching.

docs.title: The secret sails
docs.text:
This summer Dunstan asked Tegan to make the sails for the new race boat, and to make them in secret. He gave her the measurements on a scrap of paper and told her nothing about the hull, not even when she asked. She has patched and recut his race boats' sails for years, but she has never been asked to hide them before, and she is enjoying it very much. She sews the race sails after dark with the loft door barred and tells anyone who asks that she is making a new mainsail for a coaster. She will not tell even Alwyn, and the look on his face when she refuses is, she says, worth the extra lamp oil.

What she has not told Dunstan is that a sailmaker can learn a great deal about a boat from the measurements of its sails. She has done some quiet sums in the margin of that scrap of paper, and she has her own idea of what the new hull looks like. She keeps that to herself as well. It would spoil the secret, and it might be wrong.

docs.title: What she wants, and what she fears
docs.text: Tegan wants to see her sails cross the finish line first, and she wants someday to hand the loft to someone whose seams are straight enough to deserve it. She has not yet found that person. She fears very little that she will admit to, but she does not like the sails that have come back to her this year from deep water with long, straight tears that no wind made.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Tegan keep the race sails hidden from a nosy visitor, fetch a special bolt of canvas before the race, or find out whether Brisa, who sleeps right above the loft and hears the needle at night, has worked out what Tegan is sewing.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Alwyn: friend

docs.title: Thaddeus
docs.text:
Retired Captain

Town Bain Harbour Where Waterfront Role Resident Age Elder In the game Thaddeus

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Grand, nostalgic and fond of his own voice. He tells the same stories often but tells them well.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Thaddeus is a retired captain, and he spends his days on a bench by the water on the Waterfront, where he can see every boat in the bay and comment on all of them. He is seventy-nine, grand, nostalgic and fond of his own voice. He tells the same stories often, but he tells them well, with his hat pushed back and one hand drawing the course in the air, and even people who have heard them a dozen times tend to stop and listen to the end.

docs.title: The Cormorant
docs.text:
Thaddeus went to sea as a boy and was master of his own coasting ship, the Cormorant, for thirty years. She was a handsome, fast, slightly vain ship, he says, much like her captain, and he ran timber, salt and anything else that paid along the coast of Veligor. He gave up command at sixty-five, fourteen years ago, and sold the Cormorant to a captain from another harbour, who still sails her. He does not like to talk about that, which makes it the only subject he does not like to talk about.

He was married for forty years to Loveday, who mended sails on the Waterfront and was the only person in Bain Harbour who could make him stop talking by raising one eyebrow. She died ten years ago. Since then Thaddeus has lived alone in a little house a few steps from his bench, and the bench, the bay and the young sailors passing it have become his company.

docs.title: The race
docs.text:
The story everyone has heard is the race. Thirty-three years ago, Thaddeus skippered Bain Harbour's boat in the summer race around Veligor. He was forty-six, at the top of his powers, and he had wanted the helm for twenty years. So had Captain Annis of the Saltlark. They had been rivals since they were young sailors racing each other across the bay at every chance, and that summer they quarrelled so long and so loudly over who should skipper the race boat that the council very nearly gave it to someone else to shut them both up. In the end the helm went to Thaddeus.

He led for most of the way around the island. He tells you about every headland, every squall and every sail change. Then, in the last mile, the wind dropped where he was and held where Goa Harbour's boat was, and Goa crossed the line a boat's length ahead. He never skippered the race again; the next summer the helm went to another captain. He never had it again, and Annis never had it at all.

Annis has told him ever since that she would have won. Thaddeus says she would have lost by two. They have had this argument several hundred times, on his bench, at the Salt and Bread and once across a whole council meeting, and both of them would be lost without it. He thinks she is the finest sailor in the harbour. He would rather lose by ten lengths than tell her so.

docs.title: The coach
docs.text:
Thaddeus coaches young sailors from his bench whether they asked or not. Most hurry past. His current project is Lowen, the fisherman's son, who has just signed on as a deckhand on the Heron and wants a place on this summer's race crew. Thaddeus has decided the boy has the makings of a racing sailor and tells him so, along with a great deal about trimming sails, reading wind on the water and never trusting a calm in the last mile. Lowen has started taking the long way round. Thaddeus has noticed, and has also noticed that Lowen's knots and sail-handling have improved in exactly the ways he said they should. He is enormously pleased and has told nobody.

Lorcan, the shanty singer, has lately been buying him a drink in exchange for the story of the race, for a verse in his new shanty. Thaddeus has told it to him four times, with a different wind each time.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Thaddeus wants to see Bain Harbour win the race by more than a boat's length, and to have had a hand in it, even from a bench. He fears that he will be remembered only for the one he lost, and, though he would never say so, that the sea he raced on is not the sea out there now.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could find the old logbook from Thaddeus's race and the inshore course he swears would have won it, settle his argument with Annis with a race across the bay between two old captains, or help him find out where the Cormorant is sailing now.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Lowen: reluctant pupil
  • Annis: old racing rival

docs.title: Tristram
docs.text:
Harpooner

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Adventurer Age Adult In the game Tristram

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Patient, still and serious, a man who can wait for hours without moving. He laughs rarely but completely.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tristram is a harpooner, and the captains of Bain Harbour hire him to stand at the bow in deep water and watch. He is thirty-nine, patient, still and serious, and he can wait for hours without moving a muscle, his harpoon held loosely in one hand, as if he were part of the ship. He laughs rarely, but when he does he laughs completely, with his head back and his eyes shut, and people who have heard it tend to remember where they were.

docs.title: The big fish
docs.text:
Tristram learned the harpoon from his father, who hunted big fish out of the harbour in a narrow boat called the Patience and died in his bed, at a great age, ten years ago. The harpoon Tristram carries was his father's; the shaft has been replaced three times and the head never. From the age of eighteen Tristram hunted the deep water himself, alone in the Patience, for the great fish that come along the coast in late summer. It is slow, quiet work, and he loved it: days of waiting, then a few moments in which everything matters.

Then the deep water changed. The big fish stopped running where they always had, and the things that came up in their place did not behave like fish. Tristram hauled the Patience up on the beach below the Waterfront, where she still lies under a sailcloth, and went to work for the captains instead.

docs.title: At the bow
docs.text:
Captain Corwin of the Heron is his regular employer. Corwin is the most careful captain in the harbour and grumbles at the council about what adventurers cost him, but he pays Tristram without complaint and thinks him worth every coin. Tristram likes Corwin because Corwin never asks him to talk. On the Heron he stands at the bow from the moment the ship passes the headland until she is back inside it, and in all the voyages he has made, he has thrown the harpoon at something only twice. He does not describe either time. He says only that he missed once.

On shore he works with Keziah, the sword for hire who sails with Captain Seraphine. They met in her first week in the harbour, when the same captain turned them both down on the same morning, and that afternoon they cleared the rocks below the headland of crabs big enough to take a boot off. She watches everything and he waits for everything, and they have been partners since. She is the only person who can make him laugh on purpose. He has noticed that she goes grey as a sail every time she steps aboard a ship. He has not mentioned it, and he will not.

docs.title: The spear
docs.text:
On the docks Tristram is the man Warriors are sent to when they want to fight with a spear. He has never called himself a teacher, and he has never had a pupil for long, but he has spent his life with a long shaft in his hands at the bow of a moving ship, and that is the whole of what the Spearman's way asks: reach, patience and knowing exactly where you stand. A Warrior who has reached the thirtieth year of their training and asks him to teach it gets a long look, a nod and a harpoon to hold for an hour without moving.

The trial comes after the hour. Tristram sends the Warrior along the Inner Cut to the ironback crabs in the timber ponds, then into the holds of the old wreck after the mimics that hide among the cargo, and last out to the Outer Cut, where the sawbill fry run in the shallows faster than a blade can follow. He does not care how many they kill. He cares whether they kept the reach, struck from where they stood, and never let anything come inside the point. When it is done he says "good" once, which from Tristram is a speech, and Keziah, who has seen it, says the Warrior should take it as a medal.

docs.title: Nerissa
docs.text: Tristram's sweetheart is Nerissa, the pearl diver, who is fearless, quiet and happiest underwater. They suit each other: neither of them says more than they need to, and they can sit together on the harbour wall for an evening without saying anything at all. On her last dive beyond the harbour wall, Nerissa saw something move in the dark below the reef, and she has not gone down since. She will not say why, even to him. Tristram has not pressed her. It frightens him more than anything he has seen from the bow, because he has never known her afraid of the water.

docs.title: What he wants
docs.text: Tristram wants to know what is down there, before anyone else does. He does not want to kill it. He wants to see it clearly, once, and understand it, the way he used to understand the big fish. He fears that by the time anyone understands it, it will be too late to matter.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could stand the bow watch with Tristram, help him get the Patience back in the water for one more voyage of his own, or go down below the reef to find what Nerissa saw.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Keziah: adventuring partner
  • Nerissa: sweetheart
  • Corwin: employer

docs.title: Tully
docs.text:
Dockworker

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Worker Age Adult In the game Tully

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Strong, easygoing and always hungry. He thinks every problem looks smaller after lunch.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tully is a dockworker on the Bain Harbour docks, and he is probably the strongest man in the harbour, though he would never say so and would much rather talk about lunch. He is twenty-six, broad, easygoing and always hungry. He thinks every problem looks smaller after lunch, and he has found, over the years, that he is right about this more often than people who skip it.

docs.title: A boy on the docks
docs.text:
Tully has carried crates on the docks since he was a boy. His father, Treve, was a porter there before him, and Tully spent his early years sitting on coiled rope at the head of the pier, watching his father carry things. When Tully was eleven, Treve slipped on a wet gangplank with a barrel on his shoulder and hurt his back, and he never really mended; he died that winter. Tully came down to the docks the next spring, at twelve, asking for work, and Garrow, who had been foreman for two years then, looked at the size of his hands and gave him some. His mother, Lamorna, went to live with her sister in a fishing village up the coast a few years later. She writes to him twice a year, mostly to ask whether he is eating properly, and he writes back to tell her that he is.

Fourteen years on, Tully can lift more than any two other men on the docks, and he carries the things nobody else wants to: the lead-lined tea chests, the iron, the barrels that leak. Garrow shouts at him for eating on the job and then saves him the last of his own bread at the end of the day. Tully knows perfectly well that Garrow gives him the extra shifts first, and Garrow knows that he knows, and neither of them has ever said a word about it. Tully thinks Garrow is the best foreman on Veligor and that Garrow's second pier is a fine idea, and he has told several captains so, loudly, while Garrow pretended not to hear.

docs.title: His day
docs.text:
Tully's day starts before the first ship is tied up, with something to eat, and it goes on in the same way. He carries cargo off the ships and into the warehouses, where Hobart counts every crate he brings in and has never once taken Tully's count for it. He carries Finch, the dock office's errand boy, on his shoulders when the boy is too tired to run, and he shares his lunch with him on the warehouse step, which means that Finch eats well and Tully eats twice. He eats bread from Merchant Street, smoked fish from the Fish Market and whatever is left at the Salt and Bread at the end of the night, and he will talk to anyone at all, as long as there is food involved.

This spring Garrow stopped unloading at the far end of the outer pier after dark. Tully does not know why. It means the late cargoes have to be carried a long way round, and he grumbled about it for a week and then stopped, because Garrow would not look him in the eye about it, and Tully has decided that if Garrow does not want to tell him, there is a good reason.

docs.title: The boat
docs.text:
Tully is saving every coin he can to buy a small boat of his own. He has been saving for six years, in a tin box with a stone on the lid at the bottom of his sea chest, and he counts it every week on the night before his day off. He has about two thirds of what a small, plain boat from Dunstan's yard would cost, if Dunstan had time to build one, which this summer he does not. Tully wants to fish the bay in the mornings and carry small cargoes along the coast in the afternoons, and never again to carry anything for anyone but himself. He has walked down to the beach below the Waterfront more than once to look at the old boat that lies there under a sailcloth, and he has never quite worked up the nerve to ask whose it is.

He has heard the stories from the deep water like everyone else, and he has heard that Cobb no longer takes his boat past the middle of the bay. Tully says that he only wants a little boat for the bay anyway, and that the bay is a friendly place. He says it a little more often than he used to.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text: Tully fears very little that can be carried, and is not afraid of hard work or of anybody's temper. What he does fear, privately, is that by the time he has saved enough, there will be nothing left out on the water worth having a boat for.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might find Tully a boat sooner than he hoped, help him carry something too heavy even for him, or have Hobart ask him at last to move the four old iron-bound crates at the back of the oldest warehouse, which nobody has shifted in living memory.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Garrow: foreman

docs.title: Wenna
docs.text:
Net-Mender

Town Bain Harbour Where Fish Market Role Resident Age Elder In the game Wenna

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Sharp-tongued, proud and quick with her fingers. She knows everyone's business and approves of very little of it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Wenna mends nets on the fish market steps, as she has done all her life, and from her step she sees everyone who comes into the Fish Market and knows the business of most of them. She is seventy-one, sharp-tongued, proud and quick with her fingers, and she approves of very little of what she sees. Her netting needle moves so fast it blurs. Her opinions move faster.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
Wenna's mother mended nets on the same steps before her, and Wenna sat beside her from the age of five, filling needles with twine and learning every knot a fishing net can hold. By the time she was twelve she could mend a hole faster than her mother, and she has never let anyone forget it. Every fishing family in the bay brings her their nets, and she can tell, by looking at a tear, what made it: rocks fray, dogfish chew, seals bite round holes, and careless fishermen leave knots she describes to their faces at length.

She married Davey, a fisherman of the bay, who fished from the Puffin, the little open boat his own father had built. Davey was the quietest man in the harbour and the only one who could make Wenna laugh without trying. He died of a winter fever twelve years ago. She mended his last net the week after and gave it to their son.

That son is Cobb, who fishes from the Puffin now and is as quiet as his father was. Wenna thinks this is a great mercy, since the rest of the family is not. Cobb married Gwennol, the fishmonger, whose voice carries across the whole market, and Wenna has argued with her daughter-in-law about the price of fish, the gutting of fish and the raising of children for twenty years. Gwennol is the only person in the Fish Market who argues back properly, and Wenna respects her more than she will ever admit.

docs.title: The grandchildren
docs.text: Her grandson Lowen has just signed on as a deckhand aboard Captain Corwin's Heron, against his father's wishes. Wenna told the whole market that the boy was a fool, and then sewed him a new canvas kit bag with a double seam, because a fool should at least have a bag that does not split. Her granddaughter Bree is bossy, fearless and runs a business in crab shells from the rock pools; Wenna says she gets it from her mother and is privately sure she gets it from her grandmother.

docs.title: The day Kenver died
docs.text: Wenna was mending beside Kenver, the lighthouse keeper's husband, sixteen years ago on the morning he died. One moment he was singing over his nets, the next he was gone. She sent a boy running for Clemence, the healer, and held Kenver's hand until she came, though there was nothing anyone could do. She has never said much about that morning. She still keeps his place on the step clear, and she still finishes mending on the side of the steps where he sat.

docs.title: The torn nets
docs.text:
Twice this year Cobb's nets have come up torn clean through, both times in the deeper water just inside the headland. Wenna mended both. They were not frayed or chewed or bitten. They were opened in long straight rents, longer than her arm, as clean as if a blade had been drawn through them, and yet the edges were not cut but pulled. She announced to the whole market that no fish she ever knew made tears like that, and she has repeated it to everyone since. She has also kept a strip of the torn net, which she has shown nobody, rolled up in her basket under the spare twine.

What frightens her is not the tears. It is that Cobb has stopped going out past the middle of the bay, and that her son, who has never been afraid of the water in his life, has not said why.

docs.title: The steps' company
docs.text: Barnacle, the harbour cat, sleeps in the sun on the steps beside her and accepts fish heads from Wenna with great dignity. Wenna says Barnacle is the only creature in the market with any sense. Lately Nerissa, the pearl diver, has taken to sitting on the step below hers on days she would once have spent diving. Wenna has asked her nothing, which for Wenna is a kindness of enormous size.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could take Wenna's strip of torn net to someone who might know what made it, go out with Cobb to the place where the nets were torn, or win Wenna's approval, which nobody in living memory has managed on the first try.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Cobb: son
  • Bree: granddaughter

docs.title: Wilmot
docs.text:
Ropemaker

Town Bain Harbour Where Waterfront Role Craftsman Age Elder In the game Wilmot

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Slow, kind and endlessly patient, he believes any problem can be solved with the right knot. He hums sea songs older than anyone else remembers.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Wilmot is the ropemaker of Bain Harbour, and he has walked his rope walk on the Waterfront for fifty years. He is seventy-two, slow, kind and endlessly patient, and he believes that almost any problem in the world can be solved with the right knot, and that the rest can be made a good deal better by one. He hums while he works, always, and the songs he hums are sea songs older than anyone else in the harbour remembers. Ask him where he learned them and he will tell you: from the man who taught him rope, who learned them from the woman who taught him.

docs.title: Fifty years of rope
docs.text:
Wilmot came to the rope walk at twenty-two, a fisherman's son who had found he was better with lines than with fish. The rope walk then belonged to old Penrose, a ropemaker so particular that he made Wilmot spin yarn for a whole year before he would let him lay a single rope. Wilmot did not mind. He has never minded waiting for anything. When Penrose died, Wilmot took over the rope walk, and he has kept it ever since: a long, low shed that runs along the back of the Waterfront, so long that the boys of the harbour race from one end of it to the other and arrive out of breath.

His wife, Hedra, worked beside him for most of those years, spinning yarn at the far end of the walk while he laid rope at the near one, and they used to sing to each other down the whole length of the shed. She died eighteen years ago. They had no children. Wilmot still hums her half of the songs as well as his own.

docs.title: His day
docs.text:
Every morning Wilmot walks backwards down the rope walk, paying out hemp from the bundle at his waist and twisting it into yarn, while a child turns the great wheel at the far end. He pays whichever child he can find a copper for it, and he finds fewer every year. Then the yarns are twisted into strands, and the strands laid into rope, slowly, the whole length of the shed, until he has a coil that will hold a ship to a quay in a gale.

His rope goes everywhere. Merriwether the chandler buys most of it and sells it to every ship that leaves the harbour, along with a great many lists. Tegan the sailmaker buys her bolt rope from him directly, and says nobody else's rope sits as true along a seam, which Wilmot considers the finest thing anyone has said about him in years. More of it goes up to Kaldemor every autumn in the harvest carts. Lately Merriwether has been asking him for heavier and heavier lines, thick cables and hawsers for captains who want to be sure of their anchors, and Wilmot makes them, though they are hard work for old hands. He has not asked what the captains want them for. He thinks a man can guess.

docs.title: The last apprentice
docs.text:
Wilmot worries that no young person in Bain Harbour wants to learn his trade. He has had only one real apprentice in fifty years: Tamar, who came to the rope walk as a boy of fourteen and turned out to have the best hands Wilmot had ever seen. Tamar married Morwenna of the Saltlark, and he died of a lung fever the winter after their son Ossie was born, seven years ago. Wilmot has not had an apprentice since. He has never met a young person who wanted to walk backwards down a shed for a living, and he does not blame them, but he does not know what will become of the rope walk when his legs give out.

The nearest thing he has to a pupil is Kit, Dunstan's grandson, who came to him knowing a great many knots already and went away knowing a few more. Wilmot taught them slowly and kindly, humming between each one. Kit wants to be a shipwright, and Wilmot knows it. He teaches him anyway, because a knot taught is never wasted.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Wilmot has never seen the piece of rope that Ossie keeps under his pillow, tied in a knot nobody can name, though he would know Tamar's work anywhere. A quest might bring the boy and the old ropemaker together, find Wilmot a young person willing to turn the wheel for longer than an afternoon, or help him lay a cable heavier than any he has made before. Lorcan once asked him for the words to one of his oldest songs, and Wilmot found, to his surprise, that he knew the tune but had forgotten the last verse. Someone in the harbour may still remember it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Merriwether: customer

docs.title: Ysolde
docs.text:
Keeper of the Light

Town Bain Harbour Where Lighthouse Role Service Age Elder In the game Ysolde

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Solitary, wry and clear-sighted, she counts ships the way other people count sheep. She has opinions about every captain in the harbour and shares them freely.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ysolde is the Keeper of the Light, and she has kept the lighthouse on the headland lit for forty years without missing a single night. She is seventy, solitary, wry and clear-sighted, and she counts ships the way other people count sheep. She has an opinion about every captain in Bain Harbour, formed from the top of her tower over decades of watching them come in, and she shares it with anyone who climbs high enough to hear it.

docs.title: Forty years of nights
docs.text:
Ysolde was the lighthouse keeper's daughter. Her father, old Peder, kept the light before her, and she grew up on its stairs, learning to trim a wick before she learned to tie her shoes. When Peder died forty years ago, the harbour council asked who would keep the light, and Ysolde, then thirty, said she already was. Nobody has asked since.

She married Kenver, a fisherman with a fine voice and no sense of time, who used the lighthouse as his clock and said he could find home in any fog by the sound of his wife being cross with him. Their daughter Morwenna was born in the lighthouse two years after Ysolde took the light. Kenver died sixteen years ago, quite suddenly, mending his nets on the fish market steps. Ysolde lit the lamp that night as usual, because ships were out, and nobody in the harbour has ever forgotten it.

docs.title: The tower and the harbour
docs.text:
Every afternoon Ysolde trims the wicks and polishes the great lamp, and every dusk she climbs the hundred and seventeen stairs to light it, more slowly than she used to. Her knees complain. Her friend Clemence, the harbour healer, climbs up once a week with a salve for them, and the two of them sit at the top of the tower drinking tea and agreeing about most people in Bain Harbour. Clemence is the only visitor Ysolde actually invites.

From the gallery she sees everything. She thinks Captain Annis is the only captain left who sails as if the sea were listening. She thinks Captain Corwin is a clock with a hull on it, which she means as a compliment. She thinks Captain Seraphine comes into the harbour far too fast and will one day meet the harbour wall, and she tells her so whenever she can. She watched Quenna learn to sail as a deck girl, and she says the Harbour Master has been deciding things too quickly ever since, and has usually been right.

Morwenna has sailed with Annis for twelve years, and while she is at sea, Ysolde's grandson Ossie lives at the lighthouse. He is eight, solemn and full of questions, and he has decided to be a lighthouse keeper too. Ysolde pretends this is a bad idea and has started teaching him everything she knows.

docs.title: The lights
docs.text:
Three summers ago, on a still night, Ysolde saw pale lights moving under the water far out past the headland, where there should have been nothing at all. They moved slowly, together, like a shoal of lanterns, and then they were gone. She has seen them again since, on perhaps a dozen nights, always far out, always in deep water, and, she thinks, a little closer each summer.

She has told no one. Not Clemence, not the council, not her daughter, who has troubles of her own at sea, and certainly not Ossie. She has not even written them in the lighthouse log, which Peder kept honestly before her and she has kept honestly since. She marks them instead in the margin, in a little sign of her own, and tells herself that is honest enough. She does not know what the lights are. She has her guesses, and she does not like any of them.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text: Ysolde is not afraid of the dark, or of storms, or of growing old in a tower. She is afraid that the lights will come close enough for everyone to see them, and that she will have to explain why she did not say so sooner.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could climb the tower to keep the light on a night Ysolde's knees will not let her, decipher the marks in the margin of her log, or carry what she has seen to someone who can do something about it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Morwenna: daughter
  • Ossie: grandson
  • Clemence: friend

docs.title: People of Cavelor
docs.text:
The 15 people of Cavelor in the game's first release.

Name Role Marrun Keeper of the Oath Brask Captain of the Deep Watch Thera Warden of the Seal Oswin Master of the Ledgers Kell Apprentice Archivist Halvara Head of the Root Gardens Ysra Healer of the Halls Gorran Smith of Cavelor Doran Warden Back from the Surface Varn Scout of the Outer Tunnels Annick Singer of the Oath Grisel Retired Warden Ottel Child of the Root Gardens Rhenna Child of the Oath Hall Corvan Keeper of the Stores

docs.title: Annick
docs.text:
Singer of the Oath

Town Cavelor Where Oath Hall Role Performer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Lively, teasing and generous with her voice. She can turn the gloomiest Warden's shift change into a sing-along.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Annick is thirty-one, the Singer of the Oath, and the keeper of the old songs that the first guardians brought down into the roots. She is lively, teasing and generous with her voice, and she can turn the gloomiest shift change on the Deep Watch into a sing-along before the outgoing Wardens have finished handing over their lanterns. Cavelor is a serious city with a serious duty. Annick is one of the main reasons it has never been a gloomy one.

docs.title: The keeper of the songs
docs.text:
The songs Annick keeps are older than the city. Some came down with the Savage warriors who stayed below, some with the Magicians who helped make the seal, some with the Commons diggers and the Aristocrat officers, and over the centuries they have been sung together so often that they have braided into one tradition. There are walking songs for the passages, counting songs for the roster, lullabies, mourning songs and the long chant of the Oath Below itself. Very few are written down. They live in Annick's head and in the heads of the people she has taught.

She learned them from old Singer Aldra, who chose her at nine because she could not stop humming, and who sang with her every day until Aldra died eleven years ago. At sixteen, still Aldra's pupil, Annick sang the Oath songs in the Oath Hall on the day Queen Aveline and Keeper Marrun swore their alliance, and she has never been so frightened or so proud in her life.

Now she teaches the songs to every child in Cavelor. Her favourite pupil, though she tries not to have one, is Rhenna, Ysra the healer's daughter, who is shy and serious and already knows the whole Oath by heart. Annick is trying to teach her to sing it loudly. It is going slowly.

docs.title: Corvan
docs.text:
Annick's sweetheart is Corvan, Keeper of the Stores at the top of the Upper Stair. He is cheerful, chatty and an incurable haggler, and the two of them can keep a conversation going through an entire meal without either drawing breath. She teases him about his hidden jar of surface honey, which she is not supposed to know about and which she has found three times. Neither of them is in any hurry to settle anything. They are happy as they are, and Cavelor is small enough that everyone already treats them as a pair.

She takes her own turns on the Deep Watch like every adult in the city, and she is a better Warden than people expect. Even on the lowest passages she sings under her breath, very quietly, because she says the silence down there is too heavy to carry alone.

docs.title: The song about the sun
docs.text:
Since Doran came back from the surface last autumn, Annick has been trying to write a new song: a song about the sun. No one in the long tradition ever wrote one, because for centuries no one in Cavelor saw it, and none of those who have climbed the Stair since the expedition was a singer. Doran gives her more stories than she can use, and every verse she writes from them feels wrong: too bright, or too borrowed, or like a song about a lantern with grand ideas. She has started to suspect that she cannot write it properly without seeing the sun herself, and she has not decided what to do about that.

She worries, too, about the old songs. The Wardens are tired. The children ask harder questions than they used to. Annick believes a song can hold a city together in a bad hour, and she is quietly afraid that one day she will need to find the right one.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Annick finish her sun song, perhaps by bringing back something from the surface that Doran's stories cannot. Or someone might help her recover a lost verse of an old guardian song, half-remembered and tucked into the Archive's margins.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Corvan: sweetheart
  • Rhenna: pupil
  • Doran: source of sun stories

docs.title: Corvan
docs.text:
Keeper of the Stores

Town Cavelor Where Upper Stair Sells Dried mushrooms, root-fruit, lamp oil and lantern glass

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Halvara: supplier
  • Annick: sweetheart

docs.title: Doran
docs.text:
Warden Back from the Surface

Town Cavelor Where Upper Stair Role Adventurer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bright, restless and impossible to keep quiet about the sky. He squints at every lantern now and calls it "almost as good as noon".

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Doran is nineteen, the younger child of Gorran the smith and the younger brother of Thera, and since last autumn he has been the most talked-about young Warden in Cavelor. He went up the Upper Stair last summer with one of Keeper Marrun's messengers, and he came home a different person. People started calling him "Sunward" within a week of his return, half as a joke and half because there was no better word for him. He did not mind. He thought it was the best name anyone had ever been given.

docs.title: Growing up below
docs.text:
Doran grew up in the noise and heat of his father's forge by the Upper Stair, where the old vents carry the smoke up through the rock. His mother, Maelis, died in the damp fever sixteen years ago, when he was three, and he remembers her only as a voice singing in the next room. Gorran raised both children alone, loudly and lovingly, and Thera, three years older, decided early that someone in the family had to be sensible. Doran decided just as early that it would not be him.

He learned the Oath Below before he could read, like every child in Cavelor, and took his first turn on the Deep Watch at sixteen. He was a good Warden, quick and sharp-eared, but even then Brask had to remind him more than once that a lantern is for watching the passage, not for making shadow puppets on the wall.
