He has believed it since he was eighteen, when Isaura took him on as her student and gave him his first box of reports to sort.

Every theory he has built so far has fallen apart. He keeps them all in a drawer of his desk labelled "wrong", in his own furious handwriting. There are thirty-one of them. He reads through the drawer once a year, on the anniversary of the first, to remind himself which mistakes not to make again; he says it is the most useful book in the Heart Tree.

docs.title: The people around him
docs.text:
Isaura, Keeper of the Old Records, has been his mentor for twenty years. She is stern with him and careful with her praise, and he would not admit to anyone how much he wants it. He sometimes suspects she knows more about the records than she tells the other scholars, and he cannot decide whether that is duty or doubt.

Juniper, the wilds naturalist, is his closest colleague. She travels the roads recording how creatures have changed and brings her notebooks back to him, and the two of them spend long nights spreading her sketches across the floor of his study, arguing about what they mean. Neither has found it yet.

Wynne, Isaura's granddaughter, is his rival, which embarrasses him, because she is nineteen and a copyist and he is supposed to be the scholar. She is quiet and observant and notices what he skips, and twice now she has pointed out, very politely, a date he copied wrong. Both times she was right. He has not forgiven her for either. He does not know that she has found something in the records that she has not yet decided whether to tell him.

Tansy at the Dewdrop Tea House keeps a honey cake aside for him on nights when the Heart Tree's lamps are still burning at midnight, and he usually remembers to thank her the following week.

docs.title: Where he comes from
docs.text: Caelum was born on the Lantern Paths, the son of a lantern-glass grinder. His parents are both gone now. He came to the Grove School at nine and was the kind of student teachers remember: the one who asked why, and then asked why again, and then went to the library to find out without permission.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
He wants to be right once, about the one thing that matters. He fears that he is looking at the problem from the wrong side entirely, and that the answer is not in the records at all.

A quest might bring Caelum a fresh report from the roads he cannot get any other way, or put the list that Hesper, Mistress of the Herb Gardens, keeps of what has attacked her patients in front of him; he has never seen it, and it might be exactly the kind of record he has been missing. It might also, very carefully, persuade him to sleep.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Isaura: mentor
  • Wynne: rival
  • Juniper: colleague

docs.title: Celandine
docs.text:
Herbalist

Town Fairy Forest Where Herb Gardens Sells Healing salves, herb teas and potions In the game Celandine

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hesper: mentor
  • Merrow: husband

docs.title: Corisande
docs.text:
Keeper of the Old Wing's Key

Town Fairy Forest Where Lantern Paths Role Resident Age Elder In the game Corisande

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Proud, a little prickly and quietly lonely, she has kept a duty nobody remembers giving her. She is hurt that nobody ever asked her to use it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
Corisande is eighty-one, small, upright and sharp-eyed, and she lives in a tree home halfway along the Lantern Paths with a key on a cord round her neck. It is a long key of dark bronze, as long as her hand, its bow worked into the shape of a curled leaf, worn smooth by three lifetimes of thumbs. It opens the door to the oldest wing of the Grove School, which has been sealed since before anyone's teacher's teacher can remember. Corisande has kept it for fifty-four years. She has never once been through the door.

She is proud, a little prickly and, though she would sooner bite her tongue than say so, quietly lonely. She has kept a duty that nobody remembers giving her, and what hurts is not the keeping. It is that in all those years nobody has ever asked her to use it.

docs.title: Three keepers
docs.text:
The key came to her from her mother, Melusine, who had it from her own mother, Eglantine. Corisande remembers her grandmother well: a tall, stern woman who wore the key outside her dress, so that people would see it, and who told the little Corisande that it was "kept for when it is wanted". Wanted by whom, or for what, Eglantine never said, and Corisande has come to suspect she did not know either. Whether Eglantine had it from someone before her, nobody can now say. The family has no papers about it. The Grove School has none that anyone has shown her. It is simply theirs to keep, and they have kept it.

Melusine took the key when Eglantine died, and Corisande took it when her mother died, fifty-four years ago, when she was twenty-seven. She remembers sitting on the step of the school that evening with the key in her lap, waiting for somebody to come and tell her what to do with it. Nobody came. Nobody has come since.

docs.title: The door
docs.text:
Every morning, before the Grove School opens, Corisande walks round behind it to the bramble-grown door of the old wing and looks at it. She does not touch the lock. She checks that the door is shut, that the brambles have not been hacked at, and that no student has carved a name in it, and then she goes home. When she finds children daring each other to touch the door, which is often, she tells them sharply to go away, and then, when they have gone, she is sorry she did.

She has wondered, all her life, what is on the other side. Over the years she has watched living trees grow through and around the old wing until it is hard to say where the walls end and the grove begins, and she has heard, on still nights lately, a faint rustling behind the door, like pages turning in a wind. She has told nobody about the rustling. Nobody asks her about the door, and she will not be the one to bring it up.

docs.title: Her life
docs.text:
Corisande never married. She kept bees on the Lantern Paths for most of her life and sold honey along them, and the hives stand empty behind her home now, because her hands are no longer steady enough for the frames. She has a small gift, enough to make a candle lean toward her and no more, and she has always thought it a fair joke that the keeper of the school's oldest door was the least gifted person in her family.

Her oldest neighbour on the Lantern Paths is Aspen, the retired treewright, who tells the story of the day the news of the Children came to anyone who will sit still. She has heard it more times than she can count, and she corrects his improvements under her breath. In all the years they have been neighbours, Aspen has never once asked her about the key. She cannot decide whether that is tact or forgetfulness, and it nettles her either way.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: She has no daughter to give the key to, and that is what keeps her up at night. She fears that she will be the last of the keepers, that the key will go into a drawer at the Heart Tree when she dies, and that nobody will ever know why her family kept it. What she wants, though it embarrasses her to want it, is for someone to come to her door, ask her properly, and let her open the old wing herself, just once, before she goes.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could bring Corisande the first real reason anyone has ever given her to open the old wing, and walk in beside her with a lantern. Afterwards she might let anyone with the nerve go back in, and stand at the door with her key, very straight, looking as if she had been waiting all her life for exactly this. She has.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Aspen: old neighbour on the Lantern Paths

docs.title: Calyra
docs.text:
Eldest of the Grove

Town Fairy Forest Where Heart Tree Role Ruler Age Elder In the game Calyra

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Patient and dry-humoured, she lets everyone finish speaking before she answers, and her answers are short. She still corrects students' spellwork out of habit.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Calyra taught at the Grove School for forty years, and she has never quite stopped. She is seventy-four now and Eldest of the Grove, but she still corrects students' spellwork out of habit, sometimes in the middle of a Council meeting, sometimes in the middle of someone else's lesson. She is patient and dry-humoured, she lets everyone finish speaking before she answers, and her answers are short. Her former students say the shortness is the point: she has always believed that most people already know the answer, and only need to be left enough quiet to hear it.

docs.title: The teacher
docs.text:
Calyra came to the Grove School at twenty-five to teach the youngest students the first, simplest magic: how to listen to the forest before asking anything of it. She taught that and a dozen other things for forty years, and a remarkable number of the forest's teachers learned from her. Amaryl, who now teaches the coaxing of living wood, was one of her students, and still sometimes calls her "teacher" in Council by mistake. Calyra never corrects that particular mistake.

Nine years ago, when old Eldest Ferris died, the forest's teachers and elders gathered to choose from among themselves who would lead the Grove Council. Two names were spoken most often, Calyra's and Thessaly's, and Calyra won by a handful of voices. Thessaly took it graciously and has been Calyra's sharpest critic and most reliable ally ever since. Calyra would not want it any other way; she says a council with no Thessaly in it would agree itself off a cliff.

docs.title: The Heart Tree
docs.text: Calyra leads the Grove Council from the Heart Tree. Ilwen, her steward, keeps the Council's records and greets every visitor on the stair, and she has been trying for two years to make him take a holiday. Isaura, who keeps the old Magician records, is her confidante, and the two of them talk late into the night in a room of the Heart Tree where nobody else is allowed to bring a lantern. Halcy, among the first of the Children of the Tree to settle in the forest, is her friend, and Calyra sometimes asks Halcy for advice over a basket of flowers, because Halcy notices things about the forest that its oldest Magicians have long since stopped seeing. Calyra has never married. Her students were her family, and the forest is her house.

docs.title: The friend from the highlands
docs.text:
Forty-seven years ago, in Calyra's third year of teaching, a young Brenna envoy named Odda got lost on the Lantern Paths after dark in her first week in the forest. Calyra found her sitting under a lantern pretending she had meant to stop there, and walked her home without teasing her once that night. She has teased her about it ever since.

Odda stayed three winters. She taught Calyra Brenna bonesetting and the uses of highland herbs, and Calyra taught her forest plant-lore and how to read the oldest Magician script. Every spring since, Odda has written a letter ahead and then come to the forest herself a few weeks later, carrying a bundle of highland herbs, and gone home with forest herbs for the Brenna healers. Odda leads the Brenna now, and Calyra thinks the highlands are lucky to have her. Odda thinks Calyra has been telling people what to do since she was twenty-seven, and Calyra cannot honestly deny it. The spring visit is the one week of the year when Calyra sets the Council aside entirely.

docs.title: Her quiet worry
docs.text:
Calyra's quiet worry is the seal scholars. Since the expedition damaged the seal fifty years ago, the forest's scholars have studied the old records day and night, trying to understand how it might be strengthened. Isaura leads them, and Calyra watches them sleep too little and find too little. She fears they will burn themselves out before they find anything, and she fears, even more privately, that there may be nothing in the records to find.

A quest might bring a missing spring letter from Odda, help the Council persuade an exhausted scholar to rest, or carry something from Isaura's records that Calyra does not want anyone else to read.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Thessaly: old rival and friend
  • Ilwen: steward
  • Amaryl: former student
  • Isaura: confidante
  • Halcy: friend
  • Odda: old friend

docs.title: Faelan
docs.text:
Lantern-maker's Apprentice

Town Fairy Forest Where Lantern Paths Role Craftsman Age Young In the game Faelan

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Dreamy and clumsy with his hands, but with a real eye for colour. He hums while he works.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Faelan is apprentice to Ondine, Keeper of the Lanterns, and he has broken more lantern glass than any apprentice she has ever taken. He knows this because she has told him, more than once, and because Vesper, her daughter, keeps a tally of it chalked on the back of the workshop door. He is twenty-one, dreamy and clumsy with his hands, and he hums while he works, which is when most of the breakages happen. He also has the best eye for colour anyone in the lantern workshop can remember, and that is why, after five years and a great deal of broken glass, he is still there.

docs.title: The workshop
docs.text:
Faelan grew up on the Lantern Paths, where every bridge and stair is lit by the lantern-makers' work, and as a child he used to lie on his back under the bridges at dusk and watch the lights come on one by one. He had a small gift and a large imagination, and at sixteen he talked his way into Ondine's workshop by describing, in great detail, a lantern he wanted to make one day. Ondine, who is exacting and proud and secretly sentimental, said the idea was impossible and took him on the same afternoon.

Five years later, he can cut, set and seal glass, mix glow-oil and hang a lantern so it does not swing in a storm, all of it slowly and with frequent accidents. What he can do that nobody else in the workshop can is choose colours. He can look at a stretch of path and know exactly which shade of amber will make it feel safe, which green will make a bridge feel like a branch, which pale gold will let a tired traveller see the next step without being dazzled. Ondine has started asking his opinion about the glass for the outer paths, where she has been making the lanterns brighter every year. Faelan has noticed that, and noticed that she does not like to talk about why.

Vesper, who sells the workshop's lanterns, has none of her mother's patience with him. She tells him exactly what each broken pane cost and then, when no one is looking, sells the pieces he got right at the best prices in the shop.

docs.title: Linnet
docs.text:
Faelan's sweetheart is Linnet, the young Keeper of Living Homes along the Lantern Paths. They met about two years ago, when he was hanging a lantern from the branch of a tree home she was mending, dropped it, and showered her hair with coloured glass. Linnet, who is patient, practical and a little too serious for her age, picked the pieces out one by one and then made him apologise to the tree. He did, out loud and at length, and she laughed, and he has been coming to find her ever since. Far too often, according to her master.

Oriel, Master Treewright and Linnet's master, disapproves of Faelan on principle, because he is clumsy, hums and has never grown anything. Faelan knows this and has decided to be cheerful about it. He has also caught Oriel, more than once, almost smiling at one of his jokes, and is quietly counting those too.

docs.title: The lantern
docs.text:
Faelan is saving up to make a lantern of his own design as a gift for Linnet. It is not the impossible lantern he described to Ondine at sixteen; it is better. He wants it to throw light the way sunlight comes through leaves, so that wherever Linnet hangs it, the walls of a room look as if they were standing in a young grove at noon. It needs glass in eleven shades of green and gold, some of which he will have to buy from the glass-grinders of the Lantern Paths, and some of which do not exist yet and he will have to mix himself. He keeps the coins in a jar under his workbench. He has broken the jar twice.

He has not told Linnet. He has not told Ondine either, though he suspects she knows, because lately the off-cuts of good green glass have been ending up on his bench instead of in the scrap bin.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Faelan wants to finish the lantern without breaking it, and to see Linnet's face when she lights it. He fears that he will always be the clumsy apprentice, and that Linnet, who is so careful with everything she touches, will one day decide she wants someone just as careful.

A quest might ask a traveller to fetch a rare coloured sand or mineral for Faelan's glass, to help him keep the gift a secret from Linnet until it is finished, or to replace a pane he broke on the outer paths before Ondine notices it is out.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ondine: mentor
  • Linnet: sweetheart

docs.title: Galen
docs.text:
Staff and Wand Seller

Town Fairy Forest Where Grove School Sells Staves, wands, spell scrolls and practice robes In the game Galen

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Aurel: brother

docs.title: Halcy
docs.text:
Garland Weaver

Town Fairy Forest Where Children's Glade Role Merchant Kind Child of the Tree Sells Woven baskets and glade-flower garlands In the game Halcy

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Kind, practical and welcoming, Halcy remembers everyone's name after one meeting.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Halcy weaves baskets and glade-flower garlands in the Children's Glade, and sells them to anyone who stops to admire them, which is nearly everyone. Halcy is kind, practical and welcoming, and remembers everyone's name after a single meeting: the name, the face, and usually the name of whatever the person was carrying at the time. Visitors who wander into the glade unsure whether they are welcome tend to leave an hour later with a garland and the feeling that they have been expected all along.

docs.title: Among the first
docs.text:
Halcy was among the first of the Children of the Tree to come down and settle in Fairy Forest, in the days when a Child on the Lantern Paths was still a rare sight. Halcy does not talk much about life in the Tree, and when asked, usually answers with a question about the asker's own home instead. Whether that is privacy, politeness or something else, nobody in the forest has quite decided. Old Aspen, who helped coax homes for some of those first arrivals, says Halcy was the one who asked the most questions about how everything worked, and remembered every answer.

What Halcy will talk about, at length, is the forest: which paths flood in spring, which lantern-maker to ask for a lamp that will not frighten a newcomer, where the quietest benches are, and who in the Herb Gardens will give honest advice about a cough. Halcy learned all of it the slow way, and decided early that nobody coming after should have to.

docs.title: The guide
docs.text: So when newer Children come down from the Tree, it is usually Halcy who meets them and helps them find their way. Halcy finds them a place to sleep, introduces them to the right neighbours, explains the forest's customs, and stays close until they are ready to manage alone. Niv, who is shy, gentle and easily overwhelmed by crowds, was one of these, and Halcy still checks on Niv often. Halcy introduced Niv to Oriel, the master treewright, whose tended tree home Niv now lives in, and was glad to see the two of them become friends. Halcy has noticed Niv standing at the edge of the glade looking toward the World Tree, and has decided not to ask why until Niv is ready to say.

docs.title: The Eldest's friend
docs.text:
Calyra counts Halcy as a friend. They met long before she was Eldest, when Halcy began coming to sit quietly at the back of her listening lessons at the Grove School, not to learn magic, but to learn how the forest's people learned. Calyra noticed, said nothing for a month, and then asked Halcy's opinion of her teaching. Halcy gave it honestly. They have been friends ever since.

Now Calyra sometimes visits the glade and asks Halcy's advice over a basket of flowers. She says Halcy notices things about the forest that its oldest Magicians stopped seeing long ago. Halcy's advice is usually short and practical, and Calyra usually takes it.

docs.title: Trade
docs.text: Halcy's best customer is Tansy at the Dewdrop Tea House, who buys garlands for every table and baskets to carry her honey cakes, every week without fail. Halcy delivers them personally, partly because Tansy always has a cup of dew tea waiting and partly because the tea house is the best place in the forest to meet newcomers.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Lately Halcy has been weaving more garlands than the market needs, and setting the spares aside without explanation. A quest might ask a traveller to help Halcy settle a newcomer who is struggling, to carry a basket and a quiet message to the Heart Tree, or to gather a flower that grows only in a corner of the forest Halcy can no longer safely reach.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Calyra: friend
  • Tansy: customer
  • Niv: friend

docs.title: Hesper
docs.text:
Mistress of the Herb Gardens

Town Fairy Forest Where Herb Gardens Role Healer Age Elder In the game Hesper

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Blunt, kind and always smelling faintly of mint. She treats grown adults exactly the way she treats children with scraped knees.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hesper is Mistress of the Herb Gardens, the terraced beds and glasshouse-hollows below the Heart Tree where Fairy Forest grows its healing plants. She is seventy, blunt and kind, and always smells faintly of mint. She treats grown adults exactly the way she treats children with scraped knees: she sits them down, tells them they were foolish, cleans the wound, gives them something that tastes awful, and sends them off with a honey drop for being brave. Hardened adventurers have been known to come back for the honey drop.

docs.title: A life in the gardens
docs.text:
Hesper came to the Herb Gardens at fifteen as a weeding girl under old Mistress Yarrow, who taught her that every plant in the beds was either a medicine or a poison depending on how much you gave, and that most people were the same. Hesper rose from weeding to brewing to teaching, and when Yarrow died thirty-three years ago, the gardens passed to her. She has tended them for most of her life and taught half the forest's herbalists, and she still kneels in the beds every morning before anyone else is awake.

She never married. She says the gardens took all the patience she had and left none for a husband, and that she has never once regretted the trade.

docs.title: Her people
docs.text:
Celandine, her apprentice, runs the remedy stall by the garden gate and makes most of what she sells. She is gentle, orderly and a little anxious, and Hesper thinks she is the most careful herbalist she has ever trained, which she has told her exactly once. Celandine's husband Merrow does the digging, weeding and watering that keeps the gardens alive. He is slow-talking and big-hearted and fiercely protective of his seedlings, and Hesper would not trade him for three quicker men.

Ailo, one of the Children of the Tree, helps in the gardens and has become Merrow's close friend. Hesper says the gardens have never grown so well since Ailo came. She has asked why more than once. Ailo only smiles, and Hesper, who is not used to being smiled at instead of answered, has decided for now to be grateful instead of curious.

Briony, who taught herb-lore at the Grove School for decades and now sits on the Grove Council, is Hesper's oldest friend. Briony still spends more time in the gardens than at the Heart Tree, mostly on the bench beside Hesper's potting shed, and the two of them settle the forest's affairs over tea long before the Council ever hears of them.

docs.title: The list
docs.text:
More hurt travellers come to Hesper every year, carried in from the roads by the edge watch or limping in by themselves. Two years ago she began keeping a list: who came, where they were hurt, and what attacked them. She writes it in the back of her seed book in a plain, firm hand. At first it was only so she would know which salves to brew. Now it has grown long enough that she can see things in it: the same creature appearing on a road where it was never seen before, wounds that should not have come from the animal that made them, a season when everything seemed to bite at once.

She has not shown the list to anyone at the Heart Tree. She is a gardener, not a scholar, she says, and the scholars have enough to read. She is not sure that is the real reason.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Hesper wants Celandine ready to take the gardens when she is gone, and she wants the roads safe enough that she can stop keeping her list. She fears neither will happen soon. She also knows Celandine longs to go to the Forest Edge after a plant that grows only there, and she has not told her whether she approves.

A quest might ask a traveller to gather herbs from a road too dangerous for her gardeners, to carry her list to the seal scholars, or to bring back word of what attacked a traveller who did not reach her in time.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Celandine: apprentice
  • Merrow: gardener
  • Briony: friend

docs.title: Ilwen
docs.text:
Steward of the Heart Tree

Town Fairy Forest Where Heart Tree Role Official Age Adult In the game Ilwen

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Calm, tidy and endlessly polite, with a habit of answering questions with the exact page and shelf where the answer can be found.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ilwen is Steward of the Heart Tree, and if you climb the great stair that winds around its trunk, he will be at the top of it, waiting to greet you. He is thirty-four, calm, tidy and endlessly polite, and he has a habit that visitors find either wonderful or maddening: ask him a question, and he will answer it with the exact page and shelf where the answer can be found. Ask him where the Eldest is, and he will tell you that too, along with when she will be free, what she will probably say, and which chair to sit in while you wait.

docs.title: The steward's work
docs.text:
Ilwen keeps the Grove Council's records: its minutes, its meeting days, its letters in and out, and its guest list. He knows who is coming up the stair this week and who came up it ten years ago, and why. He writes down everything the Council decides, in a small, even hand, and files it where he can find it again in the time it takes to say the date. He keeps the chamber swept, the lamps trimmed and the long table polished. He also waters the vines that grow over the walls and ceiling of the Council chamber, morning and evening, because nobody else remembers to, and because the one time somebody else did, they drowned half of them.

He came to the Heart Tree at twenty-two as steward to old Eldest Ferris, who taught him that a council runs on paper as much as on wisdom, and that a good steward is the one nobody notices until he is gone. When Ferris died nine years ago and the elders chose Calyra, Ilwen stayed. He has served her ever since, and he likes her very much. She is patient and dry and lets everyone finish speaking, which makes his minutes far easier to write.

docs.title: The holiday
docs.text: Ilwen has been Steward for twelve years and has never once taken a holiday. Calyra has been trying to make him take one for two years. She has suggested it, recommended it, put it on the Council's agenda as a joke and, once, very nearly ordered it. Ilwen would like, just once, to go. He has even chosen where: he has read every account in the Heart Tree of Kaldemor's harvest fair, and would like to see it for himself and eat something someone else has cooked. But he cannot think who would water the Council chamber's vines, and every time he tries to imagine handing the watering can to anyone else, he finds a reason to stay.

docs.title: The people he serves
docs.text:
Thessaly, the sharpest of the councillors, keeps her own ledger of every promise the Council makes. She checks it against his minutes after every meeting, and about once a season she finds a difference. Ilwen enjoys this more than he would ever admit. Her sister Briony brings him gossip and seedcake, in that order. He knows, because it is in his minutes, exactly how many times Seren, Warden of the Forest Edge, has come up the stair to ask for more guards, and exactly how many she has been given. He has never said the numbers aloud. He has started underlining them.

He also keeps the guest list, which means he knows the rhythm of the forest's visitors: the chieftain of the Brenna, who comes every spring to see the Eldest, and the week the Council is set aside for it; the wilds naturalist Juniper, who comes up the stair with muddy boots to spread her notebooks across Caelum's floor; the hurt and the hopeful and the merely curious.

docs.title: Wynne
docs.text:
His friend is Wynne, Isaura's granddaughter, the young copyist of the old records. He met her on the stair the day she arrived from Selsior at fourteen, a quiet girl with a bag of books and a stubborn chin, and he showed her where everything was, down to the page and shelf. Now they eat lunch together on the landing of the great stair on fine days and talk about handwriting, ink and the shocking way some people treat a spine.

Lately Wynne asked him, very sideways, whether the Heart Tree had any list of its oldest shelves older than the one in use. He told her exactly where such a list might be, and did not ask why. He is a steward; he knows when not to ask. But he has noticed that she has been quieter than usual since spring, and he has started leaving the stair landing free for her at lunch even on rainy days, in case she wants to talk.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Ilwen wants one week away, and the vines alive when he comes back. He fears, very quietly, that the Council's records are filling with requests that have not been answered quickly enough, and that one day someone will turn to the right page and shelf and ask why nobody acted sooner.

A quest might ask a traveller to water the Council chamber's vines for a week so Ilwen can finally take his holiday, to deliver the Council's letters to somewhere the roads have made difficult, or to help him find a misfiled record he is certain he never misfiled.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Calyra: employer
  • Wynne: friend

docs.title: Isaura
docs.text:
Keeper of the Old Records

Town Fairy Forest Where Heart Tree Role Scholar Age Elder In the game Isaura

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Stern, careful and secretive by duty rather than nature. She is gentler with her granddaughter than with anyone else.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Isaura is Keeper of the Old Records, and the Heart Tree's oldest secrets sleep in rooms she holds the keys to. She guards the forest's most ancient Magician writings, including what little remains about how the great seal was made, and she leads the scholars who study it. She is stern, careful and secretive, and those who know her best say the secrecy is duty rather than nature. She is gentler with her granddaughter Wynne than with anyone else alive, and Wynne is the only person who can make her put down her pen in the middle of a page.

docs.title: Fifty years of reading
docs.text:
Isaura is seventy-two. She came to the Heart Tree's record rooms at twenty-two, as reader and assistant to old Keeper Anselm, in the same summer that the Great World Tree Expedition came home. She remembers the forest gathering under the Heart Tree to talk about the Children, and Anselm muttering that there would be nothing in the records about them, and being right.

What nobody yet knew that summer was that the expedition had hurt the seal. When the wilds began to change, and it became clear what had happened, the forest turned to its records, and the records turned out to be thinner than anyone had hoped. The Magicians who made the seal had guarded the knowledge so closely that much of it was never shared even with their own people. Isaura became Keeper when Anselm died thirty years ago, and she has led the seal scholars ever since.

Fifty years of reading have taught her a great deal about the seal: what it was meant to hold, roughly where its strength was placed, which old Magicians worked on it and what they argued about. They have taught her nothing yet about how to strengthen it. Lately she has begun to suspect that some of the oldest pages were never written down at all: that the most important parts of the making were passed from one Magician to another by word of mouth, and that the last mouth closed a very long time ago. It is not a thought she shares with her scholars. It would take the heart out of them.

docs.title: The people she trusts
docs.text:
Calyra, the Eldest, is her confidante. They have known each other most of their lives, and late at night the two of them talk in the innermost record room of the Heart Tree, where nobody else is allowed to bring a lantern. Isaura tells Calyra things she tells no one else, including her doubts. Calyra listens, as she always has, and says very little, which Isaura finds a comfort.

Caelum has been her student for twenty years. He is the most brilliant scholar she has trained and the one most likely to wear himself to nothing, and she is harder on him than on anyone because she fears for him most. She has never told him that his drawer of wrong theories is the most honest work in the Heart Tree.

Wynne came to live with her five years ago, at fourteen, from Selsior, where Wynne's mother, Isaura's daughter Mirren, lives with her husband and keeps a bookbinder's shop. Isaura's husband Corvin died fifteen years ago, and the house had been very quiet until Wynne came. Wynne now copies crumbling records onto fresh paper so the originals can rest. Isaura does not know that Wynne has found a gap in the numbering of one old seal record, as though pages were taken out long ago. If she knew, it might bear on her suspicion in a way she has not considered.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text:
Isaura fears that the answer was lost before she was born. She fears even more that it was not lost, but hidden, and that she has spent fifty years reading around a hole she should have seen.

A quest might ask a traveller to retrieve an old record from a ruined Magician site, to help Wynne decide whom to tell, or to carry a sealed letter from Isaura to Calyra that must not be opened on the way.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Calyra: confidante
  • Caelum: student
  • Wynne: granddaughter

docs.title: Juniper
docs.text:
Wilds Naturalist

Town Fairy Forest Where Forest Edge Role Adventurer Age Adult In the game Juniper

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Curious, fearless and careless about her own safety, she sketches creatures while they are still trying to bite her.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Juniper is a wilds naturalist, which is to say she walks into places sensible people walk out of, sits down, and starts drawing. She is thirty-four, curious, fearless and quite careless about her own safety. She has sketched creatures while they were still trying to bite her, and on one famous occasion finished the drawing first and dealt with the bite afterwards. Her notebooks are the most detailed record anyone in the kingdom keeps of how the wild creatures of Veligor have changed during the Age of Disturbance. Nobody yet knows what the changes mean.

docs.title: Beetles first
docs.text:
Juniper grew up in the forest and was, by every account, a child who could not walk past a log without turning it over. At the Grove School she was a middling Magician and a remarkable observer. The listening lessons, which most children endure and which Calyra taught in those days, were the only lessons she loved, because she was allowed to sit still and watch things that did not know she was there. She filled her first notebook with beetles at eleven and has not stopped filling them since.

For twelve years now she has travelled the wilds. She goes out along the roads and then off them, into the woods and hills and broken country between the towns, and she watches. She records which creatures live where, how they behave, what they eat, how many there are, and how all of that differs from what the old books say, or from what she saw in the same place a year before. The notebooks have grown into a shelf of more than forty. She cannot always say what she is looking for. She only knows that she will recognise it when she sees it, and that she has not seen it yet.

docs.title: What she has seen
docs.text: What she has seen is a great deal of change. Creatures that were once shy now walk up to a traveller's fire. Kinds she knew from one valley turn up three valleys over, where nobody has seen them before. Some animals seem larger than their grandparents in the old drawings, or bolder, or simply angrier, as if something in them had been sharpened. In some places the change is sudden; in others it creeps along over seasons. She draws all of it as carefully as she can and writes down the date, the place, the weather and what she had for breakfast, because she has learned that you can never tell which detail will matter.

docs.title: The people she comes back to
docs.text:
When Juniper comes back, she comes back to the Heart Tree, where Caelum, the seal scholar, is her closest colleague. She climbs the great stair with mud on her boots and spreads her sketches across the floor of his study, and the two of them argue for half the night about what they mean. Caelum wants a pattern that points to the seal's weak places. Juniper wants to understand the creatures for their own sake, and suspects he looks for the pattern too hard. They have not found it yet, either of them, but she has never met anyone who listens to her notes as hungrily as he does, and she makes sure he eats while she is there.

Her other friend is Seren, Warden of the Forest Edge, who keeps the watch at the last lanterns. Seren has twice gone out past the lanterns to bring Juniper back from somewhere she should not have been, sketchbook still in hand. The first time, Juniper was annoyed at being interrupted. The second time, she was very glad, and has never quite admitted it. She always stops at the Edge on her way out and on her way back, partly so the watch knows where she is and partly because Seren worries about her more than about anyone, and Juniper would rather be worried about than not.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Juniper wants to understand what is happening to the creatures of Veligor. She does not need to be the one who fixes it; she only wants to see it clearly. She fears that the answer is in her notebooks already, plain on some page she has read a hundred times, and that she is too close to see it. She has another fear she rarely says aloud: that one day, drawing something too closely, she will not get to finish the sketch.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Last autumn Juniper lost a notebook in the wilds, dropped while she was climbing out of a ravine with something large below her, and she has wanted it back ever since. It holds a season's notes from a place she has not been able to reach again. A quest might ask a traveller to recover it, to guard her while she draws something that would very much rather she did not, or to carry her latest notebook to Caelum when she is too stubborn to come in from the wilds herself.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Caelum: colleague
  • Seren: friend

docs.title: Kestrel
docs.text:
Wandering Magician

Town Fairy Forest Where Forest Edge Role Adventurer Age Young In the game Kestrel

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Restless, cocky and loyal, she treats every monster on the road as a personal insult.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Kestrel is a wandering Magician, which is a polite way of saying she is almost never anywhere for long. She is twenty-three, restless, cocky and fiercely loyal, and she treats every monster on the road as a personal insult. Where other travellers see a dangerous stretch of path and go around it, Kestrel sees an affront to be corrected, and corrects it, usually with more fire than strictly necessary.

docs.title: From the orchards to the Grove
docs.text:
Kestrel was not born in the forest. She grew up in an orchard family on the farmland near Kaldemor, where her parents still grow apples and still write to ask when she is coming home for the harvest. At ten she set a hayrick alight by sneezing near it, and the family decided, after the fire was out, that the Grove School might be a better place for her than the orchard. The forest's schools teach anyone with the gift, from any town in the kingdom, and the forest took her in.

She was not a model student. She loved the spellwork and loathed the listening lessons, and she spent a great many mornings sitting under a tree being told to hear it, while hearing only how much she would rather be somewhere else. She learned anyway, in the end, mostly so she could stop being made to sit there. She finished at nineteen and went straight out onto the roads the same week.

docs.title: The roads
docs.text:
For four years now Kestrel has walked the paths between the towns, clearing monsters from them. Nobody pays her to do it, though merchants and carters often buy her supper. She does it because the roads were safe once, according to everyone old enough to remember, and she cannot see why they should not be safe again. She knows the bad stretches better than almost anyone alive, and which creatures have turned up where they never used to be.

Between journeys she stops at the Forest Edge to rest, trade news and eat someone else's cooking. Seren, the Warden of the Edge, is her friend, one of the few people whose advice she actually takes. Kestrel brings Seren reports from the roads; Seren gives her a bed in the watch hut and tells her, in very few words, which of her plans are foolish.

docs.title: Thorne
docs.text: Thorne, one of Seren's edge guards, is her rival, and Kestrel would not have it otherwise. He is brash and eager for a fight, and so is she, which is exactly the trouble. They argue over who has seen worse monsters, who reacted faster, and whose method of dealing with them is less reckless. Kestrel teases him every time she visits. Lately he has been complaining that someone keeps moving his things in the night, and he half suspects her. She is not the culprit, and has told him so truthfully, and enjoys very much that he does not believe her.

docs.title: Admirers
docs.text: Alder, a student from a harbour town, has decided Kestrel is a hero. He follows her around the Edge whenever she visits, asking about the roads, and she is far more flattered than she lets him see. She knows he dreads the journey home at the end of term. She has been thinking about offering to walk him there, and has not yet worked out how to say it without sounding kind.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Kestrel wants the roads clear, and she wants to be the one who clears them. She fears, though she would never say it, that she is only holding back a tide: that every monster she drives off is replaced by two, and that the thing making them is far beyond the reach of any Magician with a staff.

A quest might send a traveller out with her to clear a stretch of road, ask them to carry her report back to Seren when she is too stubborn to come in wounded, or help her escort a nervous student home.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Alder: admirer
  • Seren: friend
  • Thorne: rival

docs.title: Linnet
docs.text:
Keeper of Living Homes

Town Fairy Forest Where Lantern Paths Role Craftsman Age Young In the game Linnet

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Patient, practical and a little too serious for her age. She talks to the trees she tends as if they were old neighbours.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Linnet keeps the living-tree homes along the Lantern Paths: the rooms, stairs and branch-bridges that families live in and walk across every day without once thinking about the trees that hold them up. Linnet thinks about the trees all the time. She is twenty-two, patient, practical and a little too serious for her age, and she talks to the trees she tends as if they were old neighbours, asking after their roots, apologising when she has to bind a split, and telling them the news of the path. People who overhear her find it charming or odd, depending on the person. The trees, as far as anyone can tell, do not mind.

docs.title: Learning the work
docs.text:
Linnet grew up on the Lantern Paths, and as a small girl she used to sit on the branch-bridges watching old Aspen, who kept the homes there then, coax a new room out of a trunk over a whole summer. At the Grove School she was one of Amaryl's steadiest students in Growing, never the quickest but never once the one who snapped a branch to save time, and Amaryl, who praises rarely, told her at the end of her schooling that she had good hands. Linnet has kept that.

Six years ago, at sixteen, she became apprentice to Oriel, the Master Treewright, who tends the oldest homes around the Heart Tree. Aspen had just retired, his hands too stiff for the work, and the Lantern Paths homes needed a keeper. Oriel is gruff, gentle-handed and slow to trust anything that grew in less than a century, and he trusted Linnet slowly, a season at a time. He pretends to find her habit of talking to the trees foolish. She has noticed that he stops whatever he is doing to listen when she does it.

docs.title: The homes
docs.text:
Linnet's days follow the trees. In spring she walks every home on the path, laying a hand on the bark and checking the new growth. In summer she coaxes new rooms for families that need them, slowly, a hand's width at a time. In autumn she braces the branches that will carry snow, and after every storm she is out before breakfast mending what the wind split. She knows which home has a stair that creaks when rain is coming, which bridge sulks if too many people cross it at once, and which old beech will only grow toward the morning sun.

Aspen still lives on the Lantern Paths among the homes he kept for forty-odd years, and he checks her work whenever she is not looking. She knows. She lets him. Sometimes she leaves a mend a little unfinished on purpose, so that he can have the pleasure of telling her about it at the Dewdrop, and then she listens to every word, because he is usually right.

docs.title: Faelan
docs.text:
Her sweetheart is Faelan, Ondine's apprentice in the lantern workshop, who is dreamy and clumsy and hums while he works. They met about two years ago, when he dropped a lantern from the branch of a tree home she was mending and showered her hair with coloured glass. She made him apologise to the tree. He did, at length and with feeling, and she laughed for the first time that week. He comes to find her far more often than Oriel thinks proper. Linnet does not mind at all. She is a careful person who works all day with slow, careful things, and she finds it restful, more than she can say, to be with someone who is neither.

She does not know that he is saving up to make her a lantern of his own design. She does know he is hiding something, because he is very bad at it, and she has decided to let him have his secret.

docs.title: The seedling
docs.text: Linnet hopes, one day, to grow a home from a seedling herself: not to coax a room from a tree someone else planted, but to raise one from the start, as the first Magicians did. Oriel has told her she is not ready. She believes him, mostly. But on a quiet bend of the Lantern Paths, where nobody else walks, she has picked out a young tree no taller than her shoulder, and she visits it every evening and tells it about her day. She has not told Oriel about it. She is not asking it to grow into anything yet. She is only, she says, getting to know it first.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Linnet wants to be the kind of treewright Oriel is, and one day to grow something that outlasts her. She fears that the woods are changing faster than she can learn them, and that one day a tree will tell her something is wrong and she will not understand what it means.

A quest might ask a traveller to help Linnet mend storm damage on a high bridge before nightfall, to fetch water or soil for her secret seedling from somewhere beyond the paths, or to keep Faelan's gift hidden from her until it is ready.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Oriel: mentor
  • Faelan: sweetheart

docs.title: Liri
docs.text:
Grove School Student

Town Fairy Forest Where Grove School Role Child Age Child In the game Liri

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bright, bold and impatient, she wants to learn the exciting spells first and the listening never.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Liri is nine years old, and she has decided that she has waited quite long enough. She is bright, bold and impatient, and she wants to learn the exciting spells first, the ones with light and noise and sparks, and the listening never. She has been at the Grove School for a year, which in her opinion is a year of sitting still that nobody will ever give back to her.

docs.title: The tea house girl
docs.text:
Liri was born in the forest and has lived all her life at the Dewdrop Tea House on the Lantern Paths, where her mother Tansy serves dew tea and honey cakes to everyone who passes. Her father, Edrin, kept the bees whose honey goes into those cakes; he died of a winter fever when she was one, and she does not remember him. She knows him from the hives her mother still tends and from the way some of the older guests look at her and say she has his chin.

Growing up in a tea house has taught Liri two things. The first is that if you sit quietly under a table, grown-ups forget you are there and say interesting things. The second is that the most interesting things are always about the roads: what travellers met on the way, which paths have turned bad, what the creatures beyond the Forest Edge look like now. Liri has heard a great many of these stories. She has never seen a monster, and it seems to her deeply unfair that she should live so close to them and never see one.

docs.title: School
docs.text:
Liri's teacher for the first and oldest lesson is Sorrel, who teaches listening: to trees, wind and creatures, before trying any magic at all. Sorrel's lessons are mostly silence. Liri finds silence unbearable. She likes Sorrel, which makes it worse, because she cannot even be properly cross with him. She has learned to sit still in his lessons for almost a quarter of an hour at a time, which he says is progress, and which she says is torture.

What she wants is to be like the wandering Magicians who come through the tea house with singed sleeves and stories, and to go out onto the roads herself one day and make them safe.

docs.title: Lumi
docs.text: Her best friend is Lumi, one of the Children of the Tree, who joined the Grove School to learn the forest's ways. Lumi asks the questions nobody else dares to and laughs at most of the answers, and Liri thinks Lumi is the most interesting person she has ever met. They sit together in every lesson, share every honey cake, and get into trouble roughly once a week.

docs.title: The plan
docs.text:
Liri has a plan. She is going to sneak out to the Forest Edge, past the last lanterns, and see a real monster with her own eyes; only for a moment, she tells herself, and only from very far away. She has worked out when the edge watch changes, which path has the fewest lanterns, and how long she can be gone before her mother notices. She has told only Lumi.

She has not noticed that Lumi has been quiet about it lately, or that her mother has started watching her a little too carefully at supper. She is nine, and she is quite sure nobody suspects a thing.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text:
Liri would never admit to being afraid of anything. But she is afraid, a little, of what her mother's face would look like if something went wrong, and she has not let herself think about that part of the plan for very long.

A quest might ask a traveller to keep an eye on the paths near the Edge on the night Liri chooses, to help Lumi decide whether to tell, or to find some safer way for a bold girl to see what she so badly wants to see.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Sorrel: teacher
  • Lumi: best friend
  • Tansy: mother

docs.title: Lumi
docs.text:
Glade Dweller

Town Fairy Forest Where Children's Glade Role Resident Kind Child of the Tree In the game Lumi

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Endlessly curious and happily blunt, Lumi asks questions nobody else dares and laughs at most of the answers.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Lumi is a Glade Dweller from the Children's Glade, one of the Children of the Tree, and a student at the Grove School, and Lumi is very possibly the most curious person in Fairy Forest. Lumi is endlessly curious and happily blunt, asks the questions nobody else dares to ask, and laughs at most of the answers. The laughter is never unkind. It is the laughter of someone who has just been told something wonderful and slightly ridiculous, and who would like to be told a great deal more.

docs.title: The questions
docs.text:
Lumi joined the Grove School to learn the forest's ways, and has been asking about them ever since. Why do the lanterns along the outer paths burn brighter than the ones near the Heart Tree? Why does the Council need a ledger of its promises, if everyone on it means to keep them? Does a tree mind being listened to, and would it be rude not to listen back? Why do grown-ups say "we'll see" when they mean "no"?

The teachers have learned to brace themselves. Aurel, the junior teacher, who writes out every lesson word for word, has never once had notes for a question of Lumi's, and has slowly come to understand that Lumi's laughter at his answers is how Lumi learns. Sorrel, who teaches listening, answers Lumi's questions with silence, and Lumi finds this the funniest answer of all, and then, after a while, goes quiet and actually listens. Sorrel considers this one of his finest achievements.

Lumi is not always tactful. Lumi once asked Caelum, the seal scholar, in the middle of the Dewdrop Tea House, why he kept a drawer of wrong ideas instead of throwing them away, and then, before he could answer, said that it was the cleverest thing Lumi had ever heard of. Caelum did not know what to do with that and went home without his honey cake.

docs.title: Liri
docs.text: Lumi's best friend is Liri, Tansy's daughter, who is nine, bright, bold and wants the exciting spells first and the listening never. The two sit together in every lesson, share every honey cake, and get into trouble roughly once a week, usually because Liri had an idea and Lumi asked the question that made it worse. Lumi thinks Liri is the bravest person in the forest. Liri thinks Lumi is the most interesting. Both are probably right.

docs.title: Sefa
docs.text: Lumi's other great friend is Sefa, the glade storyteller, who trades stories with the forest's children in the Children's Glade every afternoon. Lumi comes most days, brings Sefa the news from school, and asks for a story in return. Sefa always gives one, and Lumi always asks afterwards whether it was true. Sefa never says. Lumi has decided that this is the best game in the forest and is keeping score.

docs.title: The secret
docs.text:
Liri has a plan. She is going to sneak out past the last lanterns to the Forest Edge and see a real monster, only for a moment, only from far away. She has worked out when the edge watch changes and which path has the fewest lanterns. She has told only Lumi.

At first Lumi thought it was a wonderful plan, and asked a great many questions about it, all of which Liri had answers to. But Lumi has been listening, too: to the travellers at the Dewdrop who come in off the roads with bandaged arms, to the edge guards who eat standing up, to Sorrel saying the forest sounds uneasy at its edges. And Lumi has started asking questions Liri does not have answers to, and stopped asking them out loud.

Now Lumi is torn. Telling Tansy would keep Liri safe, and might cost a best friend. Keeping the secret would keep the friend, and might cost far more. Lumi has noticed that Tansy has been watching Liri a little too carefully at supper, and wonders whether Tansy already knows. Lumi asked Sefa, without saying what the secret was, what a friend should do. Sefa told a story in reply. Lumi has been thinking about it for a week and still cannot decide whether it meant tell or don't.

docs.title: What Lumi wants and fears
docs.text:
Lumi wants to know everything about the forest and the people in it, and wants Liri to see her monster and come home laughing. Lumi fears, for the first time, a question with no good answer.

A quest might ask a traveller to help Lumi decide whether to tell, to go along to the Edge and keep both friends safe, or to find some other way for Liri to see what she so badly wants to see, so that Lumi never has to choose.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Liri: best friend
  • Sefa: friend

docs.title: Lyra
docs.text:
Singer of the Old Songs

Town Fairy Forest Where Lantern Paths Role Performer Age Adult In the game Lyra

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bright, theatrical and generous, she will sing for anyone who asks and many who do not.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Lyra is the Singer of the Old Songs, and on any evening when it is not pouring with rain, you can find her somewhere on the Lantern Paths singing them. She is thirty-two, bright, theatrical and generous. She will sing for anyone who asks and for a great many people who do not, and she sings everything, from children's counting rhymes to the long, dark songs of the Balrog War, as if it were the most important song in the world and you were the only person she had ever wanted to sing it to.

docs.title: Where the songs came from
docs.text:
Lyra learned most of her songs from her grandfather, Aspen, the retired treewright. Her mother Fennel, Aspen's only child, had a fine voice too, and sang her to sleep with the old lullabies; Lyra's father, a travelling fiddler, died before she was old enough to remember him, and she has only a story or two about him and the tunes her mother said were his. When Lyra was ten, twenty-two years ago, Fennel died of a fever in a hard winter. Lyra went to live with Aspen and her grandmother Elda, and when Elda died four years later, it was Aspen alone who raised her.

Those were long evenings, and often neither of them could sleep. So Aspen sang. He knew the songs his own grandparents had sung, the songs the treewrights sang while they worked, the songs about the first Magicians and the Listening Woods, and the old war songs nobody sang at parties. He sang them all, badly and with great feeling, and Lyra learned every one. She says he saved her life with them, and Aspen, who is talkative about everything else, goes quiet when she says it.

He still comes to hear her nearly every evening and sits as close to the front as he can. He also corrects her when she changes a word, and she changes one now and then just to watch him do it.

docs.title: The bridge by the tea house
docs.text: On fine evenings Lyra sings on the branch-bridge outside the Dewdrop Tea House, so that the guests inside can hear her through the open windows. Tansy, who keeps the tea house, is one of her oldest friends. When Lyra first came to live on the Lantern Paths, a grieving ten-year-old, Tansy's mother Hollyn fed her honey cakes in the kitchen, and Tansy, then fourteen, let her stand on a chair in the tea room and sing to the guests. Lyra has been singing for the Dewdrop's guests ever since, and Tansy has never once let her pay for a cake. Lyra pays her back with songs, and with Liri, whom she has been teaching rhymes since the girl could talk.

docs.title: The war songs
docs.text: Among the songs Lyra sings are the ones about the Balrog War: the First Burning, the truce, the long days at the foot of the World Tree, the Savage front line that held, and the Magicians who worked the seal. They are not cheerful songs. Lyra sings them anyway, every few evenings, because she thinks people ought to know them, and because lately she has noticed that people are listening to them differently. Travellers who have come in off the roads go very still during the war songs, and do not clap afterwards.

docs.title: The verses nobody remembers
docs.text:
Lyra is collecting the verses nobody else remembers. She asks every old person in the forest to sing her what they know, and writes down every verse that differs from Aspen's. She has found lullabies with extra lines, work songs with whole verses missing from the common versions, and a war song that three different old singers each knew a different ending to. Each spring, when the highland visitors come from Midbarium to see the Eldest, she trades songs with them, and has learned that some of the old war songs are sung in Midbarium too, with the same tunes and different words.

One fragment troubles her. It belongs to one of the oldest songs about the Magicians at the Tree, and it does not fit: a few lines about what the Magicians did, in an order that seems to matter, with words in them that nobody she has asked can explain. Aspen knew only half of it. An old woman on the lower paths knew a little more, and died last winter before Lyra could ask her again. Lyra does not know what it means, or whether it means anything at all. It has never occurred to her that the scholars at the Heart Tree might want to hear it. She thinks of songs as songs.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Lyra wants every old song in the forest written down and sung, so that none of them ends with her. She fears that the old singers are going faster than she can find them, and that the verse that mattered most was lost with someone she did not reach in time.

A quest might ask a traveller to find an old singer in a distant village who might know the rest of a verse, to carry Lyra's book of songs to the Heart Tree, or simply to sit on the bridge outside the Dewdrop one evening and request a song nobody has asked for in years.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Tansy: friend
  • Aspen: grandfather

docs.title: Merrow
docs.text:
Gardener

Town Fairy Forest Where Herb Gardens Role Worker Age Adult In the game Merrow

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Big-hearted, slow-talking and fiercely protective of his beds of seedlings.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Merrow is the gardener of the Herb Gardens, which means that every bed, terrace and seedling tray in them has passed through his big, careful hands at least once. He does the digging, weeding and watering that keeps the gardens alive, and he does it without hurry and without complaint. He is forty-one, big-hearted and slow-talking, and fiercely protective of his beds of seedlings. Students who cut across them on the way to the school learn very quickly not to do it twice.

docs.title: The gardener
docs.text:
Merrow grew up on the forest's lower paths, the son of a deadfall gatherer who collected fallen wood for the forest's hearths and never took a living branch. Both his parents are gone now. He was a slow scholar and a slower talker, and the Grove School found that his gift was small; but Hesper, Mistress of the Herb Gardens, watched him carry a bird's nest out of a bed he was meant to be clearing and set it carefully in a hedge, and offered him work the same afternoon. He has been in the gardens ever since, more than twenty years now.

Hesper is his employer and, though neither of them would use the word, something close to a second mother. She is blunt with him and he is patient with her, and between them they keep the gardens in better order than any herbalist can remember.

docs.title: Celandine
docs.text: Merrow's wife is Celandine, the herbalist who runs the remedy stall by the garden gate. They have been married twelve years. She is gentle, orderly and a little anxious, and labels everything twice; he grows half of what she brews, and is quietly, enormously proud of her remedies. He will tell any customer at the stall that his wife's salve is the best in the kingdom, and then go red and return to his digging. They have no children, and the seedlings, Celandine says, get all the fussing a child would.

docs.title: Ailo
docs.text: Ailo, one of the Children of the Tree, came to help in the gardens and has become Merrow's close friend. Ailo is calm and unhurried and can work for hours without a word, and Merrow, who is the same, found that he had never worked so happily beside anyone. The two of them can spend a whole morning on one terrace and part at noon without having said ten words, both perfectly content. Hesper says the gardens have never grown so well. Merrow has never asked Ailo why. He thinks it would be rude, and besides, he is not sure he would understand the answer.

docs.title: The Forest Edge
docs.text:
Merrow is quietly afraid of the Forest Edge. Years ago, carrying compost to a garden plot near the outer paths, he saw the edge watch bring in a guard who had been badly hurt by something from the woods beyond, and he has not forgotten the guard's face or the sound of the stretcher. He goes nowhere near the Edge if he can help it.

Celandine, though, wants to go there. There is a plant that grows only near the Forest Edge, and she is sure it would make a better remedy than anything in the gardens. She keeps asking. Merrow keeps begging her not to go. He knows she is right about the plant, and he knows he cannot stop her forever, and he cannot think what he will do on the day she decides to go anyway.

docs.title: What he wants
docs.text: Merrow wants his wife safe, his seedlings undisturbed, and a quiet life in the gardens until he is too old to dig. A quest might ask a traveller to go to the Edge in Celandine's place, or with her; to help Merrow find the courage to go himself; or to track down whatever has been digging up his seedling beds at night.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hesper: employer
  • Celandine: wife
  • Ailo: friend

docs.title: Niv
docs.text:
Glade Dweller

Town Fairy Forest Where Children's Glade Role Resident Kind Child of the Tree In the game Niv

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Shy, gentle and easily overwhelmed by crowds, Niv is fiercely loyal to the few people Niv trusts.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Niv is a Glade Dweller from the Children's Glade, one of the Children of the Tree, and one of the quietest people in Fairy Forest. Niv is shy, gentle and easily overwhelmed by crowds, and a market day on the Lantern Paths, with its noise and press and everyone talking at once, can send Niv home before noon. But the few people Niv trusts have learned that Niv's quiet is not weakness. Niv is fiercely loyal to them, and will stand between any one of them and trouble without a moment's thought.

docs.title: Coming down
docs.text: Niv is one of the newer Children to settle in the forest, and like most newer Children, Niv was met by Halcy. Halcy, who was among the first to come down and has made a habit of helping those who came after, found Niv somewhere quiet to sleep, explained the forest's customs one at a time instead of all at once, and stayed close until Niv was ready to manage alone. Niv still finds that the hardest part of the forest is how many people there are in it, and how much they all want to say. Halcy has never once asked Niv to say more than Niv wanted to, and Niv has never forgotten that. Halcy still looks in on Niv often, usually on the way to somewhere else, and never staying longer than Niv can manage.

docs.title: Oriel
docs.text:
Not long after Niv came down from the Tree, Halcy brought Niv to Oriel, the Master Treewright, who tends the oldest living-tree homes around the Heart Tree. It seemed an unlikely match. Oriel is gruff and seventy-six and slow to trust anything that grew in less than a century, and he distrusts most new things on principle. He found, to his own surprise, that he did not distrust Niv at all.

What suits Niv about Oriel is his silence. He does not ask how Niv is feeling. He does not fill the quiet. He walks the old homes, lays a hand on the bark and listens to the wood, and Niv walks beside him and listens too. Niv now lives in a tree home that Oriel tended, a small, sheltered one with a single round window, and visits him almost every day. Some days they say a dozen words between them. Some days they say none, and both count it a good day.

Niv knows that Oriel has been worried lately, though Oriel has not said about what. He has been spending longer in a few of the oldest homes, standing very still with his hand on the bark, and coming out with his mouth set. Niv has not asked. Niv thinks a person is entitled to their own silence, which is the same thing Oriel thinks about Niv.

docs.title: Looking toward the Tree
docs.text: Niv often stands at the edge of the glade, at the place where the trees thin, looking toward the World Tree. Sometimes it is a moment; sometimes it is an hour. Niv has never told anyone why. Halcy has noticed and has decided not to ask until Niv is ready to say. Oriel has noticed and has never asked at all. Other people in the glade have asked, kindly or curiously, and Niv has only smiled and gone home. Whether it is homesickness, or habit, or something else entirely, nobody in the forest knows, and Niv is not saying.

docs.title: What Niv wants and fears
docs.text:
Niv wants a quiet life among a few good people, and wants those people safe. Niv fears crowds, loud voices and sudden changes, and fears, though Niv has said this to nobody, anything happening to Oriel, who is old and works alone.

A quest might ask a traveller to help Niv carry something through a crowded market day, to find out what has been troubling Oriel so that Niv can help, or simply to stand beside Niv at the edge of the glade for a while, saying nothing, which is a great compliment if Niv allows it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Oriel: friend
  • Halcy: guide

docs.title: Ondine
docs.text:
Keeper of the Lanterns

Town Fairy Forest Where Lantern Paths Role Craftsman Age Elder In the game Ondine

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Exacting, proud and secretly sentimental. She can tell which of her lanterns is dimming from across the forest.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ondine is Keeper of the Lanterns, and every light on every path, bridge and stair in Fairy Forest is, one way or another, her responsibility. She leads the lantern-makers who make, hang and tend them, and she can tell which of her lanterns is dimming from across the forest. Nobody quite knows how. She says she simply looks, and that anyone else could if they bothered. She is sixty-eight, exacting and proud, and secretly sentimental, a secret she keeps very badly from everyone except herself.

docs.title: The workshop
docs.text:
Ondine grew up on the Lantern Paths and came to the lantern workshop at fourteen, as a sweeper of glass dust for old Keeper Lisbet, who made the lanterns before her. Lisbet taught her to cut glass, to mix glow-oil, to seal a lantern against rain and to hang it so it would not swing in a storm, and above all to look at a stretch of dark path and ask what the person walking it would need to see. When Lisbet died thirty-one years ago, the workshop and the title passed to Ondine. She has made the forest's lanterns ever since, and she still sweeps her own glass dust at the end of every day, because she does not trust anyone else to find every splinter.

She was eighteen when the Great World Tree Expedition came home, and she remembers the outer paths as they were then: a few soft lanterns for mushroom-pickers and courting couples, lit late and left to gutter. That is the forest she was taught to light.

docs.title: The outer paths
docs.text: For the last nineteen years, Ondine has made the lanterns along the outer paths a little brighter every autumn. She began quietly, after an edge guard told her that something had come right up to the last lantern and stopped. Now the outer lights are the strongest in the forest, and the edge watch walks among them at night with spears. Ondine keeps a book in her workshop recording every increase, year by year and lantern by lantern. She has never shown it to the Heart Tree. She does not like what the numbers say, and she does not like that nobody has asked her for them.

docs.title: Faelan
docs.text:
Her apprentice is Faelan, who has broken more lantern glass than any apprentice she has ever taken, and she has told him so, often. Five years ago, at sixteen, he talked his way into her workshop by describing a lantern he wanted to make one day. She told him the idea was impossible and took him on the same afternoon. She has never told him why: it was the first time in years that anyone had described a light by how it would make a person feel.

He is clumsy and he hums, but he has the best eye for colour the workshop has known, and lately she has started asking his opinion about the glass for the outer paths. She knows he is saving for a lantern of his own design, and suspects it is for Linnet, the young treewright he walks out with. She has said nothing. She has simply started leaving the off-cuts of good green glass on his bench. She also keeps, in a box under her own bench, the prettiest of the coloured panes he has broken, because the colours were right even when his hands were not.

docs.title: Vesper
docs.text: Her daughter Vesper sells the workshop's lanterns, and her own travelling lights, from the shop at the front. Vesper has none of her mother's patience and all of her skill, and the two of them argue about the shop's prices every single day. Ondine thinks Vesper charges too much for travelling lights to people who have no choice but to use the roads after dark. Vesper thinks her mother charges too little for everything else, and that sentiment does not pay for glass. Each is right about half of it, which is why the argument never ends. Ondine is prouder of Vesper's travelling lights than she has ever said aloud.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Ondine wants every path in the forest lit well enough that nobody walking it is afraid. She fears that one autumn she will make the outer lanterns brighter and it will not be enough, and she fears, too, the day she has nothing left to make them brighter with.

A quest might ask a traveller to replace a dimming lantern on a path too far out for the workshop to reach safely, to fetch a rare mineral for a stronger glow-oil, or to carry Ondine's book of lantern brightnesses to someone at the Heart Tree who ought to read it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Faelan: apprentice
  • Vesper: daughter

docs.title: Oriel
docs.text:
Master Treewright

Town Fairy Forest Where Heart Tree Role Craftsman Age Elder In the game Oriel

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gruff, gentle-handed and slow to trust anything that grew in less than a century.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Oriel is the Master Treewright of Fairy Forest, and he tends the oldest living-tree homes around the Heart Tree: the rooms and stairways and sleeping-hollows that the first Magicians coaxed from the trunks long before the Age of Division ended, and that families still live in today. He is seventy-six, gruff, gentle-handed and slow to trust anything that grew in less than a century. That includes most people. It does not include trees.

docs.title: Hands and bark
docs.text:
Oriel was apprenticed young to old Master Brannoc, who held the forest's oldest homes before him and who died many years ago. Aspen came to Brannoc four years later, a talkative boy who could not keep still, and Oriel decided on the first day that he did not like him. They have been friends for more than half a century. Aspen talks; Oriel grunts; neither of them has ever found anyone else who understood the work so well. Aspen retired six years ago when his hands grew stiff, and Oriel has not forgiven him for it, because he now has nobody his own age to complain to about the young.

Oriel's work is slow and almost silent. He spends his days walking the old homes, laying a hand on the bark, listening to the wood, coaxing a split to close or a new room to open over a season or a year. He has never cut a living branch in his life and says he never will. He never married. The trees, he says, are company enough, and they do not ask him how he is feeling.

docs.title: Linnet
docs.text:
When Aspen retired, the living homes along the Lantern Paths needed a keeper, and Oriel took on Linnet as his apprentice to keep them. She is patient, practical and a little too serious for her age, and she talks to the trees she tends as if they were old neighbours, which Oriel pretends to find foolish and privately thinks is exactly right. She hopes one day to grow a home from a seedling herself. Oriel has told her she is not ready. He has not told her that he thinks she will be, sooner than he would like.

He knows about Faelan, the clumsy lantern apprentice who hums while he works and comes calling for Linnet far too often. Oriel disapproves of him on principle and has caught himself liking the boy anyway.

docs.title: Niv
docs.text: Niv, one of the Children of the Tree, lives in a tree home Oriel tended, and visits him almost every day. Halcy brought Niv to him not long after Niv came down from the Tree, and Oriel, who distrusts most new things, found that he did not distrust Niv at all. Niv is shy and gentle and easily overwhelmed, and Oriel's silence suits Niv better than anyone's conversation. They sit together in the old homes while he works, and Niv sometimes stays beside him for a whole morning, listening to the wood as he does. Oriel has seen Niv standing at the edge of the glade looking toward the World Tree, and has never asked why. He thinks a person is entitled to their own silence.

docs.title: The homes that will not wake
docs.text:
Lately a few of the oldest homes around the Heart Tree have been slow to wake in spring. Their buds come late, their sap runs thin, and the rooms feel colder than they should. It is only a handful, and only the very oldest, the ones the first Magicians shaped. Nobody else has noticed yet. Oriel wants to know why before anyone does.

He has thought of disease, of drought, of old age. None of them fits. He has thought, late at night, of the forest's roots, which are said to reach all the way to the World Tree's, and of what else lies under the World Tree. He has put that thought away each time, and each time it comes back.

A quest might ask a traveller to fetch soil or water from a distant root, to help Oriel quietly examine a sleeping home without alarming the family inside, or to keep Aspen from noticing, since Aspen would tell everyone by supper.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aspen: old friend
  • Linnet: apprentice
  • Niv: friend

docs.title: Orla
docs.text:
Glade Dweller

Town Fairy Forest Where Children's Glade Role Resident Kind Child of the Tree In the game Orla

docs.title: Personality
