docs.title: Hob
docs.text:
Miller

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Park Role Worker Age Adult In the game Hob

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Easygoing and dusty from head to toe, he whistles along with the creak of the sails. He worries about the weather the way other people worry about money.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
You can hear Hob before you see him. He whistles along with the creak of the windmill sails, a tune that changes with the wind, and when the wind drops the whistling stops and he goes out to look at the sky. He is forty-four, easygoing, broad in the shoulder and dusty from head to toe; the flour has settled so deep into his eyebrows that his daughter says he was born with white ones.

Hob runs the windmills in Kaldemor Park and grinds the flour for half the town. Rosa's terrace oven comes first, always, and every morning before the sun is properly up the first sacks of the day go down to the Market for her. Then come the farm kitchens, the Sleepy Snail, and the households that still bake their own. In autumn he grinds the harvest grain for the carts that go down to Bain Harbour, and the mill runs from dark to dark.

docs.title: The woodcutter's son
docs.text:
He is the son of Orin and Wren. Orin felled trees for forty winters, and in Kaldemor the sons and daughters of woodcutters have always taken up the axe after their parents. Hob is the only one who never wanted to. As a boy he was handed a hatchet and spent the afternoon not chopping wood but watching the windmill sails turn on the far side of the Park, and he has been watching them ever since. At fourteen he began carrying sacks for the old miller, Tibbet, and by twenty he was greasing the gears and dressing the millstones himself. When Tibbet died, Hob was the only person in town who knew how the mills were put together, and the mills became his.

Orin was disappointed for about a week and has been proud ever since. He tells everyone who will listen, which is everyone in the Park, that his son "fells wheat instead of trees". Hob has heard the joke perhaps a thousand times and still laughs, because his father enjoys it so. Wren never minded which he chose, so long as he came home for supper.

docs.title: Mabel and Nell
docs.text:
Hob married Mabel the potter twelve years ago. They met over a broken flour crock: he brought it to her to mend, she told him it was past mending and threw him a new one while he waited, and he came back the next week with another crock he had broken on purpose. She knew, and said nothing, and threw him that one too. Their house stands near the windmills, and its shelves are full of crocks.

Their daughter Nell is eight and spends her afternoons flat on her back in the square counting clouds. Hob understands her better than most people do. A miller spends his life looking up, judging the wind by the clouds, and he was the one who stitched her little tally book from the brown paper his flour sacks come wrapped in. He has never asked her how big the number is. He suspects it is very large and does not want to spoil it.

docs.title: Weather
docs.text:
Hob worries about the weather the way other people worry about money. Too little wind and the stones stand still and the town goes short of bread; too much and he has to reef the sails in a hurry before they tear. A wet summer spoils the grain. A dry one stunts it. He knows the sky over Kaldemor better than anyone except his daughter, and he does not like what he has seen of it lately: the winds coming in from the woods past the hills have changed, and twice this spring, on mornings with no wind at all, his sails shuddered and the stones rattled in their beds, as if the ground had shrugged beneath the mills.

He has not told anyone about that, not even Mabel. He has decided it was nothing. He checks the foundations every morning anyway.

docs.title: What he wants
docs.text: Hob wants plenty of grain, a steady westerly, and his father to stay well enough to sit on his bench in the afternoons. He would like Nell to be a miller one day, and knows she will probably be something no one has thought of yet. He is quietly glad that Fen carries his flour to Rosa twice a week, because it means someone is looking after Rosa, who he thinks has been lonely for years.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin when a millstone cracks before the harvest, and the only stone fit to replace it lies in an old quarry past the hills where the snails are thick. Or a traveller might help Hob find out why his sails shudder on still mornings, and whether something is moving beneath the ground when they do.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Orin: father
  • Wren: mother
  • Mabel: wife
  • Nell: daughter
  • Rosa: best customer

docs.title: Jem
docs.text:
Fiddler

Town Kaldemor Where Town Square Role Performer Age Young In the game Jem

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cheerful, restless and always tapping a foot, he cannot sit through a conversation without humming. He makes up songs about whoever is listening.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: You will hear Jem before you see him, and if you stop to talk to him, he will be humming before you have finished your first sentence. By the end of your second, he will have made up a song about you. It will rhyme your name with something unfortunate, and he will play it on his fiddle in the square that afternoon, and by evening half of Kaldemor will be whistling it. He is twenty-four, cheerful and restless, all elbows and knees and a foot that never stops tapping, with a battered brown fiddle that he carries everywhere, even to bed, his landlady says.

docs.title: The fiddle
docs.text:
Jem was born in Kaldemor, in a narrow house behind the Market. The fiddle belonged to his grandmother, Nan Dilly, who played every harvest dance in Kaldemor for forty years and who taught him to hold the bow before he could hold a spoon. When she died, nine years ago, Jem was fifteen, and that autumn he stood up on the cart at the harvest fair and played the dances himself, badly, and then a little better each year. His parents moved to Selsior when he was eighteen to keep a lodging house, and wanted him to come; he would not leave the fiddle's town, and they live there still and write when they remember to. No harvest dance in Kaldemor has started without him since.

By day he plays in the town square, for the children and the visitors and anyone waiting for Pell's cab. By night he plays at the Sleepy Snail, where Molly feeds him in exchange, rather more than he can eat, and scolds him for not finishing it. Molly is the nearest thing he has to family in Kaldemor now, and she knows it, and fusses accordingly. He lodges in the room over her kitchen. Fewer travellers come in from the east these days, and the ones who do arrive tired and frightened, and Jem plays them something soft and does not make up songs about them.

docs.title: The song
docs.text:
For a year now, Jem has been writing a song for Daisy the painter.

He has written a great many songs, about everyone in Kaldemor, and every one of them took him an afternoon. This one has taken a year and is not finished. He has written verses about her paint-spotted nose and her colours and her laugh, and each time he gets to the end, he decides it is not good enough, and starts again. He has played pieces of it in the Workshops lane, where she works, and stopped halfway and played something else. He has written forty-three verses. He has crossed out forty-one of them. He made up a song about Lia and Clem in an afternoon, and Clem begged him not to play it, and Jem thought that was very unfair, since it was a good song.

Daisy has no idea. Or she pretends not to. Jem does not know which, and is too frightened to find out. Her grandfather Bertie knows exactly what is going on and winks at Jem in a way that makes him miss notes.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Jem wants to finish the song, play it to Daisy, and live through it. He would like, too, one day, to play in the streets of Selsior, where his grandmother always said the crowds danced longest on Veligor. He fears that the song will never be good enough. He fears, more quietly, that the roads are becoming too dangerous for fiddlers, and that one autumn the harvest carts will not go down to Bain Harbour at all, and there will be no fair to play, and the old tunes his grandmother taught him will have no one to dance to them.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Jem has heard there is an old dancing tune his grandmother used to play, one he never learned, known by heart only to the oldest people in town. A traveller might be asked to coax it out of Orin, or Ned, or Wren, a verse at a time. Or he might at last decide the song for Daisy is finished, and need someone to make sure she is in the square, without paint on her nose, at exactly the right moment.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Daisy: friend
  • Molly: innkeeper

docs.title: Lia
docs.text:
Town Guide

Town Kaldemor Where Town Square Role Official Age Young In the game Lia

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bright, quick and endlessly patient with visitors and young adventurers, she answers the same question for the tenth time as if it were the first. She always knows the latest news in town before anyone else.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "Welcome to Kaldemor!" says Lia, and she means it every single time, which is a great many times a day. She is twenty-three, bright, quick and endlessly patient, with a cheerful face, a satchel full of folded maps nobody ever needs, and a habit of turning up at your elbow just as you were about to look lost. She meets every visitor in the town square, in front of the great treehouse, and shows them the way to the Market, the Park and the fields beyond. If you ask her the same question ten times, she will answer it the tenth time as if it were the first, and she will look pleased that you asked.

docs.title: The roadside inn
docs.text:
Lia was not born in Kaldemor. She grew up at a small inn on the Royal Road, a day's walk toward Selsior, which her parents still keep; they are well, they write every month, and they play no part in her life here beyond the letters. At the inn she learned two things: how to make a tired stranger feel at home before they have even put their bag down, and how to hear every piece of news on the road before the carters had finished their first cup. Travellers told her everything. She found she remembered all of it.

At sixteen she came up the road to Kaldemor on a harvest cart, to sell her mother's preserves at the fair, and Mayor Tobin found her in the square giving directions to three lost carters, a goat and a very confused adventurer, none of whom she had been asked to help. He offered her a job on the spot. That was seven years ago.

docs.title: Tobin
docs.text:
Lia learned half her job from Tobin: every family's name, most of their grandparents', and the story of the one seed, which she can tell in three different lengths depending on how long the visitor can stand still. Tobin says she does the job better than he ever did, and tells her so often. She sends every visitor to him first, because he wants to meet each one, and he always asks her afterward what she thought of them. He is her mentor, and the closest thing she has to a grandfather in Kaldemor, and she worries about him more than she lets him see. She has noticed, the way she notices everything, that Mildred worries about him too.

She tells visitors the practical things: that the Market is east of the square, that Bram sells red potions and that you should carry five before you go anywhere near the fields, that people with a light over their heads have a job for you, and that the snails nibble but a potion mends it.

docs.title: The news
docs.text:
Lia always knows the latest news in Kaldemor before anyone else. Nobody quite knows how. Mostly it is because she talks to everyone, and partly because people find themselves telling her things they meant to keep. She was the one who first spread word, this spring, that the clock tower had stopped: she heard the silence from the square before breakfast and had told half the town before Ewan had come back down the tower stairs. She feels a little guilty about that, because Ewan was very upset. She went up to sit with him afterward, and told every visitor that week that old Ewan might like some company.

She has also heard, from the carters and the hunters and the farmers, a good deal that she does not tell visitors: about the Snail King in the hollow, about the cart that never reached the harbour, and about what Pell will not say ran at his cab. She keeps those for Tobin.

docs.title: Clem
docs.text:
Lia is courting Clem the orchard keeper, and she pretends nobody has noticed. Everybody has. She asked him to dance at last autumn's harvest fair, while Jem was playing, and he went the colour of one of his own apples and said yes. Since then she walks out to the orchards most evenings to tell him the day's news, and he listens to all of it, from the top of a ladder, and she has found that she likes the news far better when he is the one listening. She waves at him across the square whenever he comes in, to make him blush. It works every time.

He has told her about the roots of his trees near the woods. She has told no one, which for Lia is a declaration of love.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Lia wants every visitor to feel at home, Tobin to stay mayor for ever, and Clem to ask her a certain question before she loses patience and asks him. She fears the day she has news to spread that she cannot bear to say aloud.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A traveller Lia has welcomed might be asked to help her track a rumour back to its source before she repeats it, for once. Or Lia might ask a young adventurer to carry a message out to the orchards, because she has heard something about the woods that Clem needs to know before dark.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Clem: sweetheart
  • Tobin: mentor

docs.title: Lottie
docs.text:
Schoolteacher

Town Kaldemor Where Town Square Role Scholar Age Adult In the game Lottie

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Kind, curious and a little scatterbrained, she loses her spectacles on her head several times a day. She never answers a child's question with "because".

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Lottie's spectacles are on her head. They are nearly always on her head, and she is nearly always looking for them, and the children in her schoolroom have long since stopped telling her, because watching her find them is the best part of the morning. She is thirty-four, kind, curious and a little scatterbrained, with chalk on her sleeves and ink on her thumb, and she teaches every child in Kaldemor who is old enough to sit still and several who are not. She has one rule for herself, and she has never broken it: she never answers a child's question with "because".

docs.title: The schoolroom in the tree
docs.text:
Lottie's schoolroom is at the very top of the great treehouse, behind the town square, in a round room whose windows look out over the roofs of the mushroom houses to the windmills and the hills. The floor creaks, the walls lean a little where the living tree has pushed them, and on windy days the whole room sways very gently, which the children love and Lottie pretends not to notice. Alfie and his carpenters keep it in repair. Lottie keeps it in chalk, slates and pressed leaves, and in a great many questions.

She was born in Kaldemor, the daughter of a cart-painter and a beekeeper, both dead now, and she was a pupil in the same room herself. Her own teacher was old Philippa, who taught Kaldemor's children for more than forty years and who once answered the small Lottie's question about the stars by taking the whole class up onto the treehouse roof at night. Lottie decided that evening what she wanted to be. She went to Selsior at eighteen to study in the Scholars' Quarter, came home at twenty-five when Philippa grew too frail to climb the stairs, and has taught in the treehouse for nine years. Philippa died the following winter, and Lottie still keeps her ruler on the windowsill, though she has never once used it on anything but a straight line.

docs.title: Nell, Fen and the rest
docs.text: Her pupils are as different as the mushroom houses. Nell, the miller's girl, is very good at sums and very bad at looking at the board, because she is usually looking at the sky through the window; Lottie once spent a whole lesson explaining why clouds float, and Nell wrote down every word and then asked why they bother. Lottie did not have an answer, and said so, and went to look one up. Little Fen asks "but why?" until even Lottie has to go and look something up, and Lottie thinks this is the finest thing a pupil can do. It was Lottie who first told Fen the story of the one seed and the generous soil, and she has since found small holes in odd corners of the schoolroom's window boxes, where Fen has been checking.

docs.title: The one-seed story
docs.text: Lottie collects every version of the one-seed story she can find. Everyone in Kaldemor knows the plain one: a traveller crossing the eastern meadows planted a single seed, slept beside it, and woke to find a tree taller than a tower. But the old people tell it differently. In one version the traveller sang to the seed. In another the traveller wept on it. In one the tree was already there, small and hidden, and the traveller only noticed it. Lottie writes each down in a fat green notebook, with who told it and when, and she has nearly two hundred pages. She has asked Orin, Wren and Ned, and Ned told her a version so short and grumpy that she wrote it down twice to be sure. Some say the seed came from the World Tree. Lottie would dearly like to know, and has written that question on the inside cover, where she will see it every time she opens the book.

docs.title: Hard questions
docs.text: Lately the children ask her harder things. They ask why there are more snails in the meadow, and what is in the hollow past the woods, and why Rufus reads the road warnings in a softer voice now. Tam asked her last week whether the old seal under the World Tree was going to break. Lottie told them what the history books say: that the four peoples sealed the Balrog away long ago, that the seal was damaged fifty years ago, and that the guardians below still keep watch. Then a small voice asked what would happen if it broke, and for the first time in nine years Lottie did not know what to say. She did not say "because". She said, "Nobody knows yet, and I would rather tell you that than make something up." Then she went home and did not sleep.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Lottie wants her children to grow up curious rather than frightened, and she wants a true ending to the one-seed story. She fears that one day a question will come that she ought to answer and cannot, and that a child will learn from her face what she would not say aloud.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: One version in Lottie's green notebook, told to her long ago by an old woman of the farms, says that the traveller left a sign on the tree before walking on, "so it would know her when she came back". Lottie has never found the sign and would like a traveller's help looking. She would also be very grateful for anyone who could bring her a version of the story from another town.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Nell: pupil
  • Fen: pupil

docs.title: Mabel
docs.text:
Potter

Town Kaldemor Where Workshops Role Craftsman Age Adult Sells Pots, jugs and bowls In the game Mabel

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Calm, practical and good with her hands, she can tell what a pot is for before it leaves the wheel. She laughs from the belly.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Mabel throws the pots of Kaldemor. If you have eaten soup in this town, it was out of one of her bowls; if you have bought pickles from Old Marta, they came out of one of her crocks; and if you have drunk cider at the Sleepy Snail, the jug was hers too. She is thirty-nine, calm, practical and good with her hands, with clay drying grey to the elbow most of the day, and she can tell what a pot is for before it leaves the wheel. When something amuses her she laughs from the belly, loud enough to be heard three workshops down, and the whole Workshops lane has learned to smile when it hears her.

docs.title: Learning the wheel
docs.text:
Mabel was born in Kaldemor, the daughter of a thatcher and his wife, both long dead now. She was never any good on a roof. At fifteen she went to sit in the doorway of the pottery on the Workshops lane and watch Primrose, the mayor's wife, throw a jug, and she sat there every day for a week until Primrose put a lump of clay in her hands to make her stop staring. Mabel worked under Primrose for twelve years. Primrose taught her to centre the clay, to pull a wall thin and even, to judge a kiln by its colour, and to talk to customers as if they were neighbours, which in Kaldemor they always are.

When Primrose fell ill in her last year, Mabel ran the wheel for her. Primrose died twelve years ago, and the workshop passed to Mabel. Mayor Tobin still comes by now and then to sit on the stool by the door, as he used to when his wife worked there, and tells Mabel she pulls a handle exactly as Primrose did. Mabel keeps one of Primrose's jugs on the top shelf. It is not for sale, and she has never put anything in it.

docs.title: Hob
docs.text:
It was in that last year, with Primrose ill, that a dusty young miller came in with a broken flour crock and asked whether it could be mended. Mabel told him it was past mending and threw him a new one while he waited. The next week he came back with another broken crock. She knew perfectly well he had broken it on purpose, and she said nothing, and threw him that one too. They were married twelve years ago, a few months after Primrose died, and Mabel moved into Hob's house near the windmills. The shelves there are now full of crocks, which she says is his own fault.

Hob's mother Wren tells Mabel she is the best thing that ever happened to him. It embarrasses them both, and Mabel secretly agrees.

docs.title: Nell
docs.text: Their daughter Nell is eight and spends her afternoons flat on her back in the town square, counting clouds. Mabel says that Nell learned to look up before she learned to walk, and that it was the windmill sails over her cot that did it. For years Mabel stood in the doorway at dusk calling her in. Nell never came. Mabel long ago gave up, and now simply sends supper out to the square in a covered bowl when the light goes, and the bowl comes back empty and the girl comes back later. She has never asked how big the number in the tally book is. She thinks a child should be allowed one secret that is entirely her own.

docs.title: The kiln and the carts
docs.text: Mabel works hard all year and hardest in late summer, when she fills the crates of pottery that go down to Bain Harbour on the harvest carts. Last autumn one of those carts never arrived, and with it went a whole season's worth of her best blue-glazed bowls. She was cross about the bowls for a day and frightened about the drivers for a good deal longer. They were not hers, but she had packed their straw.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Mabel wants a good kiln, a dry autumn and her family round her table, which is harder than it sounds with a husband who goes out to look at the sky and a daughter who will not come in from it. She has noticed that Hob has started checking the mill foundations every morning, and that he says it is nothing. She has decided to believe him until he tells her otherwise. What she fears is the thing she cannot shape: the roads, the woods and whatever is making the town talk in low voices.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: On one still, windless morning this summer, a row of Mabel's new jugs walked themselves to the edge of the drying shelf, and one fell. She blamed the mill. A traveller who mentions it to Hob may find out that she is not the only one who has noticed. Mayor Tobin, too, has asked for great crocks to keep the ground snail shell dry for his garden fence, bigger than any Mabel has thrown, and she will need help digging the clay for them from the bank past the farms, where the snails are thick.

docs.text:
• Hob: husband
  • Nell: daughter
  • Old Marta: customer

docs.title: Meg
docs.text:
Snail Hunter

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Park Role Adventurer Age Young In the game Meg

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cocky, quick and brave a step past sensible, she keeps a running count of every snail she has beaten and adds a few. Underneath the boasting she cares a great deal about the farms.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "One thousand, four hundred and twelve," says Meg, before anyone has asked. That is her count of snails beaten, and it goes up by a few every time she says it, whether or not she has been out to the meadow in between. She is eighteen, small, quick and sunburnt, with a short sword she keeps sharper than it needs to be and a hunter's habit of never quite standing still. She is cocky, she is brave a step past sensible, and she would very much like you to know both. What she would rather you did not notice is how much she cares about the farms.

docs.title: The holding at the meadow's edge
docs.text:
Meg was born on a small holding at the far edge of the meadow, east of the town square, where her parents grew turnips and kept geese on land that was always a little too close to the snails. She learned to swing a stick before she could spell her name, mostly at snails, and by the time she was twelve she was the one her father sent out at dusk to clear the rows. The snails grew thicker every year. Two years ago, after a spring when they ate three plantings in a row, her parents gave up the holding and went east to live with relatives in the countryside past the end of the Royal Road. They are well, and they write, and they play no part in her days. Meg was sixteen. She refused to go. She said someone had to stay and pay the snails back, and she has been doing it ever since.

She rents the loft of the old seed shed by the windmills in the Park, and she eats wherever someone will feed her, which in Kaldemor is most places.

docs.title: The Gauntlet and the fountain
docs.text:
Meg ran Quill's Gauntlet last summer and passed the hanging course on her first try, ropes, swinging logs and all, which nobody in the Park had seen done before. Quill said nothing at all, which she knows is how he says well done. That same afternoon, still glowing, she walked along the rim of the Park fountain on her hands to show the recruits how it was done, and fell in. Garrick saw it from his ledge above the fountain and applauded. Digby saw it too, and Digby has never let her forget it, any more than she lets him forget the hanging course, which he has now failed eleven times.

They needle each other at every turn. She calls him the farmer; he calls her the fish. Neither of them would admit that she has, at least once, followed him home from the meadow at a distance to make sure he got there, or that he has done the same for her.

docs.title: Hale's scout
docs.text:
Meg hunts the meadow for Hale's bounty, thirty snails at a time, and scouts the edge of the woods for him when he is busy. Hale has never told her she is good, because she would never stop saying it, but he sends her where he would not send anyone else, and she knows exactly what that means. She would walk into the woods past the hills for him without a second thought. She already has, further than she has admitted to anyone.

This spring, before anyone in town had heard of the Snail King, she went past the hills and through the woods to where the trees thin out on the far side, simply to see what was there. Standing in a clearing beyond the woods, she felt the ground shake under her feet. It was not the grinding sound Hale later described, a cart of stone tipped out, but a long low shudder, as if something far below had turned over in its sleep. She ran all the way home and told no one. She is not sure, now, whether she was frightened of what she felt or of being told off for going there.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Meg wants the meadow cleared, the farms safe and her parents' holding back under turnips one day. She wants Hale to say she is good, once, out loud, and she would die rather than ask him to. She fears the shudder she felt past the woods, and fears more that she ran from it.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Meg means to go back past the woods and find out what shook the ground, and she would rather take a traveller than go alone, though she will put it as a dare. Another quest might begin when Hale, who has noticed more than she thinks, asks a traveller to follow her quietly and make sure she comes home.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hale: mentor
  • Digby: rival

docs.title: Mildred
docs.text:
Town Clerk

Town Kaldemor Where Town Square Role Official Age Adult In the game Mildred

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Neat, dry and exact, she has never misspelled a name in the town ledger. Her rare smile is worth waiting for.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Mildred's desk stands in the little office on the ground floor of the great treehouse, where the light is good in the morning and the mayor can be found in the afternoon, if he can be found at all. She is fifty-seven, neat, dry and exact, with grey hair pinned so firmly that it has not moved in thirty years and a pen she wipes after every line. She has never misspelled a name in the town ledger. Not once. She has a smile, but it is rare, and people in Kaldemor who have earned it tend to mention it at supper.

docs.title: The ledgers
docs.text:
Mildred keeps the town's books: the ledgers of the town purse, the mayor's letters, the records of the harvest carts and the fair, and, most precious of all, the list of every family in Kaldemor. It is a long book bound in green leather, and every birth, marriage, death, arrival and departure in the town goes into it in her small upright hand. When Digby walked in from the east at fourteen, Mildred wrote him in. When Archie arrived on his father's timber cart and refused to leave, Mildred wrote him in, and then, after a pause, wrote his father's name beside his so that somebody would know where the boy belonged. She writes in the newcomers, the adventurers who settle here from other towns, and the snail hunters who move into lofts and sheds, and she crosses out no one without a reason written next to them.

She was born in Kaldemor, the only child of a schoolmaster's assistant and a seamstress, both dead now, and she has never married. She came to the treehouse office at twenty-four as assistant to old Pomfrey, the clerk in the last years of Mayor Hettie, and when Pomfrey's eyes failed seven years later she took the pen. That was twenty-six years ago, four years into Tobin's time as mayor, and she has kept his books ever since.

docs.title: Tobin
docs.text:
Mildred knows Tobin better than almost anyone, and she would rather be boiled than say so. He counts the town by knocking on doors; she counts it in the ledger, and her count is right. Just under three hundred people live in Kaldemor, Tobin says. Mildred could tell you exactly how many: two hundred and ninety-four at the last count, not including the snails, which Tobin always adds and she always crosses out.

She writes his letters for him, or rather she takes the ones he dictates while walking round the office and makes them say what he meant. She files the ones that come in. She has filed four from Ewan the clockkeeper about Garrick the climber, each more indignant than the last, under a heading that reads, in her neat hand, "Clock tower, climbing of". She files the bounty receipts from Hale and notices when the ranger has quietly paid one out of his own purse; she says nothing, and writes it in a separate column so that one day she can pay him back.

docs.title: Rufus
docs.text: Every evening Mildred writes the next morning's notices for Rufus the town crier: the fair days, the lost cats, the price of flour at Hob's mill, and lately more and more road warnings. Rufus reads them in a voice that rattles the treehouse shutters, and he adds words of his own, and Mildred pretends to mind. This spring she began writing the road warnings in shorter, plainer words, so that he would not have to shout them quite so loud for the children. She has not told him why. She thinks he knows.

docs.title: What she worries about
docs.text: Mildred has counted the town more carefully than anyone, and she has counted Tobin too. He is seventy-one. He has been mayor for thirty years. He climbs the treehouse stairs a little slower every autumn, and he sat up nine nights in a row with Ewan this spring and was grey for a week after. Lia has noticed that Mildred worries about him; Mildred has noticed Lia noticing, and they have an understanding about it without ever having discussed it. Mildred does not worry about who will be mayor next. The town will choose, as it always has. She worries that the next mayor will not know every family's grandparents, and that something, some day, will need knowing.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Mildred wants the ledger to balance and the list to be complete. She fears the day she has to write a name into the column of the dead because of something on the roads, and she fears, though she has said it to nobody, the day Tobin decides to rest.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Mildred has noticed something in her own ledger that she does not like: the far farms by the woods have reported more losses this year, of geese and hens, of pumpkins, of young orchard trees, than in any five years before. She would like a traveller to go and count for her. Another quest might ask a traveller to deliver one of Tobin's letters down the road, where the mail no longer goes as surely as it did.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Tobin: mayor
  • Rufus: town crier

docs.title: Molly
docs.text:
Innkeeper of the Sleepy Snail

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Market Role Service Age Adult In the game Molly

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bustling, motherly and nosy in the nicest way, she knows every traveller's business before their soup is served. She cannot stand an empty plate.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: You cannot leave the Sleepy Snail hungry. People have tried. Molly will see the edge of a plate from across the room, and she will be at your elbow with the pot before you have set down your spoon. She is fifty-two, round, quick and pink-cheeked, with flour to the elbows and a voice that carries from the kitchen to the stable yard, and she runs the inn at the edge of Kaldemor Market, where travellers stop for a last good night before the eastern countryside. She is bustling, motherly and nosy in the nicest possible way. By the time your soup is on the table, she will know where you are going, why, who is waiting for you there, and whether your boots will last the journey.

docs.title: The Sleepy Snail
docs.text:
The Sleepy Snail is a long, low inn of honey-coloured timber with a mossy roof, nine rooms upstairs, a big kitchen at the back and a common room with a fire that Molly has never let go out between the first frost and the last. Its sign shows a fat green snail asleep in a nightcap, and it was Molly's grandfather who first hung it, because, he said, nobody in Kaldemor had ever seen a snail hurry and nobody should be made to hurry under his roof. Molly's parents kept the inn after him, and Molly and her younger sister Hilda grew up in it, carrying trays before they could see over them. Their parents are both dead now. Molly took the inn when she was twenty-seven and has run it for twenty-five years.

She has never married, and she says she has never had the time, since she has nine rooms of other people's children to worry about every night. Daisy painted the inn's doors, and once its shutters, the exact brown of Jem's fiddle. When Molly asked her why, Daisy said she had had some brown left over and went pink under the paint, and Molly, who misses nothing, has been watching both of them very closely ever since, with enormous satisfaction.

docs.title: Jem and Hilda
docs.text:
Jem the fiddler lodges in the room over Molly's kitchen and plays in the common room every night. In exchange she feeds him, rather more than he can eat, and scolds him for not finishing it. His parents moved away to Selsior, and Molly has quietly decided that somebody in Kaldemor must see that the boy eats vegetables, and that it may as well be her. She knows all about the song for Daisy. She has heard every one of the forty-three verses through the kitchen ceiling, and she has her favourite among the two he has not crossed out.

Her sister Hilda keeps the town's storage, across the lane, and the two of them could hardly be less alike. Molly talks; Hilda listens. Molly knows everyone's business; Hilda knows where everyone's things are and will never say what they are. Molly sends every guest with a heavy pack across the lane to her sister, and tells them, "She will keep it safer than you would," which from Molly is very high praise.

docs.title: Fewer from the east
docs.text: The Sleepy Snail has always been busiest in summer, when the traders and pedlars come in from the eastern countryside with wool, hides and cheese, and go out again with Kaldemor's pottery and tools. This summer there are fewer of them. Some rooms stand empty for a week. The travellers who do arrive come in late and tired, and they talk at her fire in low voices about things on the road: carts that went into the dark and did not come out, creatures that came at the wheels, lights in the trees where nobody lives. Molly would rather not believe a word of it. She feeds them, fusses over them, gives them the warmest rooms and the second helping, and goes down to the kitchen afterwards and stands very still for a minute before she starts the washing up.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Molly wants every room full and every plate empty. She wants Jem to finish his song, and to be there when he plays it. She fears the night a traveller who promised to stop on the way back does not come back at all, and she keeps a list of those who have promised, folded small, in her apron pocket.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: One of the travellers on Molly's folded list, a pedlar who stops every summer on his way east and back, is now three weeks late, and Molly would like a traveller to go and look for him along the road. Or a guest has left something odd in one of her rooms and gone, and Molly, who cannot bear not to know things, would like someone to find out what it is before she asks Hilda to keep it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hilda: sister
  • Jem: fiddler
  • Mott: summer guest

docs.title: Mott
docs.text:
Travelling Pedlar

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Market Role Merchant Age Adult Sells Tinware and ribbons, every summer In the game Mott

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cheerful, chatty and incurably hopeful, he can sell a ribbon to a scarecrow. He takes in any creature that looks lost.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Mott is the travelling pedlar who stops at the Sleepy Snail every summer, and he could sell a ribbon to a scarecrow. He has, in fact, once, in a field outside a village with a very dry sense of humour, and the farmer paid. He is forty-one, round-faced, cheerful, chatty and incurably hopeful, with a laugh you can hear across a market and a pack on his back that clanks when he walks. He takes in any creature that looks lost. He always has. This summer that has turned out to be most of his trouble, and most of his comfort.

docs.title: On the road
docs.text:
Mott was born on the road, more or less, to a pedlar called Peg who walked the royal roads with a pack twice his size and a voice that could be heard two fields off. He walked beside her from the time he could walk, learned to count in ribbons and to bargain in tin cups, and slept in more haylofts than he can remember. When Peg died, twenty-one years ago, he took up her pack and her round, and he has walked it every year since. He has no house. In winter he lodges wherever the snow catches him, and in summer he walks.

His round brings him to Kaldemor every summer, along the Royal Road from the west, to the Sleepy Snail, where Molly gives him the small room at the end with the crooked window, feeds him far too much, and writes his name on the folded list in her apron of travellers who have promised to stop on the way back. He stops on his way east and again on his way home, and he has never missed a summer. He sells tinware, cups, pans, ladles and lanterns that shine like new money, and ribbons in every colour he can get, and the children of Kaldemor have been known to wait at the Market steps for him.

docs.title: The Deepwood
docs.text:
This summer he never reached the Snail. On the last stretch of the road, where the farm track turns off toward the woods, he saw a fat cat trotting away from the farms toward the trees, looking, he says, entirely too pleased with herself to be anywhere near a wood. He went after her to carry her home. He followed her further than he meant to, then further than was sensible, and then the mist came down and he could no longer tell which way home was.

Somewhere deep in the Deepwood, under great blue-capped mushrooms, the Shrooms found him. They came in a crowd, bolder than any he had ever seen, tore his pack open and carried off every piece of tinware he owned, every cup, pan and lantern, anything that shone. They left the ribbons. Mott still does not know whether to be relieved or insulted.

He found shelter in an old woodcutters' hut in Breezy Hollow, a quiet corner of the Deepwood, with a sound roof, a spring nearby and a rusty tin of old meal on a shelf. The cat found him there the same evening, as if she had meant to all along. He has tried to walk out twice, and twice the mushrooms around the hollow have driven him back. He has been there three weeks.

docs.title: Company
docs.text:
A week ago, on a misty morning, a lamb came out of the trees and stood at the hut door, bleating: a small speckled lamb with a bent ear, much too young to be out alone. Mott took it in, of course. He has tied a blue ribbon round the lamb's neck and a red one round the cat's, so that, he says, they look like somebody's, which they plainly are. The lamb grazes the clearing, the cat hunts mice and brings him the best ones, and in the evenings he talks to them both about Molly's pies.

He does not know whose they are. He has decided that somebody somewhere is missing a lamb and a cat very badly, and that he is not leaving this hut without them.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Mott wants to walk into the Sleepy Snail with a lamb under one arm and a cat under the other and see Molly's face. He would also like his tinware back, every cup of it. He is a little afraid, though he will not say it even to the cat, that the woods have changed for good, and that the roads he grew up on are not the roads he will grow old on.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A hunter searching the Deepwood might find Mott's torn pack strap among the blue caps, and then, deeper in, the hut and all three of them inside. Later, someone might follow the Shrooms to wherever they have carried his tinware, and bring back enough of it for Mott to set out his wares at the Snail again.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Molly: innkeeper

docs.title: Ned
docs.text:
Cobbler

Town Kaldemor Where Workshops Role Craftsman Age Elder Sells Boots and shoes In the game Ned

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Grumpy, honest and very slow, he will tell you your boots are a disgrace before he mends them beautifully. He does not trust anything that was made in a hurry.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "Disgrace," says Ned, looking at your boots. "An absolute disgrace." Then he holds out his hand for them, without getting up, and you will get them back in a week, or two, or three, mended so beautifully that you will not recognise them. He is seventy-nine, bent and bony, with a leather apron worn shiny, a mouthful of tacks he talks around, and spectacles so old that the frames have been mended with waxed thread. He is grumpy, honest and very slow, and he does not trust anything that was made in a hurry, including most people.

docs.title: Fifty years of boots
docs.text:
Ned has made the boots of Kaldemor for fifty years. His shop is a dark little room near the Park end of the Workshops lane, smelling of leather, beeswax and lamp oil, with a bench by the window where the light is best and a row of wooden lasts along the wall, one for every regular customer, each with a name inked on its heel. There are hundreds of them. Some of the names belong to people long dead, and Ned keeps those lasts too.

He was born in Kaldemor, the son of a drover and a dairymaid, both long gone, and was apprenticed at fifteen to old Joss, the cobbler of those days, who was slower and grumpier even than Ned is now. Joss made him stitch the same seam on a scrap of leather every day for a year before he let him near a customer's boot. Ned thought it was cruel. He now thinks it was the only sensible thing anyone ever taught him. When Joss died, Ned was twenty-nine, and the shop and the lasts came to him. He has never married. He says he was waiting for someone who walked properly, and never met her.

He judges people by how they walk, and he is rarely wrong. He can tell a farmer from a carter by the wear on a heel, a liar by a toe that turns in, and a warrior who will not last by a sole worn down on the outside edge. When Wilbur's farmhand Digby left the farm last year to be a warrior, Wilbur came in for a pair of good boots for him, and Ned made them himself, double-stitched, with a heel built a little wider than usual, because he had watched the boy walk and knew he would fall a great deal. Digby has fallen off Quill's hanging course eleven times in those boots, and not one stitch has gone.

docs.title: Orin
docs.text: Ned and Orin the woodcutter have been friends since they were boys, which is more than seventy years, and they have spent most of it arguing about a race. They ran it, they agree, when they were small. Neither of them remembers where it was, or how long, or what it was to, or who was watching. Each is perfectly certain that he won. Ned is a year older than Orin, and says that is why he won; Orin says it is why Ned was slower. They meet on the bench in the Park every few days, when Ned's knees allow, and take it up where they left off. Wren knits beside them and does not take sides. Ned made Orin's woodcutting boots for thirty years and says they were the best he ever made, because Orin was the only man in Kaldemor who walked like a tree falling, straight and sure.

docs.title: Slow
docs.text: The young people of the Market think Ned is too slow, and they are right. He is slower every year. They take their boots to him anyway, because nobody else in Kaldemor can do what he does, and because the warriors who go out to the meadow now come back with soles torn by things that are not stones. He has been working by lamplight this spring, which he has not done in twenty years, and his eyes do not thank him for it.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Ned wants an apprentice who will stitch the same seam for a year without complaining, or with complaining, so long as they stitch it. He wants, very badly, to win the argument about the race before one of them dies. He fears that the lasts on his wall will outlive the skill to use them.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Ned has a pair of boots on his shelf, unfinished, that he started for someone forty years ago and never completed. He will not say whose they were, but he might ask a traveller to find the right leather to finish them. Another quest could begin when someone digs up the truth about the race, and has to decide which old man to tell.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Orin: oldest friend

docs.title: Nell
docs.text:
Cloud Counter

Town Kaldemor Where Town Square Role Child Age Child In the game Nell

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Dreamy and very serious about her counting, she shushes grown-ups who interrupt. She sees snails, carts and teapots in every cloud.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
If you cross the town square of Kaldemor on a fine afternoon and nearly tread on a small girl lying flat on her back in a knitted cap, that is Nell, and you have just interrupted her. She will tell you so. "Shh," she says, without looking away from the sky, "I am counting the clouds." Then she will go on counting, and you will be forgiven only if you stand very still until she has finished.

Nell is eight years old. She is the only child of Hob the miller and Mabel the potter, and the granddaughter of Orin and Wren, who spend their afternoons on a bench in the Park. She was born in the family's house near the windmills, and some of her first memories are of the sails turning against the sky above her cot. Her mother says that is where the trouble started: Nell learned to look up before she learned to walk.

docs.title: The tally book
docs.text:
Nell does not simply watch clouds. She counts them, and she is very serious about it. She keeps a little book with a stitched spine, which her father made for her from the brown paper the flour sacks come wrapped in, and in it she keeps a tally of every cloud she has ever counted. Each day gets a line. Each line gets its marks, and beside the marks she writes down what the best clouds looked like: a snail, a cart, a teapot, a snail again, a cat asleep on a fence, Grandpa's nose. Snails come up more often than anything else, which she says is because Kaldemor has so many of them that even the sky has caught the habit.

She will not tell anyone how big the total is. Not her mother, not her teacher Lottie, not Mayor Tobin, who has tried to guess it at least once a month for a year. She says that if you say a number like that out loud it stops being yours. Her grandfather Orin, who counts trees from his bench the way she counts clouds, is the only person she has ever shown the last page, and he swears he could not read it without his glasses, which is probably true.

Her grandmother Wren knitted the cap she wears, a soft blue thing with a lopsided bobble, and Nell has not willingly taken it off since. Wren knits caps for every child in Kaldemor; Nell is the one who wears hers to bed. Her mother long ago gave up calling her in from the clouds and now simply sends supper out to the square when the light goes.

docs.title: Friends and lessons
docs.text:
Nell's two best friends could not be less like her. Tam is loud and swings a stick at anything that looks like an enemy; Fen notices every small thing and asks a question about each of them. The three of them can usually be found together, Tam shouting, Fen asking and Nell shushing them both. Tam is not allowed to swing his stick within reach of the tally book. Fen is allowed to help count, but only the small clouds.

At Lottie's school in the great treehouse, Nell is very good at sums and very bad at looking at the board. Lottie, who never answers a question with "because", once spent a whole lesson explaining why clouds float, and Nell wrote down every word and then asked why they bother.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Nell wants to count every cloud there is, which she admits might take a while. Lately she has a second ambition: to find out where the clouds go after they pass the hills, and whether they are counted again somewhere else. She is a little afraid that someone in another town is counting the same clouds, and that it would not be fair.

What she really fears she does not write in the book. Since the spring, she has seen her grandfather fall asleep on his bench more often, and she counts a little faster in the afternoons, as if she could get more done while he is still awake to hear about it.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: On three evenings this summer Nell has written something odd in her book: a low grey cloud above the woods past the hills that did not move with the others, and that was gone by morning. She drew it as a snail, like all the rest, and has not shown the page to anyone. A traveller who earns her trust might be the first to see it. Another quest might begin the day the tally book goes missing from the square, and Nell, for once, cannot stay quiet about it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hob: father
  • Mabel: mother
  • Orin: grandfather
  • Wren: grandmother
  • Tam: friend
  • Fen: friend
  • Lottie: teacher

docs.title: Orin
docs.text:
Retired Woodcutter

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Park Role Resident Age Elder In the game Orin

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Slow, warm and a little deaf, he tells the same stories over and over and enjoys them more each time. He still judges every tree he sees by how it would fall.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "Good day," says Orin from his bench in the Park, a little louder than he needs to. "Sit a while, if your legs allow." He is seventy-eight, slow, warm and a little deaf, and he has a story for whoever sits down. It will probably be one you have heard before, if you have sat on that bench before, and he will enjoy it more than he did last time. His wife Wren, knitting beside him, will tell him when he is shouting.

docs.title: Forty winters
docs.text:
Orin was born in Kaldemor to a family of woodcutters, and he took up the axe at eighteen, as his father had and his grandfather before him. For forty winters he felled trees in the woods past the hills, west of the town, where the oaks and birches grow tall: timber for the carpenters, for the beams of new cottages, for barns and carts and fence posts, and firewood for every hearth in Kaldemor. He worked from the first frost to the last, because a tree felled in winter is drier and truer, and in summer he split and stacked and sharpened.

He knew those woods better than anyone in town. He knew which trees were sound and which were hollow, which would fall clean and which would twist, and he still cannot look at a tree without judging how it would fall. He judges the trees in the Park, the trees along the Royal Road, and, on bad days, the great treehouse itself, though only in a whisper.

He put the axe down twenty years ago, at fifty-eight, when his back told him to. Now he counts the trees from his bench instead. He says the treehouse was a sapling when his grandfather was a boy. Everyone in Kaldemor knows it is far older than that, and nobody has the heart to argue.

docs.title: Wren, Hob and Nell
docs.text:
Orin married Wren fifty-three years ago, in the Park, under the clock tower, which he points out has kept time for them ever since. He says he chose her because she was the only girl in Kaldemor who laughed at his stories. She says she was laughing at something else. In more than fifty years she has never once tired of his stories, though she has tired, frequently, of their volume.

Their only son Hob is the miller. Hob was the only woodcutter's child in Kaldemor who never wanted to swing an axe, and Orin was disappointed for about a week. Since then he has been proud, and he tells everyone that his son "fells wheat instead of trees". He has told it a thousand times. Hob still laughs. Orin's granddaughter Nell lies in the square counting clouds; Orin counts trees, and he thinks they understand each other perfectly. She has shown him the last page of her tally book. He told her he could not read it without his glasses, which was true, and kind.

His oldest friend is Ned the cobbler. They have been friends since they were boys, and they still argue about who won a race they ran as boys. Neither of them remembers the race itself, where it was or what it was to, but each of them is perfectly certain he won it.

docs.title: These days
docs.text:
Orin sits in the Park every afternoon, because Wren says the Park is nicest in the afternoon, and he has learned that Wren is right about most things. He greets everyone who passes. He was the first on the bench to notice when the clock stopped this spring, and he asked Wren whether she had heard it, rather loudly, for nine days running.

He worries about the woods. He hears, from the young warriors who pass his bench, that the Shrooms are bolder than ever and that something big has settled in a hollow past the trees. He knew every hollow in those woods once. He would like to know which one.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Orin wants one more walk in the woods past the hills, to see the old trees he left standing on purpose. He fears, though he jokes about it, the day his legs will not get him as far as the bench. Wren will not let him talk about that, so he talks about trees.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Orin marked a great old oak in the woods, forty years ago, as the finest tree he ever left standing, and cut his sign into its bark. A traveller who brings him word of it, or a twig from it, would make him very happy, and might find that the hollow everyone fears lies very near.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Wren: wife
  • Hob: son
  • Nell: granddaughter
  • Ned: oldest friend

docs.title: Pell
docs.text:
Taxi Driver

Town Kaldemor Where Town Square Role Service Age Adult In the game Pell

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Steady and plain-spoken, he never hurries a fare and never misses one either. He has opinions about every road on Veligor.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "Cab for hire!" calls Pell from the stand by the signpost in the town square, and then, if you look like you might be thinking about it, "The road to Selsior is long on foot. My cab is quicker." He is fifty-two, broad and weather-browned, with a flat cap, a leather coat cracked at the elbows and a whip he has never once used on the horse. He is steady and plain-spoken. He never hurries a fare and he never misses one either, and he has an opinion about every road on Veligor, which he will share whether or not you asked, from the first turn of the wheels to the last.

docs.title: The cab
docs.text:
The Kaldemor cab is a tall, green, two-wheeled thing with a hood that folds back in fine weather, a step that squeaks and a bench that seats two comfortably and three if they are friends. Percy the wheelwright built it eighteen years ago, from the axle up, and has kept it rolling ever since; Pell brings it into his yard every spring to be gone over, and Percy tells him it will not last the year, and it always does. It is pulled by Turnip, a patient brown mare with a white nose, who knows every stand on Veligor by heart and stops at each one whether Pell asks her to or not.

Before the cab, Pell drove a carrier's wagon for a Kaldemor carter, up and down the Royal Road and along the lesser roads between the towns, from the time he was eighteen. He was born in Kaldemor, to a family that ran the old posting stable behind the Market, and he could harness a horse before he could tie his own boots. His parents are both dead now, and he has no wife or children. He says the cab is his family, and Turnip is the sensible one.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
The cab runs between towns that have a taxi stand, and never into the wilds. It runs for a fixed fare, the same for a mayor as for a farm girl. And Pell will drive you only to a town you have walked to yourself at least once, and not before. Visitors think this is an odd rule. Pell thinks it is the only one that matters. A person ought to know the road they are paying to skip, he says: where it bends, where it floods, where to stop for water and where not to. If the cab ever breaks down halfway, they will need to know the way on foot. Lia, who sends him most of his fares, has heard him explain this to hundreds of visitors, and she still sends them with a smile.

He knows the roads the way Ned knows feet. He knows which bridge on the Royal Road rattles and which one only sounds as if it does, which inn on the way to Selsior waters its cider, and how many potholes lie between the signpost and the first milestone. He has opinions about all of them. He thinks the road to Selsior is the finest road on Veligor and the most badly mended, both at once.

docs.title: Last month
docs.text:
Lately Pell drives the Royal Road a little faster than he used to. Turnip does not mind. His fares notice, and some of them ask why, and he tells them that he has a supper waiting.

Last month, coming home toward Kaldemor at dusk with an empty cab, something ran at it out of the trees by the road. Pell will not say what it was. He drove the rest of the way at a gallop, which Turnip had not done in ten years, and came into Percy's yard late that evening with two spokes cracked and a splinter torn from the felloe. Percy mended it overnight and did not ask twice. Pell has told nobody what he saw, not Percy, not Lia, not the mayor. Lia has heard something of it from a carter, and keeps it to herself. Pell has started carrying a lantern on the cab even in daylight, and he does not look at the trees on that stretch of road.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Pell wants every fare delivered and every road open. He wants to grow old on the cab bench and die there, ideally in fine weather, ideally at a stand. He fears that one day a road he has driven all his life will be closed, and that he will have to tell a fare he cannot take them home.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Pell might ask a traveller to ride beside him on the Royal Road at dusk, on the stretch he no longer likes, and keep their eyes on the trees while he keeps his on the road. One day he may decide to say what ran at his cab, and he will want to tell someone who has seen worse.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Percy: wheelwright

docs.title: Percy
docs.text:
Wheelwright

Town Kaldemor Where Workshops Role Craftsman Age Adult In the game Percy

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Methodical, gloomy in a comfortable way and secretly very kind, he expects every wheel to break and is glad when it does not.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "It will break," says Percy, running his hand round the rim of a brand-new wheel. "They all break, in the end." Then he hangs it on the cart, steps back, watches it turn, and looks, for a moment, almost happy. He is fifty-six, long, stooped and patient, with sawdust in his eyebrows and a pencil behind each ear, and he is Kaldemor's wheelwright. He builds and mends the carts, the barrows, the harvest wagons and the town cab, and he expects every one of them to fall apart. When they do not, he is quietly delighted. He calls this being prepared. Everyone else calls it gloom, and nobody minds it, because Percy is also, very secretly, the kindest man in the Workshops.

docs.title: The wheelwright's yard
docs.text:
Percy's yard is near the Market end of the Workshops lane, a long open shed stacked with seasoned oak and ash, with a pit for setting tyres and a great iron ring on the wall that he uses to true his wheels. His father was the wheelwright before him and taught him every joint; Percy started sweeping the yard at eight and made his first wheel at fifteen, a barrow wheel that wobbled so badly his father hung it over the door as a warning. It still hangs there. His father died twenty-two years ago and Percy has worked the yard alone since. He never married. He says a wheelwright is married to the weather.

A wheel, Percy will tell you, is a hundred small agreements: hub and spoke, spoke and felloe, felloe and tyre, and every one of them must hold at once. He buys his iron tyres and axle-pins from Gareth the smith, for whom Percy is the best customer in the Market, and who is the only man in Kaldemor who can match him for gloom. The two of them can spend an evening agreeing that everything is going to go wrong, and both go home cheerful.

docs.title: Pell's cab
docs.text:
The town cab is Percy's work from the axle up. He built it eighteen years ago for Pell, who drives it from the stand by the signpost, and he has kept it rolling ever since. Pell is his friend and his best customer, and the two of them have an old arrangement: Pell brings the cab in every spring for Percy to go over, and Percy tells him it will not last the year, and it always does.

Last month it nearly did not. Pell brought it in late one evening with the near rear wheel cracked through two spokes and a long splinter torn out of the felloe, and would not say what had happened. Percy did not ask twice. He mended it overnight, put in two new spokes of his best ash, and charged Pell for one. Pell will not talk about what ran at the cab. Percy has not pressed him. But he kept the old felloe, and he has looked at it a great deal.

docs.title: The marks
docs.text:
Percy has mended more broken wheels off the Royal Road this year than in any year he can remember, and it is not the wheels he minds. It is the marks. Most of them are what you would expect: stones, ruts, a wheel driven too fast into a ditch. But some of them are not. Some have deep gouges set in a curve, as though something had closed on the rim and pulled. One had its iron tyre bent inward, which takes a force Percy does not like to think about. He has shown a few to Gareth, who looked at them a long time and said nothing, which from Gareth is a great deal.

It weighs on him for another reason. Last autumn one of the harvest carts that went down toward Bain Harbour never arrived, and Percy built that cart. He built it well. He knows he built it well. He lies awake some nights wondering whether it broke, and whether it was the wheel.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Percy wants every cart that leaves his yard to come home, and every driver with it. He wants to know what makes the marks, so that he can build a wheel that will stand up to it. He fears that he already knows the answer, which is that no wheel will.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Percy would like a traveller to walk the Royal Road and bring back any broken wheel or splintered felloe they find, so that he can read the marks; he and Gareth have a wager about what made them, and neither will say what he guessed. Or the missing harvest cart might one day be found, and Percy will want to see its wheels before anyone else does.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Pell: friend and customer
  • Gareth: smith

docs.title: Quill
docs.text:
Drillmaster

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Park Role Guard Age Adult In the game Quill

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Stern, clipped and fair, he barks orders but never mocks a fall. He believes footwork wins more fights than muscle.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "Chin up. Eyes front." That is how Quill greets everyone who comes to the Kaldemor Gauntlet, whether they are a nervous recruit, a seasoned adventurer or the mayor. He is forty-nine, lean and upright, with a voice that carries across the whole Park and a habit of standing with his hands clasped behind his back. He is stern, clipped and fair. He barks orders, but he has never once mocked a fall, and he never will. He believes footwork wins more fights than muscle, and he says so roughly forty times a day.

docs.title: The road
docs.text:
Quill is not from Kaldemor. He grew up in Selsior, the son of a lamplighter and a laundress, both dead now, and he went out on the Royal Road at twenty-two as a hired guard for the merchant caravans that ran between Selsior and the eastern countryside. He had been on the road two years when the caravan master paired him with a quiet young man from Kaldemor called Hale, on Hale's very first trip.

They rode together for six years. Quill did the shouting and Hale did the watching, and between them they learned to sleep in shifts, to read tracks from a wagon seat and to stand back to back when something came out of the dark beyond the firelight. Each of them is fairly sure he saved the other's life at least once. Quill's version involves a flooded ford, a wolf and Hale standing in the wrong place. Hale's version, which he tells only with a nod, is a different night altogether. They have never agreed, and neither of them would want to.

When Hale went home to be Kaldemor's ranger, Quill stayed on the road for nine more years, as a guard and then as the man who trained the caravans' new guards. It was there that he learned what he knows best: that most people who die on the road die from a bad step, not a weak arm.

docs.title: Coming to Kaldemor
docs.text:
Ten years ago Hale wrote to him. It was a short letter, as Hale's letters are. Kaldemor had young people who wanted to fight for the fields and nobody to teach them, and Mayor Tobin would pay. Quill came within the month. He laid out the Gauntlet in the Park himself, and Alfie's carpenters built it to his drawings: the yard where he turns the monsters loose, the hanging course of ropes, logs and platforms that will not wait for anyone, and the ring for the last stand, where a runner must hold out for one full minute. Potions are allowed. Scrolls are not. Fall, flee or run out of time, and it is over, and Quill will send you in again at once.

He and Hale now work a short walk apart, see each other most days, and say very little. It suits them both.

docs.title: His recruits
docs.text:
Quill has more recruits this year than ever before, because there are more snails in the meadow than ever before, and he is not sure whether to be proud or worried. He sends no one in until they are seasoned enough to have a chance. He is hardest on the ones he thinks will go farthest. Meg passed the hanging course on her first try, and Quill has never told her she was good, because she already knows. Digby has failed it eleven times. Quill has told him his footwork is improving, which is true, and has quietly lowered nothing, because a course does not care how brave you feel.

Then there is Tam, Wilbur's boy, who hangs on the fence with his stick every afternoon and asks to run the Gauntlet. Quill tells him the same thing every time: when you are bigger. He pretends not to notice the boy watching every run. He does notice, and he shouts his footwork lessons a little louder when Tam is at the fence.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Quill wants every one of his recruits to come home from the meadow on their own two feet. He has buried friends from the road, and he does not intend to bury any from the Gauntlet. What he fears is the day the course stops being practice. Hale kept the thing in the hollow past the woods from him until he knew what it was, and Quill has forgiven him for that, mostly. Since he heard, he has started training the last stand a little longer than one minute.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Quill has quietly begun designing a fourth stage for the Gauntlet, modelled on the Snail King's sweeps, and he needs a traveller who has faced Mano to tell him whether it is fair. Or, one day, Tam will slip under the fence and into the yard, and someone will have to get him out before Quill sees, or after.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Digby: recruit
  • Hale: old comrade
  • Tam: would-be pupil

docs.title: Rosa
docs.text:
Baker

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Market Role Merchant Age Adult Sells Bread, buns and her famous mushroom bread In the game Rosa

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Warm, floury and a born feeder, she calls everyone "dear" and saves the heel of the loaf for her friends. She is private about the things that matter most to her.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Rosa calls everyone "dear", and she means it. She is forty-five, warm, round-armed and floury to the elbow, and she bakes in the terrace oven at the top of the Market steps, where half the town comes up before noon and the other half after. She is a born feeder: nobody leaves her bakery without something warm in their hands, and her friends get the heel of the loaf, which she says is the best part and saves for them alone.

docs.title: The oven
docs.text:
The oven is older than Rosa, older than her mother, and very nearly as old as the clock tower. Her grandmother Ada built it with her own hands, brick by brick, the year the whole town raised the tower in the Park, when she was a young woman newly come to Kaldemor with nothing but a starter dough in a crock. Ada used to say that a bakery without a warm oven is only a shop, and she made sure hers never went cold. It has not gone cold since. Rosa's mother kept it lit for thirty years after Ada, and when her mother died sixteen years ago, Rosa took the long paddle down from its hooks and has kept it lit alone ever since. On winter nights she banks the embers before bed and gets up twice to look at them.

She rarely tells that story. A baker's oven is public, she says, but its history is family, and Rosa is private about the things that matter most to her. A customer may hear about the weather, the price of flour and the latest from Lia; only a friend hears about Ada.

docs.title: Her bread
docs.text:
Rosa bakes round loaves, long loaves, buns, and, above all, her famous mushroom bread, which the whole town swears by and the mayor eats every day. It needs good flour, which Hob's windmills grind for her before anyone else's; mushroom spores, which Wilf gathers in the woods; and a pinch of ground blue snail shell, which is the part she will not explain. Wilf recently went away to visit his sister, and Rosa had to ask a young adventurer to bring her spores from the Shrooms and shells from the blue snails in the meadow. Now Wilf is back, and says the Shrooms have grown too bold for him to gather alone, and Rosa has begun to worry, quietly, about where next month's spores will come from.

Every autumn, when Quenna the Harbour Master comes up from Bain Harbour for the harvest fair, she and Mayor Tobin settle the year's prices over Rosa's bread. Rosa makes them a special loaf and pretends not to listen to the haggling.

Little Fen carries her flour up from the mills twice a week, and Rosa pays her in warm buns and sometimes the heel. Rosa has no children of her own and has never married, and she would tell you, if you asked, that Fen is payment enough.

docs.title: Bram
docs.text:
Nine years ago, Rosa and Bram the potion seller were the closest friends in the Market. He ate at her table every week, argued with her about cauldrons and ovens, and tasted every new loaf before anyone else. Then, the morning of the harvest fair, he "improved" a batch of her mushroom bread with a spore tincture of his own, sure it would make the loaves rise higher. They rose, all right, and came out greenish and bitter, in front of the whole fair. Rosa told him he could keep his tinctures out of her oven and himself out of her kitchen. He said he had been right in principle. Neither of them has said much of anything to the other since.

She has never mended it, and she wishes she had. She still sets aside the heel of the loaf on Bram's old day, out of habit, and gives it to the birds. She will not say what she has missed most. If she ever does decide to send word, it will be something small and plain, and she will trust only a friend to carry it.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Rosa wants the oven warm, the town fed, and her old friend back at her table, though she would admit only the first two. She fears the day the oven goes cold, and she fears, a little more than she shows, that the woods are becoming too dangerous for the spores her bread depends on.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A traveller who earns Rosa's trust may be asked to carry a message to the far end of the Market: only that the oven is warm. Another quest could follow the spores themselves, out into woods where Wilf no longer dares to go alone.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Wilf: spore supplier
  • Hob: miller
  • Bram: estranged friend
  • Tobin: regular customer
  • Fen: flour carrier

docs.title: Rufus
docs.text:
Town Crier

Town Kaldemor Where Town Square Role Official Age Adult In the game Rufus

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Booming, jolly and impossible to ignore, he cannot say anything quietly, not even good morning. He loves a good announcement more than a good dinner.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "GOOD MORNING, KALDEMOR!" It is the first thing the town hears every day, after the clock and before the cockerels, and some people in the farthest farms swear they hear it before the clock. Rufus does not know how to say anything quietly. He has tried. He is forty-four, big, red-bearded and barrel-chested, in a green coat with brass buttons and a hat with a feather that has seen better years, and he is the town crier of Kaldemor. He is booming, jolly and impossible to ignore, and he loves a good announcement more than a good dinner, which, for a man of his size, is saying something.

docs.title: The bell
docs.text:
Every morning at the stroke of eight, Rufus stands on the step of the signpost in the town square, rings his handbell three times, and reads the news. Fair days, market days and the price of flour. Births and weddings. Who has a cart going to Selsior and who has room on it. Lost cats, of which there are a great many in Kaldemor, and found cats, of which there are fewer. When the clock stopped this spring, Rufus rang the bell at eight anyway, by the sun, for nine mornings, and announced each time that the clock was being seen to and that Ewan sent his apologies. Ewan had sent no such thing. Rufus thought he would have, if he had thought of it.

The bell was given to him by old Ludo, the crier before him, who rang it for thirty years and had a voice like a barn door in a gale. Rufus was Ludo's runner as a boy, sent round the farms with notices for anyone who lived out of earshot, and when Ludo's voice finally went, fifteen years ago, he handed Rufus the bell and said, "Louder." Rufus has done his best. Ludo died the next winter, and Rufus rang the bell for him on the morning of the burial so loudly that the whole town came out of doors, which was what Ludo would have wanted.

Rufus was born in Kaldemor, the son of a carpenter and a market-woman, both dead, and grew up in the lanes behind the Market. He has never married. He says no one could stand the noise, and he is very likely right.

docs.title: Mildred
docs.text: Every evening Mildred the town clerk writes out the next morning's notices in her neat, upright hand, and every morning Rufus reads them out with a great deal more feeling than she put in. He adds words. He adds exclamations. He once added a short poem about a lost goat. Mildred pretends to be appalled. Rufus pretends not to notice that she has started leaving a little more room at the bottom of the page.

docs.title: Gently
docs.text: These days more of the notices are road warnings: snails on the meadow path, Shrooms in the woods, a stretch of the Royal Road to avoid after dark, the harvest carts to travel with guards. Rufus reads them all, because it is his job and because people need to hear them. But he has noticed the children in the square going quiet when he does, and Tam asking afterwards what the words meant, and so he has started reading the warnings a little more gently. Not quietly. He cannot do quietly. But slower, and kinder, and he follows every one with a lost cat or a fair day as fast as he can. This spring Mildred began writing the warnings in shorter, plainer words. Rufus has not asked her why. He thinks he knows.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
