docs.text: Rufus wants to announce something wonderful: the Snail King gone, the roads safe, the harvest carts home. He has the words ready and practises them in his head. He fears that one morning Mildred will hand him a notice he cannot read gently at all, and that he will have to stand in the square and read it anyway, in front of the children.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Rufus has a backlog of lost cats and would be delighted if a traveller found any of them, especially Mistress Whiskers, who has been missing three weeks and was last seen heading toward the woods. Another quest might ask a traveller to carry his announcements to the farthest farms, where folk have stopped coming in to hear them.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Mildred: clerk who writes his notices

docs.title: Tam
docs.text:
Would-be Warrior

Town Kaldemor Where Town Square Role Child Age Child In the game Tam

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bold, loud and only a little afraid of snails, he swings a stick at anything that looks like an enemy. He hates washing behind his ears.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
Tam is going to be a warrior when he grows up. He will tell you so before he tells you his name, and he will tell you again when you leave, in case you forgot. He is nine years old, bold, loud and only a little afraid of snails, and he carries a stick everywhere he goes, which he swings at anything that looks like an enemy: hedges, washing lines, fence posts, and once, memorably, Mayor Tobin's hat.

He is the son of Wilbur the farmer and Hattie the beekeeper, and he grew up on the biggest farm east of the square, among the pumpkins, turnips and beans, with the hives humming at the edge of the fields. From his father he has a loud voice and a grudge against snails. From his mother he has, so far, only her red cheeks, though she lives in hope of the patience.

docs.title: The snail feud
docs.text:
Tam's war against the snails began last autumn. The week before the harvest fair, the snails got into the patch where his father had been growing his prize pumpkin all summer and ate a hole in it big enough for Tam to put his head through, which he did. His father has sworn it will not happen again. Tam has sworn it louder. Every morning he patrols the pumpkin rows with his stick, which he has named Shellbreaker, and every evening he reports to his father how many snails he has defeated. The number is always large and usually includes a few he only frightened.

He says he is not afraid of snails. Much. The blue ones are fine. The red ones are fine from a distance.

docs.title: The Park and the Gauntlet
docs.text:
Most afternoons Tam can be found at the Park, hanging on the fence by Quill's Gauntlet and watching the young warriors run the monster yard, the hanging course and the last stand. Quill is the greatest hero Tam knows, and Tam has asked him to be allowed to run the Gauntlet more times than anyone has counted. The answer is always "when you are bigger", which Tam takes to mean "soon". Quill pretends not to notice him watching every run, but Tam has noticed that Quill shouts his footwork lessons a little louder when he is at the fence, and he practises them afterwards in the square with Shellbreaker.

He also watches Digby, who has failed the hanging course eleven times and gets up grinning every time. Digby used to work on Tam's father's farm, and Tam thinks this means they are practically brothers in arms.

docs.title: Friends and family
docs.text:
His two best friends are Nell, who counts clouds, and Fen, who counts everything else. Nell will not let him swing Shellbreaker near her tally book. Fen asks him questions about warrior things that he cannot answer, which is annoying, so he makes the answers up.

Mayor Tobin once told Tam that he could even be mayor one day, if he washes behind his ears. Tam is considering it. Being mayor seems to involve a lot of talking, which he is good at, and some washing, which he is not. He hates washing behind his ears more than he hates red snails.

His mother wants him to be careful, and his father wants him to be brave, and Tam wants to be both, which he thinks is exactly what a warrior is. He does not yet know that his mother lies awake some nights over it. Wren has knitted him a cap, too, and he wears it, but only when nobody from the Gauntlet is looking.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Tam wants a real sword from Gareth's forge, a turn on the Gauntlet, and to be the one who finally beats the snails that ate the pumpkin. He has heard grown-ups in the square talking in low voices about something big in a hollow past the woods, and about road warnings Rufus reads out more gently than he used to, and he wants very badly to be old enough to help.

What he fears, though he would never say it, is being left behind: that everyone will go and fight the big thing in the woods while he is still being told he is too small.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: One morning Tam will not come home from his pumpkin patrol, and his trail of flattened beans will lead toward the meadow and the red snails, Shellbreaker in hand. Or a traveller who has run the Gauntlet might be asked, very seriously, to teach him one real move, and to swear not to tell his mother.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Wilbur: father
  • Hattie: mother
  • Tobin: kindly mayor
  • Quill: hero
  • Nell: friend
  • Fen: friend

docs.title: Tobin
docs.text:
Mayor of Kaldemor

Town Kaldemor Where Town Square Role Ruler Age Elder In the game Tobin

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Warm, chatty and proud of his town, with a story for every occasion and a joke about the snails for every other one. He knows every family by name and most of their grandparents too.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tobin has been mayor of Kaldemor for thirty years, and he will tell you, if you stand still long enough, that the great treehouse has outlived three mayors, himself included. Nobody has ever been able to explain to him why that joke does not work, and he has stopped listening to anyone who tries. He is seventy-one, warm, chatty and endlessly proud of his town, and there is not a family in Kaldemor whose name he does not know, along with most of their grandparents.

docs.title: From barrels to the square
docs.text:
Before he was mayor, Tobin was a cooper. He made barrels for cider, flour and pickles in a workshop behind the market, and he still taps every barrel he passes to hear whether it is sound. The town chose him at forty-one, after old Mayor Hettie died, mostly because he already knew everyone and nobody could imagine a town meeting without him talking at it. He has stood in front of the treehouse ever since, greeting visitors, settling squabbles about fences and snails, and telling the story of the seed to anyone who will listen. Every great town starts with one seed, he says, and he believes it.

He was married for many years to Primrose, a potter, who died twelve years ago. They had no children, and Tobin says that is why he has so many: every child in Kaldemor is his to worry about. Tam, who means to be a warrior, has been told he could be mayor one day if he washes. Lia, who meets every visitor in the square, learned half her job from Tobin and now does it better than he ever did, which he tells her often. Mildred keeps his ledgers and letters, and Tobin knows perfectly well that she has counted the town more carefully than he has; he just prefers to count it by knocking on doors. Ewan, the clockkeeper, has been his friend since they were boys, and when the great gear went missing from the clock tower, Tobin sat up with him every night until it came home.

docs.title: The harbour bargain
docs.text:
Much of Kaldemor's good fortune travels by cart to Bain Harbour, and that trade rests on an old partnership. Nineteen years ago, a young captain named Quenna, then twenty-seven and newly master of her own ship, walked up to Kaldemor because she was tired of paying the middlemen in Selsior. She arrived in the square with salt on her boots and argued with Tobin about the price of cider for an entire afternoon. He liked her immediately. Every autumn since, Kaldemor's harvest carts have gone down to the harbour loaded with cider, flour, pottery and woodwork, and come back with salt, dried fish, rope and spices.

Quenna is Harbour Master now, but she still comes to Kaldemor for the harvest fair each autumn to settle the year's prices with him over Rosa's bread. Tobin says she is the only person alive who can out-talk him, and that she is a far shrewder bargainer than she lets on. He has been down to Bain Harbour only twice in all those years, and still talks about the smell of tar.

docs.title: What he worries about
docs.text:
Just under three hundred people live in Kaldemor, not counting the snails, and Tobin means to see every one of them safe. His current project is a new fence around the gardens, with ground snail shell mixed into the mortar; he swears it will make the wall tougher, and he is paying young adventurers to bring him shells. Hale's reports from the park and the woods worry him more than he shows, and so does the road to the harbour. Last autumn one of the harvest carts never arrived, and now every cart travels with hired guards.

He does not like to think about the day he stops being mayor. He suspects Mildred thinks about it for him.

A quest might follow the missing harvest cart down the road toward the coast, or help Tobin finish the fence before the snails find another way in.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Lia: trusted guide
  • Mildred: clerk
  • Hale: ranger
  • Rosa: baker
  • Ewan: old friend
  • Tam: admirer
  • Quenna: trading partner

docs.title: Wilbur
docs.text:
Farmer

Town Kaldemor Where Farms Role Worker Age Adult In the game Wilbur

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Big, cheerful and stubborn as a turnip, he loves his fields and talks to his pumpkins. He takes the snails personally.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Wilbur is big, cheerful and as stubborn as a turnip, and he would take that as a compliment. He is forty-three, sunburnt from April to October, with hands like spades and a laugh that carries across three fields. He grows pumpkins, turnips and beans on the biggest farm east of the square, and he loves every row of it. He talks to his pumpkins. He says they grow better for it, and nobody in Kaldemor has ever been able to prove him wrong.

docs.title: The farm
docs.text:
The farm has been in Wilbur's family for four generations. His father Amos worked it before him, and Amos's mother before that, and Wilbur grew up in the farmhouse kitchen with mud on his boots and a pumpkin seed in every pocket. Amos died nine years ago, the autumn Wilbur's boy Tam was born, and Wilbur has run the farm alone since, with his wife Hattie and whatever farmhands he can find at harvest.

He sells most of what he grows to Old Marta at the Market. Marta is the only person in Kaldemor who frightens him. She squeezes his turnips, scolds him about his beans and pays him fairly, and every year she slips something extra into his basket for Tam, and every year she pretends she did not. Wilbur has been selling to her for more than twenty years and considers the arrangement one of the great friendships of his life, though he would never say so in her hearing.

docs.title: Hattie and Tam
docs.text:
Wilbur married Hattie the beekeeper eleven years ago. Her hives stand at the edge of his fields, and he says the bees did the courting for him: they kept his bean flowers so busy that summer that he had to go round and thank her, and kept going round to thank her until she married him. Hattie is calm and softly spoken where Wilbur is loud, and between them they have found most of the answers a farm needs.

Their son Tam is nine and means to be a warrior. Wilbur thinks this is splendid. Hattie wants the boy to be careful, and Wilbur wants him to be brave, and they have had more quiet talks about it at the kitchen table than Tam knows. Wilbur has started to suspect that his wife is right, which worries him, because she usually is.

docs.title: The snails
docs.text:
Wilbur takes the snails personally. Last year he grew the finest pumpkin of his life, a great orange thing he had talked to every morning since it was the size of his fist, and he meant it to take first prize at the harvest fair. The week before the fair, the snails got into the patch overnight and ate a hole in it big enough for Tam to put his head through. Tam did. Wilbur has sworn it will not happen again. This year's prize pumpkin sleeps under a net, with a ring of crushed shell around the patch, and Tam patrols the rows every morning with his stick. Wilbur has been known to sit up with a lantern.

He has also noticed that the snails are thicker in his fields than they have ever been, and bolder, and that they come from the direction of the meadow in lines, almost as if something were driving them. He has said this to Hale, who nodded and said nothing, which Wilbur did not find reassuring.

docs.title: Digby
docs.text: For four years Wilbur's best farmhand was Digby, an earnest, clumsy young man who came to Kaldemor from a smallholding further east with nothing but a willingness to work. Last year Digby decided to become a warrior instead, and Wilbur gave him his blessing and a good pair of boots from Ned. Digby still comes back to help at harvest, and Wilbur still pays him, whether he likes it or not. Wilbur thinks Digby will pass Quill's hanging course one day out of pure stubbornness, and he should know.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Wilbur wants the prize at this autumn's fair, a good harvest for the carts that go down to the harbour, and his boy to grow up whole. He fears losing the crop to the snails, and, more lately, he fears what drives them.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A traveller might be asked to guard the prize pumpkin through the last night before the harvest fair. Or Wilbur, who never asks for help, might ask for it the morning he finds a trail across his fields too broad to have been left by any ordinary snail.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hattie: wife
  • Tam: son
  • Digby: former farmhand
  • Old Marta: grocer

docs.title: Wilf
docs.text:
Spore Gatherer

Town Kaldemor Where Farms Role Worker Age Adult Sells Mushroom spores and caps In the game Wilf

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Wiry, wry and happiest in the damp, he knows every mushroom by smell. He grumbles about everything except mushrooms.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Wilf smells of leaf mould, and he would take that as a compliment. He is forty-six, wiry and weathered, with a nose that has been broken once and a basket that has never been empty, and he gathers mushroom spores and caps for half of Kaldemor. He grumbles about everything: the weather, the price of baskets, the Market, the mayor's jokes, the noise of the windmills and the state of his own knees. Everything, that is, except mushrooms. About mushrooms he will talk with a quiet, glowing reverence for as long as you care to listen, and he knows every one of them in the country round Kaldemor by smell alone.

docs.title: The cottage in the damp
docs.text:
Wilf lives at the far end of the farms, in a squat stone cottage that stands in the wettest hollow of the lane, where nobody else would build. That is the point. Behind it, under a sagging roof of old sacking and willow, he grows a few beds of caps in rotted straw and oak dust: brown caps, orange caps and a tray of pale ones he will not name and will not sell. He was born in that cottage. His father gathered before him and taught him the woods; his mother dried and sorted the spores on the kitchen table, and he still uses her sieves. Both are dead now. He has never married. He says he would have to marry somebody who did not mind the smell, and that he has never found anybody that sensible.

His only family is his sister, three years older, who married a farmer and lives in a village a long way south of the hills. They see each other once in a few years and write at midwinter. This spring she was ill, and Wilf went to her, the first time in nine years he had left Kaldemor for more than a night. He stayed a month, until she was on her feet and scolding him, and came home at the start of summer.

docs.title: Rosa and Bram
docs.text:
Wilf's spores go into two things above all: Rosa's mushroom bread at the top of the Market steps, and Bram's potions under the striped awning at the far end of the Market. He supplies them both and has done for twenty years. Rosa takes the finest and pays on the nail. Bram takes the most and argues about every bag.

Nine years ago those two stopped speaking, over a spore tincture and a batch of greenish bread, and Wilf has been the only bridge between them ever since. Rosa asks him, in a careless voice, whether Bram is well. Bram asks him, in a careless voice, whether Rosa is still using too much salt. Wilf answers both of them truthfully and briefly, and grumbles about it all the way home, and would not stop carrying the news for anything. He thinks they are a pair of fools. He also thinks they are his two oldest customers, and he would like them both at his funeral, preferably standing next to each other.

docs.title: Too bold
docs.text:
While Wilf was away, Rosa had to send a young adventurer out for spores, and Bram ran low and made do. When Wilf came home, he went straight to the woods past the hills with his basket, and came back early, empty-handed and pale.

The Shrooms had always been there. Wilf has spent his whole life slipping past them; they are shy of a man who stands still and smells of the woods, and they used to scatter at a cough. Not any more. They came out of the leaf litter at him in threes and fours, following him between the trees, and they did not scatter when he shouted. One knocked the basket off his arm. He says they were too bold for him to gather alone, and that is as much as he will say. He has heard about the great gear the Shroom took from the clock tower. He does not think it is funny.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Wilf wants the woods back the way they were: quiet, damp and his. He wants someone to walk with him while he gathers, though he will complain the whole time that they are treading on things. He fears that Rosa and Bram will both run short at the same time, and that the woods he has known since he was a boy have turned into something else.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Wilf needs an escort into the woods past the hills to gather spores for Rosa and Bram, and he will teach a patient traveller to tell one mushroom from another by nose. He has also noticed that the Shrooms in the deepest part of the woods are carrying things, shiny things, away toward the same place, and he would very much like to know where.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rosa: customer
  • Bram: customer

docs.title: Winnie
docs.text:
Weaver

Town Kaldemor Where Workshops Role Craftsman Age Adult Sells Wool, cloth and blankets In the game Winnie

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Chatty, warm and always half-listening to her loom, she can weave and gossip at the same time. She keeps a scrap of every cloth she has made.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: The loom in Winnie's workshop goes clack and thump all day, and Winnie talks over it. She is fifty-eight, plump and rosy, with spectacles on a cord, a pencil stuck through her bun and a laugh that carries halfway down the Workshops lane. She can weave and gossip at the same time, and frequently does both at once to three different people. She is always half-listening to the loom while she talks, and if the rhythm of the shuttle goes wrong she will stop mid-sentence, frown, and put it right before she remembers what she was saying. She weaves the cloth and blankets of Kaldemor, sells wool to anyone who knits, and spins the yarn for every cap Wren has made in thirty years.

docs.title: The loom and the scraps
docs.text:
Winnie learned to weave from her mother, on the same loom, in the same narrow workshop halfway down the lane, between the potter's and the joiners'. Her mother is long dead, and so is her father, a shepherd on the hills who brought home fleeces for her to card before she could reach the treadles. She married young, a cheerful carter called Gilly, and lost him to a fever when she was thirty; there were no children. She has lived over the workshop alone ever since, and says the loom makes better conversation than most husbands, which nobody who has met her believes she means.

She keeps a scrap of every cloth she has ever made. There are thousands of them, each a finger long, pinned in rows to great sheets of sacking that hang round the walls of her back room, so that the whole room is a slow history of Kaldemor in wool. There is a scrap of Hob and Mabel's wedding blanket, and of Nell's cradle cloth, and of the cloak Tobin wore at his first harvest fair as mayor. There is a scrap of the grey blanket she wove for Wren's mother, the first thing Winnie ever sold. Ask her about any of them and she will tell you who it was for, what the weather was doing that week, and who was courting whom, which is the part she enjoys.

docs.title: Wren
docs.text: Winnie and Wren have been friends for more than thirty years, since Wren first came to the workshop to complain about a skein. They can talk for an afternoon over a basket of yarn without either of them dropping a stitch. Wren is the gentler of the two and Winnie the louder, and between them there is very little that happens in Kaldemor that they do not hear about, kindly. Every autumn Winnie spins Wren's yarn first, before anyone else's, so that the caps are done before the frosts.

docs.title: Dottie
docs.text:
Winnie's wool comes from Dottie's sheep. Dottie is ten and minds her grandmother Elsie's flock on the hills above the farms, and she sells the fleeces to Winnie herself, with great seriousness and a firm grip on the price. Winnie pays her fairly and has never once told her she is too young. She is very fond of the girl, though she is careful not to fuss, because Dottie hates fuss nearly as much as Elsie does.

This summer Dottie has brought less wool than she should, and has not looked Winnie in the eye when she brought it. Winnie noticed that at once. Then, walking up to the hill pasture a few days ago with a bag of buns as an excuse, she counted the lambs, the way you count stitches without meaning to, and came to eight. There should be nine. The speckled one with the bent ear, the one Dottie calls Button and promised Winnie the first clip of, was not there. Winnie has said nothing to anyone but Wren, and even to Wren she has only said that she thinks the girl is keeping a worry to herself. She believes Dottie will tell when she is ready, and she would rather wait than take that from her. But she has found reasons to walk up with buns twice more since, and she lies awake on the nights the count is still eight.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Winnie wants a full basket of fleece, a loom that runs sweetly and every child in Kaldemor warm by midwinter. She fears for Dottie, and fears too that the cap Wren is knitting in grey wool, the big strange one she will not explain, is a sign Wren knows something she has not shared.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Winnie would like a traveller to go up to the hills and quietly help Dottie, without letting the girl know Winnie sent them. Another quest might ask a traveller to find the source of a scrap of cloth that turned up on a thorn by the woods, which Winnie swears she wove herself, for someone who left Kaldemor long ago.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dottie: wool supplier
  • Wren: friend

docs.title: Wren
docs.text:
Orin's Wife

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Park Role Resident Age Elder In the game Wren

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gentle, patient and gently teasing, she never tires of Orin's stories, though she tells him when he is shouting. Her knitting needles are never still.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "Hello, dear," says Wren, and her needles do not stop. She is seventy-five, small and silver-haired, gentle, patient and gently teasing, and she spends her afternoons on the bench in Kaldemor Park beside her husband Orin, knitting. She never tires of Orin's stories, though she does tell him when he is shouting, which is most of the time. "Orin," she says, without looking up, "you are shouting again." He never notices that she says it fondly.

docs.title: A knitter's life
docs.text:
Wren grew up in a cottage by the farms, the daughter of a shepherd, and she learned to knit before she could read, sitting on a fleece by the fire while her mother spun. Her parents are long gone now, and the cottage with them, but she has never lost the habit of keeping her hands busy. Her needles are never still. She knits on the bench, at the supper table, in the queue at Old Marta's stall and, Orin swears, in her sleep.

She knits caps for every child in Kaldemor, a new one for each child each autumn before the frosts, and has done for as long as anyone can remember. Some of the children even wear them. Her granddaughter Nell never takes hers off: a soft blue cap with a lopsided bobble, which Nell wears even to bed. Tam wears his only when nobody from the Gauntlet is looking. Fen has asked for one with a pocket, for squirrels, and Wren is working on it.

Her yarn comes from Winnie the weaver, who spins it from the wool of Dottie's sheep. Winnie is one of Wren's dearest friends, and the two of them can talk for an afternoon over a basket of skeins without either of them dropping a stitch. Lately Winnie has had less wool to spin, and Wren has noticed that Dottie looks worried, and the two old friends have been wondering together, quietly, what the girl is not saying.

docs.title: Orin
docs.text:
Wren married Orin fifty-three years ago, under the clock tower in the Park. He likes to say he chose her because she was the only girl in Kaldemor who laughed at his stories. She says she was laughing at something else, and will not say what, and after fifty-three years he has stopped asking. She has heard every one of his stories more times than she can count, and she still listens, because she likes the way he tells them, and because she has noticed that he tells them a little differently each time.

For forty winters he went out into the woods past the hills with an axe, and for forty winters she did not sleep properly until he came home. She has never told him that. She was glad, more glad than she let him see, when his back made him stop.

docs.title: Hob and Nell
docs.text: Their son Hob is the miller, and Wren never minded that he would not be a woodcutter, so long as he came home for supper. She thinks Hob's wife Mabel is the best thing that ever happened to him, and tells Mabel so, which embarrasses them both. Nell is her joy. Wren is the one person Nell lets interrupt the counting, because Wren never asks how big the number is.

docs.title: Why the afternoon
docs.text: Wren spends her afternoons in the Park because the Park is nicest in the afternoon, when the sun comes round past the windmills and the clock tower throws its shadow over the fountain. She will tell you so with great conviction. The truth, which she keeps to herself, is that she began sitting there in the afternoons when Orin retired, so that he would have somewhere to tell his stories and someone to tell them to.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Wren wants every child in Kaldemor to have a cap before the frosts, and Orin to be warm. She fears, more than anything, the quiet that will come when he is not on the bench beside her, and she knits faster when she thinks of it.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Wren has started a cap she does not mean to give to any child in Kaldemor: a large, odd thing, far too big, in grey wool. She will only say that it is for someone who will need it before the winter, and smile. A traveller might also be asked to fetch wool from the hills, if Dottie's worry turns out to be what Wren suspects.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Orin: husband
  • Hob: son
  • Nell: granddaughter
  • Winnie: friend

docs.title: Ahvi
docs.text:
Song-Keeper

Town Midbarium Where Brenna House Role Scholar Age Elder Family Brenna In the game Ahvi

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Soft-voiced, exact and gently stubborn; Ahvi corrects anyone who gets a chieftain's name wrong, however important they are.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
Ahvi keeps the long songs of the Brenna, the songs that name every chieftain of the four families and every Old One back to the Age of Division, and she has never once got a name wrong. She is seventy-six, soft-voiced, exact and gently stubborn. She will correct anyone who gets a chieftain's name wrong, however important they are, and the families still tell the story of the feast at which she stopped Old One Varra herself mid-toast to point out that the deed Varra had just praised belonged not to the chieftain she named but to his grandfather, two names further back in the song.

Varra could take the correction. She was Ahvi's older sister.

docs.title: Two sisters
docs.text:
Ahvi and Varra grew up in Brenna House, eleven years apart. Varra was the loud one, patient and funny and very hard to argue with, and Ahvi was the quiet one who sat in corners listening. The song-keeper of those days, old Hadda, noticed that the quiet child could repeat a whole evening's singing the next morning, word for word, and took her as a pupil when she was eight. Ahvi has been learning the long songs ever since, and she has kept them as song-keeper for thirty-five years, since Hadda died.

When Varra was chosen Old One thirty-one years ago, Ahvi sang the long song at her choosing and added her sister's name to the end of it. Six years ago, when Varra died in her sleep at Brenna House, aged eighty-one, Ahvi sang the long song again, through the whole night of Hask's choosing, while Thrun drummed and her cousin Odda hosted and Dorrek argued for the Kragvar. At dawn she added Hask's name after her sister's. She says it was the hardest verse she has ever sung, and the most important, because a song that stops when it grieves is not doing its job.

docs.title: Neffa
docs.text:
Ahvi has never married, and has always said the songs keep her company enough. Four years ago, she took a new pupil: Neffa, Odda's granddaughter, then six, solemn and serious and already muttering verses under her breath. Neffa wants to recite the whole long song of the Old Ones at a gathering, without a single mistake, before she turns twelve. Ahvi has told her this is very ambitious and has privately concluded that it is entirely possible. She is a demanding teacher. She makes Neffa start again from the beginning after any mistake at all, and Neffa, to Ahvi's quiet delight, has never once complained.

Her friend outside the family is Imre, the stargazer who came to Midbarium for its night skies. They meet on the high terrace on clear nights and trade stories: Imre's about the stars, Ahvi's about the families' oldest songs, many of which turn out to mention the same stars. Ahvi thinks Imre should be invited to recite at a gathering one day, and has not yet decided whether to say so.

docs.title: The verse
docs.text:
Deep in the oldest part of the long songs, among the chieftains of the Age of Division, there is a short verse that is almost never sung. It tells of a season before the Burning came, when the beasts of the plateau grew wild: goats that bit, cats that hunted men, birds that would not settle. Then the song moves on to the war, and never mentions the beasts again.

Ahvi has sung that verse alone in her room every night this summer. She has heard Lessa count monster bites, Yarrek describe his wild-eyed goats and the Uskari report sightings closer to town every season. She does not know what the verse means, or whether it means anything at all. She knows only that the song remembered it for a reason. She has asked Odda whether she should sing it at the next gathering, and Odda has not yet answered.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could search the other peoples' old songs and records for the same season of wild beasts, or sit with Ahvi on the night she must decide whether to sing.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Neffa: pupil
  • Odda: cousin
  • Imre: friend

docs.title: Bekk
docs.text:
Trail Watch Scout

Town Midbarium Where Uskari Rim Role Guard Age Young Family Uskari In the game Bekk

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cocky, quick and kind to children, who follow him around in a small admiring crowd.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Bekk is the fastest climber on the Uskari Rim, and he knows it. He is eighteen, cocky, quick and grinning, a scout of the trail watch who goes up a cliff face the way other people go up a staircase. He is also kind to children, endlessly and without being asked, and there is nearly always a small admiring crowd of them trailing after him along the rim, copying the way he walks.

docs.title: Son of the captain
docs.text:
Bekk is the son of Skarra, captain of the trail watch. His father, Haldo, was an Uskari hunter who went out alone onto the far slopes thirteen years ago to track one of the great horned beasts of the plateau, and was gored and killed by it. Bekk was five. He remembers his father's laugh, the smell of his oiled bowstring, and very little else. He remembers his mother's face the day the hunters carried Haldo home much better, and that, though he would never say so, is the reason he grins so much.

Skarra raised him on the rim among the patrols, and he could climb before he could properly run. The Uskari take scouts onto the trail watch at sixteen, after a year of carrying water and messages for the patrols; Bekk did his year at fifteen, joined at sixteen, and has been the fastest scout on the watch ever since. His mother gives him no special favour on patrol, and is noticeably harder on him than on anyone else, which he complains about loudly and secretly understands.

docs.title: The admiring crowd
docs.text: Children follow Bekk because he lets them. He shows them handholds, teaches them knots, and tells them stories of the trail that are thrilling and mostly true. His most devoted follower is Korrin, the Kragvar chieftain's youngest child, who wants to join the trail watch himself, ties his boots exactly the way Bekk does and has started squinting at the horizon the way Bekk does, as if something is always about to appear on it. Bekk noticed the boots weeks ago and has said nothing, because he remembers doing the same thing to older scouts when he was nine. He makes sure Korrin's knots are tied properly, and pretends not to.

docs.title: The beast on the high pastures
docs.text:
Something has been raiding the high pastures this season: goats taken from the edges of the Tolmach herds, and tracks left behind that Bekk has measured with his own hand, wide, heavy and deep in the dry ground. He wants to track it. He has told himself it is because the Tolmach need their herds and the patrols are stretched too thin to spare anyone. That is true. It is also true that he wants to prove himself to his mother, to the watch and to the rim, and that he has heard Thrun the drummer lamenting that the great drum needs the hide of a great horned beast. Bekk has wondered, more than once, whether the beast on the pastures might be one of those.

His mother has forbidden him to try it alone. She has not said why, and she does not need to.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Bekk wants to be the scout people tell stories about. He fears, though he has never put it into words, that the only way to become that scout is the way his father went, and that he will try it anyway.

A quest could go with Bekk to track the beast on the high pastures, so that he is not alone, or find him when he slips away to track it by himself.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Skarra: mother
  • Korrin: admirer

docs.title: Brakka
docs.text:
Apprentice Mason

Town Midbarium Where Kragvar Quarter Role Craftsman Age Young Family Kragvar In the game Brakka

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Eager, restless and quick with a chisel; Brakka would rather carve something new than mend something old.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Brakka is nineteen, the elder child of Dorrek, chieftain of the Kragvar, and Gorra, keeper of the cisterns. She is eager, restless and quick with a chisel, and she would rather carve something new than mend something old. This makes her an excellent apprentice mason in every respect but one, because in Midbarium almost everything a mason does is mending.

docs.title: Stone and string
docs.text:
Brakka was chiselling patterns into her parents' doorstep before she could spell her name, and at fifteen she was apprenticed to her father's cousin Vosk, master of bridges, who keeps every rope-and-plank bridge in the town sound and has taught three generations of Kragvar to splice a cable. Vosk is careful, dry and suspicious of anything that sways. Brakka is none of those things. For four years they have worked side by side in a state of mutual exasperation that has slowly become mutual respect. She has learned to tie a knot he will trust, which she is told is rare. He has learned that she will finish a long job faster than anyone in the quarter, provided he tells her it is impossible first.

Most of her days are spent replacing worn planks, re-pointing terrace walls and hauling rope, and she does it well and complains about it cheerfully. But every flat stone in the Kragvar Quarter carries one of her drawings.

docs.title: The stairway
docs.text:
Brakka dreams of carving a new stairway down the cliff to the valley floor, the first new route down from the town in a hundred years. The last was Durra's Stair, cut by a Kragvar mason of that name when Brakka's great-great-grandparents were young, and every Kragvar child knows the song about it. Since then, the Kragvar have only mended what their ancestors cut.

She was eight when her great-uncle Baruk, then chieftain, died in the rockfall on the old north cliff stair. She remembers her father coming home with his hands torn from digging, and she remembers that the stair was patched afterwards, not rebuilt, because nobody had the heart to cut a new one. Her stairway would run along sounder rock farther south, with landings set into the cliff rather than hung from it, so that no landing could be swept away again. She has never told anyone that this is why she drew it.

Her mother has studied the sketches more carefully than Brakka knows, and asked only where the builders would get their water. Her father calls the whole plan foolish, loudly and often. Brakka has no idea that he keeps a copy of it under his bed.

docs.title: Family and friends
docs.text: Her little brother Korrin, ten years younger, climbs everything and wants to join the Uskari trail watch, which the family finds very funny. Brakka laughs with the rest, but she once climbed up alone and inspected the little stone wall at the boys' secret lookout above the terraces, and found it surprisingly sound. She has said nothing to Korrin, because he would never stop boasting about it. Her grandfather Ulm keeps the council fire in the great hall, and she brings him wood when she remembers, which is less often than she should.

docs.title: What troubles her
docs.text: Twice this season, she and Vosk have climbed out to the far canyon bridge at dawn and found its ropes gnawed half through. Vosk does not know what is doing it, and that frightens Brakka more than the ropes do, because Vosk knows everything about bridges. She has started to wonder whether any new route down the cliff would only be a new way for something to come up. She has not stopped drawing. But she has started drawing gates.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could help Brakka survey the rock for her stairway, which would mean climbing the cliff below the town where few have gone in years, or sit up with her on the far bridge to see what comes for the ropes.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dorrek: father
  • Gorra: mother
  • Vosk: mentor

docs.title: Corwell
docs.text:
Keeper of the Trading Post

Town Midbarium Where Trading Post Sells Lowland goods, lamp oil, salt, tools and travel supplies In the game Corwell

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Harra: friendly rival trader
  • Ennek: guide for hire
  • Imre: lodger

docs.title: Dorrek
docs.text:
Chieftain of the Kragvar

Town Midbarium Where Kragvar Quarter Role Ruler Age Adult Family Kragvar In the game Dorrek

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Blunt, broad-shouldered and stubborn as granite, but scrupulously fair once he has made up his mind.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Dorrek is broad-shouldered, blunt and as stubborn as the granite his family cuts, and the Kragvar would not have him any other way. He is forty-five, the son of Ulm, keeper of the council fire, and he grew up among masons and their songs: songs about the first terraces, the great hall's beams and the Kragvar fighters who never came home from the Balrog War but stayed beneath the World Tree to keep watch.

docs.title: The rockfall
docs.text: Dorrek did not expect to lead. Eleven years ago, his uncle Baruk, Ulm's younger brother and then chieftain of the Kragvar, was inspecting the old north cliff stair when a rockfall swept the landing away beneath him. The family gathered around its fire the next night and chose Dorrek, who had dug for his uncle until his hands bled. He has never forgotten it. To this day he climbs the highest scaffold himself before he lets any mason on it, and he will not hear arguments about whether that is wise for a chieftain. A chieftain leads from the front, he says, and the front is wherever the stone is loosest.

docs.title: The family
docs.text:
Dorrek is married to Gorra, who keeps the stone cisterns that water the terraces and knows to the bucket how long the town could last in a dry year. He thinks she is the cleverest person in Midbarium, and he tells her so roughly once a decade. Their daughter Brakka is learning the mason's trade from Dorrek's cousin Vosk, master of bridges, and she has sketched her dream of a new stairway down the cliff on every flat stone in the quarter. Dorrek pretends to find the plan foolish and secretly has a copy of it under his bed. Their youngest, Korrin, wants to join the Uskari on the trail watch when he grows up, which the whole Kragvar family finds very funny and slightly insulting. Dorrek laughs with them, and then quietly asks the Uskari how young they take recruits.

His father Ulm tends the council fire in the great hall and has never let it burn low. Dorrek visits him there most evenings, and the two of them say very little, which suits them both.

docs.title: The council
docs.text:
Six years ago, when Old One Varra of the Brenna died and the families met to choose who would follow her, Dorrek argued long in council for a Kragvar Old One. He believed it was the Kragvar's turn, and he believed the town's walls and bridges needed a voice at the head of the hall. The families chose Hask of the Uskari instead. Dorrek lost, said so plainly, and has stood by that decision without a word of complaint ever since. He is Hask's bluntest critic in council and one of his most loyal supporters outside it, and he sees no contradiction in that. He respects Hask as a fair and steady Old One; he simply thinks Hask could stand to talk more and listen less.

Dorrek is scrupulously fair once he has made up his mind, which can take a while. He settles disputes in the Kragvar Quarter by hearing both sides out on the scaffold, where nobody can storm off.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text:
Lately his worries have a shape. Vosk has found ropes on the far canyon bridge gnawed half through in the night, twice this season. Gorra has a cistern losing water through a crack nobody can find. The stone itself seems uneasy, and Dorrek, who trusts stone more than people, does not like that at all. He fears a second rockfall, a bridge failing with a caravan on it, or something in the canyons that has learned what rope is for.

A quest could send someone to sit up on the far bridge at night to see what gnaws it, or to help Dorrek inspect the north stair where his uncle fell.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Gorra: wife
  • Brakka: daughter
  • Korrin: son
  • Ulm: father
  • Vosk: cousin
  • Hask: respected chieftain

docs.title: Ennek
docs.text:
Canyon Guide

Town Midbarium Where Trading Post Role Service Age Young Family Tolmach In the game Ennek

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Easygoing and confident, with a herder's eye for weather and a habit of whistling on dangerous ledges.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ennek is twenty-two, easygoing and confident, and he whistles on the most dangerous ledges in the highlands. Traders who climb to Midbarium with him for the first time find this alarming. Traders who have climbed with him before find it reassuring, because they have learned that Ennek only stops whistling when something is actually wrong.

docs.title: A guide's son
docs.text:
Ennek is the son of Sennu, chieftain of the Tolmach. His father, a herder named Torvo, was lost in a winter storm on the high pastures when Ennek was four, and Ennek remembers him mostly as a big laugh and a smell of wet wool. He grew up following his mother and his grandmother Mabbu from camp to camp, and Mabbu taught him the old paths the way she had taught Sennu: every turn, every overhang, every place a goat can stand and a man cannot, and above all every spring that runs in a dry year. Ennek can still recite the springs of the south path in order, the way Brenna children recite the long songs.

The Tolmach have led travelers up into the mountains since the founding, when their guides first brought traders from Kaldemor and Selsior up the canyons. Ennek took his first caravan up alone at sixteen. He is good at it. He reads weather by the colour of the dust and the behaviour of the birds, he knows which traders will panic and which will simply go quiet, and he has a way of making the worst stretch of a climb sound like a pleasant walk. Corwell, keeper of the Trading Post, hires him for nearly every caravan that comes up from the lowlands, and the traders who make the climb every year now ask for him by name. His mother is quietly proud of this, and Ennek pretends not to know.

docs.title: Family and friends
docs.text:
His aunt Harra sells the herds' wool and cheese at the Trading Post, and Ennek often finds himself standing between her and Corwell while they haggle like old enemies who secretly enjoy it. Harra's son Kesh is his young cousin, a chatterbox who asks Ennek about every road he has walked and every traveler he has led. Ennek tells him the funny stories and leaves out the frightening ones, and suspects Kesh knows exactly what he is leaving out.

Ennek's sweetheart is Ketta of the Uskari. They grew up teasing each other across the camps and the rim, and when she left home at seventeen to adventure across Veligor, it was Ennek who guided her down the canyon road. Last spring, leading a caravan up the south path, he came round a bend and found her sitting on a rock with a new scar and a pack full of stories, waiting for someone to walk home with. They have been sweethearts since the summer. She tells him every story but one, and he has never pressed her about the deep canyon cave. He has a secret of his own, after all.

docs.title: The dry spring
docs.text:
A few weeks ago, at the start of this summer, Ennek led a caravan down the south path and found the Greywater spring dry. It sits in a cleft halfway down the path and has run for as long as anyone remembers; Mabbu says it ran in the driest year of her girlhood, when spring after spring on the path failed around it. Now there is only damp stone and a few dead reeds. Ennek has been carrying extra water skins for his travelers ever since, and he has not yet told his mother.

He tells himself he is waiting to be sure. The truth is that he knows what it will mean to Sennu, who has always said she fears the day a spring that has always run goes dry, and he does not want to be the one who brings her that day. He has started looking for where the water went.

Ennek also teaches Sure Footing, the canyon guide's trick of keeping your feet near a drop and your grip on a rope however hard you are struck, to anyone willing to walk the narrowest ledges of the canyon path behind him.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could follow Ennek up the cleft to find where the Greywater spring's water has gone, or help him find the words, and the courage, to tell his mother before somebody else does.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Sennu: mother
  • Kesh: cousin
  • Ketta: sweetheart
  • Corwell: employer

docs.title: Gorra
docs.text:
Cistern Keeper

Town Midbarium Where Terraces Role Worker Age Adult Family Kragvar In the game Gorra

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brisk, practical and always counting; Gorra measures water the way merchants measure coin.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Gorra keeps the stone cisterns that water Midbarium's terraces, and she measures water the way merchants measure coin. She is forty-three, brisk, practical and always counting: buckets drawn, buckets poured, days since the last rain, days until the next feast and how many extra mouths it will bring. Ask her how long the town could last in a dry year and she will tell you, to the bucket, and then tell you what you could do to make it last longer.

docs.title: Learning the water
docs.text:
Gorra was born in the Kragvar Quarter and was cutting stone with the other Kragvar children before she was ten. She was good at it, but what fascinated her was not the stone itself. It was what the stone held. The Kragvar cut the cisterns into the mountainside in the earliest days of the town, deep stone tanks that catch every drop of rain and the overflow of the terrace springs, and the young Gorra spent whole afternoons lying on her stomach beside them, watching the water rise and fall.

Old Marn, who kept the cisterns then, noticed her there and put her to work. He taught her how to read the stains on a cistern wall like the rings of a tree, how to tell rainwater from spring water by taste, and how to sit perfectly still in the dark and listen for a leak. When Marn died eighteen years ago, Gorra took the cisterns over, and nobody in the family thought to question it. She has kept them ever since. She knows every one by name and by temper, and she keeps a tally of every one of them, scratched in neat columns on the wall of her cistern house above the terraces.

docs.title: Family
docs.text:
Gorra married Dorrek, now chieftain of the Kragvar, when they were both young, and she has never once let him climb a scaffold without telling him exactly what she thinks of it. He climbs anyway; she counts the minutes until he comes down. He tells her she is the cleverest person in Midbarium roughly once a decade, and she keeps a tally of that too.

Their daughter Brakka is apprenticed to Dorrek's cousin Vosk and wants to carve a new stairway down the cliff. Gorra has looked at the sketches more carefully than Brakka knows, and her only question was where the stairway's builders would get their water. Their son Korrin climbs everything and wants to join the Uskari trail watch, and Gorra has given up telling him to come down from things; she now simply tells him where the handholds are loose. Dorrek's father Ulm keeps the council fire, and Gorra sends him a jug of the coldest cistern water every evening.

Her neighbour at the cisterns is Yarrek of the Tolmach, a gentle goat herder whose family draws water from the same terrace tanks. The two of them have a sharing arrangement that is fair to the bucket and argued over weekly, and both would be lost without it. Korrin and Yarrek's son Kesh became best friends hiding under one of Gorra's cistern lids, which she has forgiven, mostly.

docs.title: The crack
docs.text:
This season, the oldest cistern on the upper terrace, which the Kragvar call the Founders' Cistern, has started losing water. Not much: a finger's depth every few nights. But it has not rained, nobody has been drawing from it, and Gorra has checked every wall and seam she can reach. She cannot find the crack. She has sat in the dark beside it three nights running and heard nothing but a faint trickle that seems to come from somewhere deeper than the cistern itself.

She has not told Dorrek how worried she is, because he already has a bridge and a stair to worry about. She would quietly reward anyone who could track the leak down.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could follow the lost water through the rock beneath the Founders' Cistern, perhaps to wherever the water of the south path's dry spring has gone, or help Gorra work out how long the town could last if the leak grows.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dorrek: husband
  • Brakka: daughter
  • Korrin: son
  • Yarrek: water-sharing neighbour

docs.title: Hallek
docs.text:
Kragvar Mason

Town Midbarium Where Kragvar Quarter Role Craftsman Age Adult Family Kragvar In the game Hallek

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Steady, stubborn and slow to complain, he would rather mend a wall than talk about what bit him. He has started checking every rope twice.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hallek is a Kragvar mason, thirty-six years old, broad in the back and slow in the speech, and the sort of man the family sends when a wall has to stand for another hundred years. He is steady, stubborn and very slow to complain. Ask him how his arm is and he will tell you about the wall he is mending instead, in some detail, until you give up. Since the spring he has started checking every rope twice, and he does not explain that either.

docs.title: Stone and anchors
docs.text:
Hallek was born in the Kragvar Quarter and put to stone, like every Kragvar child, as soon as he could hold a mallet without dropping it on his foot. His father was a terrace mason who died of a winter cough when Hallek was small; his mother, who cut steps for the terraces until her hands stiffened, died six years ago. He never married. He lives alone in a narrow stone house near the top of the quarter, and he says the house is quiet, which suits him, and the walls are straight, which suits him better.

His trade is the part of a bridge nobody looks at. Every rope-and-plank bridge on Midbarium's cliffs is tied into the rock at both ends, through anchor stones set in seats cut into the living cliff, and Hallek has spent the last twelve years cutting those seats and setting those stones under Vosk, the master of bridges. Vosk ties the knots; Hallek makes sure there is something worth tying them to. They suit each other. Neither talks much on the job, and both of them would rather do a thing twice than once badly. Vosk is the only man in the quarter Hallek will let check his work, and Vosk checks it every time, and Hallek has never once minded.

docs.title: The far end
docs.text:
Earlier this year, before anyone found the ropes gnawed, Hallek was out at the far end of the far canyon bridge, on the ledge where its ropes are tied into the rock, resetting an anchor stone that the frost had loosened. He reached down over the lip of the ledge to feel for the lashing ring below it, and something bit him.

He never saw it. That is the part he tells, when he tells it at all. He felt claws scrabble on the rock under his hand, smelled something like wet rope and old straw, and then there were teeth through his sleeve and into his forearm, a short row of them, deep. He pulled back hard, and heard whatever it was go down the cliff face below him faster than anything should climb. When he looked over the edge there was nothing but red rock and the drop.

He walked home across the bridge holding his arm, which he now admits was foolish. By evening the bite was hot and swollen, and Lessa, the bonesetter of Brenna House, cleaned it with her grey bitter rimwort while he sat very still and she tapped a slow beat on the table. He had a fever for three days. The bite closed in the end, but the arm has never come back quite right. It is stiff in the mornings and weak when he lifts above his shoulder, and he works around it without a word.

docs.title: Back on the terraces
docs.text:
Lessa would have kept him off the bridges for good if she could. Vosk, who has since found the ropes gnawed twice on the side away from town, will not send anyone out alone any more, and he worries over Hallek more than he says. So for now Hallek is back on the terraces, mending retaining walls and resetting steps, work he could do in his sleep. He is grateful and he is bored, and he is ashamed of being bored.

He thinks about the far end a great deal. He knows how a bridge fails: rot, frost, wind, a bad knot, a bad stone. He did not know a bridge could be eaten. He wants to know what lives under that ledge, and he wants to be there when someone finds out, stiff arm or not.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text: Hallek fears being made careful for the rest of his life. He fears that one day he will reach over an edge and hesitate, and that the hesitating will cost someone more than the bite cost him.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could sit with Hallek on the terrace wall while he finally tells the whole of what he did not see, or carry his description to Lessa so she can match it to the bites she has been counting. Later, someone who has been to the far end and back might bring him a reason to set a new anchor stone there himself.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Vosk: master of bridges
  • Lessa: bonesetter

docs.title: Harra
docs.text:
Wool and Cheese Seller

Town Midbarium Where Trading Post Sells Wool, hides, goat cheese and travel rations In the game Harra

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Mabbu: mother
  • Sennu: sister
  • Yarrek: husband
  • Kesh: son
  • Corwell: friendly rival trader

docs.title: Imre
docs.text:
Stargazer

Town Midbarium Where Terraces Role Scholar Age Adult Family none In the game Imre

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Dreamy, absent-minded and delighted by everything; Imre forgets meals but never forgets a star.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Imre is Midbarium's stargazer, and on any clear night the highest terrace above the town has a small lantern on it, a scatter of charts weighed down with stones, and Imre lying flat on a sheepskin looking straight up. Dreamy, absent-minded and delighted by everything, Imre forgets meals, forgets boots, forgets which day of the week it is, and has never once forgotten a star.

docs.title: From the lowlands to the plateau
docs.text:
Imre grew up in the lowlands and learned the heavens from the old star tables in the Scholars' Quarter of Selsior, where the city's lamps wash out half the sky. Every book on the stars said the same thing in the end: if you want to see them properly, go up to the highlands of Midbarium, where the air is dry, the nights are cold and the stars over the plateau are famous across the kingdom. Five years ago Imre finally did, meaning to stay one summer.

That summer, Imre arrived at a Tolmach fire on the canyon road after dark, hungry and with a lantern out of oil, and was given water, food and a place to sleep without a single question, as highland custom demands. Imre never got over it. One summer became a winter, and the winter became five years. Imre stayed for the stars and for the hospitality, in that order on clear nights and the other order on cloudy ones.

docs.title: Lodger at the Trading Post
docs.text: Imre lodges with Corwell at the Trading Post, in a narrow room above his storeroom that smells of lamp oil and salt. Corwell is talkative, round and comfortable, a lowlander who came up the canyon himself twenty years ago and never went home, and he recognised a fellow stray at once. He feeds Imre whenever Imre remembers to come down, reminds Imre about the rent with heroic patience, and takes part of it in star charts, which he pins up behind his counter and explains wrongly to customers. Imre has never corrected him, because Corwell's versions are better stories.

docs.title: Star nights with Ahvi
docs.text:
Imre spends nights on the highest terrace charting the heavens, and swapping star stories with the Brenna, who know the sky by entirely different names. Imre's dearest friend there is Ahvi, the old song-keeper. On clear nights the two of them meet on the high terrace: Imre tells the lowland tales of the stars, and Ahvi answers with the families' oldest songs, and again and again the songs turn out to mention the same stars under highland names. Imre has filled a whole book with these matches, in two columns, and treasures it above every chart.

Imre's great hope is to be invited one day to recite at a gathering of the four families, and has been quietly working on a star song in the Brenna manner, matching every lowland star story to its highland verse. Imre has not dared to mention this to Ahvi. Ahvi, as it happens, thinks Imre should be invited, and has not yet decided whether to say so. Neither of them knows what the other is thinking, and both have been not saying it for some time.

Imre came to Midbarium after Hask's choosing and has never seen the great drum called a gathering for a choosing. Imre hopes to hear it one day, and then feels guilty for hoping, since a choosing only comes when an Old One dies.

docs.title: What Imre has noticed
docs.text:
This year, on a handful of cold, still nights, the stars low in the direction of the island's heart have shimmered as if seen through the heat of a fire. Imre has written down the dates and cannot explain them. Cold air does not do that. Imre has mentioned it to nobody but Ahvi, who listened and said nothing.

A quest could help Imre gather the old star verses from the Brenna for the song, or sit up on the terrace on one of the shimmering nights and look where Imre is pointing.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ahvi: friend
  • Corwell: landlord

docs.title: Kesh
docs.text:
Young Goatherd

Town Midbarium Where Tolmach Camps Role Child Age Child Family Tolmach In the game Kesh

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Chatty, curious and fearless; Kesh asks every traveler where they came from and what the road was like.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Kesh is nine years old, and there is no traveler in Midbarium he has not asked where they came from and what the road was like. He is chatty, curious and fearless, the son of Harra, who sells the Tolmach's wool and cheese at the Trading Post, and Yarrek, the family's gentle goat herder. Between a mother who can be heard across the whole market and a father who can go a whole morning without a word, Kesh seems to have inherited all of the talking and none of the quiet.

docs.title: The kids of the herd
docs.text:
Kesh was born in the Tolmach camps and has never slept more than a few nights under a roof. Like every Tolmach child, he was put to work with the herds as soon as he could walk without falling over a goat. His father has trusted him with the kids of the herd since last year: the young goats, all knees and appetite, who wander off the moment anyone stops watching them. Kesh has named every one of them, as his father taught him, though his names tend to be things like Grumble, Biter and Lady Snort, which Yarrek pretends to find dignified.

He is not yet trusted with the grown goats. He knows exactly why, and he thinks it is unfair. Lately, though, he has stopped asking. Last month three of his father's goats came back from the valley wild-eyed and biting, and Yarrek keeps them penned apart, hoping they will calm. Kesh has watched his father sit beside that pen every evening, talking softly to animals that will not let him near, and it is the first thing in his life that has ever made Kesh go quiet.

docs.title: Family
docs.text:
His grandmother Mabbu keeps the home camp now that her knees will not follow the herds, and Kesh spends long afternoons with her, being scolded and fed in the same breath. She remembers every spring that ever ran, out loud, and Kesh is the only one of her grandchildren who asks her to tell it all again. His aunt Sennu is chieftain of the Tolmach. His cousin Ennek is a canyon guide, thirteen years older, and the most interesting person Kesh knows: Ennek has walked every road to the lowlands and met traders from every town in Veligor. Kesh questions him relentlessly. Ennek tells him the funny stories and leaves out the frightening ones, and Kesh has noticed exactly where the gaps are.

At the Trading Post, Kesh runs errands between his mother's stall and Corwell's counter. He has learned that his mother and Corwell argue loudly about prices all day and share a pot of tea when the market closes, and that this is apparently what friendship looks like among traders.

docs.title: Korrin and the lookout
docs.text:
Kesh's best friend is Korrin, the youngest child of the Kragvar chieftain. Their families share water on the terraces, and the boys met as small children hiding under the same cistern lid from their respective parents. Korrin climbs and Kesh talks, and between them they get into a remarkable amount of trouble.

Above the terraces they have a secret lookout, a ledge with a little stone wall the two of them built, where they watch for monsters coming up the canyons. So far they have mostly seen eagles. Kesh keeps a count of them with notches on a stick, which he learned from watching Korrin's mother keep her cistern tallies. He also keeps a second, much shorter stick, for things he cannot name. It has two notches, both for something moving on the far canyon bridge after dark.

docs.title: What he wants
docs.text:
Kesh wants to see the lowlands, all of them, and then come home and tell everybody about it. He wants to be trusted with the grown goats. And he wants his father's three goats to get better, more than he has ever said aloud.

A quest could ask Kesh what is on his second stick, or help him find out what happened in the valley to make his father's goats wild.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Yarrek: father
  • Harra: mother
  • Ennek: cousin
  • Korrin: best friend

docs.title: Ketta
docs.text:
Returned Adventurer

Town Midbarium Where Uskari Rim Role Adventurer Age Young Family Uskari In the game Ketta

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bright and talkative about everything except one subject, which makes her go suddenly quiet.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ketta is twenty-one, bright and talkative, and she can tell a story about almost anywhere in Veligor. Ask her about the tavern brawl in the capital, the night she slept in a hayloft outside Kaldemor, the storm that kept her stuck in a harbour inn for nine days, or the time she got gloriously lost under the lanterns of Fairy Forest, and she will talk until the fire burns down. Ask her what she saw in the deep canyon cave on her way home, and she goes suddenly, completely quiet.

docs.title: A child of the rim
docs.text:
Ketta was born on the Uskari Rim to a family of hunters. Her father died before she could remember him, and her mother, a tracker named Sarra, fell from the rim on a winter hunt when Ketta was twelve. The Uskari look after their own, and Ketta was raised after that by the whole rim at once, eating at whichever fire was nearest and sleeping wherever she ended up.

The person who took her in hand was Zirra the bowyer, the Old One's older sister, who judges people by how they hold a bow. Zirra watched the girl shoot for an afternoon, told her that her stance was a disgrace, and spent the next five years correcting it. Ketta learned to string a bow, to make one, to shoot one in a crosswind on a narrow ledge, and to tolerate Zirra's sardonic commentary, which she eventually realised was the bowyer's way of showing affection. Ketta is still Zirra's former pupil before she is anything else; the first thing she did when she came home was to show Zirra her new bow, and the second was to be told what was wrong with it.

docs.title: The wide world
docs.text:
At seventeen, like many young Uskari, Ketta left home to adventure. Her friend Ennek of the Tolmach guided her down the canyon road, whistling the whole way, and she spent the next three years wandering Veligor: the capital's crowded streets, the farms around Kaldemor, the harbour towns, the strange bright streets of Urbanograd and the forest of the Magicians. She hunted monsters for bounties, guarded caravans, and learned that the rest of the kingdom thinks highlanders are taller than they actually are.

Last spring she came home. Ennek, leading a caravan up the south path, came round a bend and found her sitting on a rock waiting for someone to walk home with. She had a new scar across her left shoulder and a pack full of stories. They have been sweethearts since the summer. He has never once asked her about the cave, and she loves him for it, though she has not quite said so.

docs.title: The silence
docs.text:
Somewhere in the canyons below the town, on the last days of her journey home, Ketta sheltered from a dust storm in a deep cave. That is all anyone knows. She will not say what she saw there, or how long she stayed, or whether the scar came from it. She has told three different stories about the scar, each funnier than the last, and nobody believes any of them.

Tavi, her chieftain, worries about her more than about any monster on the trails. Tavi left the rim at seventeen too, and knows that kind of silence from the inside. Ketta has noticed Tavi watching her at the patrol fires, and has started taking the night watches nobody else wants, which worries Tavi even more.

She has joined the trail patrols since she came home, and she is very good. But she will not walk the canyon trail that passes the cave, and she always finds a reason to trade that stretch to someone else.

docs.title: What she wants
docs.text:
Ketta wants to be the person she was before she went into that cave: the girl who could talk about anything. She is not sure she can be. She fears that what she saw is still there, and that one day the patrols will find it without her warning them.

A quest could earn Ketta's trust enough to hear where the cave is, or go there with her when she finally decides she has to see it again.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Zirra: teacher
  • Tavi: chieftain
  • Ennek: sweetheart

docs.title: Korrin
docs.text:
Chieftain's Son

Town Midbarium Where Terraces Role Child Age Child Family Kragvar In the game Korrin

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bold, scabby-kneed and always climbing something he was told not to climb.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Korrin is nine years old, the youngest child of Dorrek, chieftain of the Kragvar, and Gorra, who keeps the stone cisterns that water the terraces. He is bold, scabby-kneed and always climbing something he was told not to climb, and the whole Kragvar Quarter has learned to look up first when it hears a small boy laughing somewhere it cannot see him.

docs.title: A Kragvar who looks the wrong way
docs.text:
Every Kragvar child grows up with stone in their hands. Korrin's sister Brakka, ten years older, was chiselling patterns into the doorstep before she could spell her name, and she is now apprenticed to their father's cousin Vosk, the master of bridges. Korrin has tried. He can split a flat stone well enough, and he once carved a goat that his grandfather Ulm kindly said looked very like a goat. But Korrin does not look at stone the way his family does. When a Kragvar looks at a cliff, they see what could be cut from it. When Korrin looks at a cliff, he sees a way up.

What he wants, more than anything, is to join the Uskari on the trail watch when he grows up. He has said so at the family table more times than anyone can count, and every time the Kragvar laugh: a chieftain's son, born to the oldest masons in the highlands, walking the rim with a bow like a hunter. They find it very funny and slightly insulting, and Korrin has learned to laugh with them and change his mind not one bit. His hero is Bekk, Skarra's son and the fastest climber on the Uskari Rim, who is kind to children and lets Korrin trail after him in the small admiring crowd that always seems to follow Bekk around. Korrin has copied the way Bekk ties his boots, and the way he squints at the horizon as if something is always about to appear on it.

He does not know that his father, after laughing loudest at the table, has quietly asked the Uskari how young they take recruits.

docs.title: Kesh and the lookout
docs.text:
Korrin's best friend is Kesh, Harra and Yarrek's son from the Tolmach camps. Their families are neighbours over water: Gorra and Yarrek share the terrace cisterns and argue amiably about every bucket, and the two boys met as small children hiding under the same cistern lid. They have been inseparable since. Kesh talks and Korrin climbs, and between them they know every handhold and every rumour on the terraces.

Above the terraces, on a ledge only two boys would think was safe, they have a secret lookout. They built a low wall of stones there, which Korrin insists is proper Kragvar work and which Brakka has privately inspected and found surprisingly sound. From the lookout they watch the canyon trails for monsters. So far they have mostly seen eagles, a lost goat and, once, Tavi of the Uskari walking the worst stretch of trail at dusk, which they agreed was the bravest thing they had ever seen.

docs.title: Grandfather and the fire
docs.text: Korrin is the only person in Midbarium who is allowed to sit on the woodpile beside the council fire while his grandfather Ulm tends it. Ulm tells him the old Kragvar songs about the fighters who stayed beneath the World Tree, and Korrin, who loves a good climb and a good fight, thinks they must have been the bravest Kragvar of all. He has asked his grandfather whether they had to climb down to get there. Ulm said nobody knows, and Korrin has been thinking about it ever since.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Lately, the eagles are not the only things the boys have seen from the lookout. Twice they have spotted something moving along the far canyon bridge after dark, and they have told no one, because then they would have to explain where they were. A quest might coax the secret out of them, or begin with Korrin missing after supper and his parents searching every ledge in the town.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dorrek: father
  • Gorra: mother
  • Ulm: grandfather
  • Kesh: best friend
  • Bekk: hero

docs.title: Lessa
docs.text:
Bonesetter

Town Midbarium Where Brenna House Role Healer Age Adult Family Brenna Sells Herbal salves, splints and highland remedies In the game Lessa

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Calm in a crisis and fussy everywhere else; Lessa will set a broken leg without blinking and then complain about the mud on your boots.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Lessa is the best bonesetter in the highlands, and she will tell you so only if you ask, and then only to explain why you should sit still. She is forty-two, calm in a crisis and fussy everywhere else. She will set a broken leg without blinking, stitch a torn scalp while chatting about the weather, and then complain at length about the mud you have tracked across her clean floor.

docs.title: Brenna House
docs.text:
Lessa is the daughter of Odda, chieftain of the Brenna, and Thrun, the drummer whose great drum calls the four families together. She grew up in Brenna House among healers, storytellers and drummers, and she was the only child in her generation who preferred the herb room to the drum. Her mother taught her bonesetting, as Odda had once taught it to her friend in Fairy Forest, and every spring Odda came home from the forest with bundles of forest herbs and new uses for them, which Lessa wrote down in a book she still keeps by her bed. From her father she learned that a frightened patient calms faster to a steady rhythm, and to this day Lessa taps out a slow beat on the table while she works.

She set her first bone at fifteen, a Kragvar apprentice's wrist, and began healing in earnest at twenty. In the twenty-two years since, she has splinted every kind of break the highlands can produce: falls from scaffolds, falls from rope bridges, goat kicks, rockslides, and an astonishing number of children who were climbing something they were told not to climb. Korrin of the Kragvar alone has kept her busy for years.

docs.title: Family
docs.text:
Lessa married Corrick, a Brenna storyteller with a gift for voices, and their daughter Neffa was born ten years ago. Corrick died of a lung fever in a hard winter when Neffa was two. Lessa does not speak of him often, but she keeps his voice alive in her own way: when Neffa practises the long songs under her breath, Lessa sometimes hears him in the rhythm, and has to leave the room for a moment.

Neffa is learning the long song of the Old Ones from Ahvi, Odda's cousin and the family's song-keeper, and wants to recite it whole at a gathering before she turns twelve. Lessa is proud of her and slightly bewildered by her; she cannot hold a verse in her head for more than a day, and her daughter holds hundreds.

docs.title: Patients
docs.text: Her most loyal patient, and her most difficult, is Mabbu, the old mother of the Tolmach camps, whose knees no longer let her follow the herds. Lessa walks to the home camp every few days with salve for those knees, and Mabbu grumbles the entire time, tells her she is doing it wrong, feeds her far too much, and would be deeply offended if she ever stopped coming. Lessa secretly enjoys these visits more than any other part of her work.

docs.title: A hard year
docs.text:
This year has been unlike any other. Lessa has treated more monster bites in the past few months than in her first ten years of healing put together: patrollers from the Uskari Rim, herders from the Tolmach camps, and once, a Kragvar mason bitten on the far canyon bridge by something he never saw. Bites from the canyon beasts fester in a way ordinary wounds do not, and the only thing Lessa trusts to clean them is rimwort, a grey, bitter herb that grows only on the far slopes beyond the canyons. Her stock is nearly gone. The Uskari used to bring it back from their hunts; now the patrols have no time to gather herbs, and nobody else will go so far.

Lessa fears the day someone is carried into Brenna House with a bite she cannot clean. She has started rationing rimwort, and she has started keeping a count of the bites in the back of her herb book, the way Gorra counts buckets.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could gather rimwort on the far slopes for Lessa, or bring her the beast behind the strange bites so she can learn what she is treating.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Odda: mother
  • Thrun: father
  • Neffa: daughter
  • Mabbu: grumbling patient
  • Hallek: patient

docs.title: Mabbu
docs.text:
Elder of the Camps

Town Midbarium Where Tolmach Camps Role Resident Age Elder Family Tolmach In the game Mabbu

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Sharp-tongued, sharp-eyed and endlessly hospitable; she will scold a guest and feed them in the same breath.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Mabbu is seventy-seven, and she has walked every herding path in the highlands at least a hundred times. She is sharp-tongued, sharp-eyed and endlessly hospitable, and she will scold a guest and feed them in the same breath.
