docs.title: Joan
docs.text:
Keeper of the Crooked Lantern

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Service Age Adult In the game Joan

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brisk, big-hearted and hard to fool. She runs her tavern like a ship and her lodgers like a family.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Joan is forty-four and keeps the Crooked Lantern, a tavern in the old quarters with a lopsided sign, a low beamed common room and nine rooms upstairs that she rents to adventurers for less than they are worth. The lantern on the sign has hung crooked for longer than anyone remembers. Joan straightened it once, when she first took over the house, and the regulars complained so much that she put it back.

docs.title: A house built on stories
docs.text:
The Crooked Lantern was her mother's before it was hers. Beatrix kept it for more than thirty years, and she married a young adventurer named Roland who kept coming back to it between journeys, because, he said, it was the only tavern on Veligor that never asked him to leave early. Joan was born upstairs, in the room over the kitchen, and grew up running plates between the tables.

Her father was away more often than he was home in those years. When he came back, he came back with stories: the Greenwood at night, the highland passes, the long roads down to the harbours, the things he had seen and the things he swore he had seen. Roland adventured when the wilds were far quieter than they are now, and his stories were mostly about weather, bad maps and worse cooking, with a monster in them now and then for flavour. Joan grew up on them. She loved them. She also grew up watching her mother look at the door every evening he was gone, and she learned that from Beatrix as surely as she learned the stories from him.

Roland gave up the road for good when his knees gave up on him, and he has been sitting in the corner of the common room ever since, giving advice to anyone younger than him, which is everyone. Beatrix died twelve years ago, and Joan has kept the Lantern alone since then. She never married. She says she has a tavern, a father and a house full of lodgers, and that is quite enough people to worry about.

docs.title: Running the Lantern
docs.text:
Joan is brisk, big-hearted and very hard to fool. She runs the Lantern like a ship: everything stowed, everything in its place, everyone with a job, and the keeper's word final. Lodgers who pay late are forgiven once. Lodgers who lie about paying late are not. She knows which adventurers are hungry and too proud to say so, and their bowls come back fuller than they ordered. She knows which ones drink to forget a bad fight, and she sits down beside them and does not ask.

Her lodgers are her family, more or less, and she treats them like it. Just now they include Thurstan, who takes every bounty posted at the gate and eats like three men, and Constance, his partner, who keeps notes on every monster they fight and once showed Joan two pages of them. Joan read them, and made Constance promise to be more careful, and has thought about those two pages more than she lets on. Roland has taken Thurstan under his wing, which Joan considers a mixed blessing: the boy needs the advice, but he does not need to be told that he reminds Roland of himself.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Joan worries every time her lodgers head out of the gate. Her father's stories were full of quiet roads, and the roads are not quiet now. She keeps a slate behind the bar with the name of every lodger who is out and the day they said they would be back, and she rubs each name off herself when they come through the door. Lately she has had to leave names on the slate longer than she likes. She has never yet had to rub one off for the wrong reason, and she means to keep it that way.

What she wants is simple: a full house, an empty slate and her father still in his corner, telling the same story wrong.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with a lodger's name that has stayed on Joan's slate three days too long, and Joan asking someone she trusts to go and find out why. Or it might begin with Roland, who has started telling one story he never told when Joan was a girl, and will not say why now.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Thurstan: lodger
  • Constance: lodger
  • Roland: father

docs.title: Jocelyn
docs.text:
Vault Clerk

Town Selsior Where Royal Vault Role Official Age Adult In the game Jocelyn

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brisk, organised and impatient with mess. She labels everything, including her lunch.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Jocelyn is thirty-four, clerk of the Royal Vault, and she labels everything. Her ledgers are labelled, and her shelves, and the drawers in her desk, and the boxes inside the drawers, and the pen tray, and the lid of the ink. Her lunch is labelled, in a neat square hand, with the day it was made. When Wulfric, the vault's warden, once asked her why, she said that a thing without a label is a thing waiting to be lost, and then she labelled the hook where he hangs his cloak. She is brisk, organised and impatient with mess, and in the cool, quiet rooms beneath the palace she is entirely in her element.

docs.title: Learning the ledgers
docs.text:
She came to the vault at nineteen, fifteen years ago, from a clerk's stool in the palace counting room, where she had made herself famous by finding an error in a sum that three senior clerks had checked. Aldous, the Keeper of the Royal Vault, heard about it, came up the stairs himself to look at her, and asked her one question: how many times did she count? "Until it comes out the same twice," she said. Aldous, who counts twice and smiles once, smiled.

He taught her the vault's ledgers, which is to say he taught her everything, because the vault is its ledgers. It keeps the kingdom's treasures and records, and the belongings of any citizen who asks, and every one of them is written down: what it is, whose it is, when it came in and when it may go out. Aldous has sat at the vault desk for thirty years and boasts that not a coin has gone missing in all that time, and Jocelyn intends to make the same boast thirty years from now. It is understood by everyone, including Aldous, that she will take his desk one day. Neither of them is in any hurry, and she would no more push him from it than she would leave a ledger open overnight.

docs.title: Wulfric
docs.text: Her husband is Wulfric, the Vault Warden, who guards the vault doors and has never once had to draw his sword there. He is huge, quiet and soft-spoken, and for years, without being asked and without saying a word, he carried her ledgers up the stairs whenever they had to go up to the palace. It took Jocelyn a surprisingly long time to notice that he was never anywhere else when the ledgers needed carrying. When she finally did, she asked him straight out whether he was going to say anything, and he blushed to the ears and said he had been working up to it. They married four years ago. He still carries the ledgers. She has labelled his lunch, too.

docs.title: The box
docs.text:
Last winter, while she was relabelling the back shelves of the oldest records room, Jocelyn found a record box she had never seen in any ledger. It is plain, heavy and iron-bound, with the vault's old mark stamped on the lid and a lock that no key in the vault will open. The label has faded almost to nothing. She has entered it in her own ledger as "unlisted box, one, locked", which hurts her to look at, because a box that is not in the ledgers should not exist. Aldous says it was there before his time and that he does not know what is in it. Jocelyn believes him, mostly, and she has noticed that he did not seem surprised.

She cannot stop wondering. She has checked every key ring in the vault and every ledger back to the oldest, and she has started, on her free afternoons, looking at keys in other people's hands.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Jocelyn wants a vault in which everything is listed, labelled and accounted for, and she wants to know what is in the box so she can write it down. What she fears is opening it and finding something that belongs in no ledger at all.

A quest might begin with Jocelyn asking a traveller to find out whether anyone in the palace collects old keys, or with a second label, under the faded one, that she has only just learned how to read.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aldous: mentor
  • Wulfric: husband

docs.title: Kenric
docs.text:
Smith's Apprentice

Town Selsior Where Crown Market Role Craftsman Age Young In the game Kenric

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Earnest, sooty and a little clumsy outside the forge. He hums while he hammers.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Kenric is eighteen, apprentice to Selene the weaponsmith in the Crown Market, and you can usually hear him before you see him. He hums while he hammers. He does not know he does it, and he does not know that the tune changes with the work: slow and low for drawing out a bar, quick and bright for the finishing strokes, and no tune at all, just breathing, when the steel is at its most difficult. Selene can tell from across the forge how a piece is going by what Kenric is humming. He is earnest, sooty to the eyebrows and a little clumsy outside the forge, where he walks into doorframes and drops his change, but at the anvil he is careful as a cat.

docs.title: Two brothers
docs.text:
He grew up in the old quarters, in two rooms near Gytha's washing yard, where his mother Cristin worked the coppers. His father died in a fall from a builder's scaffold when Kenric was seven and his little brother Wat was a baby, and Kenric remembers him: big hands, a habit of whistling on the stairs. Wat does not. From the day of that fall, Kenric has felt that his brother was partly his to look after.

At fifteen, three years ago, he went to Selene and asked to be apprenticed. He had hung around her forge since he was small, watching the sparks, and she had noticed that he never once flinched from them. She took him on. That same winter Cristin died of a fever, and Kenric, fifteen and paid an apprentice's pittance, found himself all the family Wat had. Selene let the two boys sleep in the loft above the forge, which is warm in winter and far too warm in summer, and they sleep there still.

It was not enough, that first year. Kenric knows it now. He worked from dark to dark and brought home what he could, and Wat told him he was earning the rest running errands. Two summers ago Reynold, the Warden of the Crown Market, walked Wat up to the forge one evening and told Kenric the truth: his little brother had spent most of a year picking pockets in the market and had finally tried for the warden's own purse. Then Reynold told him the rest, that he had timed the boy's run and given him a job. Kenric did not know whether to shout or cry, so he did neither and thanked Reynold three times. He has never stopped feeling that the pickpocketing was his failure rather than Wat's. Wat teases him about everything except that.

docs.title: The forge
docs.text:
Selene forges blades from the capital's own steel and believes a good blade makes the road shorter. Lately she has set herself a harder problem: a sword light enough for any new recruit and strong enough for any monster, because the Knights' Court is full of recruits and the roads are full of monsters. Kenric works her bellows and her striking hammer and watches everything she does. He has made knives, hinges, a hundred nails and a poker that Selene says is the best poker in Selsior, which he chooses to take as praise.

This winter, if Selene judges him ready, he will forge his first sword from start to finish on his own. He thinks about it constantly. He has drawn it on the back of every scrap of paper in the loft, and he has decided, without telling anyone, that it will be balanced for a short arm.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Kenric wants to make a sword good enough that Selene puts her mark beside his, and he wants Wat to grow up never needing to steal again. What he fears is failing his brother a second time, and, much more quietly, that his first sword will break.

A quest might begin with Kenric needing a particular ore or a better coal for his first sword, or with Selene's newest light blade going missing from the forge on a night when Kenric was the only one in the loft who was not asleep.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Selene: master
  • Wat: brother

docs.title: Lambert
docs.text:
Street Juggler

Town Selsior Where Plaza Role Performer Age Young In the game Lambert

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Showy, cheeky and kind to children. He never drops a ball unless it makes the crowd laugh.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Lambert is twenty-two, a street juggler, and he draws the biggest crowds in the plaza. He juggles balls, clubs, rings, apples, other people's hats, and once, memorably, three of Piers's pies, of which he ate the third without breaking the pattern. He is showy, cheeky and kind to children, and he never drops a ball unless it makes the crowd laugh. When he does drop one, it rolls exactly to the feet of the smallest child watching, and he bows to them as if they had caught it.

docs.title: The puppeteer's apprentice
docs.text:
He was born in Selsior, in rooms over a shop at the bottom of Theatre Row, and he spent his childhood loitering at the puppet booth of Rafe, the puppeteer, who runs a show for the Row's children. Rafe is quiet, clever and more expressive with his hands than his face, and he speaks best through his puppets. One afternoon, when Lambert was about ten, Rafe noticed that the boy had stayed after the show again, and without a word he picked up three spare wooden puppet heads and began to juggle them. Then he handed them over. That was the first lesson. There were a great many more, nearly all of them silent, and by the time Lambert was fifteen he could keep five things in the air and make a crowd watch his face instead of his hands, which Rafe says is the real trick.

His parents, a shopkeeper and his wife, left the city for a quieter life in the farming country when Lambert was sixteen. He stayed. He had a pitch in the plaza by then and no intention of giving it up, and they write to him from time to time to ask whether he has found a proper job yet.

docs.title: The plaza
docs.text:
His pitch is on the plaza steps, beside the flower stall of Emmeline, who sells posies and makes the garlands for every festival in the square. They have been courting for a year. She can sell a posy to a man on his way to buy bread, and Lambert, who has watched her do it a hundred times, swears she could sell one to a juggler with his hands full; she proved it once by tucking a flower behind his ear mid-cascade. When his crowd disperses, they wander over to her stall, and when her customers wait, they watch him. They are, as Piers likes to tell everyone, very good for each other's business.

The children of the plaza adore him, none more than Mab, the pie seller's daughter, who copies every trick she sees and practises cartwheels at the foot of the Great Bell. Lambert has taught her to juggle two balls and is working on three, and he lets her pass the hat after his best shows. She keeps an honest count. Hugh, the Warden of the Great Bell, disapproves of all of it on principle and has been seen, more than once, counting the catches under his breath.

docs.title: For the queen
docs.text: Lambert wants to juggle for the queen at the next royal festival. Not in the crowd, where any juggler might stand, but properly, invited, on the palace steps, with the court watching. He has worked out the routine to the last catch: seven rings, then the clubs, then a finish with a crown, borrowed from the Gilded Stage's prop room and very much not real. The trouble is that nobody seems to know how a street performer gets invited. He has asked Clement the herald, who was kind about it and promised nothing. He has thought about asking Gideon, the old herald up the ladder, who must have seen a hundred festivals.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Lambert wants that invitation, and after it a shop of his own with Emmeline's flowers in the window. What he fears is the night a crowd stops laughing, because he has never found out what he would do then.

A quest might begin with Lambert needing someone to carry a request to the palace, or with the prop crown he borrowed for his routine turning out to be a good deal more valuable than the Gilded Stage believed.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Emmeline: sweetheart
  • Rafe: teacher

docs.title: Lavinia
docs.text:
Mistress of the Gilded Stage

Town Selsior Where Theatre Row Role Performer Age Elder In the game Lavinia

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Grand, theatrical and ruthless about box-office takings. She treats every conversation as a performance.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Lavinia is seventy-two, Mistress of the Gilded Stage, and she has never in her life simply entered a room. She arrives in it. She pauses in the doorway, lets the room notice her, and then crosses it as if there were an audience in the gallery, which, on Theatre Row, there very often is. She is grand, theatrical and utterly ruthless about box-office takings, and she treats every conversation as a performance, including the ones with her accountant, which are among her best.

docs.title: The oldest house on the Row
docs.text:
The Gilded Stage is the oldest theatre on Theatre Row, a tall, gilt-and-crimson house with a cheap gallery under the roof and a box kept for the palace that no one from the palace has sat in for many years. Lavinia walked through its stage door at fifteen, fifty-seven years ago, and asked for anything at all. She swept the stage for a season. Then an actress fell ill, and Lavinia, who had learned every line in the play from the wings, went on in her place and never came off again. For the next thirty-five years and more she played every great part in the house: queens and shepherdesses, murderesses and saints, the heroines of the war plays and the villains of the comedies.

The old manager who owned the house had no heirs, and thirty-five years ago, when he died, he left it to her. She has run it ever since. She played her last great part eighteen years ago and has played only the parts she chooses since, a wicked aunt here, a ghost there, so that audiences never quite forget whose house they are in. She never married. She says she has been married to the Gilded Stage for fifty-seven years and that it has been more faithful than any man and much more expensive.

docs.title: Her company
docs.text:
She has an eye for talent and no mercy in using it. Twenty-three years ago a girl from the old quarters called Rosamund came in and asked for a part, and Lavinia, still playing the great parts herself, gave her a line and a half as a maid with a letter. Rosamund made the audience applaud the letter. Lavinia has never quite forgiven her and has given her the best parts in the house ever since. Ten years ago she cast Rosamund opposite Percival, the Row's favourite hero, for the first time, and the two of them quarrelled so thoroughly on stage and off it that Lavinia has cast them together ever since, because the audiences love it and the box office loves it more.

Crispin has been her house playwright for fifteen years, and his comedies have paid for the roof twice. Tibb works her ropes and trapdoors and keeps the actors from killing each other, which Lavinia considers the most important job in the building after her own. Edith the costumer, who dressed her in the great parts, still argues with her about budgets every week, and they have both enjoyed it for decades.

docs.title: The bet
docs.text:
Lavinia wants one last triumph before she hands the Gilded Stage on. She has bet everything on it: the theatre's savings, a loan against the building, and her own name. The play is Crispin's Balrog War, the whole of it, from the First Burning to the weaving of the seal, the largest thing the Row has ever attempted. Crispin has written four acts and cannot find a fifth. Rosamund wants to play the play's Magician and will not share the stage with Percival. Percival wants the play's Savage warrior, who stands for the whole front line that held the Balrog at the Tree. Lavinia reminds Crispin roughly once a day that she has bet everything on him, in case he forgets. He has not forgotten.

She has not said to whom she will hand the theatre. People on the Row speculate about it constantly, which she enjoys.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Lavinia wants a full house on opening night, a standing audience at the final curtain and the palace box occupied, just once, by the queen. What she fears is an empty gallery: audiences have begun going home earlier, and she can count the seats as well as anyone.

A quest might begin with Lavinia needing a rare prop or a real relic of the Balrog War for the stage, no questions asked, or with an anonymous letter promising that the play will never open.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Crispin: playwright
  • Tibb: stagehand

docs.title: Leofric
docs.text:
Queen's Consort

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Council Age Adult In the game Leofric

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gentle, absent-minded and happiest with ink on his fingers. He forgets supper but never a road.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Leofric is forty-seven, the queen's consort, and he is happiest with ink on his fingers. The palace staff know to look for him in one of two places: in front of the great map of the royal roads that covers a whole wall of the room beside the queen's study, or bent over a table somewhere with a ruler, a compass and a cold supper he has forgotten to eat. He forgets meals, appointments and occasionally which day it is. He has never once forgotten a road.

docs.title: A surveyor's life
docs.text:
He grew up in the Scholars' Quarter, the son of a copyist who made fair copies of other people's maps, and he learned to draw a straight line before he learned to write his name. Both his parents are dead now. At twenty he went out on the royal roads with a young cartographer named Gervase, and the two of them spent the better part of seven years walking, measuring and arguing their way between the towns. Gervase talked and paced and could not bear a blank space on a page; Leofric was quiet and patient and would walk the same mile three times to be sure of it. They made a good pair, and they are still old colleagues and old friends.

It was a road that brought him to the queen. Twenty years ago, in the Scholars' Quarter, a young woman who was not yet queen told him that the road on his map was in the wrong place. Leofric, politely and at considerable length, proved that it was not. She was very hard to fool, and very hard to argue with, and he had done both in one afternoon. They were married before the year was out. Four years later she was crowned under the Great Bell, and Leofric found himself the consort of Wonder Kingdom with no clear idea of what a consort does. He decided, after some thought, that he would keep doing what he was good at.

docs.title: The great map
docs.text:
So he made the map. It shows every royal road on Veligor, every town, ford, bridge and milestone, drawn in his small, careful hand, and it took him years. For a long time it was simply the most accurate map in the kingdom. Now it is something else. Each week, the reports come in from Edric, Lieutenant of the Road Patrol, and Leofric marks on the map every place the patrols met monsters: a small red mark for each, with the date beside it in tiny figures.

He does not like how the marks are spreading. They used to cluster in a few wild places. Now they creep along the roads themselves, and each season they reach a little further toward the towns. Every week Queen Aveline comes to stand in front of the map with him, and the two of them look at it for a long time without saying much. Gervase is making his own map of the same thing, across the city in the Scholars' Quarter, and when the two of them compare, the marks agree. Leofric was rather hoping they would not.

docs.title: Family
docs.text: He adores his wife and his children, and is, in the gentlest possible way, a little lost among them. Alaric asks him questions about roads and Leofric answers them at length, with sketches, which Alaric keeps. Elinor is harder. She is bold and restless and stubborn, and Leofric has a feeling there is something she is not telling him, but he is absent-minded about people in a way he never is about maps, and he has not yet worked out what it is.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Leofric wants the roads to be safe enough that the map can go back to being just a map. What he fears is the pattern. He is a surveyor, and he knows a line when he sees one, and the marks on his wall look less and less like scattered trouble and more like something with a direction.

A quest might begin with a stretch of road on the great map that has no recent reports at all, which worries Leofric more than any red mark, or with a survey he needs walked again by someone who can defend themselves.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aveline: wife
  • Elinor: daughter
  • Alaric: son
  • Gervase: old colleague

docs.title: Lettice
docs.text:
Rat Catcher

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Worker Age Young In the game Lettice

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cheerful, grubby and proud of her trade. She knows the old quarters' cellars better than anyone.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Lettice is twenty-one, the rat catcher of the old quarters, and she is proud of it. She will tell you so before you have asked, cheerfully, with a smudge on her nose and a sack over her shoulder that you had better not ask about either. She is grubby, quick, loud and good-humoured, and she knows the cellars, drains and undercrofts of the old quarters better than anyone alive. Every house in the lanes has a door to the street and a door to the dark, she says, and she has been through most of the second kind.

docs.title: The trade
docs.text:
Her parents are both dead, and she went to work at twelve for the old rat catcher of the lanes, a bent, cheerful man who smelled of cellar and peppermint and called rats "the neighbours". He taught her traps and baits, how to read droppings and gnaw marks, how to hear a nest behind plaster, and the one rule of the trade: never go somewhere you cannot back out of. When his knees gave out, when she was sixteen, he gave her his traps and his customers and went to live with his daughter in the country, where, he wrote, there were no neighbours worth mentioning.

She works with her traps, a lantern, a long hooked pole and her terrier, Nip, a wiry little brown dog with one torn ear who is afraid of geese and nothing else in the world. Nip can find a rat through a stone wall and Lettice trusts his nose over her own eyes. They work cellars, larders, drains, inn yards and, now and then, a theatre.

docs.title: Ida and the lanes
docs.text: Some nights, when a job runs late, Lettice and Nip walk a lane or two with Ida of the night watch. Ida's father mended the old drains, and the two of them can talk about the tunnels under the city in a way nobody else can follow. Ida trusts Nip's nose as much as her own ears, and lately she has asked Lettice more than once what the dog makes of the gratings. Nip, lately, does not like the gratings.

docs.title: Tibb
docs.text:
Two years ago Lavinia hired her to clear the cellar under the Gilded Stage, and Tibb, the stagehand who works the ropes, watched her do it and fell in love. He has courted her ever since by bringing her the theatre's mice, live, in a covered basket, across the whole city. Lettice says it is the most insulting present a rat catcher has ever been given. She keeps count of them in chalk on her cellar door, and the count is past two hundred, and she has never once told him to stop.

Lately the mice have moved. They are gone from the theatre's under-stage and up in the flies and the costume racks, as high as they can get. When Tibb told her, she stopped laughing and asked him which wall of the cellar was nearest the old drains.

docs.title: The deep tunnels
docs.text: The rats in the old drains have grown bigger and bolder this year. She has seen ones the size of a cat, which she would once have called a tavern tale, and they no longer run from a lantern. She has started charging double to go into the deep tunnels, and she means it as a warning as much as a price. This spring she came out of one with a long scrape down her forearm that Edwina stitched, and when Edwina asked what made it, Lettice said only that she had not had a good look. That is true. It is not all of it. What she will say, to Ida and nobody else, is that the rats in the deepest tunnels are not hunting any more. They are moving up.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Lettice wants a cellar door with a thousand chalk marks on it, and Tibb to work out what he is asking her. What she fears is the day Nip will not go into a tunnel, and she has to decide whether to go without him.

A quest might begin with Lettice needing someone to hold the lantern at the mouth of a deep tunnel while she goes in, or with Nip digging, all one night, at a cellar wall in the old quarters that has nothing behind it but earth.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Tibb: sweetheart

docs.title: Lucan
docs.text:
Bargemaster

Town Selsior Where Riverside Role Worker Age Adult In the game Lucan

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Booming, sociable and fond of a wager. He knows every bend of the river and every tavern on it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Lucan is forty-six, a bargemaster of the Riverside, and you can hear him coming round the bend before you see his barge. He has a voice built for shouting across water, and he uses it for everything: greeting every landing he passes, hailing Osmund's ferry, ordering his bargehands about, and telling the whole riverbank what odds he will give that the rain holds off till noon. He is booming, sociable and fond of a wager, and he knows every bend of the river and every tavern on it, and he is not entirely sure which he knows better.

docs.title: Born on the water
docs.text:
He was born on a barge, or so he says, and nobody on the river has ever been able to prove otherwise. His father was a bargehand who worked other men's boats all his life, and Lucan grew up sleeping on grain sacks and learning the river from the deck: where the shoals shift after a flood, which banks undercut, where the current will take a heavy barge sideways if you let it. His father died when Lucan was twenty, and his mother, who kept a tavern kitchen at one of the river landings, not long after. Lucan has no brothers or sisters. By twenty-five he had saved enough, and won enough, to buy his first barge, and he has never worked another man's boat since.

He now runs three barges, carrying grain, stone and timber up and down the river: grain to Hereward's great mill and the city's bakers, stone from the quarries upstream for the builders of Selsior, timber for the carpenters and the boatyards. He is fond of saying that half of Selsior was carried into it on his decks, and he is only exaggerating a little.

docs.title: Friends and wagers
docs.text:
His oldest friend is Bennet, the boatwright, who built two of his three barges and mends all of them. Bennet is patient, wry and proud of his joinery, and he can tell a boat's age by knocking on it. Lucan likes to say that Bennet's barges are the only things on the river he would never bet against. They have a standing wager, older than either will admit, about which of them will retire first, and the stake has grown so large and so strange over the years that neither of them can now remember what it is.

Bennet is designing a faster barge for the river trade and needs someone brave enough to test it. Lucan has told him, loudly and in front of witnesses, that he will happily bet on it but will not be standing on it, and Bennet has not stopped reminding him of it.

docs.title: The river trade
docs.text:
River travel has become popular now that the roads are dangerous. Merchants who used to send their goods by cart now send them by water, and passengers who used to walk now ask to ride on top of the cargo. Lucan has never had so much work, and he cannot hire bargehands fast enough to carry it. The ones he has are tired, and some of them are frightened. Aldith the herb wife has treated one of his hands for a bruise on the leg in the shape of something that gripped him, and two more have left for safer work in the city.

So Lucan employs Tristan, the river scout, who walks the banks ahead of the barges and warns them where creatures lurk. Tristan is quiet and quick and would rather track a beast than fight it, and Lucan trusts him completely, which is the only thing on the river he does not make a wager on. He pays Tristan well and listens to every word he says, even the words he would rather not hear.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Lucan wants the river busy, his barges full and his crews whole. What he fears is the stretch of water Tristan has started asking him to pass at speed, without explaining why.

A quest might begin with Lucan needing hands for a barge that must sail tonight, whatever the river is doing, or with a wager he has made with a stranger in a riverside tavern that he is now very much afraid of winning.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Bennet: friend
  • Tristan: scout

docs.title: Mab
docs.text:
Pie Seller's Daughter

Town Selsior Where Plaza Role Child Age Child In the game Mab

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bold, giggly and fearless. She tries every trick she sees the street performers do.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Mab is ten, the pie seller's daughter, and she has never in her life walked across the plaza when she could cartwheel across it. She is bold, giggly and entirely fearless, and she tries every trick she sees the street performers do, usually within the hour, usually somewhere she has been told not to. She has skinned both knees so many times that her father Piers says she has knees like pie crust, and she has taken it as a compliment.

docs.title: The cart and the Bell
docs.text:
Her father sells pies from a cart by the palace steps, and he claims his recipe is older than the Great Bell. Piers is jolly, round and full of gossip, and he knows who bought what pie and why. He is raising Mab alone. Her mother is not part of her life, and Mab, who does not remember her, has never pressed him about it; Piers talks about the cart instead, and Mab has learned that the cart is how her father says most of the things he means. He hopes she will take it over one day. She helps at it when she has to: she can count change faster than he can, she knows which customers want gravy and which want gossip, and she can sell a cold pie by standing beside it looking hungry.

When she can, which is whenever Piers looks the other way, she practises cartwheels by the Great Bell. The flagstones around its dais are the smoothest in the plaza, and the dais itself makes a perfect audience: tall, still and very grand. Hugh, the Warden of the Great Bell, tells her off every afternoon. Mab has noticed that he has never yet actually stopped her, and that on the day she landed her first handspring he looked away very quickly and polished something.

docs.title: The most famous performer in Selsior
docs.text: Mab wants to be the most famous performer in Selsior, and she has studied the competition. Lambert the juggler is kind to children and has taught her to keep two balls in the air; she is working on three, and he lets her pass the hat after his best shows. She copies Mirabel's spins at dusk, badly, and Mirabel laughs and shows her how to spot a turn. She has watched Rafe's puppet show on Theatre Row so many times she can do the voices, and she sits under Fulke's lute with her chin on her knees. Her father says she would rather run off with the circus. Mab says Selsior is the circus, and she is not wrong.

docs.title: Wat and Hodge
docs.text: Her two best friends are Wat, the errand boy, who knows every alley shortcut in the city, and Hodge, who runs across the rooftops of the old quarters. Between the three of them there is no corner of Selsior they cannot reach: Mab handles the crowds, Wat handles the ground and Hodge handles everything above it. When one of them is in trouble, the other two turn up, usually from an unexpected direction. Mab is the loudest of the three and the one most likely to be caught, and she has never once given up the other two. She knows Hodge practises with a broom handle at dawn; she has offered to teach him a proper flourish, and he has declined, which she thinks is his loss.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Mab wants a stage, a real one, and her name on a playbill twice the size of anyone else's, like Rosamund's. Failing that, she will settle for the plaza on festival day with every eye in it on her. What she fears, though she would never say so, is that her father is right, and that she will be selling pies at the palace steps when she is as old as he is.

A quest might begin with Mab attempting a stunt somewhere very high to impress a crowd, or with her spotting, from the middle of a cartwheel, something on the Great Bell's dais that nobody else in the plaza has noticed.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Piers: father
  • Hodge: friend

docs.title: Margery
docs.text:
Baker

Town Selsior Where Crown Market Sells Bread, buns and honey cakes baked the Kaldemor way In the game Margery

docs.text:

  • Alys: mother

docs.title: Marigold
docs.text:
Child Actor

Town Selsior Where Theatre Row Role Child Age Child In the game Marigold

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Precocious, dramatic and very sure of herself. She knows everyone's lines better than they do.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Marigold is ten years old, a child actor of the Gilded Stage, and she has never in her life made an ordinary entrance. She does not come into a room; she arrives, the way Lavinia does, with a pause in the doorway to let the room notice her. She is precocious, dramatic and entirely sure of herself, and she knows every line of every play in the house, including the ones she is not in, better than the actors who are supposed to say them.

docs.title: Born in the second act
docs.text:
She is the daughter of Crispin, the house playwright, and Rosamund, the most famous actress in Selsior, and she has been on stage for as long as she can remember, which is longer than she can actually remember. As a baby she was carried on in a basket in the second act of The Baker's Wager. Edith the costumer sewed the lining of that basket, and still keeps a scrap of it in her attic; Marigold has asked for it twice and been refused twice, which she considers an outrage and also a very good scene. Since she could walk she has refused to leave the stage at all. She has played lost children, pages, a talking cat and the youngest of three princesses, and she has upstaged grown actors in every one.

She grew up in the wings, as her father did. She learned to read from prompt books, to count from the rows of the gallery, and to tell time by the interval bell. Tibb, who works the ropes and trapdoors, has taught her which boards creak and which ones drop, and she has sworn on her life never to use the trapdoor without asking. She has kept that oath for nearly a year, which is the longest she has kept any.

docs.title: Everyone's lines
docs.text:
Marigold prompts from the wings whether anyone asks her to or not. She can do Percival's heroic speeches with his exact pause before the last word, and she does them for the stagehands, who pay her in sweets. She can do her mother's faint and her mother's laugh. Rosamund, who recognises the type because she was the type, watches her daughter with pride and something close to alarm. Crispin finds her useful, which is worse: she remembers lines he cut three drafts ago and asks him why.

She has seen Mab, the pie seller's daughter, turning handsprings by the Great Bell, and she has made a point of saying, loudly, that the plaza is not a real stage. She has also practised a handspring in the dressing room, alone, and failed, and told no one.

docs.title: The part
docs.text:
Lavinia has bet everything on Crispin's new play about the Balrog War, and Marigold wants a part in it. Any part. There is no part for a child in it yet, and she means to fix that. She has suggested a refugee girl in the first act, a messenger at the truce, a drummer at the Last Stand, and a ghost, and her father has said "we'll see" so many times that she has stopped believing it.

So she has moved to stronger methods. Marigold knows where Crispin keeps his discarded endings. She has let him know that she knows, with a look over the breakfast table that she copied from her mother's best villainess. She has not said what she would do with them, which is, she has learned from the theatre, far more frightening than saying. Her father knows perfectly well that one of those endings is the one Lavinia would hate most, and that Marigold could find her way to Lavinia's office in her sleep.

She has not actually decided whether she would do it. She suspects she would not. But nobody else needs to know that.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Marigold wants her name on a playbill, even small, and she wants the play to be the greatest thing Theatre Row has ever seen, because she would like to have been in it. Underneath the drama she is a child who has heard the grown-ups talking in low voices about the theatre's savings and the loan on the building, and what she fears is the night the Gilded Stage goes dark and there is nowhere left to make an entrance.

A quest might begin with one of Crispin's discarded endings going missing, and Marigold being the first suspect and, for once, innocent. Or it might begin with Marigold needing someone to fetch a prop from somewhere she has been forbidden to go, so that she can prove she deserves a part.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rosamund: mother
  • Crispin: father

docs.title: Mariota
docs.text:
Academy Student

Town Selsior Where Scholars' Quarter Role Scholar Age Young In the game Mariota

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bright, impatient and argumentative. She has opinions on everything and evidence for half of them.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Mariota is nineteen, a student at the Royal Academy, and she has never in her life heard an opinion she did not want to argue with, including her own from the week before. She studies the stars and the old histories, which she says are the same subject looked at from opposite ends: one is the record of what happened down here, and the other is the record of what was happening up there at the time. She has opinions on everything and evidence for about half of them, and she is working, very hard and very loudly, on the other half.

docs.title: A house full of books
docs.text:
She and her younger brother Tobe grew up in the Scholars' Quarter, in two rooms over their father's bindery. Ranulf bound books for the Academy and the libraries, and the bindery was always full of them, half-sewn, waiting for covers, stacked on every chair. Their mother, Sabine, died of a fever twelve years ago, when Tobe was five and Mariota seven, and after that it was the three of them and the books. Mariota read the histories. Tobe read the manuals. They argued about which was more useful across the supper table every night, and Ranulf, who had bound both, refused to take sides.

He died two winters ago, of a bad chest that would not clear. The bindery went to pay what was owed on it. Mariota had already won a place at the Academy by then, on the strength of an essay that argued with its own examiners, and Bartholomew, the Master, who welcomes students from every town and likes nothing better than one who answers back, made sure she kept it. Tobe found work fetching and shelving in a Scholars' Quarter library and read every book on swordsmanship in it. This spring he took everything he had read to the Knights' Court.

docs.title: Stars and histories
docs.text:
At the Academy, Mariota studies under Theobald, the stargazer, whose charts of the night sky go back sixty years. Theobald talks to the stars as if they owe him money and forgets to eat, and Mariota adores him and tells him so by correcting his arithmetic. Her friend Everard, who sleeps through lectures and passes every exam, drives her to distraction. She has worked out that he is far cleverer than he lets anyone see, and she has made it her business to catch him at it.

What she wants is to be the first to explain why the monsters changed. Everyone in Selsior agrees that they have. The creatures on the roads are wilder than they were in the old books, and there are more of them every year. Mariota wants to know why, properly, with evidence, and she has decided that if the answer exists anywhere, it is written down somewhere already, in the sky or in a chronicle. So she has set herself to read both. She has been going through Theobald's charts year by year, looking for anything in the heavens that changed around the time the creatures did, and through the Academy's old histories, looking for any account of beasts turning strange before. She has not found anything she can prove. She has found three things she is fairly sure of and one she is afraid of, and she will tell anyone about the first three.

docs.title: Tobe
docs.text: She teases Tobe without mercy for reading about swords instead of using them, and she visits the Court every week to see whether he has got past the third cut yet. He has not. She tells him that reading a book does not make you a swordsman, and he tells her that reading a chart does not make her an astronomer, and they are both right. Underneath it she is fiercely proud of him, and frightened for him in a way she would never let him see, because he is the only family she has left.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with Mariota hearing that an adventurer at the Crooked Lantern keeps notes on every monster she fights, and wanting them very badly. Or it might begin with the fourth thing, the one she has not told anyone, when she finally needs somebody to help her check it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Tobe: brother
  • Theobald: teacher
  • Everard: friend

docs.title: Maud
docs.text:
Housekeeper

Town Selsior Where Crown Market Role Service Age Adult In the game Maud

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bustling, bossy and warm. She shops like a general on campaign and expects the crowd to mind her baskets.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Maud is fifty-two, housekeeper to Dame Orsa, and every dawn she goes into the Crown Market like a general taking a city. She carries two baskets, one on each arm, and a list she does not need, and she moves through the busiest market on Veligor at a pace that clears a path in front of her. "Mind the baskets!" she calls, and the crowd, which has known her for years, minds them. Eggs first, while they are still warm. Bread next, from Margery's stall, before the rest of the city wakes up and wants it. Then fruit, the best in Selsior, which is never at the same stall two days running and which Maud always finds.

docs.title: A market child
docs.text:
She was born a few streets from the Crown Market, the daughter of a fruit seller who kept a barrow at its edge, and she spent her childhood under that barrow, sorting bruised apples from good ones and learning to tell a ripe pear by its smell from three stalls away. Her mother taught her that a market is a war fought politely, and that the only way to win it is to arrive first and leave last. Maud swears the Crown Market opens at dawn and closes only when the stalls run out, and she means to be there for both. Both her parents are long dead now, and the barrow went with them, but Maud still stops at the corner where it used to stand, out of habit, and buys something from whoever has it now.

She has kept house for Dame Orsa for twenty-two years, in the rooms above and behind the general store, and she has never married. She says one household that needs running is plenty, and that Dame Orsa's needs running more than most.

docs.title: Dame Orsa's house
docs.text:
Dame Orsa is grand, motherly and shrewd. She calls every customer "dear" and remembers every debt, and she runs a shop that stocks everything a traveller forgets, from rope to scrolls home. Maud runs everything else: the kitchen, the linen, the coal, the accounts that are not the shop's, and the steady stream of travellers who come round to the back door to ask Dame Orsa for one more favour. The two of them are very fond of each other and disagree about almost everything, loudly, over breakfast.

Dame Orsa earned her title long ago for service to the crown and has never explained what it was. In twenty-two years Maud has never found out. She has dusted every room in the house and has found no medal, no letter and no portrait, and she has decided that this is suspicious in itself. She has several theories, most of them involving pirates, and she tells a new one to Margery roughly once a month.

docs.title: Friends at the market
docs.text:
Margery the baker is Maud's oldest friend in the market and her first stop every morning. Margery learned to bake in Kaldemor and sells out by noon, and Maud is her loudest champion; she tells everyone who will stand still that Margery deserves a bakery big enough to bake through the night, and that someone ought to give her one. Margery's mother, Alys the cheesemonger, lets Maud taste her cheese now, which took about ten years.

And then there is Biscuit, the dog from the gate, who follows his nose to the Crown Market every morning and has learned that the bustling woman with two baskets is a soft touch. Maud keeps rinds and scraps from Dame Orsa's kitchen in her apron pocket for him and tells everyone she is only getting rid of them. Nobody believes her, least of all Biscuit.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Maud wants the market to stay as it is: loud, crowded, full and safe. Lately the carts come in later, the prices from the other towns are higher, and some mornings a stall she has known for years is simply not there. She fears the day the roads close and the stalls run out before noon and do not fill again.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with Maud's dawn list containing something that cannot be found anywhere in the market, which has never happened before. Or it might begin with Maud deciding, after twenty-two years, that she is finally going to find out what Dame Orsa did for the crown.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dame Orsa: employer
  • Biscuit: favourite dog
  • Margery: friend

docs.title: Melisende
docs.text:
Mistress of the Envoys' Hall

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Official Age Adult In the game Melisende

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Polished, patient and fluent in every town's manners. She never raises her voice and never loses an argument.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Melisende is fifty-one, Mistress of the Envoys' Hall, and she has never been seen to hurry, raise her voice or lose an argument. She hosts the envoys that every town keeps at the palace, and she knows each of them better than their own households do: who takes highland tea and who takes it with honey, who wants sea salt on the bread, who wants the windows open in winter and who wants them shut in summer, and who will say yes to anything after a good supper and no to everything before one.

docs.title: Raised among the envoys
docs.text:
She was born in Selsior, in one of the old envoys' houses near the plaza, where her father kept the household of an envoy and her mother kept its books. Both are dead now. As a girl she carried trays through rooms where the four peoples' manners met and collided, and she learned early that what looks like rudeness in one town is courtesy in another. A highlander who sits down without being asked is paying you a compliment. A harbour captain who interrupts you is agreeing with you. A Fairy Forest visitor who says nothing for a long time is not bored but thinking. Melisende learned all of it, the way other children learn songs, and she has added Urbanograd's habits since, which she admits took longer.

She came into palace service at twenty, in the old king's reign, as a junior clerk of the Envoys' Hall, and she rose the way water rises, quietly and everywhere at once. Queen Aveline made her Mistress of the Hall fourteen years ago, two years into the reign. Melisende has never married. She says the Hall has guests enough for any family.

docs.title: The Hall
docs.text:
The Envoys' Hall is a long wing of the palace with a dining room, a garden court and a set of rooms for every town, each furnished the way that town likes it. Melisende runs it like a household and like a negotiation, which she says are the same thing. She seats envoys at supper so that the right people quarrel early and the wrong people never meet before noon. She knows which disputes are really about trade and which are about someone's grandmother. When two towns fall out over trade, the queen sends for her, and Melisende tells her, in a few calm sentences, what each side actually wants, which is very rarely what it says.

Aveline listens to everyone to the end and then decides in one sentence. Melisende says the sentence is usually the one nobody else thought to say, and she means it as the highest compliment she has. Privately she believes the queen is the best listener she has ever served, and she would rather lose an argument than tell her so.

docs.title: Petronella
docs.text: Her closest friend in the palace is Petronella, the Royal Scribe, who copies every royal letter and decree into the palace books. They take supper together most weeks in the garden court, after the envoys have gone in. Melisende tells Petronella which envoy said what and why; Petronella tells Melisende which words in the treaty letters mean more than they seem to, and uses a great many long ones doing it. Melisende is the only person in the palace who never corrects Petronella's vocabulary and the only one who knows about the history she is secretly writing.

docs.title: What has changed
docs.text:
The quarrels have grown smaller lately. Towns that used to argue over the price of wool now argue over who will guard the carts that carry it, and then agree to share the cost. Melisende takes it as a sign of how much the kingdom holds together, and also as a sign of what it is holding together against. What worries her is the empty chairs: envoys who are late back from their home towns because the roads are slow, and messages that arrive with the seals cracked from rough travel.

What she wants is a Hall with every room full on the same night, which has not happened in some years. What she fears is the quarrel that cannot be settled over supper.

A quest might begin with an envoy who should have arrived a week ago and has not, or with Melisende needing a traveller to carry a gift to another town that must arrive before the envoy who is carrying the complaint.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aveline: queen she advises
  • Petronella: friend

docs.title: Merrick
docs.text:
Caravan Master

Town Selsior Where Selsior Gate Role Worker Age Adult In the game Merrick

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Loud, calculating and loyal to his crew. He prices danger like any other cargo.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Merrick is fifty-two, a caravan master, and you can hear him before you see him. He arrives at the Selsior Gate at the head of a line of wagons, standing on the box of the first one, shouting at the oxen, the drivers, the gate guards and the weather in roughly that order. He is loud, calculating and fiercely loyal to his crew, and he prices danger exactly the way he prices salt, wool or cider: by the weight, by the distance, and by how much worse it has got since last season.

docs.title: Up from the driver's bench
docs.text:
He started on the roads at twelve, as a boy who walked beside the oxen of somebody else's wagon and was paid in suppers. He learned the royal roads a mile at a time: every ford, every hill that breaks an axle, every inn that waters its beer. In those years he often shared a fire with a carter who hauled goods between the capital and the other towns with two small sons on the bench beside him. The carter is long dead. One of the sons is Edric, now Lieutenant of the Road Patrol, and Merrick still tells him he was a dreadful child who threw stones at the horses.

By twenty-five Merrick had his own wagon; by thirty-five he had six, and a name among the merchants of the Crown Market as the man who delivered on the day he said he would. He has kept that name for seventeen years, and he guards it harder than any cargo.

docs.title: The crew
docs.text:
Merrick's crew is the closest thing he has to a family, and he treats it like one: badly fed when the road is long, loudly scolded, and defended to the last breath against anyone else who tries it. His drivers have been with him for years, and the oldest of them taught him to grease an axle. He has never married. He says no woman alive would put up with a man who leaves for a month at a time and comes back smelling of oxen, and that the oxen, at least, do not complain about it.

When he is in the capital he sleeps at the Gate Inn, where Hamon keeps his old room at the back and sets his supper on the table before he has finished shouting at the oxen. Merrick reads Hamon's board of road stories by the door before he reads anything else, and he adds to it most times he comes in.

docs.title: Pricing danger
docs.text:
In his first years the worst thing on the roads was weather. Then it was wolves in a hard winter. Now it is everything, and it is every season. Merrick has watched the danger grow the way a merchant watches prices, and he has done what a merchant does: he has charged for it. Every load he carries now has a line for guards, and he pays them well, because he has to. Fighters who can hold a road are scarce, the Guard cannot be everywhere, and the ones who are good know exactly what they are worth.

He hires anyone capable, from any town, and he judges a fighter in one look: how they stand, how they carry their pack, and whether they look at the wagons or at the trees. He has never yet lost a driver. He has had guards hurt, and he paid every one of them in full for the season, which he will tell you was simple good business, and which was not.

Edric is his great friend, and they have shared more fires on the road than either can count. They argue cheerfully about whether the patrol should guard the caravans or the caravans should guard themselves. Both know the true answer: there are not enough swords for either.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Merrick wants to make one more run than the roads can stop him making, every season, until he is too old to stand on the box. What he fears is the day he has to tell a merchant that a load cannot be carried at any price, because that will be the day the roads have won.

A quest might begin with Merrick hiring guards for a run he will not explain, at twice his usual rate, or with one of his wagons coming in through the gate with its driver and its oxen safe and its cargo gone, and the driver unable to say what took it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hamon: innkeeper
  • Edric: friend

docs.title: Mirabel
docs.text:
Dancer

Town Selsior Where Plaza Role Performer Age Young In the game Mirabel

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Dreamy, light-hearted and impossible to hurry. She dances for the pleasure of it, and the coins are a bonus.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Mirabel is twenty-two, a dancer of the plaza, and she has never once been on time for anything except dusk. Every evening, as the light goes gold over Selsior and Baldwin crosses the plaza with his ladder, she comes to the Great Bell, slips off her shoes and begins to dance. She dances for the pleasure of it, and the coins are a bonus. She is dreamy, light-hearted and impossible to hurry, and the plaza, which hurries at everything, slows down to watch her.

docs.title: Born on the road
docs.text:
She was born on the road, to a company of travelling players who carried their stage in two wagons from town to town, and she learned to dance on the boards of it before she could talk properly. The company came to Selsior when she was six, for Queen Aveline's coronation, and set up at the edge of the plaza with half the kingdom. Mirabel was on her mother's shoulders when the Great Bell rang. She remembers the whole crowd going quiet, and the sound going through her like warm water, and she remembers thinking that she had never heard anything so beautiful and would very much like to hear it again.

At fifteen, when the players came back through the capital, she told them she was staying. Her parents still tour the towns with the company, and they send word when they can, but they play no part in her days. Mirabel rents a room up three flights of stairs off the plaza, with a window that looks at the Bell.

docs.title: Dusk at the Bell
docs.text:
Fulke, the ballad singer, plays his lute for her every evening once Baldwin has lit the lamps around the dais. They have played the plaza together for years, and he has learned to follow her rather than lead, faster when she spins and slower when she drifts. Mab, the pie seller's daughter, copies her spins and falls over, and Mirabel laughs and shows her how to fix her eyes on one spot so the world stops turning. Baldwin lights the dais lamps last, and Mirabel always dances one turn for him as the final flame catches.

Then there is Hugh, the Warden of the Great Bell, who stands beside it from dawn to dusk with his hands behind his back.

docs.title: The Bell that sings
docs.text:
Mirabel swears the Bell sings at dusk when the wind is kind. Not every evening: only when the wind comes softly across the plaza as the light goes. Then, she says, there is a note under everything, faint and sweet, like the Bell remembering how it rang. She tells travellers that it rings when the wind is kind, and she uses the word on purpose, because she knows what it does to Hugh. He tells her, every time, that the Bell has not rung since the coronation, that it rings for a crowning and for nothing else, and that the wind makes a great many noises. They have argued about it, happily, for years. She thinks it is the best conversation in Selsior.

She does not know what she hears. She has wondered whether it is the wind on the Bell's lip, or the metal of the four peoples remembering the treaty, or simply the city itself. Selsior never sleeps, she likes to say; it only hums. Fulke has written a verse about the Bell humming at dusk, and when he sings it his voice does not go up the way it does when he is lying, and Mirabel loves him for it.

On still evenings she hears nothing at all, over the lute and the crowd and her own feet on the stones, and she has always taken that as proof that it is the wind that wakes the Bell. It has never occurred to her that Hugh, who stands closer to it than anyone, might be listening on those evenings too.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Mirabel wants to hear the Bell ring properly one more time, and to dance to it. What she fears, though it is a light fear and she does not keep it long, is that one evening the wind will be kind and there will be nothing to hear.

A quest might begin with Mirabel asking a traveller to stand on the far side of the Bell at dusk and tell her whether they hear it too, or with an evening when she hears the note and the wind is not blowing at all.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hugh: friend and sparring partner in argument
  • Fulke: musician who plays for her

docs.title: Mirel
docs.text:
Apothecary

Town Selsior Where Crown Market Sells Potions, tonics and cures In the game Mirel

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Prudence: rival
  • Rosalind: herb supplier

docs.title: Morwen
docs.text:
Teacher of Magic

Town Selsior Where Scholars' Quarter Role Scholar Age Adult In the game Morwen

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Intense, precise and impatient with showing off. She believes magic is mostly patience.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Morwen is fifty-four and teaches young mages at the Royal Academy, and the first thing she tells every new class is that magic is mostly patience. The second thing she tells them, usually within the hour, is to stop showing off. She is intense, precise and impatient with anything flashy, and her students are a little afraid of her for about a year, after which the good ones discover that she is the best teacher in the Scholars' Quarter and the rest discover that she remembers everything.

docs.title: An old Magician family
docs.text:
Her family has been in Selsior since the Academy was founded by the city's first Magicians, or so the family says; Morwen, who is precise about such things, points out that nobody can prove it and that it hardly matters. What the family did keep, for certain, is a habit of collecting. For generations they gathered whatever survived of the old Magician craft from the Balrog War: notes, fragments of spells, half-copied diagrams, letters that mention a working and then break off. Her grandmother Eluned, who raised her, kept them in a chest at the foot of her bed and read them aloud to Morwen as other grandmothers read stories. Morwen grew up knowing the shape of the seal-craft before she knew her letters, and knowing just as early that most of it was missing.

Eluned died when Morwen was twenty-six, the year Morwen began teaching at the Academy, twenty-eight years ago. The chest is in Morwen's rooms now, and it is a great deal fuller than it was. She has no husband and no children; she has the chest, her classes and the work.

docs.title: The work
docs.text:
Morwen studies the old seal-craft, the Magician arts that went into weaving the seal over the Balrog at the foot of the World Tree. Nobody alive has seen that seal made, and the records are scattered, fragmentary and frequently written by people who expected their readers to know the parts they left out. She is trying to put them back together, one piece at a time, in the hope that someone will one day need it. She does not know how the seal was finished, or how it might be mended, and she says so plainly to anyone who asks. She does know more than anyone else in Selsior about how it was begun, and lately she has noticed that more people are asking.

She reads the Magician accounts of the Balrog, the ones that call it something like a wound in the world, and she does not say whether she believes them. What she will say is that a wound is a thing that can reopen, and that the news from the roads, and the rumours of warnings from Cavelor, have made her work feel less like history every year.

docs.title: Teacher and friend
docs.text:
Her oldest friend is Bartholomew, the Master of the Academy, who has known her since she was a young teacher with very firm opinions and who still answers her questions with better questions, which she finds infuriating and has come to rely on. They argue over supper about once a week and would each defend the other to the death.

Her present despair is Everard, who came from a harbour town, sleeps through her lectures, spends his evenings on Theatre Row and passes every exam she sets him. She is convinced he could be a great mage if he tried. She is not wrong, and she has not yet understood that this is exactly what frightens him.

Her old regret is Constance, who studied under her for five years and was the most careful student she ever had, and who left in her final year to take up the road. Morwen told her at the door that she would be back for the books one day. Constance comes back to borrow them fairly often. Morwen lends them every time and has never once said she is glad to see her, which Constance, being clever, understands perfectly.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with a fragment missing from Morwen's chest, the one piece of seal-craft she has never shown anyone. Or it might begin with Rosamund of the Gilded Stage arriving at her door, wanting to learn how a Magician really moves when she casts, and Morwen, against every instinct, deciding to teach her.

docs.text:
• Bartholomew: old friend
  • Everard: student
  • Constance: former student
