docs.title: Osbert
docs.text:
Royal Steward

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Official Age Elder In the game Osbert

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Precise, dry and secretly sentimental. He can tell how many candles burned last night by sniffing the hall.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Osbert is sixty-nine, the Royal Steward, and he can tell how many candles burned in the great hall last night by sniffing the air in it this morning. He is usually right to within two. He runs the palace household: its kitchens and cellars, its linen and silver, its pages and maids, its fires, its accounts, its locks. He has done so for thirty-four years, longer than Queen Aveline has worn the crown, and there is no spoon in the palace and very few secrets whose whereabouts he does not know.

docs.title: Up from the boot room
docs.text:
He came to the palace at fourteen as a boot boy, in the early years of King Bertram's long reign, and he has never lived anywhere else since. He polished boots, then silver, then carried trays, then kept the cellar book, and he learned the household the way other people learn a language, from the bottom up. When old Steward Hamlyn died thirty-four years ago, the old king gave Osbert the great ring of keys, and Osbert has carried it ever since. The palace staff who served Bertram still call him "the old king", and Osbert does too, but it was Osbert who stood at the back of the plaza when the Great Bell rang sixteen years ago, and Osbert who saw to it that the new queen's household was ready for her before she had finished being crowned.

Aveline trusts him with keys she would give to no one else, and he knows it. He has never married. When anyone asks, he says the household is the only family that has ever needed him to count its spoons.

docs.title: The household
docs.text:
Osbert is precise and dry, and his praise is so rare that the staff treasure it. Cuthbert, the royal cook, shouts at the pots and sings to the bread, and Osbert has spent years trying to make him do neither in the presence of envoys. He has failed, and secretly he is glad. Agnes, the maid who cleans the upper halls, hears everything and repeats only half of it, which in Osbert's view is still half too much. Peterkin, the page, runs everywhere, and Osbert has told him a hundred times that a royal messenger walks, and has never once meant it.

He is secretly sentimental. In a drawer of his desk he keeps the menu from the coronation feast, a beetle in a jar that Alaric once gave him as a present, and a list in his own hand of every person who has served in the household in his time, with the date each one left.

docs.title: The keys and the secrets
docs.text:
The thing Osbert wants most is to retire. He would like a small room with a window and nobody to count anything for. But retiring means handing the keys to someone, and he has not yet found a person he trusts with all of them. He has trained under-stewards. They have been honest and hard-working and not quite enough.

Part of the trouble is that the keys open more than doors. Osbert knows things. He knows that someone has been drawing the bolt of the little door in the kitchen garden wall before dawn, most mornings, and sliding it back by breakfast. He knows whose boots come back muddy. He has said nothing to anyone, telling himself that it is not a lie if nobody asks him, and that he is not quite sure. He is quite sure. He also knows what is, or is not, behind the tapestries in the throne hall, and when Prince Alaric asks him, he raises an eyebrow and says nothing at all, which he knows is the most tormenting answer available.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text:
Osbert fears the day he is asked a direct question about that garden door. He fears, too, being the steward who handed the keys to the wrong person, and so he keeps carrying them, and his knees get older.

A quest might begin with a key missing from Osbert's ring for the first time in thirty-four years, or with the old steward quietly testing someone to see whether they could be trusted with it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aveline: queen he serves
  • Cuthbert: cook
  • Agnes: maid
  • Peterkin: page

docs.title: Osmund
docs.text:
Ferryman

Town Selsior Where Riverside Role Worker Age Elder In the game Osmund

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Silent, weathered and wise about water. He speaks mostly in nods.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Osmund is seventy, the ferryman of the Riverside, and he has poled the ferry across the river since he was a boy of twelve. In fifty-eight years he has said, by his daughter's count, perhaps a thousand words to his passengers, most of them "mind the edge". He speaks mostly in nods. There is a nod for "get in", a nod for "sit down", a nod for "you are welcome" and a nod for "that will be a copper, and I can see you have one". The Riverside folk understand every one of them. Strangers learn fast.

docs.title: The river's man
docs.text:
His father kept the ferry before him, and taught him the way Osmund later taught his own daughter: by doing it in front of him until he could do it himself. Osmund knows the river better than anyone alive. He knows where it runs deep and where it lies, where the current pulls left under a calm skin, how it smells before rain and how it looks the morning before a flood. He reads it the way a scholar reads a book, all the way through and then again.

In the years when the ferry did not keep him busy, he fished as well, with a set of heavy nets he mended so many times that hardly a knot of the first ones is left. When his hands grew too stiff for the nets, he gave them to his daughter Agatha, and she mends them every evening on the step of the house, as he did. He still sits beside her while she does it, watching her fingers, and now and then he reaches over and pulls one knot tighter. That is the whole of his advice, and she takes it.

His wife Edda died twenty-two years ago, when Agatha was fifteen. After that it was the two of them on the water every day, and Osmund, who had never needed words much, found he needed even fewer with a daughter who could read his face. Agatha does the talking for both of them now, and she married Silas, who talks for everyone. Osmund approves of him with a nod he does not give to many.

docs.title: The family
docs.text:
His grandson Robin is nine, a mudlark, and the only person who claims to understand every one of Osmund's nods. Osmund lets him ride the ferry for nothing and steer it in the shallows. Last spring Robin dug an old badge out of the mud below the ferry landing and brought it to his grandfather, and Osmund looked at it for a long time and nodded once. Robin says that meant "put it somewhere safe". Osmund has never said what else it meant, if anything.

Aldith the herb wife rubs mint and comfrey salve into his stiff hands, and he nods his thanks, which from Osmund is a speech. Lucan the bargemaster hails the ferry in a voice that carries to both banks every time he passes, and Osmund lifts one hand from the pole in answer, as he has for twenty years.

docs.title: After dark
docs.text:
Osmund no longer crosses after dark. He stopped last summer, and he has not said why, not to Agatha, not to Aldith, not to anyone.

This is why. One evening at the end of last summer, crossing late with the light going, he felt the ferry lift under him in the deep channel, a hand's breadth, slowly, and settle again, as if something very long had passed beneath it without touching. Then a wake crossed the river ahead of him, against the current, with nothing at the head of it. He has seen things in the deep water before and since: shadows where no shadow should be, the surface bulging and smoothing over in still weather. He does not know what any of it is. He is sure only that it was not there when he was young.

He has not told his family because he does not know what to tell them, and Osmund does not speak unless he knows. But he watched Agatha's nets come up torn this spring, and he watched her move her fishing into the shallows without being asked, and he nodded.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Osmund wants to pole the ferry until the day he cannot lift the pole, and then to hand it on to someone who will listen to the river. What he fears is the deep channel, and the day Robin decides he is old enough to find out what is in it.

A quest might begin with Osmund, for the first time anyone can remember, asking someone he trusts to cross with him after dark, or with the ferry found one morning drifting in the middle of the river with its pole gone.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Agatha: daughter
  • Robin: grandson

docs.title: Percival
docs.text:
Leading Man

Town Selsior Where Theatre Row Role Performer Age Adult In the game Percival

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Dashing, pompous and a better actor than person, though he is working on it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Percival is forty-one, the leading man of the Gilded Stage, and he enters every room as if it had been waiting for him, which, on Theatre Row, it usually has. He is tall, golden-voiced and dashing, with a jaw made for posters and a cloak he swirls without seeming to notice. He is also pompous, vain and capable of talking about himself for an entire supper without once asking how anyone else is. He is a better actor than he is a person. The difference between Percival and most people with that fault is that he knows it, and that for the last few years he has been quietly, clumsily trying to close the gap.

docs.title: Every hero on the Row
docs.text: He came to Theatre Row at seventeen, the son of a ropemaker from the inner streets (both his parents are dead now), with a good voice, no money and a conviction that he was meant for great parts. For six years he carried spears, died in the first act and understudied everybody. Then a leading man on the Row broke his ankle on a staircase, and Percival went on as the hero that night and never went back to the spears. He has since played every hero the Row has ever written: kings and princes, lost heirs, bandit chiefs with good hearts, and at least three different founders of the kingdom. He came to the Gilded Stage thirteen years ago, when Lavinia lured him away from a rival house with the promise of the best parts in the city. She kept the promise. He has never let her forget that she made it.

docs.title: Rosamund
docs.text:
Ten years ago Lavinia cast him opposite Rosamund for the first time. They disagreed about one entrance in the first rehearsal, and they have been quarrelling ever since, on stage and off it, in the wings, in the dressing-room corridor and once, memorably, in a curtain call. The audiences love it. They come to watch the two of them fall in love on stage while knowing perfectly well they can barely share a staircase, and Lavinia sells tickets on it shamelessly. Tibb, the flyman, arranges every play so that they exit on opposite sides, and carries their messages to each other slowly and slightly edited.

What nobody would believe is that Percival thinks Rosamund is the finest actress he has ever worked with, and that the quarrel is the only way he has ever found of keeping up with her. He has never told her. Nor has he ever been told what she privately thinks of him, which is much the same.

docs.title: The Savage warrior
docs.text:
Crispin is writing a play of the whole Balrog War, and Percival wants one part in it more than he has ever wanted anything: the play's Savage warrior, who stands for the whole front line that held the Balrog at the Tree for days so the Magicians could weave the seal. He has read every account of the Last Stand that the Academy will lend an actor, and has found that none of them agree. He has been running up the Row's stairs before breakfast to build his chest, and has twice been to the plaza to watch the Midbarium envoys walk, to learn how a highlander stands.

The trouble is that Rosamund wants to play the play's Magician, who stands for the Magicians who wove the seal, will not share a stage with him, and Crispin cannot see how to write the Last Stand without both. Percival has, for the first time in his life, considered asking Rosamund what she would need from him to make it work. He has not yet done it. He is working on it.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Percival wants to play the warrior so well that the audience forgets, for one night, that he is Percival. What he fears is that they never will.

A quest might begin with Percival wanting someone to find him a real highland warrior's account of the Last Stand, or with an anonymous gift in his dressing room that looks very much like it came from Rosamund.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Rosamund: rival

docs.title: Perrin
docs.text:
Royal Courier

Town Selsior Where Plaza Role Official Age Young In the game Perrin

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fast-talking, self-important and always in a hurry. Letters wait for no one, and neither does he.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "No time to talk," says Perrin, already past you. "Letters wait for no one." He is twenty-one, the Royal Courier, and he is always in a hurry, even when he is standing still on the plaza with his satchel on his hip, rocking on his heels as if the road might leave without him. He is fast-talking, self-important and very sure of his place in the order of things, which is, in his opinion, somewhere just below the queen and well above anyone who is in his way. "Out of my way," he calls across the plaza. "Official business." Usually it is.

docs.title: Letters for every town
docs.text:
Perrin carries the crown's letters to every town in the kingdom: up into the dry highlands of Midbarium, out to both harbours, down the Royal Road to Kaldemor, to Urbanograd and its arguments, and even to the World Tree. He will tell anyone who asks, and most who do not, which towns he has letters for today, and he always ends with the one for the World Tree, because it sounds best. He does not read the letters. He would like that to be clearly understood. He knows the seals, though, and he has carried some he is very proud to have carried, and he walks a little taller on the days the queen's own seal is in his satchel.

He calls himself the fastest courier in the kingdom, and he has the blisters to prove it, from saddle and boot alike, since the highland trails are walked as often as ridden; he will show you the blisters if you are not quick. He grew up in the city's inner streets, the son of a wheelwright and a laundress who have since moved to a village down the river and write to ask when he is going to visit. He ran messages for anyone who would pay him from the age of eight, and at seventeen, four years ago, he talked his way into the royal couriers by delivering a letter to the palace that nobody had asked him to carry, faster than the courier who had. He has been insufferable about it ever since.

docs.title: Tilda
docs.text: His cousin Tilda, who drives the Selsior cab from the gate stand, is a good deal older than he is and a good deal less impressed. She tells everyone, fondly, that she can read from the mud on his boots exactly which roads he took, and that he takes the long way round far more often than he admits. He has asked her to stop. She has not. The worst of it is that she is right.

docs.title: The long way
docs.text:
The roads are not what they were, and Perrin knows it better than almost anyone, because he has ridden all of them. Stretches he used to gallop he now goes round. He knows where the wolves have moved, which bridge the boars have taken to sleeping under, and which bend of which highland trail has a thing on it he does not describe. Lately the royal couriers ride out with guards, by order of the Knights' Court, and Perrin grumbles about it at length: the guards are slow, the guards stop for lunch, the guards want to camp before dark. He grumbles less than he did. On one ride, which he does not talk about, he was glad of them.

Peterkin, the palace page, wants to be a courier when he grows up, and watches Perrin mount up in the plaza as if he were a hero in a play. Perrin pretends not to notice. He has started telling Peterkin, in a voice of great importance, which way the wind is blowing, which is the first thing he ever learned on the roads.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Perrin wants to be the courier who gets through when no one else can, and to be thanked for it, loudly, by name. What he fears is the letter he cannot deliver, and having to come back to the plaza with it still sealed in his satchel.

Perrin also teaches Courier's Stride, the short burst of running speed every royal courier learns in their first week, to anyone who can keep pace with him from the palace steps to the gate and back without dropping a letter.

A quest might begin with Perrin, for once, asking someone to carry a letter for him on a road he will not take, or with a letter in his satchel that he is certain he never picked up.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Tilda: cousin

docs.title: Peterkin
docs.text:
Palace Page

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Child Age Child In the game Peterkin

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Eager, breathless and proud of his uniform. He runs everywhere, even when nobody is waiting.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Peterkin is eleven, a page of the palace, and he has not walked anywhere since he was given his uniform. He runs. He runs with messages and he runs without them, down the long gallery, up the back stairs two at a time and round corners so fast that the maids have learned to carry their trays high. He is eager, breathless and enormously proud of his uniform, a blue coat with brass buttons that he polishes every night and that has been let out twice at the sleeves.

docs.title: Into the palace
docs.text:
He comes from a farm a few days' walk down the river, the third of a large family. His parents still keep it, and they write to him through the steward's office at harvest and midwinter, but they play no part in his days. When he was nine a carter brought him up to the palace with a letter from the village and a clean shirt, because the household needed pages and Peterkin needed, his mother said, somewhere big enough to run in. Osbert, the Royal Steward, read the letter, looked at the boy for some time, and said, "We shall see." Peterkin has been trying to prove that he saw correctly ever since.

Osbert has told him a hundred times that a royal messenger walks. He has never once meant it, and Peterkin knows. The steward's praise is so rare that the staff count it, and Peterkin has received it exactly twice: once for carrying a message to the Envoys' Hall in the middle of a storm without letting the seal get wet, and once for something he did not do, which he has decided not to mention.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
He carries messages inside the palace from the first bell to the last: notes from the kitchens to the steward's office, letters from Melisende's Envoys' Hall to Petronella's copying room, summonses from the queen's study to anyone at all. He is not allowed to read them and he does not, but he has become very good at guessing from the hand, the seal and the face of the person who gives them to him. He tells Agnes, the upper-halls maid, the guesses, and she pays him in biscuits from her father's kitchen and pays him extra for anything he guesses right.

He is up before almost anyone. He likes the palace at first light, when the corridors are empty and the only sound is the clock tower getting ready to strike, and he likes to be the first boy at the steward's door in case the day's first message is an important one.

docs.title: The race and the passage
docs.text:
His great friend is Prince Alaric, who is two years younger and asks why about everything. When Peterkin is not running messages, the two of them race the clock tower bells: from the cellars to the roof while the hour strikes, which Peterkin can now do with one stroke to spare and Alaric cannot do at all yet, though he has worked out three shortcuts and is sure of a fourth. They also practise listening at doors, which they call training.

Alaric has told him about the secret passage behind the throne-hall tapestries, and nobody else. Peterkin has felt the draught under the tapestry and heard the hollow wall, and he has not told a soul, not even Agnes, which has been the hardest thing he has ever done.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Peterkin wants to be a royal courier and carry the crown's letters between the towns on a fast horse, all the way to the harbours and the highlands. Lately the couriers ride out with guards, and come back slower and quieter, and he has heard the grown-ups say the roads are not what they were. He still wants it. What he fears is being told he is too small for it, and, more quietly, the day a courier does not come back.

A quest might begin with Peterkin trusted with a message that must not be delivered to the person it is addressed to, or with Peterkin and Alaric finding, one morning, that the draught under the throne-hall tapestry has stopped.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Osbert: employer
  • Alaric: friend

docs.title: Petronella
docs.text:
Royal Scribe

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Scholar Age Adult In the game Petronella

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Neat, serious and fond of long words. She corrects other people's spelling out of kindness.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Petronella is thirty-eight, the Royal Scribe, and she has the finest handwriting in Wonder Kingdom. This is not a boast. It is, as she would put it, an incontrovertible observation, attested by every person who has ever received a royal decree. She is neat, serious and fond of long words, and she corrects other people's spelling out of pure kindness, in the gentle voice of someone pointing out that your cloak has caught in a door.

docs.title: The north-lit room
docs.text:
She grew up in the Scholars' Quarter, the daughter of a clerk at the Academy and a schoolmistress, both dead now, in a house where every flat surface had paper on it. At fourteen she went to the back room of the Academy's great library, the cold one with the good north light, where Benedict the Head Librarian trains the copyists and scribes the palace needs. He made her copy the same page forty times before he let her touch a second one. She did not mind. She liked the page.

Benedict says she was the best pupil he ever had, and he says it in a hushed voice as if it might disturb the books. She still sends him her finest pages, and he still finds one letter on each to correct. Neither of them would give up the custom for anything.

She came to the palace as a junior copyist at nineteen, in the last years of the old king's reign, and has been Royal Scribe for nine years. She never married. She says she is already wedded to a great many books, and that they are better at keeping their promises.

docs.title: The palace books
docs.text:
Petronella copies every royal letter and decree into the palace books: great leather-bound volumes, one for each year, ruled by hand and kept in a locked press in her copying room. Proclamations, trade settlements, Guard commissions, letters of thanks and letters of complaint, all go through her pen before they go out under the seal. She reads each one twice before she copies it and once after. She notices everything, and repeats nothing, which is why Queen Aveline lets her copy the letters she does.

Peterkin brings her most of her work at a run, and she has given up asking him to slow down and asks him only to wipe his hands. Her dearest friend is Melisende, Mistress of the Envoys' Hall, who never raises her voice and never loses an argument. They take supper together most weeks, and Melisende tells her what the envoys said in the room, and Petronella tells Melisende what the envoys' letters said afterwards, which is often quite different.

docs.title: The history
docs.text:
Petronella has a secret, and only Melisende knows it. She is writing a history of her own.

It began as notes in the margins of her own commonplace book: a decree here, a date there, a letter from a town about wolves on a road, then about worse than wolves. Over nine years of copying she has watched the palace books change. The letters about trade and festivals have grown thinner. The letters about roads, patrols, guards and wounds have grown thicker. Nobody else reads all of them. Petronella does, and she has realised that she is holding a record of the Age of Disturbance as it happens, written by the people living through it, and that nobody else in the kingdom has one quite like it.

She has filled three notebooks. She does not yet know how the history ends, and she has begun to be afraid that she is not the one who will write the last chapter. She would like very much to talk to Thomasin, the historian, and to Benedict about the missing volume of the Aristocrat chronicles, which he lost the year after she left his back room for the palace and has been searching for ever since. She has not done either, because a scribe who writes history is getting above herself, and she is not yet brave enough to be.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Petronella wants her history read, and her name on the spine, written in her own hand. What she fears is a decree she cannot bring herself to copy.

A quest might begin with a page missing from one of the palace books, cut out cleanly with a blade, or with Petronella needing someone to carry a question to another town's archive that she cannot ask in a royal letter.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Melisende: friend
  • Benedict: former teacher

docs.title: Piers
docs.text:
Pie Seller

Town Selsior Where Plaza Sells Meat pies, apple pasties and hot cider In the game Piers

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Mab: daughter

docs.title: Pim
docs.text:
Recruit

Town Selsior Where Knights' Court Role Guard Age Young In the game Pim

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Keen, clumsy and endlessly cheerful. He asks for one more round of drills even when he can barely stand.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Pim is sixteen, a recruit of the Royal Guard, and the most cheerful person in the Knights' Court by a distance nobody has bothered to measure. The Guard takes recruits from the age of sixteen, and Pim was at the gate of the Court at dawn on his sixteenth birthday this spring, before the drill sergeant was awake, with a bundle of clothes and a speech he had been practising for two years. He forgot most of the speech. They let him in anyway.

docs.title: Where he comes from
docs.text: Pim grew up in the old quarters with his grandmother Gisela, who raised him after his parents died of a winter fever when he was a baby. She kept a little stall that mended pots and kettles, and she was cheerful in the same unstoppable way Pim is; he says he learned it from her, along with how to whistle and how to fix a dented pan. She died two winters ago. Pim does not talk about it much. He talks about the Guard instead, which he says is the biggest family in the city, and which he joined so that he would never again come home to a quiet house.

docs.title: Recruit Pim, reporting
docs.text:
He salutes everyone, just in case: captains, sergeants, the stablemaster, visiting envoys, the cook from the palace, and once, memorably, a statue. In his first week, flustered at meeting Captain Rhys in a doorway, he saluted smartly and told the Captain to stand at ease. Rhys did, gravely, and the whole Court heard about it by supper. Pim still introduces himself to strangers with a salute and a slightly worried look, as if he is about to make the same mistake again, and occasionally he does.

He is keen and clumsy in about equal measure. He trips over his own scabbard, drops his helmet in drill and puts his feet in the wrong place on every third cut. But he has never once asked to stop. When everyone else is sitting down, Pim is asking for one more round of drills, even when he can barely stand, and Drill Sergeant Bertrand, who swears he can turn anyone into a guard given a year and enough porridge, has quietly decided that Pim is going to test that claim to its limits. Bertrand bellows at him more than at anyone else. Pim considers this an honour.

Captain Rhys says Pim's guard is full of holes. Pim has written the remark down and pinned it above his bunk, and every evening he works on closing one of them.

docs.title: Friends and rivals
docs.text:
His best friend is Tobe, who read every book on swordsmanship in the Scholars' Quarter before he came to the Court and is still stuck on the third cut. Tobe knows the manual by heart and Pim knows nothing by heart, so they help each other: Tobe tells Pim what he is doing wrong, and Pim makes Tobe laugh when the third cut goes wrong again. They share a bench at supper and a great deal of porridge.

His rival is Avice, who walked down from the highlands to try the trials and means to be the first of their year to earn the Swordsman's rank. Avice is fierce, proud and better than Pim at nearly everything, and she trains harder when anyone is watching. Pim has decided that the best way to beat her is to watch her as often as possible. Avice has not yet worked out whether this is strategy or friendliness, and to be fair, neither has Pim.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Pim wants the Swordsman's rank, and after it a place on the road patrol, riding out with the lieutenant and the older guards to keep the roads open. He fears very little, which is part of the problem. What he does fear is being sent home: being told, kindly, that the Guard is not for him.

A quest might begin with Pim asking a passing traveller to drill with him after hours, or with him volunteering, far too early, for a patrol nobody wants.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rhys: captain
  • Tobe: friend
  • Avice: rival
  • Bertrand: drill sergeant

docs.title: Prudence
docs.text:
Alchemist

Town Selsior Where Scholars' Quarter Role Craftsman Age Adult Sells Alchemical reagents, inks and powders In the game Prudence

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Methodical, prickly and proud. Her eyebrows have grown back twice.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Prudence is thirty-six, the alchemist of the Scholars' Quarter, and her eyebrows have grown back twice. The first time was an accident with a copper salt. The second time, she maintains, was a successful experiment that happened to be louder than expected. She is methodical, prickly and proud, with ink on her cuffs, a burn scar across the back of one hand and no patience at all for anyone who says "near enough". In her trade, she says, near enough is how roofs come off.

docs.title: The workshop
docs.text:
Her workshop is the ground floor of a tall, thin house in a lane behind the Academy, with a furnace at the back, shelves of stoppered jars to the ceiling, every one of them labelled in her small, upright hand, and a chalk line on the floor that visitors are not permitted to cross. She lives in the two rooms above, which smell, like everything she owns, faintly of sulphur and lavender.

She brews reagents and inks for the Royal Academy: the powders the masters use in their demonstrations, the salts for the students' practical lessons, and the inks that the Academy's copyists and the palace's scribes swear by, a black that never fades and a red that never runs. She learned her craft as an apprentice to an old Academy alchemist, a woman with no eyebrows at all, who took her on at fifteen and left her the furnace and the jars when she died nine years ago. Prudence has kept the workshop alone since. Her own parents, a schoolmaster and his wife, are long dead. She has never married, and says no one would want to live above that furnace, which is true.

docs.title: Mirel
docs.text:
Prudence also makes tonics, and she will tell you, with some heat, that they are better than anything sold in the Crown Market. By "anything sold in the Crown Market" she means the potions of Mirel the apothecary, whose stall does a roaring trade with adventurers on their way up the road. Mirel is brisk, cheerful and a born salesman, and Prudence considers all three of these qualities suspicious in a man who handles medicine. She says his tonics are made for the bottle and not the patient. He says hers taste like ink, which, she admits, some of them do.

Their rivalry is old and well known, and it is conducted chiefly through customers, who are told by each what the other has got wrong. They do not, in fact, disagree about very much except who is better. Neither of them would ever say so.

docs.title: The moment potion
docs.text:
What Prudence is trying to brew is a potion that heals in a moment. Not a tonic that helps a wound close over days, but one that closes it while you watch. She has read of such a thing in old accounts of the Balrog War, which may be stories, and she has seen enough hurt travellers come up the road this year to believe that the kingdom needs it whether it is a story or not. She has been working on it for three years. She has made a draught that stops bleeding and turns the drinker green for a week, and one that heals a scratch beautifully and blows out the workshop's windows while doing so.

Her neighbours are trying to get her moved. They have sent a letter to the Academy, signed by eleven households, and a second, longer one after the windows. Prudence has answered both, at length, explaining the chemistry.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Prudence wants the moment potion in a stoppered jar with her label on it, and she wants Mirel to have to buy it from her. What she fears is that it cannot be done by anyone, and that she will spend her life near enough.

A quest might begin with Prudence needing a reagent that can only be gathered somewhere monsters have moved into, or with a jar in her workshop that has started, all on its own, to glow.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Mirel: rival

docs.title: Aveline
docs.text:
Queen of Wonder Kingdom

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Ruler Age Adult In the game Aveline

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Warm, quick to laugh and very hard to fool. She listens to everyone to the end, then decides in one sentence.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
Aveline was crowned under the Great Bell sixteen years ago, at twenty-eight, and the Bell has not rung since. She is forty-four now, and she still remembers the sound of it better than anything that was said to her that day. The crowd in the plaza went quiet when it started, and stayed quiet until it stopped, and she understood then that the bell was not ringing for her but for the treaty, and that she had just been handed it to keep.

She has held to that idea ever since. The crown's task, as she likes to put it, is to keep the kingdom together, not to command it. She settles quarrels between towns, keeps the royal roads open, and speaks for Wonder Kingdom when it needs a single voice, but she will not tell Midbarium how to choose its chieftains or Bain Harbour how to run its docks, and she has refused more than one adviser who wanted her to.

docs.title: The palace and the people in it
docs.text:
Aveline came to the throne after the long reign of King Bertram, who wore the crown for forty-two years and is still called "the old king" by the palace staff who served him. She runs her court very differently. She listens to everyone to the end, from envoys to kitchen boys, and then decides in a single sentence; Melisende, who advises her whenever two towns fall out over trade, says the sentence is usually the one nobody else thought to say. Osbert, the steward, has kept the household running for longer than she has been queen, and she trusts him with keys she would not give to anyone else.

Her husband, Leofric, was a road surveyor when they met over a disputed map in the Scholars' Quarter, four years before her coronation; she said his road was in the wrong place, and he proved, politely and at length, that it was not. They married twenty years ago. His great map of the royal roads now covers a whole wall of the palace, and every week the two of them stand in front of it and watch the monster marks spread.

Their children are Elinor, nearly grown, and Alaric, who is not. Alaric brings her beetles and rumours, and she takes both seriously. Elinor worries her more. The princess has been coming to breakfast with blistered hands and a look of great innocence, and Aveline, who is very hard to fool, has noticed. She has said nothing yet. She has not decided whether she is angry, proud or simply frightened.

docs.title: Allies below and letters from afar
docs.text:
The tie Aveline guards most closely is with Cavelor. It was King Bertram who sent the Great World Tree Expedition fifty years ago, and Aveline has always felt that the crown owes the guardians beneath the Tree a debt it can never fully repay. In the first year of her reign, fifteen years ago, she went down the Upper Stair herself, the first reigning monarch to do so, walked a shift of the Deep Watch beside Marrun, the Keeper of the Oath, and swore an alliance with him in the Oath Hall. The crown promised to answer every message from below; Cavelor promised to send word of every change in the seal. Their letters have come and gone each month since, and she has been down twice more. Marrun is the person outside her family she trusts most, and she fears she is failing him, because she believes every word of his warnings and cannot make the rest of the kingdom believe them half as much.

Her other great correspondent is Rook Tallow of Urbanograd. Nine years ago Rook sent her an indignant letter about Guard patrols that stopped short of the road to Urbanograd, and she answered it herself, three pages long, agreeing with half of it. The patrols were extended the next year, and the letters never stopped. They write roughly every fortnight and argue about nearly everything: guilds, theatre, the Great Bell, whether a kingdom needs a crown at all. They have met only once, on Walkout Day six years ago, when Aveline watched Juna Marrow's play standing in the crowd and Rook found her an upturned crate to sit on. She began writing to Rook long before the Open Table made Rook its Caller, and she likes to say she writes to the person, not the post. She knows Rook reads the funniest parts aloud at the Table, and now writes a few of them on purpose.

docs.title: What keeps her awake
docs.text:
The reports from the royal roads keep her up at night. Rhys, whom she made Captain of the Guard eight years ago, has more recruits than ever and less time to train them, and Leofric's map grows more crowded each week. Her fear is not that the towns will turn on one another; she knows they will not. It is that the danger will grow faster than the kingdom's patience, and that one day Marrun will send word that cannot be answered with a letter.

A quest might begin with a sealed message from Cavelor that arrives without its messenger, or with the queen quietly asking someone she trusts to find out who is teaching her daughter the sword.

docs.text:

  • Elinor: daughter

  • Osbert: trusted steward
  • Melisende: adviser
  • Marrun: sworn ally

docs.title: Rafe
docs.text:
Puppeteer

Town Selsior Where Theatre Row Role Performer Age Adult In the game Rafe

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, clever and more expressive with his hands than his face. He speaks best through his puppets.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Rafe is forty-six, the puppeteer of Theatre Row, and he is very hard to read. His face does very little. He speaks rarely, briefly and usually to the floor. But put a puppet on his hand and everything changes: the puppet blusters, sulks, flirts, weeps, falls in love and tells the children of the Row exactly what it thinks of them, and Rafe, behind it, is suddenly the most expressive man in the city. He is quiet, clever and kind, and he has long since stopped apologising for the fact that he says what he means best through a wooden head.

docs.title: The booth
docs.text:
His booth stands in a wide doorway at the bottom of the Row, between a cookshop and a theatre's stage door: a tall striped box with a painted proscenium, a curtain that rolls up on a string, and a bench in front for the smallest children. He plays it every afternoon, and twice on festival days. His company of puppets numbers over forty, all of them carved and painted by him in the room behind the booth where he lives: a king, a queen, a baker, a dragon, a goose who is cleverer than everyone, a highland warrior, a Magician with a beard that sparks, and a great many more.

He learned the trade from an old travelling puppeteer who stopped on the Row one summer when Rafe was a boy and, when he left in the autumn, found that the boy had followed him. Rafe travelled with him for six years and settled on the Row at twenty-one, with a box of puppets the old man had given him and no words at all to say thank you. He has played the same doorway for twenty-five years. The old man is long dead, and Rafe still has his first puppet, a fox with a chipped nose, on a nail above his bed.

docs.title: Lambert
docs.text:
About twelve years ago he noticed that one boy from the rooms over a shop at the bottom of the Row was staying after every show. One afternoon, without saying a word, Rafe picked up three spare puppet heads and juggled them, and then handed them over. That was the first lesson. There were a great many after it, nearly all of them silent, and the boy is Lambert, now the best juggler in the plaza. Rafe taught him that the real trick is to make the crowd watch your face instead of your hands, which is a strange lesson from a man whose face does so little. Lambert still comes by the booth, and still brings him the first apple of every autumn.

The children of the Row are his audience and, in their way, his family. Mab, the pie seller's daughter from the plaza, has watched so many shows that she can do all the voices, and Rafe has started, without comment, leaving the stool behind the booth free for her.

docs.title: The Balrog
docs.text: His most famous puppet is the Balrog. The first one he made, for a show about the Last Stand at the Tree, was as tall as he is, with red-glass eyes and a mouth on a hinge, and the smallest children screamed until their parents carried them home. He made it smaller. The second one still made a baker's boy hide under the bench for the whole second half. He made it smaller again. The one he uses now is about the size of a cat, and it is still, the children agree, the most frightening thing on Theatre Row. Rafe does not entirely know why. He thinks that whatever he puts into it comes out of the wood whether he means it to or not.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Rafe wants a full bench every afternoon and one more pupil like Lambert before his hands grow stiff. What he fears is a child who does not laugh at the end, when the Balrog goes back into its box.

A quest might begin with the Balrog puppet going missing from its box overnight, or with Rafe asking someone to carry a message he cannot bring himself to say aloud, written in the voice of the fox.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Lambert: pupil

docs.title: Reynold
docs.text:
Warden of the Crown Market

Town Selsior Where Crown Market Role Official Age Adult In the game Reynold

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Harried, honest and allergic to shortcuts. He carries a set of weights and checks everyone's scales.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Reynold is forty-seven, the Warden of the Crown Market, and he is always slightly out of breath. The Crown Market is the busiest place on Veligor, and keeping order in it is a job for three men, so Reynold does the work of three, at a fast walk, with a frown and a heavy leather case under his arm. In the case is a set of brass weights, from a pound down to a quarter-ounce, each one stamped and checked against the palace standard. He uses them on everyone's scales. Everyone's. He is harried, honest to the bone and allergic to shortcuts, and the stallholders say, half in complaint and half in pride, that there is no market on the island with fairer weight.

docs.title: The warden's round
docs.text:
He took the post eleven years ago, when the old warden retired, and he walks the market from the opening bell to the last lamp. He settles squabbles over stall space, which are endless, and over whose awning drips on whose cheeses, which are worse. He checks scales, measures and yardsticks, chases off sellers of cracked pots and watered milk, and keeps a ledger of every complaint and how it was settled, so that when the same two stallholders come to him for the ninth time he can tell them what he decided the previous eight. He has no power to fine anyone very much. He relies instead on the fact that a stall Reynold has called short-weight in front of its customers does not do much trade for a week.

He grew up in the back streets behind the market, the son of a porter. His mother sold dried peas and beans by the scoop, and when he was nine he watched a dishonest weigher cheat her out of a winter's earnings with a doctored scale, and watched her say nothing because she could not prove it. Both his parents are dead now. He has never forgotten the scale. He has never married, either. He says he would have to check her scales and it would start them off badly.

docs.title: Wat
docs.text:
Two summers ago a thin, fast boy of nine tried for Reynold's own purse in the middle of the cloth row. Reynold caught his wrist without looking round. He had noticed the boy about the market more than once that year, too quick and too thin and never buying anything, and had half suspected, without ever catching him at it. Instead of marching him to the Guard, Reynold asked him how fast he could get a message to the far end of the market. The boy told him. Reynold timed him, and gave him a job.

That boy is Wat, who is eleven now and runs Reynold's errands: messages, measures, warnings about short weights, summonses to stallholders who are about to have a very bad afternoon. The evening he hired him, Reynold walked Wat up to Selene's forge and told his elder brother Kenric everything, because he would not keep a boy's secret from the person responsible for him. Kenric thanked him three times. Reynold found it very difficult to know what to do with that, and went home and checked his weights.

Wat now tells strangers when their purses are badly tied. Reynold has never told him how proud that makes him. He suspects Wat knows.

docs.title: What the market is saying
docs.text: Lately the market is quieter in a way Reynold does not like. Carts come in late or in convoys. Prices on goods from the far towns have jumped, not from greed, as he first suspected and checked, but from the cost of guards on the road. More stalls sell blades and potions than did five years ago, and fewer sell lace.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Reynold wants a market where every scale is true and every quarrel is settled before sundown. What he fears is someone from Wat's old days turning up in the market, and having to choose between the rules and the boy.

A quest might begin with a set of weights that read true on Reynold's scale and false on everyone else's, or with Wat failing to come back from an errand to the far end of the market.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Wat: errand boy

docs.title: Rhys
docs.text:
Captain of the Royal Guard

Town Selsior Where Knights' Court Role Guard Age Adult In the game Rhys

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Steady, demanding and fair. He believes a sword is only as good as the arm behind it, and says so often.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
Rhys came to the Knights' Court at eighteen with a borrowed sword and a great deal more confidence than skill. Aubrey, then the Guard's finest Grand Swordmaster, watched him swing for about a minute and told him he fought like a man chopping firewood. Rhys spent the next two years learning to stop, and he says he is still learning. He is forty now, a Grand Swordmaster himself these ten years, and the queen made him Captain of the Royal Guard eight years ago.

Fifteen years ago, when Queen Aveline swore her alliance with Cavelor, Rhys was a young Swordsman in the guard that escorted her down the Upper Stair, and he watched the serving Swordmasters swear the new Swordmaster's oath in the Oath Hall. When he passed the Swordmaster's trial himself, he went back down and swore it before Keeper Marrun. He still remembers the cold, the lanterns and the old Keeper's voice, and he sends every new Swordmaster down to swear it with a few plain words of warning about the stairs.

docs.title: The season with Tavi
docs.text:
The spring Rhys was nineteen, a young Uskari from the rim of Midbarium walked into the Court and asked to train. Tavi was eighteen, had left home to go adventuring, and wanted to learn what the capital's swordsmen knew that the highland hunters did not. The Guard is open to anyone who can keep up, and Aubrey, who thought both young people were too fierce for their own good, paired them together so they would wear each other down.

They did not wear each other down. From spring until the first frosts of autumn, Rhys and Tavi fought a bout every evening after drill, eighty of them in all, and they kept a tally scratched into the post of the practice yard. At the end of the season it stood at forty-one to Tavi and thirty-nine to Rhys. Tavi left the Court before the Guard's trials, took no rank and has never let Rhys forget the count. Rhys still says no one ever pushed him harder, and he means it as the highest praise he knows.

They have seen each other only a handful of times since. The last was three years ago, when Tavi came down to Selsior with a party from Midbarium and the two of them could not resist one more bout in the old yard. The bell for the recruits' drill rang before either won, and both agree the bout is unfinished; each is privately certain who would have taken it. They write once a year, around midwinter, short letters that are mostly about patrols and monsters and end, every time, with the tally.

docs.title: The Captain's day
docs.text:
Rhys is steady, demanding and fair. He believes a sword is only as good as the arm behind it, and he says so often enough that the recruits mouth it along with him. He trains the Guard's warriors in the Swordsman's way and sets the trials for every rank on the road: Swordsman, Swordmaster and Grand Swordmaster. The old books name one rank more, the Sword Saint. Rhys has never met one, and when someone reaches the point where only that test remains, he sets it with the honest admission that he is passing on something older than himself. Aubrey, retired now, claims to have found a page of the true test in an old book, and Rhys listens to him with the patience of a pupil who still owes his teacher everything.

Since the Age of Disturbance began, the Guard has had more recruits than it has ever had, and the Court is full from dawn to dark. There is Pim, who salutes everyone and whose guard is full of holes; Tobe, who read every book about swords and none about how heavy they are; and Avice, who walked down from the highlands with a stubbornness that reminds Rhys, more than he admits, of a certain Uskari. Rowena teaches the advanced classes beside him, and he trusts her judgment as he trusts his own. Ida and the night watch bring him reports from the old quarters that he does not like, including a scratching under the drains that nobody can explain.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Rhys wants more time. Every season the queen asks the Guard to patrol more of the royal roads, and every season the recruits come to him with less experience and more courage than is good for them. He fears sending someone out before they are ready, and he fears, more quietly, that one day he will have to.

He would also very much like to finish that bout.

A quest could grow from the unfinished match, a message from Tavi asking for the Guard's help on a highland trail, or Aubrey's page of the Sword Saint's test, which Rhys suspects is real.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Pim: recruit
  • Tobe: recruit
  • Avice: recruit
  • Rowena: fellow instructor
  • Aubrey: former teacher
  • Ida: night watch guard
  • Tavi: old training partner

docs.title: Robin
docs.text:
Mudlark

Town Selsior Where Riverside Role Child Age Child In the game Robin

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Curious, muddy and full of treasure. He thinks every shiny thing is a lost crown.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Robin is nine years old, a mudlark of the Riverside, and he has never met a shiny thing he did not suspect of being a lost crown. When the river runs low he is down on the bank before anyone else, barefoot, with a bucket, a bent spoon for digging and the absolute certainty that today is the day. It never quite is. He has found buttons, buckles, coins from the old king's reign, a silver thimble, three keys to nothing, and more broken crockery than anyone could want. Every single piece, for a moment, was treasure.

docs.title: A river family
docs.text:
Robin comes from a family that lives by the river and on it. His grandfather Osmund has poled the ferry across since he was a boy and speaks mostly in nods; Robin is the only person who claims to understand every one of them. His mother Agatha fishes the river with nets that were once Osmund's, and his father Silas sells her catch, and fish from both harbours besides, at a shout in the Crown Market, naming every one as he goes. Robin grew up in the boat, on the bank and under the market stall, and he smells of river most of the time and is not sorry about it.

He is curious about everything, muddy almost always and generous with his finds. His mother is cheerful in any weather and his father is cheerful in any market, and Robin is cheerful in any mud, so the house is a loud and happy one. His parents let him mudlark on two conditions: never alone at the deep end of the bank, and never after dark. The second condition is newer than the first. It came in about the time his grandfather stopped crossing after dark himself.

docs.title: The curio dealer
docs.text: Robin sells the best of his finds to Jasper, the curio dealer in the Crown Market, who sells strange inventions from Urbanograd and buys almost anything with a story attached. Jasper is excitable and talkative and a dreadful salesman, and he pays Robin a little more than the finds are worth, partly because he likes the boy and partly because he cannot resist a story. Robin, in turn, tells him exactly where each thing came out of the mud and spins the rest. They get on very well. Robin thinks Jasper's shop is the best place in the whole city, and he would very much like to see inside the one box Jasper will not open in public.

docs.title: The badge
docs.text:
Last spring, at the lowest water of the year, Robin dug an old badge out of the mud below the ferry landing. It is about the size of a large coin, heavy, crusted with river and stamped with a seal. When he had cleaned it he took it straight to Jasper, who turned it over for a long time and admitted, for perhaps the first time in his life, that he had no idea. It is not the crown's seal, nor any town's that Jasper knows, nor any guild's. Osmund looked at it and nodded once, which Robin says meant "put it somewhere safe".

So Robin did. He keeps it under his pillow, and he has not sold it, though Jasper has made him two offers. He is sure it belonged to someone important. On some nights he is sure it is the start of a lost crown. On others, when the river is loud, he is less sure he wants to know.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Robin wants to find something that really matters, and to be the one who knows what it is. What he fears, though he would not say so, is the deep water. His mother's nets have been coming up torn, his grandfather will not cross at night, and Robin has started to watch the river the way they do.

A quest might begin with someone recognising the seal on Robin's badge, or with Robin finding a second one.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Jasper: buyer
  • Osmund: grandfather
  • Agatha: mother
  • Silas: father

docs.title: Roland
docs.text:
Retired Adventurer

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Adventurer Age Elder In the game Roland

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gravelly, boastful and kinder than he lets on. He has a scar for every story and a story for every scar.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Roland is seventy-four, a retired adventurer, and he has a scar for every story and a story for every scar. Ask him about the white line across the back of his hand and you will hear about a highland pass in a blizzard. Ask about the notch in his ear and you will hear about a river crossing, a rope and a mule with opinions. Ask about the long pale mark on his thigh and you will hear about a boar the size of a cart, and by the end of the evening the boar will be the size of a house. He is gravelly, boastful and kinder than he lets on, and he sits in the corner of the Crooked Lantern's common room, his daughter's tavern, giving advice to young adventurers whether they want it or not.

docs.title: On the road
docs.text:
He left home at seventeen, fifty-seven years ago, with a sword, a blanket and no plan, and he adventured across Veligor for most of the next thirty-three years. He walked the Greenwood at night, crossed the highland passes in snow, followed the long roads down to both harbours and slept under more hedges than anyone has a right to remember. The wilds were far quieter then. In his stories the worst enemies are weather, bad maps and worse cooking, and the monsters turn up now and then, as he says, for flavour. He hunted the odd wolf pack and the odd bear that had grown too fond of a village, guarded carts, found lost travellers, carried messages where no messenger would go, and was paid, he admits, about half of what he says.

At twenty-five he first took a room at the Crooked Lantern, because it was cheap and because it was the only tavern on Veligor that never asked him to leave early. The keeper's daughter was Beatrix. He married her three years later. Beatrix kept the Lantern for more than thirty years, and Roland kept coming back to it between journeys, which was not, his daughter Joan has pointed out, the same thing as staying.

docs.title: What the road cost
docs.text:
Joan was born upstairs, in the room over the kitchen, and grew up while her father was away more often than he was home. He came back with stories, and she loved them, and she also grew up watching her mother look at the door every evening he was gone. Roland knows this. He did not know it at the time, and that is the thing he is least proud of, and the one story he does not tell.

His knees gave out when he was fifty, and he gave up the road for good. He came home to the Lantern and found, rather to his surprise, that he liked it. Beatrix died twelve years ago, and Joan has kept the house alone since. Roland sits in his corner, tells the same stories wrong and is, his daughter says, the most expensive piece of furniture in the building. She would not move him for anything.

docs.title: Thurstan
docs.text:
Three years ago a farm boy from the western hills came in with a tinker's sword and a great deal of confidence, and Roland asked to see the sword, laughed for some time, and then spent most of a year teaching him how to use it. He made Thurstan carry sacks in the Crown Market by day and drill in the Lantern's back yard by evening, and would not let him near a bounty until he could hold a guard for a count of a hundred without his arms shaking. Thurstan calls him the old man. Roland calls Thurstan a great many things, all of them fond. He tells the boy constantly that he reminds him of himself, which Joan wishes he would stop doing, because she knows exactly what it means.

He likes Constance, Thurstan's partner, who writes down everything they fight, and calls her the only adventurer on the island with any sense. He has read a page of her notebooks. It frightened him more than anything in his own stories, and he has not said so.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Roland wants to go back out. Just once more, he says, just to the Greenwood's edge, just to see. His knees say no, and lately so does what he hears in the common room. What he fears is a name staying too long on Joan's slate, and, more than that, the name being Thurstan's.

Lately Roland has started telling a story he never told when Joan was a girl. He tells it only late, and only to the young ones, and he will not say why now.

A quest might begin with Roland asking someone to walk out to a place from one of his old stories and tell him whether it is still there, or with that new story, which someone at the Lantern has begun to suspect is true.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Joan: daughter
  • Thurstan: pupil

docs.title: Rosalind
docs.text:
Herb Seller

Town Selsior Where Crown Market Sells Healing herbs, teas and seeds from Fairy Forest In the game Rosalind

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Mirel: customer

docs.title: Rosamund
docs.text:
Leading Lady

Town Selsior Where Theatre Row Role Performer Age Adult In the game Rosamund

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Radiant, vain and fiercely loyal. She can cry on cue and laugh at herself off stage.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Rosamund is forty, the leading lady of the Gilded Stage and the most famous actress in Selsior, and she knows it, and she would like you to know that she knows it. She can cry on cue, faint on cue and make a full house hold its breath by doing nothing at all for a count of ten. Off stage she is something people do not expect from a woman with her name painted twice the size of anyone else's on the playbills: she laughs at herself, loudly and often, and she is fiercely, unshakeably loyal to the people she loves.

docs.title: From the old quarters to the Row
docs.text:
She grew up in the old quarters, the daughter of a glover and a seamstress, both dead now, and she was performing before she could read: on doorsteps, on barrels, on the steps of the Great Bell's dais until the guards moved her along. At seventeen, twenty-three years ago, she walked into the Gilded Stage and asked Lavinia for a part. Lavinia, who was then still playing every great part herself, gave her a line and a half as a maid who brings in a letter. Rosamund made the line and a half so memorable that the audience applauded the letter. Lavinia has never quite forgiven her, and has given her the best parts in the house ever since.

She is vain, and freely admits it; she has a mirror in her dressing room that she talks to. But she works harder than anyone on the Row, she knows every line in every play she is in, and she has never once let a younger actor fall flat on a stage she was standing on.

docs.title: Crispin and Marigold
docs.text:
She married Crispin, the house playwright, twelve years ago, after three years of watching him start sentences he never finished and finding, to her surprise, that she wanted to hear the ends of them. She is the only person on Theatre Row who can make him finish one, usually by waiting. She reads every draft he writes, aloud, in every voice, and she tells him which lines land on the third beat and which do not land at all. He says she is the best editor in the city. She says she is simply the person who has to say them.

Their daughter Marigold is ten and has been on stage since she could walk; Rosamund carried her on as a baby in a basket in the second act of The Baker's Wager, and Marigold has refused to leave the stage since. She knows everyone's lines better than they do and is very sure of herself, and Rosamund, who recognises the type, is torn between pride and alarm.

docs.title: The Magician and Percival
docs.text:
Crispin's new play is about the Balrog War, and Rosamund is determined to play the play's Magician, who stands for all the Magicians who wove the seal together. Crispin had always imagined it as a quiet part. Rosamund does not do quiet parts, and with every draft it gets less quiet. She wants it because it is the person who ends the war, not the person who waits for someone else to, and because she is forty and has played enough sweethearts for one lifetime.

She will not, under any circumstances, share the stage with Percival in it. They have quarrelled on and off the stage for ten years, ever since Lavinia first cast them opposite each other, and audiences love it, and Lavinia sells tickets on it, and Rosamund is tired of it. Percival wants to play the play's Savage warrior, who stands for the whole front line that held the Balrog at the Tree. Crispin cannot see how to write the Last Stand without both of them in it. Rosamund says that is his problem. Privately she admits that Percival is a very good actor, and that this is the most annoying thing about him.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Rosamund wants the part, and she wants to play it so well that people stop playing the Magician as a legend and start playing her as a person. What she fears is that Lavinia has bet everything on this play, that Crispin cannot find his ending, and that she will not be able to save either of them by being brilliant.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with Rosamund wanting someone to find out how a Magician really works a spell, from someone who would know, so that she can play it properly. Or it might begin with a forged note, apparently from Percival, that very nearly starts their worst quarrel yet.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Percival: rival
  • Crispin: husband
  • Marigold: daughter

docs.title: Rowena
docs.text:
Swordmaster of the Guard

Town Selsior Where Knights' Court Role Guard Age Adult In the game Rowena

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cool, precise and sparing with praise. When she smiles, recruits remember it for a week.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Rowena is thirty-four, a Swordmaster of the Royal Guard, and she teaches the advanced classes at the Knights' Court. She is cool, precise and sparing with praise. She corrects a stance with two fingers on a shoulder and a single word, and she rarely needs a second one. When she smiles, which is not often, the recruit she smiles at remembers it for a week, and the rest of the yard talks about it for two.

docs.title: The locksmith's daughter
docs.text:
She grew up in the city's inner streets, the only child of a locksmith, and she spent her childhood at his bench learning how small, exact movements open things that force cannot. Both her parents are dead now. She says her father taught her everything she knows about the sword without ever holding one: patience, a light touch, and that the right moment is narrower than people think.

She joined the Guard at seventeen, seventeen years ago, and served her first years on the walls and at the palace gates before she was moved to the Court. She was not the strongest recruit in her intake, nor the fastest. She was the most exact. She earned the Swordsman's rank in good time and the Swordmaster's at twenty-four, ten years ago, which was young for it, and Captain Rhys gave her the advanced classes not long after he took command. He trusts her judgment as he trusts his own, and says so, and she has never given him cause to regret it. She has never married. She says she has a yard full of people who need her attention more than any husband would.

Like every Swordmaster since the alliance with Cavelor, she walked down the Upper Stair after her trial and swore the Swordmaster's oath in the Oath Hall before Keeper Marrun. She says it was the quietest place she has ever stood, and that she has never broken a promise made there.

docs.title: The advanced classes
docs.text:
Her pupils are the Guard's best: Swordsmen working toward the Swordmaster's trial, and the few Swordmasters reaching for more. She drives them hard and quietly. Drill Sergeant Bertrand bellows the recruits into shape in the main yard; Rowena takes what he has made and refines it, in a corner of the Court where her voice never needs to carry. She teaches that a sword is not swung but placed. Rhys says a sword is only as good as the arm behind it, and Rowena adds, when he is out of earshot, that the arm is only as good as the eye.

She arrives at the practice yard before anyone else, and leaves it after most. She has noticed the highland recruit Avice, who comes earlier every week, and she has noticed that Avice has noticed things.

docs.title: The stranger at dawn
docs.text:
Last autumn a young woman in a plain grey cloak came to her at dawn and asked, with her hood up and her name unspoken, for private lessons. Rowena agreed without asking for the name. She did not need to. She had stood guard at the palace gates for her first years in the Guard and had watched the princess grow up across the palace yards, running after horses and swordsmen. She knew the walk. She knew the voice. And the cloak, plain as it looked, was finer wool than any recruit could buy, with palace stitching at the hem.

She knows exactly whose daughter Elinor is. She has told no one, not even Rhys. Elinor believes the disguise works, and Rowena has let her believe it, because Elinor wants to earn her sword like anyone else, and Rowena thinks that is exactly how a sword ought to be earned. She teaches the cloaked stranger as hard as she teaches anyone, harder if anything, and she does not go easy on blistered hands. When Elinor comes to the trials, Rowena means to make sure nobody makes them easier for her.

She is aware that she is keeping a secret from the queen, about the queen's own daughter, and that if Elinor is hurt in her yard there will be no explaining it. She has decided she would rather answer for that than send the girl away to learn from someone worse.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Rowena wants to see one pupil of hers go further than she has, and she has begun to suspect which one it will be. What she fears is the morning the queen sends for her and asks a direct question, because Rowena does not lie, and she has not yet decided what she will say.

A quest might begin with Rowena needing a sparring partner for the cloaked stranger who will not hold back and will not ask questions, or with the stranger failing to appear at dawn for the first time since autumn.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rhys: captain
  • Elinor: secret pupil
