docs.title: Simkin
docs.text:
Cobbler

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Craftsman Age Elder Sells Boots, shoes and repairs In the game Simkin

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Grumpy, chatty and soft at heart. He judges people by their soles.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Simkin is seventy-six, the cobbler of the old quarters, and he has mended shoes in the same narrow lane for fifty years. He judges people by their soles. Hand him a boot and he will tell you, before you have opened your mouth, whether you walk on cobbles or grass, whether you favour your left foot, whether you stand all day or run, and whether you have been lying about any of it. He is grumpy, chatty and soft at heart, and he complains about everything except the work itself, which he loves more than he will ever say.

docs.title: The shop in the lane
docs.text:
He learned the trade from an old cobbler at the gate end of the city, who took him on at fourteen to sweep up leather scraps and kept him on because the boy never stopped asking why a heel wore down on one side. At twenty-six, fifty years ago, Simkin took the little shop in the lane, with its low door, its one window and its bench under the window where he has sat ever since. It has not changed much. The lasts hang in rows on the wall, the awls sit in their old jar, and the smell of leather and wax comes out into the lane on warm days and tells the neighbours he is in.

A year after he took the shop he married Winifred, forty-nine years ago, and they have argued happily ever since. She tells stories from a stool on her doorstep every evening, and he listens from the bench, pretending to work, and corrects her when she gets the details wrong, which she does on purpose. He judges people by their soles; she judges them by their stories. The two methods agree more often than either of them admits.

docs.title: Gytha and Hodge
docs.text:
Their only child, Gytha, came late and talks faster than both of them together. She runs the washing yard in the courtyard round the corner, and she is raising her son Hodge, who is ten, with her parents' help. Simkin gives Hodge scraps of leather, small jobs at the bench and long lectures on the proper care of heels. Gytha would be glad to see the boy take up his grandfather's trade, and so would Simkin. Hodge listens politely and goes up the nearest wall.

Simkin has never seen Hodge on the rooftops. He has seen his soles. The boy's boots come to the bench worn in places no street wears them, scuffed with tile grit and roof moss, and the toes are scraped in a way that means climbing. Lately the heels have been wearing in a new pattern, the way a recruit's do from planting the back foot again and again on the same patch of ground. Simkin has noticed. He has said nothing to Gytha. He has started, quietly, stitching the boy's heels twice.

docs.title: More work than hands
docs.text:
Adventurers wear out their boots faster than they used to. There are more of them, they walk further, and they come back with soles split on stone and burned on things they do not like to name. Simkin has taken on more work than his old hands can manage, and his fingers ache by evening in a way they never did. He grumbles about it all day to anyone who comes to the window. He has never turned a pair away.

He has opinions about the boots he sees. Thurstan from the Crooked Lantern stamps through his heels in a season, and Simkin has told him so. Recruits from the Knights' Court come in with boots that were made for a different foot. He has seen boots this year with marks on the leather like teeth, and once a sole with a scorch in the shape of a print, and he has kept that one on the shelf behind him, not quite sure why.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Simkin wants an apprentice with good hands and patience, and in his heart of hearts he wants it to be Hodge, though he knows better than to say so. What he fears is the morning his hands will not close on the awl, and the lane with no smell of leather in it.

A quest might begin with a pair of boots left at Simkin's bench and never collected, with soles worn in a way he cannot explain, or with Simkin needing a rare leather from another town that the carters have stopped bringing.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Winifred: wife
  • Gytha: daughter

docs.title: Swithin
docs.text:
Gate Clerk

Town Selsior Where Selsior Gate Role Official Age Elder In the game Swithin

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fussy, precise and secretly romantic. He writes down every traveller and imagines their adventures.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Swithin is seventy, the clerk of Selsior's great gate, and he writes down everyone. He sits in a narrow office set into the gatehouse wall, at a high desk under a small window that looks straight out onto the Royal Road, and as each traveller passes under the arch he takes their name, their town, their business and the date, in a hand so small and neat that the guards say he could fit the whole kingdom on one page. He is fussy, precise and particular about his pens, his ink, his blotting sand and the exact angle of his stool. He is also, though he would deny it with some indignation, the most romantic man in the city.

docs.title: The books
docs.text:
He has kept the gate book for thirty-six years. Before that he was a clerk in a carrier's counting house by the Crown Market, adding up loads and distances, and he took the gate post at thirty-four because, he told his mother at the time (she is long dead now), he wanted to write down people instead of parcels. The old gate books fill a whole wall of shelves in his office, one fat volume for each year, and he can find any traveller in them by date, by name or by the colour of the cloak they wore, which he also writes down.

And in the margins, in an even smaller hand, he writes what he imagines. A pale young woman from the harbours, travelling alone with a sealed letter: in the margin, a lost inheritance, or a secret marriage. A grey old highlander with a sword far too fine for his coat: a hero of some forgotten fight, come to see the capital before he dies. A pair of students in a hurry: eloping, certainly. He has never told any of them. He has never asked. He has, now and then, been right, and on those days he walks home very pleased with himself.

He never married. He lodges in two rooms above a cooper's yard near the gate, and he takes his supper most evenings at the corner table of Hamon's Gate Inn, where Hamon tells him the travellers' stories and Swithin quietly corrects the dates.

docs.title: Brann
docs.text: He has written down every recruit, sergeant and visitor at the gate since before Brann was a recruit, and he wrote down Brann himself on the day the young man first stood guard under the arch, twenty years ago, with a note in the margin that said only "will stay". Brann did. The two of them are old colleagues and, though neither would ever put it so, old friends. Brann watches the faces and Swithin keeps the names, and very little gets past the gate that the pair of them do not know about. Brann pretends to find the margins ridiculous, and then asks what Swithin has written about the interesting ones.

docs.title: Fewer on foot
docs.text:
Swithin is a counter by nature, and for the last few years the counts have been changing. Fewer travellers come in on foot than used to. More come in wagons, in convoys, with hired swords on the tailboards. And more of them come in hurt, limping, bandaged, carried. He has started a new column in the book for it, which he did not want to do. He marks each one with a small cross, and passes the week's count to Brann, who passes it to the Knights' Court.

He has also noticed something he has told only Brann. Some travellers he wrote going out have never been written coming back in.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Swithin wants every name that goes out of the gate to come back through it, so that he can draw a neat line under it. What he fears is a book full of names with no return.

A quest might begin with Swithin asking someone to find out what became of a traveller who went out of the gate a year ago and never came back, or with one of his margin guesses, written about a stranger last month, coming true in a way he very much did not want.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Brann: old colleague

docs.title: Sybil
docs.text:
Royal Wardrobe Mistress

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Service Age Adult In the game Sybil

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Elegant, sharp-tongued and kind underneath. She can judge a person by their hem.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Sybil is sixty-one, the Royal Wardrobe Mistress, and she can judge a person by their hem. A hem let down tells her someone has grown; a hem taken up in a hurry tells her someone is going somewhere they should not; a hem with mud on the inside tells her rather more than its owner would like. She is elegant, sharp-tongued and kind underneath, and she keeps the royal family's clothes, from the coronation robes in their cedar chest to the princess's riding boots, with the precision of a general and the patience of a saint who has stopped expecting thanks.

docs.title: Two sisters, two halves
docs.text:
She and her elder sister Edith grew up in the city, in a house where both girls were sewing before they could spell; their parents are dead now. Edith, five years older, went to Theatre Row at eighteen and has dressed its players ever since. Sybil went the other way. She came to the palace at nineteen, in the old king's reign, as a seamstress in the wardrobe rooms, and she has been Wardrobe Mistress for twenty-five years. She altered the coronation robes for Queen Aveline sixteen years ago, working through the night with pins in her mouth and her heart in her throat, and she still says it was the finest fit she ever made.

She never married. She says she has dressed enough brides to know what it costs.

The sisters meet for supper once a week and trade gossip about who wore what: which envoy's wife wore last year's sleeves, which actor split his breeches in the third act, what the queen chose for the trade council and why. Edith says they dress the two halves of Selsior, the half that is real and the half that pretends. Sybil says that on a good week she cannot tell them apart either.

docs.title: A palace that talks
docs.text: The palace is full of people who would like to know things. Agnes, the maid of the upper halls, hears everything and repeats half of it, and Sybil is the one person in the household from whom Agnes has never got a single story. Sybil regards this as a professional achievement. She is sharp with the maids, sharper with the pages and sharpest of all with anyone who touches the coronation robes without washing their hands, and the whole household knows that under the edge she will mend a torn sleeve before a scolding is noticed, and say nothing about how it was torn.

docs.title: The cloak
docs.text:
Last autumn, Princess Elinor came to the wardrobe rooms early one morning and asked for a cloak: plain, grey, with a deep hood, nothing anyone would look at twice. Sybil looked at her, at her hands and at her boots, and fetched one from the back of a press without a word. She knew where the princess meant to wear it. She has known ever since, and she has made it her business to help. It was Sybil who suggested that "riding" was a perfectly good reason for a princess to be out early, and Sybil who keeps the riding boots polished and the riding habit worn just enough to be believed. She mends the cloak when it comes back torn. When anyone asks where that grey cloak went, she says she has no idea, in a voice that closes the subject.

She is not sure what she would say if the queen asked. She has noticed Aveline looking at Elinor's hands at breakfast, and she has noticed that Aveline has not asked anyone anything yet. Edith has noticed that there is one subject her sister goes quiet on. Sybil has noticed Edith noticing, and has served her more soup.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Sybil wants to dress the princess for one more great occasion, and she hopes privately that it will be one Elinor has earned. What she fears is the day the cloak comes back with blood on it that is not from a blister.

A quest might begin with Sybil needing a rare thread or cloth for a royal garment that must be ready by a date she will not explain, or with a garment going missing from the wardrobe rooms that Sybil did not lend to anyone.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Edith: sister
  • Elinor: mischief she covers for

docs.title: Tancred
docs.text:
Retired Drain-Mender

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Resident Age Elder In the game Tancred

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gruff, patient and fond of a long silence, he knows the city by its smells and its echoes. He trusts a lantern more than a map.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tancred is seventy-seven, a retired drain-mender of the old quarters, and he knows Selsior by its smells and its echoes. Blindfold him at any grating between the plaza and the river and he will tell you which lane you are in from the way the air comes up through it: wet brick here, old lime there, the river close by on the turn of the tide. He is gruff, patient and very fond of a long silence, and he trusts a lantern more than any map, including the good ones.

docs.title: Under the lanes
docs.text:
He went down into the old drains at eighteen, carrying buckets for the drain-menders of those days, and he never really came back up. The drains beneath the old quarters are older than the streets above them, and below them lie older works still: walls, arches and the great pillared cisterns of the first fortress-town, which the city simply built over as it grew. Tancred learned them all with a lantern and a pole, by walking them, by listening to the water and by getting lost exactly once, which he says is the right number of times.

At twenty-five he was paired with a young drain-mender named Osgood, and the two of them worked the old drains side by side for thirty years. Osgood was the talker and Tancred was the listener, and between them they cleared every channel, mended every collapse and worked every sluice in the old quarters. Osgood drew a map of the drains in chalk and ink, which Tancred teased him about for thirty years, and which his daughter Ida keeps still. Osgood's little girl carried their lamp on the short jobs, and Tancred taught her which gratings carry a voice and which swallow it. She is the night watchwoman of the old quarters now, and she still knows.

Osgood died twenty-two years ago, when Ida was sixteen. Tancred worked on alone, with whatever young help the city gave him, until his knees gave out seven years ago, and then he climbed up out of the drains for good and has missed them every day since.

docs.title: Steps Lane
docs.text:
Tancred lives in Steps Lane, the steep lane of the old quarters with steps instead of cobbles, two doors up from the house where Ida grew up. His wife, Winsome, who kept a pie stall at the bottom of the lane and called him her mole, died eleven years ago. They had no children, and he says, gruffly, that he did not need any, having had the loan of Osgood's.

At the bottom of the lane is an old iron grating, the heaviest in the quarter, over the channel where he and Osgood used to go down. Nobody gave him the keeping of it. He simply took it on. He sweeps the leaves off it, oils its hinge, and sits on the step beside it most evenings with his pipe, listening. He still has the key to the sluice gear in the cisterns below, on a cord round his neck, because nobody ever asked for it back.

docs.title: What he hears
docs.text: For some months now Tancred has not liked what he hears beneath that grating. The water sounds wrong. There is a scraping that comes and goes, slow and heavy, and a dull knocking deep down, like someone patiently taking a wall apart. The rats he used to hear by the hundred have gone quiet, and Lettice the rat catcher says they are moving up into the cellars. Ida has told him about the scratching that keeps pace with her on her rounds, and he has not told her what he thinks, because he does not know what he thinks. He knows only that nothing he ever met in fifty years below the lanes sounded like that.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Tancred wants to go down one more time, and knows his knees will not let him. He fears that whatever is down there is in the cisterns, where the water is deep and the pillars are old, and that Ida, who is as brave as her father was and twice as stubborn, will go and look without him.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin the morning the Steps Lane grating is found pushed up from below, with Tancred standing over it in his slippers. Anyone going down with Osgood's map will want Tancred first: he knows how to work the old sluice in the cisterns, which the map does not show, and he will tell them, at length and with a long silence in the middle, to trust the lantern over the map.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Ida: his old partner's daughter

docs.title: Theobald
docs.text:
Stargazer

Town Selsior Where Scholars' Quarter Role Scholar Age Elder In the game Theobald

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Dreamy, nocturnal and absent-minded. He talks to the stars as if they owe him money.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Theobald is seventy-nine, the stargazer of the Scholars' Quarter, and he has hardly been to bed before dawn in sixty years. He lives at the top of an old stone tower at the edge of the Quarter, where the roof opens onto the sky, and every clear night he is up there with his instruments, his charts and a cup of tea that went cold some hours ago. He is dreamy, nocturnal and spectacularly absent-minded. He talks to the stars as if they owe him money: "There you are. Late again. Don't think I didn't notice."

docs.title: Sixty years of charts
docs.text:
He came to the Academy as a boy from the city's inner streets, the son of a lamp-oil seller, and was meant to study law. On his first night in the Scholars' Quarter an old master of the Academy, long dead, let him look through a brass glass at the moon, and that was the end of the law. He began keeping his own charts at nineteen, sixty years ago, and he has never missed a clear night since unless he was too ill to climb the stairs, which has happened four times, and he has marked each of those nights on the chart with an apology.

The charts fill the tower. They are rolled in racks, stacked on chairs, pinned to the walls and piled on the stairs, every star he could see from that roof, night by night and year by year, with the weather, the moon and whatever he happened to be thinking in the margins. He teaches at the Academy, after a fashion, by inviting students up the stairs and forgetting they are there. Some of them have become very good astronomers. Most have become very good at making tea.

docs.title: Mariota
docs.text: His student now is Mariota, who is nineteen and argues with everything, and Theobald adores her. She corrects his arithmetic, reminds him to eat and tidies the charts into an order he cannot find anything in. She is going through all sixty years of them, year by year, looking for anything in the sky that changed when the creatures on the roads began to change. Theobald does not know what she has found. He knows she has found something, because she has stopped telling him about it, and Mariota has never in her life stopped telling anyone about anything. He has decided to wait until she is ready, which is, for him, an unusual act of patience by daylight.

docs.title: The telescope
docs.text:
Theobald buys every curious lens the market sells. His supplier, and his favourite person in the Crown Market, is Jasper the curio dealer, who sells strange inventions from Urbanograd and saves every piece of ground glass he can find for his best customer. They talk for an hour over each lens, and both of them come away happier and neither of them is sure who got the better bargain.

The lenses are for the telescope. Theobald is building one larger than his tower. This is not a figure of speech. It is a long tube of brass and wood, half finished, that runs out of the top window and along the roof, and when it is done it will need the tower to lean on and the neighbouring roof to rest its end on. The neighbours have opinions. Theobald does not hear them. He says the stars are further away than they used to be, or else his eyes are worse, and the telescope will settle which.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Theobald wants to finish the telescope and see something nobody on Veligor has ever seen. What he fears is subtler. Going back through his oldest charts with Mariota, he found a margin note in his own hand, from about fifty years ago, which he does not remember writing and cannot quite read. Three words, the last of which may be "wrong". He has not told Mariota. He has not slept well since, which for a man who does not sleep at night is saying something.

A quest might begin with Theobald needing a lens that only Urbanograd can grind, and Jasper unable to get it, or with someone helping him decipher that margin note.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Jasper: supplier of lenses
  • Mariota: student

docs.title: Thomasin
docs.text:
Historian of the Balrog War

Town Selsior Where Scholars' Quarter Role Scholar Age Adult In the game Thomasin

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Earnest, careful and quick to say what nobody knows. She hates a good story that is not true.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Thomasin is thirty-nine, the Royal Academy's historian of the Balrog War, and the most common thing she says in a lecture is "nobody knows". She says it plainly and without apology, and then she tells you exactly what each of the four peoples believes instead, and who wrote it down, and when, and why they might have wanted it told that way. She is earnest, careful and quick to admit the edges of her knowledge. What she cannot bear is a good story that is not true, and the Balrog War is full of them.

docs.title: Four grandmothers' tales
docs.text:
She grew up in a back street behind the Crown Market, raised by her grandmother Wendreda, who sold ribbons from a tray and told stories to anyone who bought more than a yard. Thomasin's parents died when she was too small to remember them, and Wendreda's stories filled the space they left. The trouble was that Wendreda told the Balrog War differently depending on who was listening. For a highland herder she told the horned giant wreathed in flame; for a forest customer, the wound in the world; for a Commons housewife, simply the Burning. When Thomasin, aged eight, asked which one was true, her grandmother laughed and said, "Whichever sells the ribbon." Thomasin did not think that was an answer. She has been looking for a better one ever since.

She came to the Academy at fifteen, twenty-four years ago, on the strength of an essay that compared two ballads of the Last Stand line by line and found they disagreed about which day of the battle it was. Bartholomew, already a senior teacher then, read it, sent for her, and asked her which ballad was right. She said she did not know yet. He has been her mentor from that afternoon, and she is, by common agreement on the Scholars' Quarter, his protegee, though he would say she was always going to be stubborn without his help. Wendreda died in Thomasin's second year at the Academy, and Thomasin still keeps her ribbon tray on her desk, full of pens.

docs.title: The work
docs.text:
Thomasin has taught at the Academy for fourteen years. Her work is simple to describe and endless to do: she sets the four peoples' accounts of the war side by side, the Savage songs, the Magician records, the Commons tales and the Aristocrat chronicles, and she refuses to call any one of them right. Her students hate this for about a season and then, the good ones, come to love it. She teaches them to ask who was standing where when a thing was seen, and who was paid to remember it.

She spends much of her time in the great library, and Benedict, the Head Librarian, has long since stopped pretending he does not keep the best desk for her. She knows the story of his missing volume of the Aristocrat chronicles as well as he does, and lately she asks him about it more often. Benedict thinks she suspects him of something. She does not. What she has begun to suspect, reading the rest of the set, is that the volume did not wander off by accident, and that someone who knew what it was wanted it out of the library. She has no proof, no name and no wish to say any of it aloud to an old man who has blamed himself for eighteen years.

docs.title: Crispin
docs.text: Her friend Crispin, the playwright of the Gilded Stage, comes to her every week with the same question in a different coat: what was the Balrog, really? She gives him the four accounts and he goes away annoyed. She reads his drafts of the Balrog War play, all four acts, and she will not choose his ending for him. Privately she likes the one where the creature never appears and the audience sees only its light on the actors' faces, because it is the only ending that does not pretend to know. She has not told him so. He would put it in a programme note with her name on it.

docs.title: The lectures
docs.text: Thomasin used to give one public lecture a season, to a polite half-full room. This spring she has been asked to speak nearly every week: by guilds, by market traders, by the parents of new Guard recruits, by a crowd at the Gilded Stage that came because the play is coming. She does not like why. The people in those rooms are not curious; they are frightened. They do not ask what happened at the Tree. They ask how it was done, and whether it could be done again, and they want her to promise that the seal will hold. She cannot promise that, and she will not tell them a good story instead.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Thomasin wants the truth of the war, even a little more of it than anyone has now, and she wants the kingdom to be brave enough to live with the parts that cannot be known. What she fears is the day a frightened crowd stops asking for history and starts asking her for a story she will not tell, and someone less careful tells it to them instead.

A quest might begin with Thomasin needing an account of the war from another town copied word for word, not retold, or with her asking someone to find out quietly who borrowed books in the great library on a particular afternoon eighteen years ago.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Bartholomew: mentor
  • Crispin: friend

docs.title: Thurstan
docs.text:
Adventurer

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Adventurer Age Young In the game Thurstan

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brash, brave and always hungry. He charges first and plans later.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Thurstan is twenty-one, an adventurer who lodges at the Crooked Lantern, and he has never once in his life read a bounty notice to the end before deciding to take it. He reads the word "reward", and the name of the beast, and he is already reaching for his sword. He is brash, brave and always hungry, and he charges first and plans later. Most of the time, thanks to his partner, there is a later.

docs.title: Off the hill farm
docs.text:
He grew up on a hill farm a few days west of Selsior, the youngest of four and the only boy, in a house where his mother and three older sisters ran everything and expected him to carry it. His father died when he was small. He spent his boyhood hauling water, chasing sheep and fighting imaginary monsters on the hillside with a stick, and listening, every time a traveller passed, to news of the real ones. When the roads started getting worse, he decided it was a sign. His mother decided it was nonsense. At eighteen, three years ago, he walked to the capital anyway, with a sword he had bought from a tinker and a great deal of confidence, and his mother and sisters are still running the farm without him and writing to tell him so.

He found the Crooked Lantern on his first night because it was the cheapest bed in the old quarters, and he has never moved out. Joan took one look at him and doubled his supper without being asked. She has been doing it ever since.

docs.title: Roland
docs.text:
The first person in the common room to talk to him was Roland, Joan's father, who adventured across Veligor in his youth and has a scar for every story and a story for every scar. Roland asked to see his sword, laughed for some time, and then spent most of a year teaching him how to use it. He made Thurstan carry sacks in the Crown Market by day to pay his rent and drill in the Lantern's back yard by evening, and he would not let him near a bounty until he could hold a guard for a count of a hundred without his arms shaking. Thurstan calls him the old man, to his face, and would walk into a fire for him.

Roland is boastful and gravelly and much kinder than he lets on, and he worries about Thurstan in exactly the way he never let anyone worry about him. He tells Thurstan constantly that he reminds him of himself. Joan wishes he would stop.

docs.title: Constance
docs.text: Thurstan took his first bounty two years ago and came back with a torn sleeve, a very small reward and a story three times its size. Constance, a mage who had left the Academy and taken a room upstairs, listened to the whole thing from the next table and then pointed out, drily, the four things he had done wrong. He asked her to come next time and show him. She has been his partner ever since. She plans every fight; he ruins every plan; between them they have not yet lost one. He does not really understand why she writes everything down afterwards, but he carries spare ink for her in his pack, and he gets very angry with anyone who laughs at her notebooks.

docs.title: The bounties
docs.text:
He takes every bounty posted at the gate. There are more of them every season, and the Royal Guard, with more recruits than it has ever had, is sending patrols after more of the beasts itself. Thurstan wants to make a name for himself before the Guard takes all the good monsters. He has never tried the Guard's trials. He says he does not take orders well, which is true, and that he would rather be paid by the head than by the month, which is half true. The other half is that he wants people in the old quarters to say his name the way they say Roland's.

He fears very little, and that is the trouble. The thing he fears most is the thing he will not say out loud: that one day he will charge first, and the plan will not catch up, and Constance will be the one who pays for it.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with a bounty Thurstan has already taken and cannot finish alone, for once, because Constance has refused to come. Or it might begin with a rival adventurer who has started taking the bounties before Thurstan can reach the gate.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Joan: landlady
  • Constance: adventuring partner
  • Roland: mentor

docs.title: Tibb
docs.text:
Stagehand

Town Selsior Where Theatre Row Role Worker Age Young In the game Tibb

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Wiry, unflappable and sarcastic. He knows every trapdoor and rope in the theatre.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tibb is twenty-two, a stagehand of the Gilded Stage, and he has spent more of his life above the stage and under it than on it. He works the ropes on the fly floor high over the actors' heads and the trapdoors in the boards beneath their feet, and between the two he knows every inch of the oldest theatre on Theatre Row. He is wiry, unflappable and sarcastic, and the worst thing that can happen on a first night, in his considered opinion, is that something goes wrong and he has to look surprised about it. It has never happened yet.

docs.title: Raised in the gallery
docs.text: His mother sold oranges in the Gilded Stage's cheap gallery, and Tibb grew up under the benches, picking up dropped coins and the plots of every play in the house. She died when he was eleven, and Lavinia, who notices everything that happens in her theatre and pretends to notice nothing, let the boy stay. She put him to work for old Fitch, the flyman, who had hung scenery in that house for longer than Lavinia had been in it. Fitch taught him knots, counterweights, the timing of a drop and the one rule of the fly floor: never trust a rope you did not tie yourself. When Fitch died four years ago, Tibb took over the ropes, and nobody, including Tibb, thought of asking anyone else.

docs.title: Keeping the peace
docs.text:
Officially Tibb works the ropes and trapdoors. Unofficially he keeps the actors from killing each other, which Lavinia considers the most important job in the building after her own. Rosamund and Percival have quarrelled on stage and off it for ten years, and Tibb has arranged the wings so that they exit on opposite sides in every play, meet only under lights, and never share a staircase. He delivers their messages to each other slowly and slightly edited. He has also learned that Crispin will hand you a scrap of paper in the middle of a sentence, and keeps a box on the fly floor full of lines the playwright has forgotten he wrote.

Marigold, the playwright's daughter, followed him about the building as soon as she could walk. He taught her which boards creak and which ones drop, partly to keep her alive and partly because she would have found out anyway. In return she swore on her life never to use the trapdoor without asking him first, and she has kept the oath for nearly a year. Tibb is privately astonished, and has not told her so, in case it breaks the spell.

docs.title: The play
docs.text: The Balrog War play frightens the rest of the house, but it interests Tibb. Crispin has an ending in which the creature never appears and the audience sees only its light on the actors' faces. Lavinia, Crispin says, would hate it. Tibb has quietly worked out how to do it anyway, with a row of lamps behind red glass and a sheet of polished tin on a rope, and has tried it once at night on an empty stage. It worked rather too well. He has not told Lavinia. He has noticed one of the Academy students in the cheap gallery watching the stagehands more than the actors, and he has a feeling the boy would want to see it.

docs.title: Lettice
docs.text:
Two years ago Lavinia hired Lettice, the rat catcher of the old quarters, to clear the cellar under the stage. She came with her traps and her terrier, talked the whole time, and left the cellar clean and Tibb thoroughly in love. He has been courting her ever since in the only way he can think of, which is to bring her the theatre's mice. He catches them live in the prop room and the under-stage and carries them across the city in a covered basket. Lettice says it is the most insulting present a rat catcher has ever been given, and keeps count of them on her cellar door. The count is past two hundred.

Lately it has been harder to keep it rising. The mice are gone from the under-stage. The ones Tibb finds now are up in the flies and the costume racks, as high in the building as they can get, and Lettice, when he told her, stopped laughing for a moment and asked him which wall of the cellar was nearest the old drains.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Tibb wants a full house on opening night, every cue on time, and Lettice to say yes, though he has not worked out what the question is. What he fears is a rope he did not tie, and, more and more, the dark under the stage that the mice have left.

A quest might begin with Tibb needing someone to go down into the under-stage cellar with a lantern to find out what the mice are running from, or with a rope on the fly floor found cut, cleanly, on the eve of the Balrog War play's first rehearsal with lights.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Lavinia: employer
  • Lettice: sweetheart

docs.title: Tilda
docs.text:
Taxi Driver

Town Selsior Where Selsior Gate Role Service Age Adult In the game Tilda

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Breezy, practical and full of road wisdom. She never forgets a route once she has driven it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "Cab for hire!" calls Tilda from the stand outside Selsior's great gate, and then, catching your eye, "Hello there. I drive the Selsior cab from the gate stand." She is forty-three, sun-browned and easy in her seat, with her sleeves rolled to the elbow and a straw hat she has worn so long it has taken the shape of her head. She is breezy, practical and full of road wisdom, and she never forgets a route once she has driven it. Ask her the way to anywhere a cab can go and she will tell you every bend, ford and milestone in order, and where the puddle is that never dries.

docs.title: The cab and Thistle
docs.text:
The Selsior cab is a tall, two-wheeled thing painted red with yellow wheels, with a folding hood, two brass lamps and a bench that seats two in comfort and three in friendship. It is drawn by Thistle, a grey gelding with opinions about bridges. Tilda took the cab over fourteen years ago from old Larkin, who had driven it from the gate stand for most of his life and taught her the job in his last two summers on the bench. When he died she bought the cab and the horse from his estate with every coin she had and a loan she paid off in three years.

Before that she drove carriers' wagons for a city carrier from the age of seventeen, up and down the Royal Road and along the lesser roads between the towns, and she learned then the trick that made her name: drive a road once with your eyes open and you never need to ask the way on it again. She can recite the whole Royal Road from the gate stand to Kaldemor, turn by turn, with her eyes shut. Passengers have tested her. She has never lost.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
The cab runs between towns that have a taxi stand, and never into the wilds. And Tilda will drive a passenger only to a town they have walked to before, at least once, on their own feet. Newcomers think this is a strange rule for a driver who wants fares. Tilda has a saying for it: walk the road to Kaldemor once, and her cab will know the way home. What she means is that a person ought to know the road they are paying to skip. If a wheel comes off halfway, she says, she wants a passenger who knows which way to walk, not one who sits in the ditch and waits to be rescued.

The rule about the wilds is older than Tilda, and she used to think it a little fussy. She does not any more. Lately, she says, it has never seemed wiser. Last autumn, coming home along the Royal Road past the Greenwood with the light going, Thistle stopped dead in the road and would not move, ears flat, for as long as it takes to say a slow prayer, while something large went through the trees beside them without once showing itself. Then he walked on as if nothing had happened. Tilda has not driven that stretch at dusk since. She leaves the far stands earlier now, and she tells her passengers it is because Thistle likes his supper.

docs.title: The gate
docs.text:
Her stand is just outside the gate, and the gate's regulars are her friends. On slow afternoons she leans against the cab and Hollis, the young gate guard, leans against the gate, and they trade the news of the road: who came in hurt, which carters are late, which passengers she turned away because they had never walked where they wanted to go. Biscuit, the gate dog, checks her stand every morning in case anyone has dropped anything near the cab overnight. Nobody ever has. Tilda has lately started dropping a crust there on purpose.

Her cousin Perrin, the royal courier, is a good deal younger than she is and a good deal louder about it. He tells everyone he is the fastest courier in the kingdom. Tilda tells everyone, fondly, that she can read from the mud on his boots exactly which roads he took to get there, and that he takes the long way round more often than he admits. He has asked her to stop. She has not.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Tilda wants every road with a stand on it open and every passenger delivered before dark. She would like, one day, to drive the cab to a town that does not have a stand yet, on the day it gets one. What she fears is the evening she has to choose between her rules and a passenger who must get home.

A quest might begin with Tilda refusing a well-paying stranger who wants to be driven somewhere off the road, and asking someone to find out where he went on foot instead, or with Thistle stopping dead again, in broad daylight, on a road he has walked a thousand times.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Perrin: cousin
  • Hollis: friend

docs.title: Tobe
docs.text:
Recruit

Town Selsior Where Knights' Court Role Guard Age Young In the game Tobe

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Thoughtful, bookish and a little anxious. He knows the manual by heart and his arms do not.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tobe is seventeen, a recruit of the Royal Guard, and he knows the Court's sword manual by heart, every stance, every cut and every footnote. His arms do not. He read every book on swordsmanship in the Scholars' Quarter before he came to the Knights' Court, and he will tell anyone who asks that not one of them mentioned how heavy swords are. He is thoughtful, bookish and a little anxious, and he is still stuck on the third cut.

docs.title: The bindery boy
docs.text:
He grew up in the Scholars' Quarter with his elder sister Mariota, in two rooms over their father's bindery. Ranulf bound books for the Academy and the libraries, and the house was always full of them, and while Mariota read the histories, Tobe read the manuals: fencing, drill, the old treatises on the sword written by masters nobody remembers. Their mother, Sabine, died when he was five. Their father died two winters ago, and the bindery was sold to pay what was owed on it. Mariota had her place at the Academy. Tobe found work fetching and shelving books in a library in the Quarter, and in the long evenings between shelves he read, as far as he can tell, every book on the sword that has ever been bound in Selsior.

He read about the ranks of the Guard, from the Swordsman to the Grand Swordmaster, and about the one the old books name beyond them, the Sword Saint. He has read six different accounts of what a Sword Saint is, and they disagree about nearly everything, which bothers him more than it bothers anyone else. This spring, at seventeen, he closed the last book, put on his only good coat and walked to the Knights' Court to try the trials, on the theory that he already knew everything except how to do it.

docs.title: Step, strike
docs.text:
The theory was mostly correct, and that was the problem. Tobe can tell you exactly where his feet should be on the third cut, at what angle the blade should leave the guard and why. Then he tries it, and the sword goes somewhere else. Drill Sergeant Bertrand, who swears he can turn anyone into a guard given a year and enough porridge, bellows at him every morning, and Tobe mouths along with the corrections under his breath, because he has read them already, and it does not help. He drills alone in the evenings, step, strike, step, strike, counting under his breath. Captain Rhys watches sometimes and says nothing, which Tobe finds far worse than shouting.

His best friend is Pim, who salutes everyone and whose guard is full of holes. They share a bench at supper and a great deal of porridge, and they have a working arrangement: Tobe tells Pim exactly what he is doing wrong, and Pim makes Tobe laugh when the third cut goes wrong again. It works better than either of them expected. Pim says Tobe is the cleverest person in the Court. Tobe says Pim is the bravest, and has privately decided that brave is the more useful of the two with a sword in your hand.

Avice, the fiercest of their year, frightens him a little. She once watched him miss the third cut four times and then told him, in five words, what he was doing wrong. She was right. He has not yet worked out how to thank her.

docs.title: Mariota
docs.text: His sister visits every week to ask whether he has got past the third cut yet, and to tease him for reading about swords instead of using them. He teases her back for reading about stars instead of looking at them. They are all the family either of them has, and they both know it, and neither of them says it.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Tobe wants to earn the Swordsman's rank and to prove that a person who learned from books can learn from bruises too. He fears that he is the kind of person who will always know the answer and never be able to do it, and that one day, on a road somewhere, knowing the answer will not be enough.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with Tobe asking a passing adventurer to show him the third cut, slowly, because the books all describe it differently. Or it might begin with a seventh account of the Sword Saint, in a book Tobe has never seen, turning up on a stall in the Crown Market.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rhys: captain
  • Pim: friend
  • Mariota: sister

docs.title: Tristan
docs.text:
River Scout

Town Selsior Where Riverside Role Adventurer Age Adult In the game Tristan

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, quick and confident on water and land. He would rather track a beast than fight it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tristan is forty-one, a river scout of the Riverside, and most people who have seen him at work did not notice him at the time. He walks the banks ahead of the barges, a long way ahead, quietly, reading the reeds and the mud and the birds, and when he finds something wrong he warns the barges before they reach it. He is quiet, quick and confident on water and on land, and he would much rather track a beast than fight one. He says a scout who has to fight has already done his job badly.

docs.title: The carter's boys
docs.text:
He and his elder brother Edric grew up on their father's cart. Their father hauled goods between the capital and the other towns, and the two boys sat on the bench beside him through most of their childhood, learning milestones, fords and where to water a horse. Their mother kept the house in Riverside, and between journeys the boys came home to it. Both parents are dead now, and the brothers have no other family. Tristan still lives in that house, a narrow place with a door on the lane and a window on the water, and Edric, who sleeps at the Knights' Court more often than not, comes down to it on his rest days.

Edric loved the road. Tristan never did. He found the cart too loud, and he would slip off at the river landings and lie in the reeds while their father watered the horses. An old fowler called Hamund, who netted ducks in the reed beds below the city and has been dead many years, found the boy there one evening and, instead of chasing him off, showed him the track of an otter. Hamund taught him to move without a sound, to read a bank like a page, and to know what had passed by from the shape of the reeds it bent. By the time Edric joined the Guard, Tristan was earning his keep scouting for any barge that would pay him.

docs.title: Lucan's scout
docs.text:
For nine years now he has worked for Lucan, the bargemaster, who runs three barges on the river and has never hired anyone to do anything quietly before or since. They are an odd pair. Lucan booms, bets on everything and greets every landing he passes; Tristan says perhaps a dozen words a day, and Lucan listens to every one of them. Lucan trusts him completely, and it is the only thing on the river he does not make a wager on. Tristan, for his part, trusts Lucan to turn a barge when he is told to, which is rarer than it sounds.

River travel has grown busy now that the roads are dangerous, and Tristan's work has grown with it. There are more creatures on the banks than there were, and bolder ones, and the water itself has started to keep secrets. Tristan was on the bank the day one of Lucan's hands came out of the river with a bruise on his leg in the shape of something that had gripped him, and he helped carry the man to Aldith's door.

docs.title: The Long Reach
docs.text:
A half-day upstream of the city, below the quarry landing, the river runs deep and slow for a long stretch between high banks. The bargehands call it the Long Reach. Early this spring Tristan found a track there: a broad swathe of reeds pressed flat from the top of the bank down into the deep water, as wide as a cart, with nothing at either end of it. The herons have gone from that reach. Once, watching a loaded barge pass over the deepest pool, he saw the water behind it rise in a slow, smooth hump, as if something underneath had turned to follow, and then settle.

Since then he has asked Lucan to pass that stretch at speed, every time, and he has not said why. He is not sure what he saw, and he will not say what he is not sure of. He also knows that Lucan would either bet on it or tell the whole river by nightfall, and that the bargehands are frightened enough already. He has told Edric. The brothers have always compared notes on how the wilds are changing, road against river, and lately their notes match more than either of them likes.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Tristan wants to know what made that track before anyone has to find out the hard way. What he fears is the day a barge cannot go fast enough, and the day he has to tell Lucan the truth because it is too late to keep it.

A quest might begin with Tristan asking someone steady to watch the Long Reach with him through a night, without a lantern, or with Bennet's new fast barge needing to be tested on exactly the stretch of river where speed matters most.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Edric: brother
  • Lucan: employer

docs.title: Vessa
docs.text:
Armourer

Town Selsior Where Crown Market Sells Mail, helms and boots, fitted while you wait In the game Vessa

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Helewise: customer
  • Selene: sister

docs.title: Wat
docs.text:
Errand Boy

Town Selsior Where Crown Market Role Child Age Child In the game Wat

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quick, cheeky and sharper than he looks. He knows every alley shortcut in the city.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Wat is eleven, the errand boy of the Crown Market, and he can get from the gate to the palace steps faster than anyone in Selsior without once using a street that has a name. He knows every alley shortcut in the city, every gap in every fence, every courtyard with two doors, and which kitchens will let a boy run straight through if he says "Errand for the warden!" loudly enough. He is quick, cheeky and a good deal sharper than he looks, and he looks quite sharp.

docs.title: Before the errands
docs.text:
His father died when he was a baby, in a fall from a builder's scaffold, and Wat does not remember him. His mother, Cristin, took in washing and worked the coppers in Gytha's yard in the old quarters, and Wat spent his first years underfoot there, among the baskets and the steam. That is where he met Hodge, Gytha's son, when they were both too small to be any use and old enough to get into everything. They have been friends ever since.

Cristin died of a fever three winters ago, when Wat was eight. His brother Kenric, seven years older, was already apprenticed to Selene the smith in the Crown Market, and he did everything he could, which was not enough to feed two on an apprentice's pay. Wat did the rest himself. He was very good at it. For the best part of a year he picked pockets in the Crown Market, and no one caught him, and he was rather proud of that, and rather ashamed of it, and told Kenric he was running errands.

docs.title: The warden
docs.text:
Two summers ago, Reynold, the Warden of the Crown Market, caught him. Reynold is harried, honest and allergic to shortcuts, and he carries a set of weights with which he checks everyone's scales, and Wat had made the mistake of trying for his purse. Reynold caught his wrist without looking round. Then, instead of marching him to the Guard, he asked Wat how fast he could get a message to the far end of the market. Wat told him. Reynold timed him, and gave him a job.

He has run errands for the warden ever since: messages, measures, warnings about short weights, summonses to stallholders who are about to have a very bad afternoon. He sleeps with Kenric in the loft above Selene's forge, which is warm in winter and much too warm in summer, and he eats more regularly than he has in years. He is honest now, mostly. He still notices every purse in the market that is badly tied. These days, when he sees one, he tells its owner, which gives him almost as much satisfaction and makes Reynold almost smile.

docs.title: Hodge and Mab
docs.text: His two best friends are Hodge, who runs across the rooftops, and Mab, the pie seller's daughter, who turns cartwheels by the Great Bell. Between them there is no corner of the city they cannot reach: Mab handles the crowds, Hodge handles everything above them, and Wat handles the ground and everything under it. When one of them is in trouble the other two turn up, usually from an unexpected direction. Wat knows Hodge trains with a broom handle at dawn and would never tell Gytha, even though she was kind to his mother.

docs.title: Kenric
docs.text: Kenric is earnest, sooty and clumsy away from the forge, and he hopes to forge his first sword this winter. Wat teases him about everything and would fight anyone who teased him back. He knows Kenric still worries about him, and he knows Kenric still feels he failed him that first winter. Wat does not think so, and has not found a way to say so that does not sound soft.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Wat wants to be useful, and to be trusted, which for a boy who used to pick pockets is the harder of the two. What he fears is someone from the old days remembering his face, and Reynold hearing about it from them first.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with Wat noticing that a great many badly tied purses in the market are being emptied by someone who is very good, possibly better than he was. Or it might begin with Wat needing a message carried somewhere his shortcuts cannot reach: outside the gate.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Reynold: employer
  • Kenric: brother
  • Hodge: friend

docs.title: Winifred
docs.text:
Storyteller of the Old Quarter

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Resident Age Elder In the game Winifred

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Twinkling, mischievous and endlessly patient with children. She tells the same story differently every time.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Winifred is seventy-four, and every evening, when the lamps are lit in the old quarters, she sets a stool on her doorstep in the narrow lane where her husband Simkin mends shoes, folds her hands in her lap and waits. She never has to wait long. Within a few minutes the children arrive, from the lanes and the courtyards and, in her grandson's case, from somewhere above, and she tells them a story. Half the children of the old quarters grew up on Winifred's stories. A good many of their parents did too.

docs.title: Where the stories came from
docs.text:
She was born in the old quarters and went to work at twelve for a seamstress who sewed for the envoys' households near the plaza: the Savage halls, the Magician houses, the Commons merchants' widows and the old Aristocrat families who still kept rooms in the capital. Winifred hemmed and pinned and carried, and above all she listened. Every household had its own stories, and every one of them told the Balrog War differently. In the Savage hall she heard of a horned giant wreathed in flame, woken from the deep earth by the noise of the old wars. In the Magician houses she heard of a wound in the world, a hunger come through a tear from somewhere else. The Commons widows called it the Burning and said it had always been under the island. The Aristocrat families showed her chronicles full of armies and burned towns and very little about the thing that burned them.

She kept all four. She has kept them for more than sixty years, and she has added to them from every traveller who ever sat down on her step.

docs.title: The same story differently
docs.text:
Winifred is twinkling, mischievous and endlessly patient with children, and she tells the same story differently every time. On Monday the Balrog comes out of the ground; on Thursday it comes out of the sky. In one telling of the Last Stand at the Tree the Savage line holds for three days, in the next for nine. The children argue about it furiously on the way home, which is, she says, the point. She refuses, absolutely and cheerfully, to say which version she believes. When anyone presses her, she says that she believes the one she is telling, for as long as she is telling it.

Lately the questions have changed. The children used to ask whether the Balrog was real. Now, with monsters on the roads and their fathers coming home from the gate with stories of their own, they ask whether it is coming back. Winifred does not know, and she does not pretend to. She tells them that the four peoples beat it once, together, and that the kingdom they made is still here. Then she tells them a funny one, so that they sleep.

docs.title: Simkin, Gytha and Hodge
docs.text:
She married Simkin forty-nine years ago, the year after he took the little shop in the lane, and they have argued happily ever since. He is grumpy and chatty and judges people by their soles; she judges them by their stories, and the two methods agree more often than either will admit. Their only child, Gytha, came late, when Winifred was thirty-nine and had stopped expecting her. Gytha talks faster than both her parents put together and runs the washing yard in the courtyard round the corner.

Winifred helps raise Gytha's son, Hodge, who is ten. Hodge's father is the one story Winifred has never told and never asked for. Gytha does not speak of him, and Winifred, who can get a story out of anyone, has decided that some stories belong to the person who carries them.

Hodge's favourite is the Last Stand at the Tree, and he has noticed that she never tells it the same way twice. What he has not noticed is that his grandmother sleeps very little, and sits at her window at dawn, and has seen a small figure cross the ridge of the roof opposite most mornings with something long over its shoulder. She has not told Gytha. She is waiting to see how the story goes.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with a traveller on Winifred's step telling a fifth version of the Balrog's coming, one she has never heard, and Winifred wanting very much to know where it came from. Or it might begin with Winifred deciding that her grandson's story has reached the part where someone ought to step in.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Simkin: husband
  • Gytha: daughter
  • Hodge: grandson

docs.title: Wulfric
docs.text:
Vault Warden

Town Selsior Where Royal Vault Role Guard Age Adult In the game Wulfric

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Huge, quiet and soft-spoken. He blushes when thanked.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Wulfric is thirty-eight, the Warden of the Royal Vault, and he is the largest man most people in the palace have ever seen. He has to duck under nearly every door below stairs and turn sideways on the narrow ones, and when he stands before the vault's great iron-banded doors in his grey mail, with his hands folded on the pommel of his sword, visitors tend to lower their voices without knowing why. Then he speaks, and it is the softest voice in the palace, and they have to lean in to hear it. He is huge, quiet and gentle, and if you thank him for anything, even for holding a door, he turns pink to the ears.

docs.title: From the quarries to the vault
docs.text:
He grew up upstream, in a quarrymen's village where the stone for half of Selsior is cut, the son of a quarryman who could lift a block two men could not, and of a mother who sang while she split slate. Both of them are dead now. Wulfric was already the size of a doorway at fifteen, and the quarry would have taken him gladly, but he wanted to see the capital, and at eighteen he walked down the river and joined the Royal Guard.

The Guard put him on the palace gates, where he stood for eight years, and where it was discovered that nobody, not even the drunkest reveller on a festival night, ever argued with him. Twelve years ago, when the old warden of the vault retired, Aldous, the Keeper of the Royal Vault, came up to the gate to look at him, counted him twice, as he counts everything, and smiled once. Wulfric has guarded the vault doors ever since. In all that time he has never once had to draw his sword there. He oils it every week anyway, and polishes the scabbard, and says the sword is a kind of promise and a promise ought to be kept bright.

docs.title: Jocelyn
docs.text:
The vault's clerk, Jocelyn, had been at her desk for three years when Wulfric arrived. He noticed her on his first day. It took him years to do anything about it. What he did, at first, was carry her ledgers. Whenever the great bound books had to go up the stairs to the palace, Wulfric was somehow there, and he would pick up the whole stack without a word and carry it up behind her, and carry it down again after. He did this for years. It took Jocelyn a surprisingly long time to notice that he was never anywhere else when the ledgers needed carrying.

When she did notice, she asked him straight out whether he was going to say anything. He blushed to the ears and said he had been working up to it. They married four years ago. He still carries the ledgers. She labels his lunch, and the hook he hangs his cloak on, and he keeps every one of the labels in a tin, though he has not told her that.

docs.title: Below the palace
docs.text: The vault is quiet, cool and very old, and Wulfric loves it. He knows its corridors by the sound of his own boots, and he can tell from the echo when a door has been left ajar three rooms away. He knows that Jocelyn has found a locked box in the oldest records room that is in none of the ledgers, and that it keeps her awake. He cannot open it for her and would not if he could. But he has started, on his rounds, walking past the oldest records room twice instead of once.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Wulfric wants a quiet watch, a full ledger and his wife's hand on his arm on the stairs. What he fears is the day he has to draw his sword below the palace, and the thing that would make him.

A quest might begin with Wulfric hearing, on a still night, an echo in the vault's deepest corridor that matches no door he knows, or with him asking a traveller, with great embarrassment, to help him choose a present for Jocelyn that she will not immediately label.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Jocelyn: wife

docs.title: Wystan
docs.text:
Stablemaster

Town Selsior Where Knights' Court Role Worker Age Elder In the game Wystan

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Grumbling, gentle with animals and rough with people. He trusts a horse's opinion over a captain's.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Wystan is seventy-two, the stablemaster of the Knights' Court, and he does not like you. He does not like most people. He likes horses, and he will tell any captain, sergeant or visiting envoy who walks into his stables in the wrong boots exactly what he thinks of them, at length, in a voice like a cart going over cobbles. Then a frightened young horse will be led in off the road, and the same man will stand at its head for an hour, murmuring nonsense, until it puts its nose in his hand. He is grumbling, stubborn, rough with people and gentle with animals, and he trusts a horse's opinion over a captain's every time.

docs.title: Forty years in the stables
docs.text: He came to the Knights' Court stables at fourteen, fifty-eight years ago, to muck out for the old stablemaster, and he has slept within sound of a horse every night since. He has been stablemaster himself for forty years. In that time he has kept the Guard's horses through hard winters, coughing sicknesses and three captains, and he knows every animal in the long stables by its name, its temper and the sound of its feet. Recruits who come to the Court learn quickly that they can be shouted at by Bertrand in the yard or by Wystan in the stables, and that Bertrand at least stops for dinner. Pim saluted him in his first week. Wystan told him not to do that near the horses, and has privately liked him ever since.

docs.title: Aylwin
docs.text:
His wife died young, when their only child, a daughter called Elswyth, was small, and he raised the girl in rooms above the stables much as he would later raise her son. Elswyth grew up, married a riverman and moved to Riverside, and fifteen years ago, in a spring flood, the river barge she and her husband were travelling on overturned, and both of them drowned. Their boy, Aylwin, was four. Wystan went down to Riverside, picked him up and carried him back to the stables, and has never said a word about that day to anyone since.

He raised his grandson the way he raises a foal: patiently, with few words and a great deal of mucking out. Aylwin learned to ride before he could read, and he learned from his grandfather to trust a horse's opinion of a stranger. He is nineteen now and rides with the road patrol under Lieutenant Edric, and Wystan is prouder of him than he has ever been of anything. He has never said that either. When the boy came back this spring from the business with the boars on the road to Kaldemor, laughing about his hat, Wystan looked him over very carefully, from boots to hair, without saying anything at all, and then went and looked his horse over the same way.

Princess Elinor has been coming down to his stables to see the horses since she was small. Wystan grumbles at her exactly as he grumbles at everyone else, which may be why she keeps coming back. He has eyes. What he has seen with them, between his grandson and the princess, he keeps to himself.

docs.title: What the horses smell
docs.text: Horses come back from the roads jumpy and wild-eyed lately. Not all of them and not every time, but more than in forty years, and on roads that used to be dull. Good, steady animals shy at nothing in their own stalls at night, kick at the walls, will not settle until he sits with them. He has checked their feed, their water and their shoes. It is not the horses. It is something they are smelling out there, on the wind past the Greenwood or on the dust of the highland trails, and he wants very badly to know what it is.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Wystan wants every horse back in its stall at night and his grandson back in the rooms above them. What he fears is a horse coming home from the road with an empty saddle, and whose saddle it might be.

A quest might begin with Wystan asking someone to ride a patrol horse out along the Royal Road and watch exactly where it starts to sweat, or with a horse from the road patrol that comes back to the stables alone, at night, unhurt, and will not go near the road again.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Aylwin: grandson
