Everyone who lives here in the first release: People of Kaldemor.

In the game

Kaldemor is in the game. Its town guide lists its maps and hunting grounds, theme dungeon, bosses, NPCs and shops, and its quests are laid out line by line.

Design notes

The atmosphere is inspired by the bright, welcoming character of MapleStory's Henesys. The seed story, the treehouse, the mushroom houses, the clock tower, Mayor Tobin and the Snail King come from the game itself. New with this page: the guess that the seed came from the World Tree, and the clock tower being raised by the whole town.

The Lands Around Kaldemor (new): the Royal Road's Kaldemor stretch (Kaldemor Woods, the Crossing, the Greenwood), the Verdant Coast Road (agreed with Bain Harbour's page), and Kaldemor's three wild bands: the Boarwood with Gnarltusk (levels 20-30), the Deepwood with the Bluecap Mother (30-50) and Stonecap Keep with the Cap King (50-70), plus the theme dungeon, the Sleeping Stones under the Park, with the Sleeper. The chain of displacement (the Cap King's rising drives the Shrooms, the Deepwood's brood drives the boars, the boars drive Mano, Mano and the boars trouble the fields) answers Hale's question of what drove the Snail King out. Real-world touches: English hedgerow farms and stiles, boar wallows, mushroom rings and mycelium, and buried stone halls in the manner of barrows and stone circles.

Still open: who built the Sleeping Stones and why; what the carving in their deepest hall and the one on the treehouse beam show, who cut them and whether the likeness means anything (the one-seed traveller included); what overturned the harvest cart in the Greenmarsh and what became of its drivers; and why the Cap King rose this spring beyond "the Disturbance".

docs.title: Midbarium
docs.text:
The Highland Settlement

Midbarium is a rugged, rural mountain town and the ancestral home of the Savages' culture. It sits high in Veligor's dry uplands, among red-rock peaks, sheer cliffs, deep canyons and steep highland trails, and its people grew strong learning to live with them.

docs.title: The Land
docs.text:
The highlands around Midbarium are a hard, beautiful country. Rain is scarce, the sun is fierce, and the wind carries red dust down the canyons for days at a time. Above the town rise wind-carved mesas and bare stone spires; below it, dry riverbeds wind through rocky valleys dotted with caves, hardy scrub and the odd twisted tree. Nights are cold and clear, and the stars over the plateau are famous across the kingdom.

Life here follows the land. There are no grand fields like Kaldemor's. Instead, families farm small stone terraces on the slopes, watered by springs and carefully kept cisterns, and they drive herds of goats and other hardy beasts between the high pastures and the valley floors as the seasons turn. Many Midbarians live not in the town itself but in scattered homesteads and camps across the highlands, coming in to trade, to settle disputes and to celebrate.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Midbarium is built into the mountainside. Its houses are thick-walled and earthen-red, made of stone and sun-dried clay that keep out the heat of the day and hold warmth through the night. Heavy timber beams carry the roofs of the great halls, and terraces, carved stairways and swaying rope-and-plank bridges join the levels of the town across the cliffs.

Out in the highlands, herding families live in sturdy hide tents and stone shelters that can be moved or rebuilt with the seasons. Painted standards and carved totems mark the camps of each family.

docs.title: The Four Families
docs.text: Midbarium is not governed like Selsior. Its people belong to four great families, clans bound by blood, oath and shared history, and each family follows a chieftain.

docs.title: The Kragvar
docs.text: The stone-cutters. The Kragvar built Midbarium. Their ancestors cut the first terraces, raised the great hall and carved the stairways that climb the cliffs, and Kragvar masons still keep every wall and bridge in the town standing. In the Age of Division they were the hardest of the Savage warriors, and in the Balrog War they stood in the front line. Kragvar songs claim that some of their greatest fighters never came home from that war, but stayed beneath the World Tree to keep watch. The family keeps the council fire in the great hall burning, and counts that as its proudest duty.

docs.title: The Tolmach
docs.text: The herders. The Tolmach are the wanderers of the highlands. Most of the family still lives in hide tents and moves with its herds between the high pastures and the valley floors, as it has for longer than anyone remembers. They know every old path through the canyons and every spring that runs in a dry year, and that knowledge kept the Savages alive through the long wars. After the founding, it was Tolmach guides who first led traders from Kaldemor and Selsior up into the mountains, and they still bring most of the town's wool, hides and cheese down to market.

docs.title: The Uskari
docs.text: The hunters. The Uskari live along the canyon rims, and they are the best trackers, climbers and scouts in Veligor. They once hunted the great beasts of the plateau, and in the old wars they were the eyes of the Savage armies. Since the Age of Disturbance began, the Uskari have taken on a new duty: they patrol the highland trails, drive off the monsters that come up from the canyons, and see travelers safely from one camp to the next. Many young Uskari leave home to become adventurers.

docs.title: The Brenna
docs.text: The keepers. The Brenna are Midbarium's healers, storytellers and drummers. They know the highland herbs and how to set a broken bone, and they keep the memory of the families: the long songs that name every chieftain and every Old One back to the Age of Division, recited at every gathering. When the Savages and Magicians were allies, it was Brenna envoys who walked to the forests to talk with them, and the family still has old friends in Fairy Forest. The Brenna host every choosing, and their drums call the families together.

docs.title: The Chieftains and the Old One
docs.text:
A chieftain is not simply born to the role. When a chieftain dies, their family gathers around its fire and chooses a new one from among its own people, for strength, wisdom and fairness. A chieftain is expected to lead from the front: to walk the hardest trail first, to judge disputes fairly, to protect the herds and to look after the weakest members of the family.

Above the four chieftains stands one leader for all of Midbarium, whom everyone calls the Old One. The name is a title of respect, not a description: an Old One can be any age. The Old One is chosen the same way. When the Old One dies, the four families come together at the great hall, around the fire that is never allowed to go out, and choose the next. By custom, no family may hold the title twice in a row, so each Old One owes the role to all four families, not to their own.

The chieftains meet in council with the Old One to settle matters that touch the whole town. Debates are long and loud, but once the Old One closes the council, every family stands by its decision. Within Wonder Kingdom, the Old One speaks for Midbarium, and the families are as loyal to the kingdom as any lord in the capital.

docs.title: Culture and Atmosphere
docs.text:
Midbarium stands for strength, resilience, independence and respect for the ancestors. Its people admire anyone who overcomes hardship, and they guard the knowledge handed down by earlier generations: the old paths through the canyons, where water can be found in a dry year, and the stories of the four families.

Hospitality is sacred in the highlands, where a traveler turned away might not survive the night. Anyone who comes to a Midbarian fire in peace is given water, food and a place to sleep, no questions asked. Feasts, storytelling, contests of strength and long nights of drumming and song mark the families' gatherings.

For all its rugged looks, Midbarium is not hostile, primitive or grim, and it holds nothing against outsiders. Today it is a peaceful, welcoming town whose people are proud of both their ancestral traditions and their place in Wonder Kingdom.

docs.title: The Lands Around Midbarium
docs.text: The town itself is safe, as every town in the kingdom is. The highlands around it are not. Since the Age of Disturbance began, the red-rock country has grown harder to walk every year, and the Uskari Trail Watch, stretched thinner each season, holds the trails between the camps. Above the town lie the high ridges and the plateau; below it, the canyons. The Uskari like to say that every monster in the highlands comes up from the canyons sooner or later.

docs.title: The Royal Road
docs.text:
The royal road from Selsior climbs northwest off the central plain into the canyons. Its lower stretch, the Canyon Road, follows a dry riverbed between red walls, past Tolmach cairns and over a rope-and-plank bridge across a dry wash. Its upper stretch is the South Path, the old Tolmach caravan path that switchbacks up the last canyon to the town, along ledges a goat can stand on and a trader would rather not. Halfway up it, in a rock cleft, is the Greywater spring, which has run for as long as anyone remembers.

Dust boggles, quick little things that whirl up out of the dry ground, pester travelers on both stretches, and woken stumps have taken to the ledges near the top. Corwell of the Trading Post pays to have the road cleared for his caravans, and Ennek, the Tolmach guide, teaches the narrowest ledges of the South Path to anyone willing to walk them behind him.

docs.title: The Northern Woodland Trail
docs.text: The old trail to Fairy Forest leaves the town along the North Ridge, a high red ridge with an Uskari watch post and a view of the far-off woods. It drops down into the Edgewood, where the red rock gives way to the first trees, and on through the Young Woods to the forest's edge. The Brenna envoys walked it in the days when the Savages and the Magicians were allies, and the Brenna chieftain's spring letters to the forest still travel along it. Woken stumps hold the ridge, and the woods have creatures of their own.

docs.title: The High Ridges
docs.text:
From the North Ridge a path climbs onto the High Ridges: Windworn Hill, the Long Ridge and the Broken Ground, bare rock and wind, where old twisted trees cling to the ledges and the nearest Tolmach high pastures lie. The trees have woken. Stumps of dead wood and living trunk now walk the ridges, swing at anything that passes and root where they please, and they have driven the herds off the nearer pastures. The oldest of them, a great split tree called Old Gnarl, has rooted itself on Howling Peak.

This is where the Old One's quiet request begins: walk the patrols, and tell him the truth about them. Skarra, captain of the Trail Watch, has red marks on the ridges she wants checked; Sennu of the Tolmach wants a safe route back to a high pasture; Yarrek wants to know what his three goats met when they strayed down a ridge gully; and Tavi, chieftain of the Uskari, walks the worst stretch personally and will take company.

At the far end of the Broken Ground, the far canyon bridge swings across the Far Canyon to the far slopes. Vosk, the master of bridges, keeps it sound.

docs.title: The Far Slopes
docs.text:
Across the bridge lie the far slopes beyond the canyons, where rimwort grows and the Uskari once hunted the great horned beasts of the plateau. Old dry-season fires have scorched much of it. Past the Far Anchor, the ledge where the bridge's ropes are tied into the rock, the land runs out over the Scorched Slopes, the Boar Runs, the Ironback Flats and the Hot Rocks to the Ash Mesa.

The animals here have gone wild in the way an old Brenna verse describes: boars and flint-hided hogs that charge anyone on sight, and on the cliff below the Far Anchor, cliff gnawers, big sharp-toothed canyon rodents that climb sheer rock, nest in chewed rope and leave bites that fester. They are what has been gnawing the bridge's ropes by night. Above them all, a great horned plateau beast the Uskari call Grimhorn, huge, ash-coated and with one horn chipped, raids the Tolmach herds and returns to the Ash Mesa.

The story of the far slopes belongs to the town: two boys with a secret lookout and a notched stick, a bitten mason, a night watch on the bridge with Vosk and his apprentice Brakka, rimwort for Lessa the bonesetter, and Bekk, the young Trail Watch scout who wants to track the raider and has been forbidden to go alone. The great drum that calls the four families needs a new hide, and only a great horned beast's will do.

docs.title: The Withered Reach
docs.text:
Beyond the far slopes lies the Withered Reach, where the Disturbance lies thicker than anywhere else in the highlands. Dry storms break over it, bringing wind and lightning but never rain; the grass is dead and the trees are swollen and grey. Through the Dry Hills and the Weathered Rocks the way leads to the Old War Camp, the ruin of a Savage camp from the Age of Division that once held the highlands' western edge, where the Trail Watch now keeps a post. In the War Camp Ruins the camp's carved war masks have been stirred into moving, and hounds of bone and red dust prowl the broken walls. Beyond them, stone hulks, rock that walks, hold the Red Ravine.

The springs of the Reach are dying one by one, and the Greywater on the South Path, which ran through the driest year in living memory, has gone dry. In a hollow beneath the Red Ravine stands the reason: a vast dead tree, the Rootdrinker, which has driven its roots down through the rock into the deep water that feeds the highland springs and is drinking them dry.

Ennek, Sennu and old Mabbu of the Tolmach are at the heart of this story, with Brakka's eye for stone and Zirra's need for staves. So is Imre the stargazer, who has noticed that the stars low toward the island's heart sometimes shimmer as if seen through heat, and whose dates, set beside the red marks on Skarra's map, fall just before the worst stirrings of the year. Nobody can say why. The story ends in the great hall, at a gathering called by a drum with a new hide, where Ahvi the song-keeper sings an old verse about a season when the beasts grew wild before the Burning, and the four families say aloud in council what each of them has been too proud to say alone.

docs.title: The Dustfall Cave
docs.text:
Below the Uskari Rim, on the Trail Watch's canyon trail, a deep cave opens in the canyon wall. Ketta of the Uskari sheltered in it from a dust storm on her way home from adventuring, and the Uskari now call it the Dustfall Cave. It is reached from the rim by the Trail Watch's rope-way, and it goes down a very long way: through the Dustfall Mouth, down the Cliff Gallery, along the Cold Draught, where a wind blows up from below and never stops, and into the frost-rimed Chill Caves. Cave drakes have filled it and are breeding there.

At the bottom, in a lake in the dark called the Sunken Pool, lives the great drake Hollowmaw, grey-blue, frost-rimed and larger than any beast Ketta met in three years on the roads of Veligor. It is what she saw, and what saw her. Hunters of every strength go down into the cave again and again, because the drakes never stop coming up.

docs.title: Leadership Today
docs.text:
The Old One is Hask, born an Uskari. He led the Uskari as their chieftain for nine years, and six years ago, after Old One Varra of the Brenna died in her sleep, the four families gathered in the great hall and chose him through a long night of argument, drumming and song. He gave up his chieftainship that night, and the Uskari chose a new chieftain before dawn. Varra had been Old One for twenty-five years, and the Old One before her was a Tolmach, so no family has held the title twice in a row.

The four chieftains today are:

Family Chieftain Since Kragvar Dorrek 11 years, after his uncle Baruk died in a rockfall on the old north stair Tolmach Sennu 13 years, after old Bekku died Uskari Tavi 6 years, chosen the night Hask became Old One Brenna Odda 20 years

docs.text:
Name Role Ulm Keeper of the Council Fire Ahvi Song-Keeper, who remembers every chieftain and Old One Skarra Captain of the Trail Watch

People

Everyone who lives here in the first release: People of Midbarium.

In the game

Midbarium is in the game. Its town guide lists its maps and hunting grounds, theme dungeon, bosses, NPCs and shops, and its quests are laid out line by line.

Design notes

The geography and look are inspired by MapleStory's Perion. Midbarium is rural and mountainous, ruled by the chieftains of four families and the Old One, with a dry highland and desert feel. It should draw on highland, canyon and steppe cultures, not on Middle Eastern or Arabian desert cultures. Still open: how a family decides between rivals when it chooses a chieftain.

The lands around Midbarium draw on Perion's ridges, burnt lands, excavation ruins and drake caves. In the game, the roads hold levels 0 to 20; the High Ridges are the 20-30 band with Old Gnarl as its boss, the Far Slopes 30-50 with Grimhorn, and the Withered Reach 50-70 with the Rootdrinker; the Dustfall Cave is Midbarium's theme dungeon. Kept open on purpose: what makes Imre's stars shimmer; whether Grimhorn is the beast that killed Bekk's father; how Ketta got her scar; what Ahvi's verse means; and whether the bone hounds and moving masks of the war camp are anything more than the Disturbance working on what the old camp left behind.

docs.title: Selsior
docs.text:
The City of Everything

Selsior is the capital of Wonder Kingdom and by far the largest city on Veligor. It is a bustling fantasy metropolis: crowded, noisy, endlessly busy and remarkably diverse. People call it the City of Everything, and they mean it. Its residents trade, craft, teach, study, perform, govern and do a thousand other things besides, in marketplaces and workshops, schools and theatres, taverns and quiet residential lanes.

docs.title: The Treaty Field
docs.text:
Before there was a city, there was a field. When the Balrog had been sealed away, the leaders of the four peoples needed somewhere to meet that belonged to none of them. They chose a broad, empty meadow on the island's central plain, a day's ride from the World Tree, where the armies of all four peoples had camped together during the last months of the war. There, under open sky, they signed the founding treaty.

The field never emptied again. Envoys stayed to make the treaty work, traders came to sell to the envoys, craftsmen came to build for the traders, and within a generation the camp had become a town. The four peoples agreed to make it the seat of the new kingdom, precisely because it had never belonged to any of them.

docs.title: Growing Into a Capital
docs.text:
The Aristocrats brought the skills of building and government, and the early city looked much like their old fortress towns: thick walls, a stone keep and straight streets. But the Commons filled it with markets and workshops, Magicians founded its first schools, and Savage clans built halls for their envoys and their feasts. Over the centuries, Selsior outgrew every wall built around it, and the old quarters grew into the winding maze they are today.

The spot where the treaty was signed is now the central plaza. The Great Bell stands there on its dais, cast from metal given by all four peoples. It rings only when a new monarch is crowned, and the guards will tell anyone who asks that it rings for no one else.

docs.title: The Palace and the Crown
docs.text:
The kingdom's monarch rules from the palace at the head of the plaza, where the throne hall's red carpet runs up the palace steps. The crown's task, as Selsior's people like to say, is not to command the kingdom but to keep it together: to uphold the founding treaty, settle disputes between towns, keep the roads safe and speak for Wonder Kingdom as a whole. Each town keeps its own leaders and customs, from Kaldemor's mayor to Midbarium's Old One.

The Royal Vault beneath the palace keeps the kingdom's treasures and records, and its keepers will also guard the belongings of any citizen who asks.

docs.title: The Knights' Court and the Royal Guard
docs.text:
The Royal Guard keeps the peace in the capital and on the royal roads. Its home is the Knights' Court, where recruits drill from dawn and its captains train warriors in the way of the sword. The Guard is open to anyone from any town who can pass its trials, and since the Age of Disturbance began, it has had no shortage of work. Its ranks run from the Swordsman to the Swordmaster and the Grand Swordmaster, and old books name one more, the Sword Saint, earned by very few.

A warrior who passes the Swordmaster's trial is not a Swordmaster until they have sworn the Swordmaster's oath. They walk down the Upper Stair to Cavelor and swear it in the Oath Hall before the Keeper of the Oath, binding the Guard's blades to the founders' duty of keeping the Balrog imprisoned. The custom began with Queen Aveline's alliance with Cavelor fifteen years ago, when every serving Swordmaster and Grand Swordmaster went down to swear it, and every new Swordmaster has sworn it since.

docs.title: The Crown Market
docs.text: The Crown Market is the busiest place on Veligor. Here, Kaldemor's bread sits beside Midbarium's wool, Bain Harbour's fish beside Fairy Forest's herbs, and Urbanograd's strange inventions beside the finest blades in the kingdom. Its shopkeepers, apothecaries, weaponsmiths and armourers serve adventurers from every town.

docs.title: The Gate
docs.text: The city's great gate faces the Royal Road, which runs east past the Greenwood to Kaldemor. Gate guards greet every traveller, and taxis wait at the gate stand to carry visitors between the capital and the other towns.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Selsior is a classic medieval fantasy city. Timber-framed houses stand on stone foundations under brightly colored roofs, towers rise over the skyline, and cobblestone streets run between the neighborhoods.

At its heart lie broad avenues, great public squares, the palace and the city's most important civic spaces. Around them sprawl dense old quarters that grew without a plan: winding streets, narrow passages, hidden courtyards, crowded homes, little local markets, and skywalks that cross above the streets.

docs.title: Culture and Atmosphere
docs.text:
Selsior is cheerful, sociable and full of energy. Street performers draw crowds on every corner, dancers turn in the plaza, festivals fill the squares, and there always seems to be something to celebrate. The city is busy not only because people work there, but because its people love city life and throw themselves into it.

Folk from every corner of Wonder Kingdom live side by side in Selsior, and nobody thinks that strange. More than anywhere else, the capital shows what the founding of the kingdom achieved: prosperity, cooperation and a shared identity, with room for every kind of life and ambition.

docs.title: The Gates and the Roads
docs.text:
Selsior has three gates. The great gate faces east, the Tree Gate faces north toward the World Tree, and the Bridge Gate opens west onto the city bridge over the river, which runs down past the city's west side from the north. Every royal road begins at one of them:

  • The Royal Road to Kaldemor leaves by the great gate and runs east up the Selsior Approach, over the rise and on toward the Greenwood.
  • The road to Bain Harbour leaves by the great gate beside the Royal Road and soon parts from it, bearing east toward the coast.
  • The road to Fairy Forest leaves by the Tree Gate with the World Tree Road and bears away northeast once the hedges end.
  • The road to Midbarium leaves by the Bridge Gate, crosses the city bridge and climbs away northwest toward the highlands.
  • The road to Urbanograd leaves by the Bridge Gate over the city bridge and runs due west.
  • The road to Goa Harbour crosses the city bridge with the Urbanograd road and parts from it to bear southwest toward the far coast.

docs.title: The World Tree Road
docs.text:
The World Tree Road runs north from the Tree Gate to the foot of the World Tree, a day's ride across the plain. It is broad and well kept, marked every mile by tall old waystones, and busier than it used to be: royal couriers ride it with letters for the Tree, and every warrior who passes the Swordmaster's trial walks it on the way to the Upper Stair. The river is never far off to the west.

Outside the gate the road runs through the Hedge Lanes, farm lanes between tall hedgerows and orchards, where slimes and snails creep along the verges. Further on it crosses the Waystone Meadows, open grass where the great waystones stand and pigs and mushrooms have grown bold enough to block the road. Last come the Rootlands, where the plain rises and the Tree's outermost roots break the turf like low walls, and stumps that have learned to walk wander among them. The road ends at the Tree's foot.

The Road Patrol keeps the World Tree Road as it keeps the royal roads, and Lieutenant Edric posts bounties on all three stretches. Two ways lead off it into wilder country: east from the Hedge Lanes onto the downs, and west from the Waystone Meadows down to the river at the Quarry Landing.

docs.title: The Selsior Downs
docs.text:
East of the Hedge Lanes lie the Selsior Downs, the open downs beyond the capital: rolling chalk grassland, thyme and clover, sheepfolds, dew ponds and white chalk banks, where Selsior's shepherds have grazed their flocks for as long as there has been a city. Lately the shepherds have brought their flocks in.

The wild bees of the downs, which nest in the chalk, have turned mean, and boars have come up onto the grass from the woods to root up the folds. The danger grows the further one walks from the road: from Downs Edge, past the Thyme Banks where the boars wallow, to the Chalk Hives, where the bees have cut their nests deep into the banks. Beekeepers in the city say their own hives have been short-tempered since spring, and the palace gardener has been stung more this year than in all his life before.

Those who have gone to the bottom of it found the reason in the Hive Hollow, a hollow in the chalk walled with old comb, where Queen Amberwing rules the swarms: a Disturbance-touched bee queen grown larger than a calf.

docs.title: The Long Reach
docs.text:
From the Waystone Meadows a track runs west to the Quarry Landing, a stone wharf where the road from the quarries meets the river barges. Downstream of it lies the Long Reach, a deep, slow stretch of river between high banks, half a day upstream of the city, which the bargehands have learned to fear.

Since the roads grew dangerous the river has never been busier, and its creatures have never been bolder. Great lizards bask in the Reed Beds, crabs as big as cartwheels scuttle along the Long Reach Banks, and in the Undercut, where the river has eaten under the banks, larger lizards still lie in wait for anything that comes to the water's edge. Barges pass the Reach at speed now, if their masters are wise.

The worst of it is Longjaw, a deeply touched river beast as long as a barge, which hunts the whole river from the Long Reach down past the city. It flattens a cart-wide path through the reeds when it leaves the water, and lairs in the Heron Pool, the deepest pool of the Reach, where the herons used to stand before they left.

docs.title: The Upstream Quarries
docs.text:
Upstream of the Quarry Landing, on rising ground, are the Upstream Quarries, where the stone of Selsior has been cut since the first city was built. Terraced grey cuts climb the hillside among spoil heaps, cranes and sledge-ways, and a quarrymen's village stands among them, quieter than it was.

The stone has started to stand up. On the Spoil Heaps rubble gathers itself into small walking shapes; on the Terraced Cuts golems of solid rock step out of the faces the quarrymen were working; and in the Deep Cut, the oldest workings still in use, they are bigger, darker and harder to break. The quarrymen have stopped cutting the oldest faces. Nobody can say whether the golems slept in the stone all along or the Disturbance made them, and the scholars of the Academy, asked, say plainly that nobody knows. What is known, from the notebooks of an adventurer of the Crooked Lantern, is that they wake in waves.

At the top of the quarries is the First Cut, the ancient face that gave the first keep its stone. Out of it has risen Old Cairn, the Ancient of the Quarries, a golem as tall as a house.

docs.title: The Old Drains
docs.text:
Selsior's oldest danger is under its own streets. The Old Drains run beneath the old quarters, and below them lie the buried foundations of the first fortress-town that the Aristocrats built on the Treaty Field: its walls, its great cisterns, even whole streets that were walled over and built upon as the city grew.

For some months the night watch has heard something scratching under the gratings, slower and heavier than any rat. The rats themselves, grown as big as cats, have stopped running from lanterns and started moving up, out of the deep tunnels and into the cellars, and the mice under Theatre Row have fled to the rafters. When a grating in Steps Lane, a steep lane of the old quarters with steps instead of cobbles, was found pushed up from below, the Royal Guard set a watch on it.

Below Steps Lane the way runs down through the Old Drains themselves, into the pillared water halls of the Cisterns, along the Buried Street, a street of the first city with its doorways and lamp brackets still standing in the dark, and on to the Delver's Burrow. Fresh tunnels cut by great claws run through all of it, straight through walls the founders' masons laid. At the end of them waits the Delver, a deeply touched burrowing beast as big as a cart, blind and tireless, which has dug its way up from somewhere below. What drove it up, nobody knows.

docs.title: Leadership Today
docs.text:
Queen Aveline has ruled Wonder Kingdom from the palace for sixteen years. She was crowned under the Great Bell at twenty-eight, after the long reign of King Bertram, who sat on the throne for forty-two years and sent the Great World Tree Expedition. The Bell has not rung since her coronation. She is married to Leofric, once a road surveyor, and they have two children, Princess Elinor and Prince Alaric.

In the first year of her reign, Aveline became the first reigning monarch to walk down the Upper Stair to Cavelor, and she swore an alliance with its Keeper of the Oath: the crown answers every message from below. Eight years ago she made Rhys Captain of the Royal Guard.

docs.text:
Name Role Rhys Captain of the Royal Guard Osbert Royal Steward, who has run the palace for over thirty years Melisende Mistress of the Envoys' Hall, who advises the queen when towns quarrel Edric Lieutenant of the Road Patrol Hugh Warden of the Great Bell Bartholomew Master of the Royal Academy Reynold Warden of the Crown Market Clement Royal Herald

In the game

Selsior is in the game. Its town guide lists its maps and hunting grounds, theme dungeon, bosses, NPCs and shops, and its quests are laid out line by line.

Design notes

Classic medieval fantasy architecture. Joyful, bustling and cosmopolitan. New with this page: the Treaty Field and the treaty signed where the plaza now stands, the Great Bell cast from all four peoples' metal, and the crown's role as keeper of the treaty. New with "The Lands Around Selsior": the Tree Gate and the Bridge Gate, the river running from north to south past the city's west side, the World Tree Road's three stretches, the Selsior Downs, the Long Reach, the Upstream Quarries, and the Old Drains over the first city's buried foundations. Still open: how monarchs are chosen; whether the golems of the quarries are new creatures or slept in the stone all along; why the monster changes come in waves; and what drove the Delver up.

docs.title: Urbanograd
docs.text:
The Town of Societal Rebels

Urbanograd is a city unlike any other on Veligor. It was founded 100 years ago, long after the four peoples had united, so its identity has nothing to do with the old wars. It grew up inside the kingdom, built by people who wanted to live their own way: free to express themselves and free of the expectations of ordinary society. Over the century since, it has grown a counterculture all its own.

docs.title: A Kingdom That Had Settled Down
docs.text:
A century ago, Wonder Kingdom had known peace for so long that peace had grown comfortable, and comfort had grown habits. In Selsior, the old guilds decided who could practice which trade, who could sell in which square and which songs could be sung in the theatres. Families expected their children to follow the trade they were born into. Even Kaldemor, for all its warmth, had firm ideas about what a good, honest life looked like.

None of this was cruel. It was simply how things had always been done, and most people were happy with it. But a restless few were not: painters whose work the galleries called vulgar, musicians who played too loud and too fast, tinkerers whose inventions no guild would license, young people who wanted to dress, love and live in ways their elders did not understand. In the capital, they gathered in cellars, rooftops and back-alley taverns, and they began to talk about leaving.

docs.title: The Long Walk
docs.text:
The spark was a small thing. When the theatre guild of Selsior banned a play by Juna Marrow, a young playwright whose comedy poked fun at the city's grandees, she performed it anyway, on a cart in the middle of the market square, to the biggest crowd the square had seen in years. The guild had her cart hauled away. That night, she told her friends she was done asking permission, and that she meant to build a town where nobody would ever have to.

A few weeks later, about three hundred people walked out of Selsior's gates together: artists, musicians, craftspeople without a guild, inventors, wanderers, and plenty who simply wanted something different. Others joined them along the road from Kaldemor, the harbours and the highlands. They called themselves the Walkers, and the day they left is still celebrated in Urbanograd as Walkout Day.

docs.title: The Empty City
docs.text:
The Walkers did not build Urbanograd from nothing. They settled in Old Grad, in the west of the island: the ruins of a walled stronghold built by the Aristocrats in the Age of Division and abandoned after the founding of the kingdom, when nobody needed fortresses anymore. For generations it had stood empty: crumbling towers, roofless halls and a maze of narrow streets slowly being taken back by weeds.

The Walkers saw something else in it. They patched the roofs with whatever they could find, strung lanterns between the towers, painted every bare wall and turned the old barracks into workshops, theatres and homes. They added the name the city still carries: Urbanograd, roughly "the city of Grad", half a joke about the grand old fortress and half a promise of what it would become.

The first winters were hard. The Walkers knew a great deal about art and very little about farming, and more than one of them went home. Those who stayed learned to trade their crafts, music and inventions for food, and travelers began to come just to see the strange new town.

docs.title: The Kingdom's Answer
docs.text:
Not everyone was pleased. Some in Selsior called the Walkers deserters, and a few guild masters asked the crown to send them home. The question went all the way to the royal court.

The answer came from the founding treaty itself. It promised that every people of Veligor could live together in peace, whatever their culture. The court ruled that the promise did not only protect the four peoples who had signed it, but any people who chose to live differently, so long as they kept the kingdom's peace and laws. Urbanograd was recognized as a town of Wonder Kingdom, with the same rights as any other.

That ruling, known in Urbanograd as the Open Charter, is the reason the city exists as it does today. Its people have never forgotten that the kingdom chose to welcome them, and that is why their rebellion has always been about how they live, never about overturning the realm that let them.

docs.title: A Century of Urbanograd
docs.text:
Over the next hundred years, Old Grad filled up. Each generation built on top of the last, so the city grew upward rather than outward: houses stacked on houses, bridges between rooftops, staircases that lead to three different places at once. New arrivals kept coming from every town on Veligor, bringing their own crafts and ideas and making the city ever more varied.

Today Urbanograd is a busy, noisy, colorful town, famous for its music, its street art, its workshops and its night markets. Juna Marrow's play is performed in the main square every Walkout Day, on a cart, as it was the first time.

docs.title: Cultural Identity
docs.text:
Urbanograd is famous as the home of societal rebels. Its people prize individuality, creativity, unconventional thinking, free expression and the right to live differently. The city draws anyone who loves alternative lifestyles and unusual art, music and fashion.

The city has no lord or chieftain. Matters that concern everyone are talked out at the Open Table, a long gathering in the old fortress's great hall where anyone who lives in Urbanograd may speak. It is loud, slow and often funny, and its people would not have it any other way.

But its people are not revolutionaries. They have no wish to unsettle the kingdom, topple its institutions or quarrel with their neighbors. Their rebellion is cultural and personal, not political.

docs.title: Relationship with Wonder Kingdom
docs.text:
Urbanograd is a full and proud part of Wonder Kingdom. Its people respect the kingdom and get along well with every other community, and the rest of Veligor accepts the city's unusual character. Its people are understood, not distrusted. Even Selsior's guilds, which once wanted the Walkers brought home, now send their apprentices to Urbanograd to see what new things its workshops have come up with.

Urbanograd shows that the kingdom's founding promise reaches further than peace between the original four peoples. Wonder Kingdom also welcomes communities that invent entirely new ways of living.

docs.title: The Lands Around Urbanograd
docs.text: Old Grad stands on its rise in the west of Veligor, and the city has only one way out: the old fortress gate at the end of the Gate Walk. Three roads leave from below it. The royal road runs east across the island to Selsior. Stonefang Pass climbs northeast into the red rock toward Midbarium. The Western Merchant Road, the Aristocrats' old road to the sea, runs southwest to Goa Harbour and is described on that town's page. Inside the walls there is nothing to fear. Outside them, the Gate Watch keeps count: Brindle chalks every sighting on the slate by the gate, and the numbers only go one way.

docs.title: The Gate Meadows
docs.text: All three roads begin in the same place: the open meadows below the gate, where Patch learned her herbs as a girl and carts pull up to wait for morning. A city that keeps building upward needs somewhere to keep its timber and stone, so half the meadows are stackyards: piles of beams and fortress stone, half-built scaffolds, rope cranes and sheds, all of it painted by somebody at some point. Creatures have learned to den among the stacks. Adders sun themselves on the warm stone, and the low, shining-eyed things Dagny sees from the gate at night come up out of the old ditches to hunt among the timber. The way into the Outworks opens from the meadows, where the old ditches run off along the foot of the walls.

docs.title: The Walkers' Road
docs.text: The royal road from Selsior is the way the Walkers came, a century ago, with their bundles and their cart, and Urbanograd has called it the Walkers' Road ever since. From the Gate Meadows it runs east past the edge of the Bristlewood to the Halfway Stone, a tall grey marker that the Walkers are said to have slept beside on their first night out of Selsior's sight. Urbanograd's builders keep a stone depot there, with a crane, a scaffold and a carters' shelter, and the crossroads is busy by day and noisy with creatures by night: rats in the stone stacks, things with too many arms in the drainage pools, adders in the verge. Beyond the stone the road runs on toward the central plain and the capital. Since the year after Rook's first letter to the queen, the Royal Guard's road patrols have ridden its whole length, all the way to the Gate Meadows.

docs.title: Stonefang Pass
docs.text: Stonefang Pass is the highland road. Wool carters bring it down from the hills, and Torvi came down it six years ago meaning to stay a week. From the Gate Meadows it bears northeast into the Seepwater Foothills, where springs seep out of the rock and turn the low ground to bog: reed beds, rotten boardwalks, mist in the mornings, and lumpish bog-lurchers that heave themselves out of the pools at anyone who leaves the planks. Beyond the foothills the pass climbs out of the wet into the Western Descent, a road of red rock ledges and switchbacks where dark, walking stumps root along the path and the axe-headed kind wait at the turns. At the top of the descent stand the needle-sharp spires that give the pass its name, and beyond them the pass comes out on Midbarium's western edge, where the highland families' own country begins.

docs.title: The Outworks
docs.text:
The Aristocrats did not trust walls alone. Around the foot of Old Grad they dug ditches, raised earth banks and built small outer towers, and when they left, all of it fell into ruin. Urbanograd calls this ring of tumbled stone, brambles and half-buried cellars the Outworks. It is reached from the Gate Meadows and runs right round the city's outward side.

For a hundred years the Outworks were a place for children's dares. This year they are where the trouble at the walls comes from. Lux finds outer lanterns smashed in the mornings, never on the same night twice. Dagny sees pairs of eyes low in the brush beyond the road. Both are true, and they are two different things. The eyes belong to gloomeyes, lizard-like creatures with great shining eyes that have crept out of the old ditches to hunt along the walls. The lanterns are the work of lampbats, a swarm that roosts in the flooded cellars under the ruin of the outermost tower, which Urbanograd calls the Fallen Tower, and that throws itself at any light on the walls.

The swarm has a leader. The Gloamwing is a bat the size of a market awning, Disturbance-touched, that hunts every second night and drives the swarm before it. It hates noise, and that is what Drum half-noticed without being able to prove it: on nights the beat in Lantern Square is loudest, the lanterns survive.

The story of the Outworks begins with Brindle, who needs someone to stand the night watch beside Dagny and find out what the eyes are. It runs through Lux's watch on the outer walls and a crate of new panes carried from Tinsel's furnace before the lanterns go dark, a basket of herbs for Patch from the meadows inside the old ditches, and Drum's rhythm, played for the first time outside the gate, to scatter the swarm. It ends under the Fallen Tower, with the Gloamwing. At the far, eastern end of the Outworks, the ditches give out among trees: the edge of the Bristlewood.

docs.title: The Bristlewood
docs.text:
East of the city, along the Walkers' Road from within sight of the city's towers almost to the Halfway Stone, lie the wooded hills of the Bristlewood: old oak and hazel, steep stream valleys and boar wallows. The road's travelers have always heard boar in it. Now the boar come out of it, in herds, and charge the carts.

Shade knows the Bristlewood's near edge well, and two of the routes Shade no longer trusts are there: the Silent Cutting, a wooded cutting where the birds have stopped singing, and the Tusk Path, a hill path where the tracks have grown too large. Deeper in, the streams spread into the Reedwater Bottoms, a marshy valley floor of reeds and black pools where the boar wallow and reed-lurkers lie in wait. At the edge of the bottoms, two days out from the city by cart, is the stream bank where Zip chased something large and tusked, fell, and broke her arm in two places last spring. At the top of that bank Torvi found tracks bigger than any boar's. Zip has named it Zip's Bank, and has asked everyone else to call it that too.

The tracks belong to Hackleback, a boar heavier than a loaded wagon, so deeply touched by the Disturbance that its bristles have gone hard as iron. It has made its home in the Wallow, a deep mud hollow at the heart of the bottoms, and it drives the lesser boar out of the trees and toward the road ahead of it.

This is the hunt that Hatch can no longer make alone. His story is a teacher's: first a test of whether the hero can read tracks at the wood's edge, then Shade's new route past the Tusk Path, then Hatch's own notes, recovered from the camp he had to abandon in the Bristlewood when his knees failed him there. Torvi goes back with the hero to Zip's Bank. Zip and Margo's spark lamp get their trial against real boar, and Zip brings the lamp back, as promised. Patch's rarest root, the one she cannot get anywhere else, is found in the Silent Cutting. Last comes the Wallow, and a hunt Hatch plans but cannot walk. Afterwards, Tick writes the fourth version of Zip's story, the first one that is true.

docs.title: The Beacon Downs
docs.text:
Beyond the Bristlewood's far end the trees thin and the land climbs onto high, bare chalk downs that roll away east toward the middle of the island. Along their crest stands a chain of ruined towers: the beacon towers the Aristocrats built to pass fire signals between their strongholds in the Age of Division. Urbanograd calls the whole country the Beacon Downs, and the tallest tower, on the highest hill, the Highbeacon.

The downs are the wild country Perch's pigeons refuse to cross. At dusk the sky above them belongs to the duskhawks, great hook-beaked hunters that strike anything on the wing, and the grass below belongs to downs howlers, shaggy horned beasts that bay at dusk, and to rams with horns like millstones. The routes the pigeons will not fly at any hour pass over the Highbeacon itself, where Stormcrest nests: a raptor with a wingspan wider than a city street, deeply touched by the Disturbance, that has taken the old tower for its eyrie.

The Beacon Downs are also the nearest high ground from which to look east toward the middle of the island, and that brings in Starling. The story of the downs begins in Perch's loft, with a message the birds refuse to carry, which the hero walks over the downs on foot and gives to a bird released on the far side. It goes on through the dusk skies and the duskhawks, a new lens carried from Tinsel's furnace to Starling's roof through the evening crowds, and long nights on the downs. On one of them, from the ruins of a lower beacon, Starling and the hero watch the far horizon waver, just as Starling has seen it from the Rooftops, and find that it wavers far beyond the downs, further east than anyone can walk in a night. It is not the downs' doing. But on the nights it comes, the duskhawks are restless and hunt late, and that is why some of Starling's dates match Perch's list and some do not.

The story ends at the Highbeacon with Stormcrest. Afterwards, the pigeons fly the dusk routes again, though not every route. The hero carries Starling's dates and Perch's list to Rook, who reads them twice, says nothing funny at all, and sends them to Queen Aveline in the next letter. What the flicker is, nobody in Urbanograd can say.

docs.title: Low Grad
docs.text:
Old Grad was built as a fortress, and fortresses go down as well as up. Under the Great Hall, behind the kitchens, is an iron door that the Walkers found locked a century ago and never had a key for. Below it lie the old fortress's buried levels: the halls of the old keep, storerooms and vaults, flooded cisterns, the sally tunnels the garrison used to leave the fortress unseen, and the quarry the Aristocrats cut Old Grad's dark stone from. The city calls all of it Low Grad, and until this summer nobody had been down.

It begins with Velvet's warm stone, and with Tick's notebook. Velvet bought the stone from a frightened wanderer off the deep roads. In his notebook, Tick has written down that same wanderer's story: he sheltered from a storm in a tunnel mouth in the hills, followed it a long way underground, and came out running, with a dark stone in his pocket that would not cool. Brindle hears the story and sees what it might mean: tunnels under the country that may run all the way to the fortress, and a way into the city that no gate guards. The Open Table argues the question for a whole night (Bastian argues both sides, and wins both), and then agrees to open the door. Hex, who learned locks before boxes, opens it, delighted by its Aristocrat lock.

Low Grad goes down in four levels. The Undercroft holds the old keep's halls and the Aristocrats' storerooms, full of rot, dust and creeping slimes. The Floodwells are flooded halls where lurkers lie in the dark water. The Deep Roads are the sally tunnels, long and narrow, roosted by bats and running out under the hills toward the wanderer's tunnel mouth. Last comes the Warm Quarry, where the dark stone is warm to the touch and creatures of that same stone have stirred. The quarry's master is the Warmstone Colossus, a giant of dark stone and the deepest-touched thing beneath the city.

The keeper of Low Grad is Leland, an old well-digger who knows more about what lies under the city's streets than anyone alive, and whom the Table has named Keeper of the Low Door. He keeps the door, the ropes and a chalk map of every level that grows a little each day, and he lets anyone with the nerve go down, as often as they like. At the end of the Deep Roads, the Watch has set an iron grate from Ferro's forge across the tunnel. A chip of the warm stone sits on Tinsel's windowsill with the other failed experiments, and it is still warm.

docs.title: Leadership Today
docs.text: Urbanograd still has no lord. Each year the Open Table chooses a Caller to convene it and keep order, and the Caller rules no one. This year's Caller, for the first time, is Rook, a chandler from Workshops Row whose great-grandparent was one of the Walkers. The Table chose Rook this spring because Rook hates making speeches and loves listening to them. Rook has also written to Queen Aveline every fortnight for nine years.

People

Everyone who lives here in the first release: People of Urbanograd.

In the game

Urbanograd is in the game. Its town guide lists its maps and hunting grounds, theme dungeon, bosses, NPCs and shops, and its quests are laid out line by line.

Design notes

The atmosphere is inspired by MapleStory's Kerning City. Juna Marrow, the Walkers, Old Grad, the Open Charter and the Open Table are new with this page. Urbanograd lies in the west of the island, as the game's world map has it. Still open: what the city looks like beyond its fortress core.

The Lands Around Urbanograd are new with this section: the Gate Meadows and their stackyards, the Walkers' Road and the Halfway Stone, Stonefang Pass's Seepwater Foothills and Western Descent (the spires and the far canyon bridge belong to Midbarium's side), the Outworks, the Bristlewood, the Beacon Downs, Low Grad, their creatures and bosses, and Leland. Still open: what the horizon flicker is; why the stone of the Warm Quarry is warm, and whether Velvet's stone is the same; and what the wanderer saw underground. None of them is tied to the Balrog here. The bosses are Disturbance-touched creatures, nothing more. The Walkers' Road follows the Long Walk in spirit; exactly which way the Walkers went is not recorded.

docs.title: Elite and Epic monsters
docs.text:
Each defeat raises the chance that the next monster to appear is Elite by 0.2% (up to 5%). After 3 elites, an Epic monster appears.

Elite Epic Modifiers 1 2 HP multiplier x8 x30 EXP multiplier x6 x25 Touch multiplier x2 x3 Attack multiplier x2 x3 Defense multiplier x2 x3 Extra drop rolls 1 2 Meso multiplier x3 x8

Modifiers an elite can roll:

  • Elemental: one of fire, ice, lightning, poison
  • Shielded: a shield of 40% of its HP that refills after 5 s without being hit
  • Regenerating: heals 2% of its HP per second after 3 s without being hit
  • Shockwave: a ground slam for 150% damage every 5 s
  • Swift: moves at 140% speed

docs.title: Agatha
docs.text:
River Fisher

Town Selsior Where Riverside Story Agatha in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Lovely day for it! Wet, cold, and the eels are biting."
  • "Silas, your prices are a disgrace! Love you."
  • "Torn again. Three rows deep. No fish did that."
  • "Robin! Not the deep end!"

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Guards for the River (gives)
  • Torn Nets (gives)
Dialogue
  • Agatha, river fisher. My father Osmund poles the ferry, and my husband Silas sells my catch in the Crown Market. Overcharges for it, too.
  • Met him across his stall. Told him his prices were a disgrace; he said mine were worse. Eleven years married and we still haven't settled it.
  • Fair, close to the bank. I've moved into the shallows lately. Don't ask me to explain it. A fisher just knows when to.
  • Long ragged rents, three or four rows at once, and nothing in the net around the hole. As if the fish were taken out before the net came up.
  • I know every fish in this river. It's none of them. And my father won't cross after dark any more, and won't tell me why.
  • Off you go! If you're in the market, tell Silas his eels are overpriced.
  • Morning, Player! Mind the nets, they're my father's and older than you. What brings you down to the water?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: How's the fishing?
    • Choice: What tore your nets?
    • Choice: Just looking.
  • Silas's guard boat goes out tomorrow. He's named it after a mackerel. Of course he has.

docs.title: Agna
docs.text:
Net-Mender

Town Goa Harbour Where Goa Harbour Story Agna in the lore Services Quests

Your knot's slipping. No, the other one.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Fifty years on this crate. The crate's held up better than my knees."
  • "That's a granny knot. Who taught you that? Not me."
  • "Not bad. That's all I'll say. Not bad."
  • "In my day we fished at night, a lantern in every bow."
  • "Another long tear. Mend and mend again."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Nets for the Boats (gives)
  • Agna's Notch (gives)
  • Torn Nets (gives)
Dialogue
  • So the water's been over my notch. Twice, the girl says. I cut that mark when I was ten. I don't like it, Player, and I'm too old to pretend I do.
  • The racks have been quiet since the gulls learned their lesson. That's one kind of tear I won't see for a while.
  • Still have your claws on my bench. I look at them now and then. They're honest, crabs.
  • Well? I can talk and mend at once. I've had fifty years' practice.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What tears the nets?
    • Choice: Tell me about the night fishing.
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Agna. I've mended the coves' nets fifty years, and my mother before me. Every boat on this shingle fishes with my knots, and they know it.
  • Sorcha's my girl. Loud as me, stubborn as me, which is why we argue. Calder's a good one, he mends without being asked. The magpie and Eilidh you'll have met. Everyone has.
  • Long bites through a dozen meshes at once. Not the ragged hole a seal leaves, not a clean cut off a rock. Always from boats that went out past the point.
  • I mend every one. And I say nothing in front of Eilidh, who notices everything. Ask me something else.
  • The crab work and the gull work I can mend half asleep. The long tears from past the point I mend wide awake. Ask me something else.
  • When I was young the boats went out on still summer nights with a lantern in every bow. From the shore you could count them, strung across the water like a second line of stars.
  • I went out with Maili more than once, her that married Varro the warden after. Nobody's fished at night here for twenty years. The young ones think I made it up. You don't. I can see.
  • Off with you. And retie that knot.

docs.title: Agnes
docs.text:
Palace Maid

Town Selsior Where Palace Story Agnes in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Beds made, grates swept, and not a soul saw me do it."
  • "I hear everything. I only say half. Lucky you."
  • "That is not garden mud. I know garden mud."
  • "One day I will get a story out of Sybil. One day."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• A Wing on the Sill (gives)
  • Bats in the Chimneys (gives)
Dialogue
  • The flue is netted and Osbert has not asked me a single question. I am almost disappointed.
  • Oh, hello! Mind the floor, it is just polished. I am Agnes; I keep the upper halls. Are you lost, or just curious? I like curious.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What happens in the upper halls?
    • Choice: Heard anything interesting?
    • Choice: I will let you work.
  • I grew up in the kitchens. That loud man shouting at the pots is my father, Cuthbert.
  • At fourteen I asked Osbert for a place in the household. Two years ago he gave me the upper halls, which from him is practically a speech.
  • Fires laid, beds made, linen counted, all before anyone notices. A good maid is never seen. A great maid sees everything.
  • Interesting? In a palace? Every day! Most of it I keep to myself, though.
  • There is one thing. Someone's boots come back muddy every morning, and it is not garden mud. A sweetheart, a secret or a horse. I like all three.
  • Bye now! If you hear anything good, you know where to find me.

docs.title: Ahvi
docs.text:
Song-Keeper

Town Midbarium Where Midbarium Story Ahvi in the lore Services Quests

Good evening, Player. Mind the names.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Varra, of the Brenna. Then Hask, of the Uskari. Just so."
  • "That is not how the chieftain's name is said."
  • "A clear night. Imre will be on the terrace."
  • "Some verses are heavier than others."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Old Verses (gives)
  • The Beast Verse (gives)
  • The Verse (completes)
  • Dates and Dots (completes)
Dialogue
  • Good evening, Player. Forgive me if I correct you later; I correct everyone who gets a chieftain's name wrong, even Old Ones. Especially Old Ones.
  • Odda gave me two verses I had half forgotten, and Thrun gave me one I had never heard, which he insists his grandmother sang while churning butter. The song is a little longer tonight than it was.
  • Imre's dates: the shimmering nights, and after each one the worst stirring of the season. I have kept songs for thirty-five years and I cannot tell you what it means. I can only tell you it is so.
  • The hounds, the masks, the wild goats, the gnawers. I have decided: the verse is true, as far as a verse can be. Whether it is sung is not mine alone to decide.
  • I sang it at the gathering, before all four families: a season when the beasts grew wild, before the Burning. The song does not say what it means. It is sung again, and the families heard it together.
  • What would you hear?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What troubles you?
    • Choice: Who is the stargazer?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Ahvi, song-keeper of the Brenna. Old Hadda taught me from the age of eight. I sang the long song at my sister Varra's choosing, and through the whole night of Hask's choosing, and at dawn I added his name after hers.
  • There is a short verse in the oldest part of the long songs, among the chieftains of the Age of Division: goats that bite, cats that hunt people, birds that will not settle, a season before the Burning. I have sung it alone every night this summer.
  • It is sung now, and it will be in Neffa's lessons. She will learn it properly. Not yet. But properly.
  • Imre and I swap star stories on the high terrace on clear nights: lowland names for Brenna stars, Brenna songs for lowland stars. Imre forgets supper and never forgets a star. I suspect a song is being written up there, though nobody has told me so.
  • Good night. Mind the names.

docs.text:
Keeper of the Tide Book

Town Goa Harbour Where The Wardens' House Story Ailsa in the lore Services Quests

Mind the desk, Player. And the stack. Especially the stack.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "High water at the quay steps, three hours past noon. As in the spring of the long frost."
  • "Halvard has straightened my notes again. Good."
  • "Someone has spelled westerly with two Ts."
  • "Bread at midday. Then the moons."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• A Hard Quill (gives)
  • Not All of It (gives)
  • Marks Where the Boats Cannot Go (gives)
  • The Verse and the Page (completes)
Dialogue
  • Sit down, Player. No, there. You may read over my shoulder today. Today only.
  • Your marks are in the book. In my hand, not yours. Yours was adequate.
  • Still writing. Still sharp. The quill, I mean.
  • Ah. Someone who knows not to touch the stack.
  • Well? The book does not write itself. I have asked it to.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Tell me about the Tide Book.
    • Choice: How is Halvard?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Ailsa. Keeper of the Tide Book, forty-six years. I came here at seventeen to copy for old Keeper Innes, the same spring Varro became a warden.
  • We are the last two from those days. He trusts my memory more than his own. I trust his eyes more than mine. Between us we used to make one very good warden.
  • You want a tide? Very well. The great storm of forty years ago, the autumn moon. Turn at the fourth hour past midnight, water two steps over the top ring of the quay, wind north-west and rising.
  • Written in by a warden whose spelling I shall not discuss. There. Now you have heard me recite. Very few people ask.
  • The oldest pages are the first camp's: Savage tally marks and a careful Magician hand. They have been rebound so often the spine is younger than the wardens.
  • The later volumes stand on the long shelf in the back room, where it is dry. The current one lies here, under the window. Every tide since the first camp. Every one.
  • Halvard is very well. He straightened my notes at eleven and again at half past. I put them crooked again each time. It is one of the small pleasures of my day. Do not tell him.
  • Off you go. Mind the stack on your way past.

  • Two lamps past the Tree Gate now, Player. Just in case. The dark seems to mind them less than I feared.
  • Baldwin. I light the lamps, fifty years now. The plaza first, around my brother Hugh's Bell, then the old quarters on the long way home.
  • The one by the palace steps? Old Odo taught me to trim it, and it burned blue for him too. Fifty years and I still do not know why. Some lamps keep their own counsel.
  • Nobody asked me to. I buy the oil from Gilbert and set a few lamps on the last stretch inside the gate. For travellers who come in late.
  • Fifty years I have watched the dark, Player. Lately the dark past the gate is not as empty as it was. Just in case, that is all.
  • Mind your step after dusk. Stay where the lamps are.
  • Evening, Player. Or near enough. What is it?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Why does that lamp burn blue?
    • Choice: Lamps by the gate?
    • Choice: Good night.

Master of the Royal Academy

  • "Highland, harbour, forest, Urbanograd, and every one of them argues. Splendid."
  • "A Master who does not teach is just a man with a large office."

docs.text:

Dialogue
  • Ah, a visitor! Mind the papers, the floor is under there somewhere. What brings you to the Royal Academy, Player?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What is the Academy?
    • Choice: You look troubled.
    • Choice: How are the downs?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Bartholomew, Master of the Academy these twenty-one years. I came here at fourteen, a shepherd's boy from the downs, with a letter from my schoolteacher and no idea what an academy was.
  • So I asked every old wizard in the building a question. I have never stopped. Now, what did you come here hoping to find out? No, wait, what did you come here hoping not to?
  • The city's first Magicians founded it. Now we take students from every town on Veligor, and I am proud to say no two of them think alike.
  • The people who built this house once fought a war over whose way of thinking was right. The least we can do is keep every way of thinking under one roof and make them eat lunch together.
  • Troubled? I was thinking about a goat I knew as a boy. Well, no. I was thinking that the roads are worse every season, and that my scholars have noticed.
  • Morwen reads the old seal-craft, Theobald and Mariota read the sky, and Thomasin lectures to frightened rooms every week. All of them looking for something they have not yet named.
  • One day someone will come down from the palace and ask this Academy for an answer it does not have. Until then, I mean to keep it asking good questions. Will you help, if I ask?
  • Off you go. And come back with a better question than the one you brought.
  • The downs are still green, and now they have dots on Gervase's map. I prefer the dots to the blank. A blank is a question nobody asked.

docs.title: Bastian 'Bellows' Krell
docs.text:
Loudest Voice at the Table

Town Urbanograd Where The Great Hall Story Bastian 'Bellows' Krell in the lore Services Quests

docs.text:

  • "I was wrong, and that was an excellent argument!"
  • "Mags, my love, have you heard my new speech? You have? Again, then!"
  • "And in conclusion: more volunteers for Brindle's watch!"
  • "I am not shouting. This is my indoor voice."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Bastian Gives His Time (gives)
  • Measure the Gap (gives)
Dialogue
  • Player! Welcome, welcome! Have you an opinion? Everyone has an opinion! Mine is about a bridge, and I warn you now, it is a long one. The opinion, I mean. The bridge too, if it comes to that.
  • Tonight, the iron door! I have two speeches: one for, one against! I have not decided which to give, so I shall give both! In order! With an interval for stew!
  • Three thirds of a bridge! Built over three years! The Table laughed for ten minutes, which I count as applause. Vane laughed too, and then quietly measured something. That is hope, Player!
  • Five words. I have them perfect now. I say them to Mags every night over the pot. She timed me at four breaths and one small extra speech. We are getting there. Not a word to Rivet!
  • What shall I tell you about, at length?
    • Choice: Tell me about the covered bridge.
    • Choice: Why do they call you Bellows?
    • Choice: How did you meet Mags?
    • Choice: What worries you?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Picture it! Lantern Square, a night of rain. The Night Market shuttered, buns soggy, Ladle's coals hissing. Now picture a roof over it all, a bridge from the Fiddler's Crossing to the far gutters, lanterns underneath, and every stall dry as a sermon!
  • I have drawings! I have costings! I have a speech on the dignity of a dry pepper bun! What I do not have is the Table's vote, and the timber, and, Vane tells me, a very great deal of sense. Two out of three is not bad!
  • The voice came first! My father was a Night Market crier; he could sell a stale bun across three streets. I learned to throw my voice off the fortress walls for fun. 'Bellows', they called me, and I thought: well, I had better make the nickname honest.
  • So I make bellows! For the forges, the kilns, the glass furnaces on the Row. Ferro's fire breathes through my leather, and so does Tinsel's. Every bellows comes with an opinion on last night's Table, free of charge.
  • Seventeen years ago I spent a whole winter praising her stew. In the middle of debates about other things. Drains. Lamp oil. A goat. I would stand up and say 'and furthermore, the stew', and the Table would groan.
  • She says she married me to stop me talking about it. She has not succeeded! It is the most persuasive campaign of my life, Player, and I won it with soup.
  • Worries? Me? I am never... hm. Close the door. Smaller voice. I worry the Table is too slow. Twenty years I have loved how slow it is. But the roads are worse every year, and Brindle needs volunteers, and something at the gate will not wait for us to finish.
  • So I end every speech with Brindle's call for volunteers now, whatever it began with. Bridges, lamp oil, the goat. 'And furthermore, the Watch.' It is the only thing I say that I never change my mind about.
  • Farewell, Player! Come to the Table! Bring an opinion! I shall disagree with it magnificently!

  • All right. Going alone was stupid. I ran out of arrows and the hogs knew it. You came, though. I owe you, and I don't forget what I owe.
  • Over the Hot Rocks, every track bigger than the last. It's a great horned beast. I guessed right. I don't feel like I won anything.
  • Grimhorn's hide is on Thrun's drum. I heard the first beat from the rim. I waited at the edge of the mesa, like I promised. I don't know what my father would have said. I'd like to think he'd have laughed.

    • Choice: Why do the children follow you?
    • Choice: Take me to the Ash Mesa.
    • Choice: Goodbye.

  • They follow me everywhere. Korrin ties his boots like mine now; I check his knots when he's not looking. Somebody should, the way that boy climbs.
  • The Ash Mesa. It paws the ground before it charges: watch for that, then move. I'll wait at the edge. I promised my mother.
  • Race you to the rim sometime.

  • Name a book and I will have it in your hands before you finish describing it. Nearly any book.
  • I came here as a boy to fetch and shelve, and I have hardly left since. Head Librarian for thirty years. I also teach the palace's scribes to hold a pen properly.

  • A volume of the Aristocrat war chronicles. I read its first pages myself, eighteen years ago, at the desk by the window. I was called away, and when I came back it was gone.

  • Lucan? Oldest friend I have. He booms, I measure. We've a wager on which of us retires first, and neither remembers the stake. I suspect a goat.

  • You listen. Each spring the houses grow, and I hollow out a new room, fit a door, set a window. I never measure. The mushroom tells me where.
  • Old Bracken taught me, long ago. He said a house that is not listened to grows crooked. He was right about most things.
  • A mushroom house, of course! You knew that, Player. You have lived among them all your life.
  • Young Fen carries my tools and asks a hundred questions, and my granddaughter Daisy paints every house I shape. I am a lucky old man.
  • Off you go, Player. Say good morning to the houses.

  • Hello! I'm Bolt, I'm Margo's apprentice. I do the sweeping and the testing. Mostly the testing finds me, actually.
  • Player! You didn't tell anyone, did you? About the question? No, of course you didn't. Sorry. Thank you. Sorry.
  • Player! The springs held all week out in the ditch, damp and everything. I wrote it all down. In the... other notebook. The private one.
  • Um. What can I do for you?
    • Choice: How did you come to work for Margo?
    • Choice: What do you test?
    • Choice: What do you think of Rivet's lift?

  • I came up from Bain Harbour two years ago. My father mends nets. I didn't want to mend nets. I walked down the Row and saw a door with scorch marks all around it and thought, there. I asked Margo if she needed a sweeper. She said yes, and also a tester. I didn't know what that meant yet.

  • I apologise to them after. The machines. Margo laughs. But they try so hard, you know? It's not their fault I'm clumsy.
  • Rivet's lift? It's, um. It's fine. It's very good. The counterweight is old fortress stones, so it never needs winding, it just... balances. It's really clever. I mean. Margo would do it with springs.
  • Springs are good too! Don't tell Margo I said the lift was clever. Don't tell Rivet either. Actually, don't tell anyone anything. Sorry.
  • Bye! Mind the... oh. Sorry. That was the bucket.

  • "Grandfather Ulm's wood! I forgot again."

  • The cliff on the Long Ridge is as good as I hoped. Now I am drawing gates for the stair. If things come up from the canyons, a stair needs a way to be shut.
  • A whole night on the Far Anchor, with Vosk and you, and the gnawers coming up off the ledge. I have never held a rope so hard. Vosk says I did well. He said it twice, so he means it.
  • The old walls in the War Camp Ruins showed me how the first Kragvar cut: rough and deep, every block leaning into the next. My gates will be built like that.

  • Vosk ties every knot himself and trusts nobody else's. I was with him at dawn both times we found the far bridge ropes gnawed. He spliced them without a word, then sat a long while looking at the far side.
  • The boys' lookout? I found it ages ago. Good wall, too: low, but they set the stones properly. I never told them I knew. Don't you tell them either.
  • Mind the steps. Some of them are older than the songs.

Dialogue
  • Brindle, captain of the Watch. Which sounds grander than it is: we are a handful of volunteers and a gate. You look like you can handle yourself, Player. That makes you interesting to me.
  • Player. Pull up a crate. I will not offer you the good one; that is Knox's, and he has carved his name in it.
  • Dagny is at the gate from sundown. Stand where the light is and let her talk. Then the Outworks.
  • Your count is on the slate, chalked in my best hand. The eyes are the eyes. The lanterns are something else. Lux is working on the something else.
  • The Fallen Tower is waiting, Player. Say the word and I will show you the way in. Say it when you mean it.
  • Every lantern on the outer wall, lit, three weeks running. I had to rub out a whole column of the slate. I nearly enjoyed it.
  • Low Grad. A whole buried city under our feet, and we posted a guard on the wrong door for a hundred years. I am trying to find that funny.
  • The Table is arguing about the iron door. It will argue all night; that is what it is for. I would rather it argued all night than one of us decided before breakfast.
  • Two doors now. The gate up here and Ferro's grate out in the hillside. I check them both twice. Knox says I check the grate three times. Knox is right.
  • Player. The outer wall is lit and the tunnel mouth is barred. Do you know how long it has been since I could say two good things in a row? Sit down before I think of a third.
  • What do you need?
    • Choice: Take me into the Fallen Tower.
    • Choice: What does the Watch do?
    • Choice: What is on the slate?
    • Choice: What about Dagny?
    • Choice: You and the Open Table?
    • Choice: Nothing. Goodbye.
  • Down the side path, into the Outworks, east under the walls till the tower lies on its side. The vault is flooded and open to the sky. Make noise. Come back.
  • When I joined, seventeen years ago, the Watch greeted late carts and settled quarrels over tolls nobody paid. I signed up for one summer, for something to do. I was meant to make rope. Rope is very quiet.
  • Now we stand between the city and whatever comes up the road, which is more every year. Knox knows every face. Dagny keeps the night. I keep the slate and ask the Table for help. Mostly it cheers and goes home.
  • Every sighting the Watch hears of, every week, chalked by road. Walkers' Road, Stonefang Pass, the Outworks. Tick reads it aloud every week, slowly, with feeling. The numbers only go one way.
  • Gloomeyes by the gate road, counted properly now. And under it, in a different chalk: lanterns smashed, outer wall, every second night. Two columns. Two different things. I would like one of them to go away.
  • The lantern column is empty. I left the chalk line under it, so nobody forgets it was ever full. The other columns still go one way. But one is empty, and I look at it every morning.
  • Dagny Roe. Came inland from Bain Harbour to haul lamp oil and put her hand up at the Table when I asked for volunteers. I gave her the night watch because nobody else wanted it.
  • She says she talks to the dark because she is too frightened to do anything else. I have watched her do it for two years. I have a word for what she does out there, and it is not frightened.
  • I have not said it to her. When I do, I want it to land, not scare her off the gate. So I am waiting for the right moment. And checking twice. Knox gives her owls in the meantime.
  • Rook is a friend, and the Table is the best thing this city has, and I stand up at it every month and ask for twenty volunteers. People listen. People nod. Bastian ends his speeches with my call for volunteers now, which is kind and very loud.
  • Then they go back to their workshops. I do not blame them; the Walkers were painters and players, not soldiers. I just wonder what happens the night something gets past the gate before we have decided whose turn it is.
  • Walk safe, Player. And check twice.
