Dialogue
  • Oh. You. I'm not sleeping, if you were going to ask. Don't ask.
  • You again. The trigger's set. Don't touch it. Don't look at it too hard.
  • A cub. Don't. I know.
  • My traps work. Every one of them. Nothing to grumble about. I hate it.
  • Caddoc. Trapper. Twenty-six years of looking at holes in the ground before breakfast. What?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Your traps.
    • Choice: Greer and the pelts.
    • Choice: Let's sit up by the trap tonight.
    • Choice: Nothing. Goodbye.
  • Highland born. A trapping family, in the hills above the hill road. I came down at sixteen with a drover's flock and never went back up.
  • My father taught me to make every part of a trap myself. A trap you bought is a trap you don't understand. Which is why I'm up at all hours with wire in my teeth.
  • You've seen my hut. Don't say it. It's a mess, I know, I live in it. Every spring and cord in there is exactly where I can find it.
  • Torva offered to tidy it once. Once. Here, your strap's buckled wrong, hold still... there. No, I don't want paying. Badly made in the first place.
  • Something's springing my big cages. Bait gone, door down, nothing inside. No hair on the wire, no blood.
  • And the ground round them swept smooth, as if something didn't want to leave tracks. I've rebuilt the triggers three times. Sprung inside a week, every time. It's a nuisance, that's all. A nuisance.
  • A fox. A grey old fox, lifting my door with its teeth and sweeping its tracks with its tail. Twenty-six years I've built cages on the notion that cleverness was ours and not theirs. I'll need a better trigger. A much better trigger.
  • The new trigger's set. Sinew, bristle, driftwood, and a bit of thinking it won't have seen before. If it learns this one too, I'll take up mending nets. I won't, but I'm saying it.
  • A cub. I built the cleverest trap on this coast and caught a cub. The old one will be laughing at me from under some root. Torva's going after it. Kenna's going after it louder.
  • My traps work. They catch what they're meant to catch, and nothing sweeps the ground. I've nothing left to complain about, and I don't care for it. And Torva still comes out at dawn, which means she's still looking at something.
  • My pelts go to Greer at the Lantern Market. Fewer trappers come down from the highlands every year, so she pays me more than she used to. It's still not enough. She says I wound her. I do my best.
  • Greer was pleased with those woodland pelts. She said so, which cost her. Then she offered me less than they were worth, which didn't. We're both very happy.
  • Go on, then. Mind the springs on your way out. No, the other way. That one.
  • Right. Something warm, something sharp, and no falling asleep.

  • Dagny. Dagny Roe. Night watch. Everyone calls me Two-Lamps, which is fair, because look: two lamps. I am awake. I am mostly awake. What can I do for you?
  • The little ones by the stackyards are young gloomeyes. I say it to them now: hello, young gloomeyes. They still do not answer. But the far ones, by the old walls, I still do not know.
  • You stood the watch with me! Nobody stands the watch with me. Knox does, a bit, but he carves, so it is more like standing the watch with a woodpile.
  • Brindle chalked your count in the good chalk. I saw. The prints are still there in the mornings, but now I know whose they are, and they are smaller in my head.
  • Every lantern on the outer wall is lit. I can see them from the gate, all along, like a necklace. I used to count the dark gaps. Now I count lights. It is a much nicer number.
  • Ask me anything. Please. It is a long night.
    • Choice: Why two lamps?
    • Choice: What do you see out there?
    • Choice: You and Patch?
    • Choice: Nothing. Goodbye.
  • My first month on the gate, late autumn, wet, my lamp went out. Just went. And there was something on the road. Moving. I stood there in the pitch black for a whole minute with my heart going like a drum.
  • It was a goat. A lost goat. I have never forgiven it. The next night I brought two lamps, and I have carried two ever since. My family renders lamp oil in Bain Harbour; I know how to keep a flame. I just like to keep two.
  • Eyes. Pairs of them, low down in the brush beyond the road, catching the lamplight and holding still. More this year than last. Some nights I can hear them breathing. So I step up to the edge of the light and talk at them. Because what else is there to do?
  • Gloomeyes. Lizards with lamps for eyes. Knowing makes it better and worse. Better, because they are only lizards. Worse, because there are so many of them.
  • Still eyes. Always eyes. But the touched ones, the ones that do not blink, there are fewer. I can tell. I still talk at them. It is a habit now. I think they would miss it.
  • Patch is my friend. On bad nights I bring the bitten ones to her door, and she scolds them while she bandages them, and then she scolds me for standing too near the road, and then she makes me a drink.
  • It is willow bark and something else she will not name, and it tastes like a boot, and it is the only reason I make it to dawn. After the last patient I walk her home with both lamps. She says it is unnecessary. She has never once said no.
  • Bye! Come back before dark. Or after. Either. Both lamps will be lit.

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Octopus Ink (gives)
  • The Oldest Volume (gives)
Dialogue
  • Hm? Oh, hello, Player. Sorry. I was writing down a heckle from three sessions ago that I only just understood. It was very good. Sit, if you like. Do not sit on the minutes.
  • One night. The Table agreed in one night. I have been through every shelf: the fastest yes in forty years, and the last one was about a goat. I have underlined it twice. I never underline twice.
  • Look at this black. Look at it. Octopus ink, Player, your octopus ink, and it sits on the page like it means it. I have copied eleven pages this week instead of three.
  • Ozzie came by this morning to argue about the goat vote. He was so happy he forgot to look for his spectacles for an entire hour. You did that. I have written it down.
  • Something for the record?
    • Choice: What do you write down?
    • Choice: Why do they call you Inkpot?
    • Choice: Tell me about the oldest books.
    • Choice: How often does Bastian change his mind?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Everything. Every motion, every vote, every speech, every heckle, every joke. Especially the jokes. The decisions are only half of what the Table is. The other half is how it got there, and that half is mostly jokes.
  • If somebody says the Table agreed to a thing nine years ago, I go to the shelves and find out whether it did. It usually did not. People remember the Table the way they wish it had gone.
  • Years ago a guild master from Selsior visited the Table, to see what all the noise was about. He leaned over my desk to read the minutes. Everyone leans on the desk. And the inkpot went over, all down his good blue coat.
  • I minuted it. Word for word. Including what he said, which I will not repeat aloud in the hall. It is on page four hundred and six if you want to look. Everybody has.
  • The record begins after the first winter. Of the winter itself, nothing; nobody knows why, and Ozzie has worn out three pairs of spectacles wondering. The first books that do survive are written on whatever the Walkers had: scavenged paper, ledgers turned upside down.
  • They are crumbling. Pages come away at the spine. I copy a page or two after every session, but the Table makes new arguments faster than I can save the old ones. One day I will open a volume and a joke will be gone that nobody alive remembers. That is what keeps me up.
  • I keep a private tally. Mid-speech changes of mind, Bastian Krell, twenty years: two hundred and twelve. Three in one sentence, once, about lamp oil. That was a good night.
  • Do not tell him about the tally. He would be proud of it, and then he would try to raise it, and I only have so much ink.
  • Go on, then. I will note that you visited. I note everything.

  • The masons swing your flint hammers all day now, and they ring true. A Kragvar knows good stone by its sound, and good work the same way.
  • You went up the old north stair, where Baruk fell. I have not been able to look at it properly since. Thank you for looking for me.

  • I argued long in council for a Kragvar Old One. The families chose Hask. I said my piece, I lost, and I stand by it; that is how it is done here. He listens, I will give him that. I still tell him when he is wrong.
  • Gorra keeps the water, Brakka carves on every flat stone she finds, and Korrin climbs everything he is told not to. He wants to join the Uskari watch. I asked Skarra how young they take recruits. Sixteen, she says. Good. That is seven years off.
  • Brakka wants a new stair down the cliff. Do not tell her I keep a copy of her sketch. A chieftain must not look soft.

  • ...You laughed. Or you coughed. Thirty years and nobody's laughed. I'll take the cough.
  • I know every sound of it. Which boats knock in a swell and which ones grind. Which warehouse door rattles in a north wind. Which lantern burns a shade low. Dunmor lights them, I count them, Dunmor puts them out. Then I sleep.
  • Old Ewart's count. One night it'll be wrong, he said. I'm sixty-six. I'd like it to be wrong on someone else's watch.
  • It was wrong once, and it was a knot. I'll take a knot. I'll take a knot every time.
  • You sat on the steps with me. Keep it between us and Ruan. I still keep my back to the wall going past them. Habit, now.
  • Off you go. I'll count you out. One.

  • Pale green as spring, pinned with bee stingers, haggled at two-thirds. My finest work this year, dear. Don't tell Isabeau.

  • The downs quiet, the quarries quiet, and Gervase drawing fewer dots. I've never written a report like it. Don't get used to it. I won't.

  • Do you know what I tell Brigid? That there's no magic in it, only knowing which herb, which tide and which hour. And then that the knowing is the magic.

  • A thing you made and send away should have a name, so it knows it was wanted. I scratch it small on the tang, under the grip, where nobody looks. Nobody is meant to look. That is not the point.
  • The heron on my door is made of old hinges. The fox on the roof is copper off a burst boiler. The thing in the yard is chain and springs and has no name yet; it has not told me one. The fiddler on the corner of Lantern Square is mine too. Saffi sits on its knee. It does not mind.
  • Every Walkout Day I weld one and give it away. Last year a small iron cat for Perch's loft. That big grey cat of Perch's sleeps beside it now. Best review I ever had.
  • Hatch. Sixteen years ago Hatch walked in with a bent spear-head and would not leave until I straightened it. A month later, back again: a pair of hunting knives, please. I said I make foxes. Hatch said foxes do not skin rabbits.
  • Now Hatch tells everyone the whole trade was Hatch's idea. It was. I grumble about it daily. I would grumble more if the roads did not need it.
  • Shut the gate. The fox does not like draughts.

  • A drawing isn't finished until it rains on it. Then all the colours run together down the gutters and go somewhere. Everywhere. That's the finished part.
  • I watch from under the edge of Ivo's awning. He lets me. He says it's the best show on the square. Better than Tinder. Don't tell Tinder.
  • SPLASH. The chimney ones. Everybody knows they're Splash's and nobody can prove it. Mum's good too. Mum's very good. But Mum paints the same old pictures every spring, line for line, because the Walkers drew them. That's a rule. I like my rule better.
  • Mind the dragon on your way out! ...That was its tail. One copper.

  • Player! The tin is heavier. Sinew and coppers. That is nearly a bow, that is. Nearly.
  • Player! You kept up! Nearly. Want to go again?
  • Player! You are my best customer. You are my only customer who does not pay in fish.

    • Choice: Anything on your mind?

  • Fionn. Stair runner. Quickest on the cliffs, ask anyone. Ask Gorm. He will pretend he is cross.
  • I live with Uncle Hamish by the windlass. I am saving coppers in a tin, for a bow. Do not ask where the tin is. It is not under anything.
  • My dad was a cove fisher. Duncan. He drowned when I was a baby. My mum got the cough after.
  • I do not remember them much. A blue shawl. A song about a gull. Uncle Hamish sings it wrong, but I let him. You can know that. Not everyone can.
  • There is the gap behind the smokehouse, that drops you two landings at once. The ledge under the third rope bridge. And the goat path that cuts the Long Stair in half, if you do not mind holding on with your fingers.
  • Old Ulric says I read his stair with the pages torn out. I do not know what he means. He just laughs.
  • Nothing! Why, did someone say something? About a bridge? Nobody said anything about a bridge.
  • I told Kestra. Everything. She did not shout. Well, a bit, about the dark. Then she said thank you, which was worse.
  • Only, Uncle Hamish is stuck at the windlass all day. If I was not around, who would bring him the news? He would have to talk to the rope.
  • Race you down! Oh. You are not racing. Bye, then!

docs.title: Iska
docs.text:
First Warden

Town Goa Harbour Where The Wardens' House Story Iska in the lore Services Boss: The Undertow, Quests

Player. Walk with me, I have a ship at the turn.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Halvard, who is due at the turn?"
  • "Four ships before dark. Kor will want all four."
  • "Dunmor says sit. I will sit when the tide does."
  • "Nessa, I heard you. I always hear you."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• The Old Mark (gives)
  • The Undertow (gives)
  • Under the Jaw (gives)
Dialogue
  • Player. The slack came on its hour this morning. I stood on the quay and watched it like a girl.
  • Player. Ruan's landings are quieter. Not quiet. Quieter. That is your doing, and Torva's.
  • You found the way in. Now finish it. Torva will not wait long, and neither will I.
  • The old mark is tarred fresh. I took a ship in on it yesterday, in a grey squall. Still the best line in.
  • Player. Sit, if you can stand to. I can't.
  • Quick, then. The tide won't wait, and neither will Halvard.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: How is the harbour?
    • Choice: What is on your mind?
    • Choice: Take me to the Scour.
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • First Warden, seven years. The wardens chose me because no one alive knows the gap better. I still take ships through it, when Halvard lets me out of the house.
  • Varro taught me from the age of seven. My mother taught me to argue. Between them they made a pilot.
  • You want to know who I am? Ask who I race. Quenna, Harbour Master of Bain. Twenty-two years ago a squall took her boat's mast off a headland, and we turned back to tow them clear.
  • I threw the line. She caught it. Neither boat finished, the race was void, and we spent the night in a cove eating their bread because ours was wet.
  • Nine wins to her, three to me, four of hers by a length. I buy the first round at the feast more often than I like. Do not repeat that. Everyone already knows it.
  • Ships in, timber out, wool on the quay. Ruan brings me his report every week, and every week it is longer. Bethoc's board says the Strandwood. Torva says the same.
  • Ruan laid it all on my table: Dougal's cord, Gorm's stone, a chewed rope of Kestra's. Something leads the climbers. I want it found, and I want it off my cliffs.
  • The climbers come fewer since the Gapclaw, and less boldly. They have not stopped. I never thought they would. Ruan still wants his lanterns.
  • The Scour is empty and the slack keeps its hour. Whatever else the water is doing, Ailsa will tell me when she is ready. She always has.
  • The inlet. I have read it most of my life, and lately it keeps things from me. The seas are rougher every year.
  • Ailsa's new pages and the old ones do not sit together the way they should. I asked her once. She said not yet. I have not asked again.
  • Your marks agree with Ailsa's pages. So it is not a careless warden, and it is not a strange year. I would almost rather it were.
  • Arlo. He thinks I do not know where he goes at dawn. I am pretending not to. It is a family habit.
  • Mind the steps. They are wet. They are always wet.
  • The lowest tide is our hour. Come. Keep to the high pools.

  • Fulke, singer of the plaza, born a street from here. My lute came second-hand from an old singer who said it had more songs in it than he had years. I am still getting them out.
  • The First Burning, the truce at one table, the Last Stand at the Tree, the warriors holding the line while the Magicians worked the seal. The four peoples tell it four ways, and I sing all four.
  • What the Balrog was? I would rather sing three guesses than pretend to one answer. Every ballad I sing is true, Player. Mostly. Watch my eyebrows.
  • At the gate, most mornings. Highland herding songs, harbour shanties, forest rounds, Urbanograd marching songs. I ask every traveller what they sing at home.
  • Lately their songs have more monsters in them, and some are not old songs at all. One day I will write the song the whole kingdom sings. I have not found it yet.
  • Come back at dusk. I play for Mirabel when the lamps are lit.
  • Ah, an audience! Player, is it? Sit, sit. A song, a story, or both?

    • Choice: Sing of the Balrog War.
    • Choice: Where do you find new songs?
    • Choice: Not today.

  • Because one pier is not enough for a harbour this busy! Ships waiting in the bay, cargo waiting on the ships, and the council waiting on next year.

Cartographer

Town Selsior Where Scholars' Quarter Story Gervase in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• An Impossible Dot (gives)
  • Blank on the Map (gives)
Dialogue
  • Come in, come in, step on the margins, not the roads! Gervase, cartographer. You've come about a map? Everyone comes about a map.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What are all these maps?
    • Choice: Why are you pacing?
    • Choice: How is the map?
    • Choice: I'll find my own way.
  • Grew up three streets from here and drew my own street at six, every door, drain and cat. At twenty-two I went out on the royal roads with Leofric, surveying.
  • Seven years! He would walk the same mile three times to be sure of it, and I would talk the whole way. Between the two of us we got the roads right.
  • The kingdom's maps, for the Academy, the palace, the Guard and anyone else who pays. I have never drawn one I thought was finished.
  • Before I'm too old to walk I mean to finish the whole kingdom: every road, every ford, every ridge, no blank spaces anywhere.
  • That one, on the far wall: where monsters have been seen. Edric of the Road Patrol sends me every report, and I mark each one with a dot of ink and the date.
  • It began as a few dots in the wild places. Now the quiet stretches between the towns are filling up, and I've had to start a second sheet for the roads near the towns themselves.
  • I'm no scholar of the war. But I know what a map looks like when something is spreading, and I've started measuring how fast.
  • Off you go! And if you see anything strange on the road, remember where. Exactly where.
  • The impossible dot is real, and I've drawn it. It doesn't spread like a stain; it wakes in places. I'm measuring. I'm always measuring.

Retired Herald

Town Selsior Where Royal Plaza Story Gideon in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Ha! A visitor! Mind the top rung, it wobbles."
  • "That is the market's opening bell. And that one is the gatehouse."
  • "I cried the king's news in that square for forty years."
  • "The pigeons have heard all my stories. They never laugh in the right places."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• A Bell He Does Not Know (gives)
  • Down the Ladder (gives)
  • Word for Clement (gives)
Dialogue
  • Ha! Player! Aldous kept the bench warm, you know. Smiled twice that evening. Twice!
  • Gideon, Royal Herald for forty years, retired sixteen! Every piece of royal news in this city came out of this mouth first. Laws, roads, fairs, births and deaths.
  • I cried the Great World Tree Expedition off the palace steps fifty years ago. Biggest crowd I ever had! And when the news of what it found came back, the hardest to make them believe. Ha!
  • Every bell in Selsior! The clock tower bells the palace children race, the drill bell at the Knights' Court, the market's opening bell, the one on the gatehouse.
  • And the Great Bell, which does not ring. I heard it twice, at King Bertram's crowning and at Queen Aveline's. The sound went straight into my chest and stayed there.
  • There is Clement, the herald now. He climbs up every week, for a social call, he says. Then a proclamation falls out of his sleeve. Ha!
  • He is far better than he believes, and I tell him so loud enough for the plaza to hear. Otherwise... well. The ladder is long, and the young have places to be.
  • Come back up any time, Player! I have sixty years of stories, and I have only told you two.
  • Ha! You climbed all the way up here for an old herald, Player? Sit, sit. The pigeons will make room.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What can you hear from up here?
    • Choice: Do you get many visitors?
    • Choice: I should go.

Candlemaker

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Story Gilbert in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:

  • "Beeswax burns clean and slow. Tallow just smokes and sulks."

  • Gilbert, candlemaker. My mother taught me candles. The bees I taught myself, from a swarm on a washing line when I was fifteen.
  • Nine hives on the roof above the shop, among the lavender and thyme. On a clear morning they fly out over half the city and bring it all home in their legs.
  • That's what you smell in my candles: a little of all of Selsior. Baldwin the lamplighter won't burn anything else.
  • Since spring they've been short-tempered. They come off the hives at a shadow, at a door closing. I've been stung more this year than in the ten before it.
  • The other rooftop keepers say the same, and I hear the palace garden bees have turned mean too. It feels like a hive before a storm. Hmm. I don't like it.
  • Mind the ladder on your way past. Hmm, hmm.
  • Oh, hello, Player. Candles, lamp oil, wax seals... or did you want to hear about bees? Most people don't. Hmm.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Tell me about your bees.
    • Choice: Your bees seem upset.
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Hear that? The old hum, or nearly. The bees came home from their flights calmer today. Hmm. Thank you.
  • The swarm's home on the roof, and the guards have stopped glaring at me. Mostly.

  • The lemon balm has taken, and the rose walk is gentler. Slow roots hold longest, Player.
  • Ah... a visitor. Good morning. Mind the roses; they are listening. I am Godwin, gardener here.
    • Choice: Who are you?

  • Below the terrace is the kingdom border: a cutting of every town's favourite flower, begged from envoys and carters over many years.

  • Go gently. Slow roots hold longest.

docs.title: Gorm
docs.text:
Master of the Stairs

Town Goa Harbour Where Goa Harbour Story Gorm in the lore Services Run: Below the Anvil, Quests

Mind that step, Player. It is sulking.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "This landing has never forgiven the winter."
  • "Kestra! Where is your line? KESTRA!"
  • "A town that stops climbing its own stairs forgets how they were made."
  • "The far cove stair will be done before the race. It will. Stop looking at me."
  • "That boy has found another shortcut. I will have words. Later."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Below the Anvil (gives)
  • The Far Cove Stair (gives)
  • The Last Flights (gives)
Dialogue
  • Player. Come and look at the lower flights. No, really look. That is good stone, that.
  • Player. You held the face below the Anvil all night. The crew still talks about it. I tell them to get back to work.
  • Player! Hamish has not stopped smiling since you went to him. I blame you.
  • Player. Stand there, on the good step. That one likes you.
  • Master of the Stairs. What can I do for you, short of finishing that stair?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Tell me about the stairs.
    • Choice: How is the far cove stair?
    • Choice: Let's go down below the Anvil.
    • Choice: Nothing. Good day.
  • Gorm. Master of the Stairs, eleven years. Born halfway up the Long Stair. My father cut stone for the quay walls.
  • Ulric taught me everything I know about stone. I still take him every difficult piece of rock. For a second opinion. Only ever a second opinion.
  • My father died of a fall when I was thirteen. I sat on the step outside our door all that winter and would not go anywhere.
  • Then Ulric sat down beside me, put a chisel in my hand, and said if I meant to sit on a step all day I might as well learn how it was made. I have never told the crews that. Nor will you.
  • Every step on these cliffs has a temper. The old stair above the quay is getting tired and wants looking after. The third landing is sulking. People laugh. Then they live here a few years and stop laughing.
  • And Ulric's little animals. A crab here, a hare there, a gull, a seal. I have walked past a thousand of them and I love every one.
  • I promised the First Warden a stair down to the far cove before the race, so the town can stand on the rocks and watch the boats go out. The rock is harder and more broken than it looked. A whole flight cracked in the spring frost.
  • And the crews will not work the lowest landings after dark. I am behind. I would sooner cut every step myself than say so. So I have not said so. You did not hear it.
  • Ulric is still on the Anvil, by daylight, slow as the tide. The crews work the lower flights again with someone watching the face. Behind, still. Less behind.
  • Three flights left, and a handrope Kestra strung like a fiddle. It will be done before the race. I said it to Iska and I will not unsay it.
  • Up or down, use the stairs. Not the basket.
  • Good. The crew is ready. Stone does not wait.

docs.title: Gorra
docs.text:
Cistern Keeper

Town Midbarium Where Midbarium Story Gorra in the lore Services Quests

Forty-one, forty-two... oh. Hello, Player. Water?

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "A finger's depth, gone. Where does it go?"
  • "Ulm's jug. Mustn't forget Ulm's jug."
  • "Every bucket counted, every night."
  • "Yarrek's family and mine share this cistern. Always have."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:

  • The Founders' Trickle (gives)
Dialogue
  • Forty-one buckets on the lower terrace, thirty-eight on the middle. Sorry, Player, I count when I am thinking. Do you need water?
  • Four cisterns, and you looked at every one. The Founders' Cistern still loses a finger's depth every few nights. I can hear the water going, somewhere deep in the rock.
  • So that is where the Founders' water went: down a crack and out under the old rock, a trickle nobody would ever have found. Sealed now, and the level holds. Thank you.
  • What can I tell you?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: How long would the water last?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Gorra, the cistern keeper. Old Marn taught me, and I have kept the stone cisterns eighteen years since he died. Every tally is scratched on the wall of my cistern house. Dorrek says I measure water the way Corwell measures coin. He is right.
  • In a dry year, with care, a season and a half. I know it to the bucket. What I do not like is a cistern losing water I cannot account for. Don't mention it to Dorrek; he has walls enough to worry about.
  • The Greywater gone dry, the old springs failing... I count every night now. Yarrek's family and mine share the terrace cisterns, and we will share the last bucket too, if it comes to that.
  • Every drop counts, Player.

docs.title: Greer

Fur Trader

Town Goa Harbour Where Goa Harbour Story Greer in the lore Services Shop: Greer's Furs

Ah, someone with taste. Or someone who needs it. Either way, welcome.

docs.text:

  • "Fewer trappers every year. Higher prices every year. Funny, that."
  • "Morag's jumpers are lovely. My cloaks are lovelier."
  • "Caddoc grumbles at every price. Then he takes it."

  • Looking, or buying? I'll know which by the time you answer.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: How is business?
    • Choice: And Morag?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Greer. I buy pelts from the hunters and the highland trappers and ship them all over the island.
  • I always know who's selling cheap and who's buying dear. It isn't magic. People talk to someone who listens, and looks good doing it.
  • Fewer trappers come down from the hills every year, and my prices climb with every one that doesn't. I pay Caddoc more than I've ever paid him. He grumbles anyway.
  • Teague brings down what he can by the hill road. Morag frets about him every trip, and between you and me, so do I. A good drover is worth more than his flock.
  • Morag and I have shared this end of the market longer than either of us admits. She sells wool, I sell fur, and we argue over who keeps the coves warmer. I'm winning. Don't tell her.
  • Come back when it's colder. You'll need me then.

docs.title: Ysmay
docs.text:
Retired Sea Warden

Town Goa Harbour Where Goa Harbour Story Ysmay in the lore Services Quests

Stand out of the light, Player. I am watching a fool take the gap.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Too wide. Far too wide. Who taught that one?"
  • "Forty years on the water and I never swung like that."
  • "My daughter is First Warden, you know. Of course you know."
  • "Arlo will be up after his supper. He writes the best of it down."
  • "Varro will be saying the same from the quay. He always does."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• A Sharp Note (gives)
  • Quills and Advice (gives)
Dialogue
  • Player. Iska came up the stairs yesterday. To ask after my back. My back is fine. Sit down.
  • Player. Varro got my note, I hear. Good. Someone has to say these things.
  • Player. Pull up the stool. Not that one. That one is Arlo's.
  • Well? Say it. I have a pilot to watch.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What do you see from the window?
    • Choice: Something on your mind?
    • Choice: Nothing. I'll leave you to it.
  • Ysmay. Forty years a sea warden, from twenty to sixty. My eyes and my back retired me. A warden who cannot see the far eddy in the rain has no business in the gap.
  • And I am Iska's mother. The First Warden. You will have heard. I tell everyone. Nearly everyone.
  • They asked me to stand for First Warden. More than once. I said a First Warden spends her days at a table, and I wanted the water.
  • That is what I said. Do not look at me like that, it is all you are getting. It is more than most get.
  • From this window I can see the whole inlet, down to the gap. Every pilot who takes a ship through goes under my eye. Most of them would rather not know what I think.
  • Varro watches from the end of the quay and I watch from up here, and we compare notes. We usually agree. It annoys us both.
  • The pilots this spring. Swinging wide where the old eddy used to be, then correcting late. Sloppy. I have said so, loudly. Varro has not argued with me. Varro always argues with me.
  • Arlo checked my complaints against Varro again. Agreed, every one. And Varro still has not argued. Forty years, and he picks now to stop. I do not care for it.
  • Off you go. And if you ever take the gap, take it tight.

  • The wood you brought is drying in the back. Do you still want to know why? Good. Keep wanting.

  • My great-aunt Seona taught me at ten, when my hands were small enough for the finest work. A hand lantern takes me days. A quay lantern, most of a month. Why would anyone want it faster?
  • How does the tide know when to turn? Some things you learn with your hands, Player, and some you never learn at all.
  • Tarran. Half his lanterns are brilliant and half do not light, and I have never had a pupil whose good half was so good.
  • Is he the one for the rest of it? I have not decided. It is not his hands I am unsure of. Tell me, what do you think a lantern is for?
  • Go carefully. Mind the dark corners.

Washerwoman

Dialogue
  • Gytha. Daughter of the cobbler and the storyteller, which is why I talk faster than both of them. Somebody had to.
  • Every shirt tells a tale. Who's been ill, who's been courting, who was at the tavern till dawn.
  • I don't repeat most of it. I don't need to. Everyone knows I know, and that keeps the lanes honest.
  • Hodge? Somewhere he shouldn't be, I expect. Half the lanes tell me he's on the roofs, and I've never once caught him.
  • He wants the Royal Guard. He's not having it. He'll learn a trade and come home every night, like a sensible boy.

  • You're dripping on my clean linen, Player. Well, you're here now. What is it?

docs.text:
Head of the Timber Crews

Town Goa Harbour Where Goa Harbour Story Haldor in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Steady. Let her come down slow."
  • "Within shouting distance. That's the rule."
  • "Thank you. Down you come."
  • "The edge-wood's thin this month."
  • "Merrin. The second half, Merrin."

docs.text:

  • The Timber Carts (gives)

  • A Pot for Haldor (completes)
Dialogue
  • Player. The carters say the Saltwood Road is as clear as it's been all year. That was you, they tell me.
  • Player. You know where the line is now. That's more than some of my cutters do.
  • Player. Tamsin sent a word back with the raft hands. It wasn't a kind word. It was a fair one, though.
  • Head of the crews, for what that's worth this year. What is it, Player?
    • Choice: Why do you thank the trees?
    • Choice: Why did you pull the crews back?
    • Choice: Tamsin and the deep timber.
    • Choice: Nothing. Goodbye.
  • A tree's never just timber. It stood there before any of us, and it'll go to sea in a hull. The least I can do is say thank you.
  • I was twenty-three. A tree that had been judged a hundred times came down the wrong way, and a better cutter than me was under it. I was close enough to hear it crack and too far to do anything.
  • Since then I put a hand on every one and thank it before it falls. The young ones grin. None of them has ever seen me skip it. I don't tell many people that, Player.
  • Twice this year. End of winter, a cutting party came back to camp and found it torn apart, and every axe-handle bitten through.
  • This spring something large followed a crew through the trees all afternoon and never once showed itself. I called them all out before dark and I've not sent them back.
  • I don't know what it was, either time, and I'll not guess. I've not lost a cutter in twelve years. I mean to keep it so.
  • Torva says the old fox is done with, and Caddoc's traps hold. Good. That tells me nothing about my axe-handles, nor about what walked behind my crew. So we stay at the edge.
  • She wants deep-forest timber for the Gap Runner. Tall, close-grained, slow-grown. She's sure it's the length she keeps losing by.
  • Maybe she's right. I'll still not send a crew in for a keel. The quay hands can tell you the rest, they've heard us often enough.
  • She still wants her tree. But Jory tells me she's using the driftwood, every pin of it, and she's not said a word about that. From Tamsin, that's thanks.
  • Go careful. Keep where you can be heard.

docs.title: Halvard
docs.text:
Clerk of the Wardens' House

Town Goa Harbour Where The Wardens' House Story Halvard in the lore Services Quests

Ah, Player. Do mind the chair, it was straight.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Captain of the Tern, late again. Underlined."
  • "No, thank you, I'll watch the boats from here."
  • "Eleven ships due, ten in. Oh. There's the eleventh."

docs.text:

  • The Count (gives)
Dialogue
  • Every ship with its tide.
  • I underlined it once, and I have not looked at it since. Well. Twice.
  • Come in, come in. I've straightened the chair for you.
  • What can the Wardens' House do for you? Within reason. And within the ledger.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What do you write down?
    • Choice: How is your family?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Halvard, clerk of the Wardens' House, fifteen years. I'm from Linmoor, inland. Farms, and a slow brown river.
  • I came to see the sea. I have seen it. I see it every day from this window, which is quite close enough.
  • Did I ever tell you about my voyage? I took passage on a timber ship at twenty-four, for the view. Three days. I saw the view for about an hour of it.
  • I came down the gangplank grey as a gull and swore I'd never sail again. I have kept that promise better than any other I have made. The quay still laughs. I've heard all the jokes. Dougal's are the worst.
  • Every ship through the gap: ship, captain, cargo, pilot, tide, and the time through. Fifteen years in my hand, and many more in the hands before mine.
  • Every morning I give the First Warden the list of who is due, who is late, and who still owes last season's fee. The captain of the Tern still owes last season's fee.
  • My sister works the farm in Linmoor. She writes once a year to ask when I'm coming home, and I write back: not yet. It is the same letter every year, and we are both very fond of it.
  • Good day. Do close the door. Not all the way, it sticks.

docs.title: Hambone

Keeper of the Theatre Cart

Town Urbanograd Where The Old Barracks Yard Story Hambone in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• A New Rim (gives)
  • Seasoned Wood (gives)
Dialogue
  • Look at her. The old rim, with Ferro's band round it, and a name inside where nobody looks. I will not tell you the name. I cried when I read it.
  • New spokes, from your wood. Do not look at the rim. Look at the spokes. Lovely spokes.
  • Did you hear Drum last night? That deep boom under everything? That is my old theatre washtub. Best sound it ever made, and it washed a lot of costumes.
  • Juna's play has gone round the square on a cart every Walkout Day for a hundred years, Player, and for forty of them it has been my cart to keep. What can I tell you?
    • Choice: Tell me about the cart.
    • Choice: Why are you called Hambone?
    • Choice: Is something wrong with that wheel?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Fenwick Corliss kept it before me, a wheelwright, and he had it from the keepers before him. Those three dark, worn planks in the middle of the stage, those are from Juna's own cart. Fenwick told me so.
  • Ozzie has never found a letter to say so, nor one to say not. So I choose to believe it. Every Walkout Day, Juna's planks go round the square again.
  • My second season, under Bellamy Stroud. I played the back half of a prize pig in one of his farces, and the crowd threw sausages. The name stuck. My real one did not. I barely remember it myself.
  • Wrong? With the wheel? Which wheel? No. Nothing. It squeaks. Wheels squeak. Why would you ask about the left rear one in particular? I never said left rear.

  • Off you go. Hm hm hmm...

Dialogue
  • Player! I have pinned Gorm's scribble over the windlass. The second lift, corrected by the Master of the Stairs himself. Someday!
  • Player! New brush, and the rope has never been so well oiled. Up we go?
  • Player! Hop in, the basket has missed you. So has the gossip.
  • Hamish, keeper of the lift! Up, down, or something put by in the shed?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Tell me about the lift.
    • Choice: Anything worrying you?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Hamish! Keeper of the rope lift these fifteen years. I took it over from old Murdo when his arms gave out. Rode it every day as a boy, whenever he would let me, and some days when he would not.
  • And I raise my nephew Fionn, in the little house by the windlass. Quickest boy on the cliffs. Cheekiest too. Did I tell you what he did last week? I will tell you on the way up.
  • Fionn is my sister Ishbel's boy. His father, Duncan, drowned when he was barely one, and Ishbel went two winters after, with a cough that would not let go.
  • I was thirty-two and had never looked after anything softer than a rope. I took him home to the windlass anyway. Best thing I ever hauled up a cliff. Do not tell him I said so, he will be unbearable.
  • A timber frame bolted into the clifftop, a great windlass, a counterweight of stone-filled baskets in its own channel, and one heavy rope I oil by hand every week. Built long before I was born.
  • It hauls goods and tired legs from the Inlet Quay to the top. And whatever you cannot carry, I keep in my store-shed by the windlass, dry and counted. Fifteen years and I never lost a crate. Never dropped one either.
  • Worrying? Me? Only Fionn, all day long. If he takes a fall while I am at the windlass with a basket halfway up, I cannot let go to run to him.
  • Gorm wrote on my drawing! On it! Moved my anchor bolt a yard over and wrote that the rock would spit it out. He is right, which is worse.
  • And lately, on still nights, the rope gives a shudder. As if something had brushed it, out on the face in the dark. I go out with a lamp and there is nothing. I do not like it.
  • Mind your fingers on the frame!

Dialogue
  • Hatch. I hunt. Hunted, more like; my knees have opinions now. If you want stories, come back after my second cup. If you want to learn something, stay.
  • Split print, deep at the toe. Say it back to me. Good. You'd be amazed how many can't.
  • I've been reading my own notes all week. My handwriting's worse than I remember, and I was righter than I remember. Don't know which bothers me more.
  • Everything's ready but you. Spear's on the shaft. Torvi's sitting on Zip. When you want the Wallow, say so.
  • There's my hunter. Sit. It's the second cup, so you get a story whether you want one or not.
  • Well? Out with it.
    • Choice: Take me to the Wallow.
    • Choice: What has changed on the roads?
    • Choice: Tell me a story.
    • Choice: About Shade and Tick.
    • Choice: Nothing. Goodbye.
  • Down through the Reedwater Bottoms to the mud hollow at the heart of it. Step aside, then strike. I'll be in this chair. Hating it.
  • When I was young, a monster was an animal that had turned mean. You could read it: hungry, scared, cornered. These days they're bolder, stranger, and closer to the towns every season. They don't read right.
  • Why? I don't know. Anybody who tells you they know, buy them a drink and don't believe a word. I write down what I see. I never used to write anything down.
  • That's the first cup. Come back for the second. Better yet, go and earn it.
  • Ferro used to make only sculptures. Herons, foxes, a spiral of chain nobody understands. I brought a bent spear-head in, sixteen years back, and Ferro mended it like it was art. A month later I talked Ferro into a pair of hunting knives.
  • Every adventurer on the Gate Walk carries Ferro's steel now. I started that. Ferro says I ruined a perfectly good sculptor. Both true.
  • My father drove a cart between the towns, and I drove my own from sixteen. Learned the land from the bench: which fords flood, which woods hold boar, which hills smell of rain a day early.
  • At thirty-three I lost the wagon and two good horses to something in a ravine that shouldn't have been there. Walked home. Sold the wheels. Bought a spear. Came to Urbanograd because it was the only town that never asked me to wipe my boots.
  • Shade's the best I ever taught. Four seasons on the roads. Now Shade walks my old routes and finds half of them gone bad. I'm prouder than I'll say, so don't repeat that.
  • Tick follows me with a notebook. I respect his father too much to tell him to take the road. So I answer every question and hope the answers make him careful. That's all I've got.
  • Walk downwind. Always.

Puzzle-Box Maker

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• The Aristocrat Lock (gives)
  • The Returned Box (gives)
Dialogue
  • Welcome, Player. Here is a riddle for the threshold: what comes in without a key, leaves without a word, and is always being asked the price? You. Customers.
  • Player! The opener of doors, or at least the carrier of news about them. Leland sends word that the iron door swings like a garden gate now. Mine is the only door on the Row with no handle, and I intend to keep it that way.
  • Player. The owl sits on my shelf and watches me work. Too clever for its buyer, the note said. Too clever for its maker too, for twenty-eight years. I have not stopped grinning.
  • Ask, and I may answer. Buy, and I certainly will.
    • Choice: How do your boxes open?
    • Choice: Where did you learn locks?
    • Choice: What is that walnut box on the shelf?
    • Choice: Nothing today.

  • I write every sequence in a book now. The book is locked in another box. The box's sequence I keep in my head. You see the weakness. So do I. I enjoy it.
  • I swept for Esmond the locksmith from the age of twelve. He said a lock is a promise and a good one is a joke. When he died I kept the shop and took the handle off the door. Velvet sells my smaller boxes in the Night Market, and tells stories about them that are better than the truth.
  • Ah. You found the embarrassment. Dark walnut, a brass key-shaped inlay on every face and no keyhole anywhere. I made it about twenty-eight years ago and sold it at the Night Market to a traveller whose face I cannot recall.
  • It came back this spring with a carter, unopened, and a note: the buyer could not solve it. Neither can I. I have forgotten my own trick. Something rattles inside, and it is laughing at me.
  • Open, at last, thanks to a bucket drummer and you. Inside: a little wooden owl and a note in my own young hand. I keep the box open on the shelf as a warning to myself about cleverness.
  • Mind the door on your way out. It has no handle, so it will not mind you.

docs.title: Ozzie Lantry
docs.text:
Historian of the Walkers

Town Urbanograd Where The Great Hall Story Ozzie Lantry in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Now where did I put my... ah. On my head. All three."
  • "That reminds me of a letter from ninety years ago. Have you a moment? Several?"
  • "The first winter. Not one line. Not one."
  • "Dog-Ear quoted me another line of Juna's script today. Only one. The scoundrel."
  • "Mind the box. And that box. And the box under that box."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• The Oldest Volume (completes)
  • Marguerite's Bobbins (gives)
  • The First Winter (gives)
Dialogue
  • Hello, hello! Do I know you? I feel as if I ought to. Forgive me; I spend most of my days with people who have been dead for ninety years, and they are much easier to remember.
  • Ah, my door-knocker! Every 'nothing' you brought me is pinned up on that board, see, with a little cross. A history is half crosses. The other half is goats.
  • The goat won, Player. I have found the diary-writer who said it lost. He voted against the goat. History is written by sore losers too, it turns out. Wonderful. Wonderful!
  • The colour of the sky on the day they walked. I have it on the very first page of the book now. Nana came and read it and said I had spelled her mother's name wrong. I had not. She was pleased anyway.
  • Now, what was I... yes. What would you like to know?
    • Choice: What are you writing?
    • Choice: Who were the Walkers?
    • Choice: What happened in the first winter?
    • Choice: What is this about Dog-Ear's script?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Urbanograd's first hundred years, told through the Walkers' own words: their letters, diaries and songs, and their children's. Eighteen years in this corner. Before that I taught children to read in my front room. Half the Table learned their letters there.
  • I would like to finish it before my eyes give out. I am not certain I will. So I write faster, and then I find a new letter, and I write slower again, because it deserves to be read properly.
  • About three hundred people who walked out of Selsior behind Juna Marrow, after the theatre guild had her cart hauled away. Painters too vulgar for the galleries, musicians too loud, tinkerers nobody would license. And more joined on the road, from Kaldemor, the harbours, the highlands.
  • My grandfather was one: a fiddler, whose songs Selsior's theatres would not hear. He sang them to me at bedtime, very badly. That is where all this began. I wanted to know who wrote them, and who sang them on the road.
  • Nobody knows. That is the honest answer, and I hate it. The Walkers wrote about the road, and about the spring after. Of the first winter itself: nothing. Not a letter. The Table's own record books begin after it.
  • Perhaps they were too cold and hungry to write. Perhaps the pages were burned for warmth. Perhaps somebody hid them. I would pay well for one page of it from an old attic. If you ever find one, run here. Walk. Do not fall.

  • I'd rather be crewing the race boat, honestly. But I haven't dared ask her. She'd laugh. She laughs at everyone who asks.

docs.title: Kenna
docs.text:
Young Hunter

Town Goa Harbour Where Goa Harbour Story Kenna in the lore Services Quests

Player! Seen anything big? Anything at all?

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Nothing on Bethoc's board worth chalking."
  • "Dull watch again. Dullest on the shore."
  • "Merrin's crew is slow today. Good."
  • "That's a fox print. And that's a boar. Anyone could learn that."
  • "I'd follow Torva anywhere. She'd just rather I didn't."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Clean Prints (gives)
  • Something to Chalk (gives)
Dialogue
  • Player. 'A boar.' That's what she wrote. 'A boar.'
  • Player! It caught a cub. A cub! The old one's still out there. Torva says wait. I'm waiting. Loudly.
  • Player. The prints were clean again this morning. Not that I check.
  • Player! Did you hear them at the Gap Inn last night? They're still talking about it.
  • Kenna. One of Torva's hunters. The newest. Not for long. What is it?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: You and Merrin.
    • Choice: Bethoc's sighting board.
    • Choice: Nothing. Goodbye.
  • I grew up on this shore, in a house so close to the trees the branches scraped the roof. My folks went along the coast for timber work. I stayed.
  • I mended nets and watched the hunters till Torva took me on last autumn. I'd follow her anywhere. I've told her so. She ignores me, which is how I know she heard.
  • Do you know what Torva's first test was? I thought it'd be a monster. She sat me at the forest edge for three days and made me tell her everything that moved.
  • Every bird. Every leaf. I still haven't decided if it was a lesson or a punishment. Don't tell her I'm still thinking about it.
  • We raced when we were nine, raft landing to the point and back. I was ahead at the turn. She came back over the rocks, and I slipped following her and skinned both knees. That's cheating. Don't tell me nobody made any rules, I've heard it.
  • The rematch is on. Sand both ways, nobody on the rocks, Bethoc holds the line. She'll try something. She always tries something. I'll be watching her feet.
  • Torva reads it, says nothing and sends us out. I read it after her, and it's boars, stumps and foxes. Nothing big enough to be talked about. Bethoc says be careful what I wish for. I'm not.
  • My tusk's on it. 'A boar,' she wrote, small, in the corner. Merrin walked past it twice and said nothing, which means she saw it. It's still not big enough.
  • Bethoc chalked Old Brushtail up in letters you can read from the door, and the whole Gap Inn is talking about it. I thought it would feel bigger than it does. Don't tell anyone that either.
  • Go on. If you see anything big, it's mine.

  • Kenric, apprentice to Selene. Bellows, striking hammer, knives, hinges, a hundred nails. And a poker she says is the best poker in Selsior. I'm taking that as praise.
  • This winter, if Selene judges me ready. Start to finish, on my own. I have drawn it on every scrap of paper in the loft.
  • I've decided how to balance it, too. But that stays a secret until it's made.
  • My little brother. He runs errands for the warden. We sleep in the loft above the forge: warm in winter, far too warm in summer. I look after him. Or I try to.
  • Mind the sparks on your way out!
  • Oh! Sorry, Player, didn't see you there. Mind the doorframe, I always walk into it. What can I do?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Your first sword?
    • Choice: Who is Wat?
    • Choice: Goodbye.

docs.text:
Salvager of the Bellcaves

Town Bain Harbour Where Bain Harbour Story Kenwyn in the lore Services Boss: The Holdfast, Quests

docs.title: Says

• "Every plank of her, I know. Every plank."
  • "She's been wedged in there longer than anyone's been alive."
  • "I'll draw you a map for nothing. Going in is your own business."

docs.text:

  • The Holdfast (gives)

Dialogue
  • Kenwyn. I salvage. Iron and good old timber, out of the old wreck in the caves. Or I did. What can I do for you?
    • Choice: Take the salvagers' short way to the Captain's Cabin.
    • Choice: What is down there?
    • Choice: Why did you stop going in?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • There's a way I never told anyone. Down the old rope, along the cave wall at low water, in through the stern windows. Straight into the cabin.
  • Hold on tight. And if it gets hold of you, let go of everything else.
  • The Bellcaves, under the south cliff. They boom like a bell when the tide's in, hence the name. And in the deepest of them, the Saltgrace.
  • A great trading ship from the harbour's early days. A storm drove her into the caves long ago and she wedged there, tilted, decks sloping down into the dark water. I've worked her for years.
  • This spring I went down the steps and she was crawling. Crabs in the holds, eels in the hatches, things I'd not seen in twenty years of salvage.
  • I came out the way I went in, with all my fingers. I'm not daft. I sit at the top of the steps now and draw maps for braver folk.
  • Fair winds, Player.

Young Goatherd

Town Midbarium Where Midbarium Story Kesh in the lore Services Quests

Where did you come from? What was the road like?

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Forty-three eagles! No, forty-four!"
  • "Grumble, stop eating my sleeve."
  • "Korrin! Wait for me!"
  • "Biter doesn't bite. Much."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• The Second Stick (gives)
  • Where Did You Come From? (gives)
Dialogue
  • Where did you come from? What was the road like? Were there boggles? Did you see an eagle? I've seen forty-three. I have a stick for them.
  • You went all the way down the Canyon Road! Ennek says the boggles throw dust in your eyes. Did they? I'm going to be a guide like Ennek, or a watcher like Bekk, or both.
  • I'm glad I told you about the second stick. It was getting heavy, even though it's only a stick. Korrin says you won't tell about the lookout. You won't, will you?
  • Ask me anything! I know lots.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What are your sticks for?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Kesh! I'm Harra and Yarrek's son. I look after the kids of the herd. Grumble, Biter and Lady Snort are mine. I'm not allowed the big goats yet. Next year, maybe.
  • This one's for eagles. Forty-three notches. The other one... that's a different stick. It's not for telling.
  • Eagles on this one, forty-seven now. The second stick has two notches, both for the far bridge after dark. I don't want to put any more on it.
  • Come back and tell me about the next road!

docs.title: Kestra
docs.text:
Rope-Bridge Builder

Town Goa Harbour Where Goa Harbour Story Kestra in the lore Services Quests

Do not look down, Player. Look at the next plank.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Every plank, every knot. Every morning."
  • "A safety line is something to trip on."
  • "Ruan tested my ropes again. Twice. Again."
  • "Tarran's lantern will work this time. It will."
  • "Something has been at the highest bridge. I will catch it."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Lashings (gives)
  • The Chewed Ropes (gives)
Dialogue
  • Player. The highest bridge has held a week now. I walk it twice a morning anyway.
  • Player. Using that Rope Slide? Good. Knees soft, hands loose, and off the end before it is off you.
  • Player. You do not look down any more. I noticed.
  • Bridges are my business. What is yours?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Tell me about the bridges.
    • Choice: What's troubling you?
    • Choice: Nothing. See you.
  • Kestra. I string the rope bridges across the clefts of the cliff, from the low spans over the quay to the highest one near the top. I can cross any of them blindfold. I have, for bets.
  • Gorm took me on as a rope-carrier at fourteen, mostly to stop me climbing things. It did not work.
  • My mother, Shona, made nets in the coves. She taught me every knot she knew before I could write my name. She died of a fever when I was fifteen, and I just stayed up on the bridges.
  • Old Agna calls my knots Shona's knots, near enough. Near enough is the nicest thing Agna says about anyone. There. Now you know where the knots come from.
  • Every morning I walk every bridge end to end, hands on the ropes, listening to the planks. What is worn I replace before it frays. What is frayed I replace before anyone notices.
  • Help me check every lashing on one of them and I will teach you Rope Slide: the quick way down a rope or ladder, and safely off its end.
  • Every morning, every bridge, end to end. Hands on the ropes, ears on the planks. You have checked my lashings yourself now, so you know.
  • Use your Rope Slide on the Saltface. That cliff is all ropes and ledges. And look where you are going, not where you might land.
  • The highest bridge. Something is chewing the ropes. Not frayed, not cut. Chewed, from below, on the seaward side, strand by strand, where nothing should be able to reach.
  • I splice them and it happens again. I have never once seen what does it. Tarran is making me a lantern to light the face under the bridge. I am waiting for it. Patiently. Do not laugh.
  • I know what is down there now. What frightens me is someone who does not know the ropes stepping onto that bridge on the night it gives. So it never gives. That is the whole job.
  • Feet first, eyes forward.

  • Every one of them is a personal insult. I take them personally.
  • Grew up in the orchards down toward Kaldemor. My parents' carts still take that road every harvest.
  • Which is exactly why nothing is allowed to sit on it.
  • Kestrel is cleaning something unpleasant off her staff.

docs.title: Ketta
docs.text:
Returned Adventurer

Town Midbarium Where Midbarium Story Ketta in the lore Services Boss: Hollowmaw, Quests

Player! Want a story? I have three years of them.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Did I ever tell you about the fish in the harbour towns?"
  • "Night watch? I'll take it. I don't sleep much anyway."
  • "Zirra pretends she didn't leave that bow at my fire."
  • "Anything but that stretch. Any stretch but that one."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Back into the Dark (gives)
  • Drakes of the Dustfall (gives)
  • Earn Her Trust (gives)
  • Hollowmaw (gives)
  • The Cave Is Held (gives)
  • Let Ketta Lead (gives)
Dialogue
  • Player! Have I told you about the harbour towns? Fish taller than a man, and a captain who swore in five languages. Or the farms by Kaldemor, or Urbanograd's market? Three years of stories. Take your pick.
  • I told you about the cave. I haven't told anyone else. I don't know why it was easier with you. Please don't go in there without me.
  • We went back in. The Mouth, the Gallery, the Cold Draught. The wind from below still makes my teeth ache. But I walked out on my own feet, and that's something.
  • Hollowmaw's dead. That thing at the lake that looked at me. I keep waiting to feel different. I think I just feel tired. Good tired.
  • I walked the canyon stretch at dawn today, past the cave mouth, on patrol. Tavi didn't say a word, just nodded. Best nod I ever got.
  • Go on, ask me anything. Almost anything.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: How did you get that scar?
    • Choice: Take me into the Dustfall Cave.
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Ketta, of the Uskari rim. I left at seventeen like half the young Uskari, and saw Selsior, the Kaldemor farms, the harbour towns, Urbanograd and Fairy Forest. Came home last spring. Zirra taught me the bow; somebody left a new one at my fire, and I know exactly who.
  • This? A bear in Fairy Forest. No, a sword-dancer in Selsior. No, I fell off a fish cart. Pick the one you like best. I have.
  • A new one for you: I wrestled a drake twice my size at the bottom of a lake, and it gave me this as a parting gift. That's not true either. But it's my favourite now.
  • The Dustfall Cave. I'll be on the rope-way right behind you. Don't look down too long, and don't stare at the dark too long either.
  • Come back with a story, Player.

  • Keziah. I guard ships for Seraphine. What do you need?

    • Choice: How do you like the sea?

  • I grew up on an apple farm in the orchard country outside Kaldemor. Guarded carts and caravans on the inland roads from seventeen.
  • End of last winter I heard the captains here were paying swords to sail. I'd never seen the sea. Three voyages on the Bright Morrow so far. Seraphine wants me for the whole summer.
  • It's lovely. Very blue. Very large.
  • Next question.
  • Fair winds, Player.

Shipwright's Son

Town Bain Harbour Where Bain Harbour Story Kit in the lore Services Quests

  • I can tie fourteen knots! Do you want to see all of them?

  • Watch. Over, under, round the tree, back down the hole. Bowline! Grandad taught me that one. The last few Mr Wilmot taught me.

  • Obviously. I'm already nearly one. I help Dad and Grandad every day after lessons.
  • I've got a secret about the race boat. I'm not telling. Not even you.

docs.title: Kite
docs.text:
Rooftop Runner

Town Urbanograd Where Urbanograd Story Kite in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Gate Walk to the Great Hall, and not one stair!"
  • "Cobble's boots. Nothing else grips a wet slate."
  • "Pounce came in early. Storm's coming. Run now, while it is dry."
  • "Tick says he will beat my record by the streets. Tick says a lot of things."
  • "The slates sing if you run them right. Listen."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Kite Laid Up (gives)
  • Rooftop Dash (gives)
  • The Crooked Tower Run (gives)
Dialogue
  • Sitting. I am sitting. Look at me, sitting, with my foot on a cushion like a grandee. Has the message gone to Perch yet? Do not answer. Just go.
  • Ankle's back! I ran the Long Lean twice this morning to make sure. Ivo says I should rest it. Ivo says that about everything.
  • There is my test runner! I have run the tower line three more times since you. It still breaks at the Long Lean. One day it will not.
  • Still landing heavy on that left foot, Player? Lean in. Let the roof carry you.
  • Kite. Rooftop runner. Record holder. You have heard of me, or you will. What is it?
    • Choice: How fast is the record?
    • Choice: Who taught you to run?
    • Choice: Which roofs should I avoid?
    • Choice: So Nana Gristle was right about that roof?
    • Choice: Who paints the chimney backs?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Gate Walk to the Great Hall, by the roofs. A sand-glass at each end, turned by somebody honest. I took the record last summer and bettered it twice since.
  • Cobble keeps the times on the back of his shop door. Tick means to beat it by the streets, and writes down everybody who says he cannot. I have not said it. I am waiting to say it at the finish.
  • My grandmother ran messages over these roofs when Cobble was young. She taught me the old routes: the long jump over the Night Market, the gutter run below the Crooked Tower, the singing slates.
  • My mother ran too, until a wet roof took her knee. She lives out near Kaldemor now and writes when the carts get through. Three of us in Cobble's boots. I am the fastest. Do not tell my mother.
  • Ask Nana Gristle on her bench in Lantern Square. She has a list as long as your arm. Half of them fell in fifty years ago and were patched. The other half... well. Ask Nana. Do not tell her I sent you.
  • Do not say it so loud. The roof over the old cooper's yard. She said it would go, and it went, and I was on it. Fine. She was right. Once.
  • Paints? What paints? I do not know anything about any paints. If I am out at night with my hands full, that is exercise. Very good exercise.
  • Mind the third slate on the Kiss, Player. It talks.

docs.title: Knox
docs.text:
Gate Watch Guard

Town Urbanograd Where Urbanograd Story Knox in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "A hare, this one. Or a fox. It decides as I go."
  • "Tick! Walk. Do not run. ...He is running."
  • "Every face that comes up that road, I know it."
  • "Quiet watch. Good. Quiet is good."
  • "Patch will have words about this splinter."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Owls for the Watch (gives)
  • The Highland Traveler (gives)
  • The Late Egg Cart (gives)
Dialogue
  • Knox, of the Gate Watch. Ten years on this gate. I am the big one; Brindle is the one with the slate. If you are going out, come back the same way, so I can count you in.
  • The egg woman asked after you. She says you have an honest face. From her, that is high praise; she says it about almost nobody, and never about me.
  • The old button-seller sewed a horn button on my coat himself. Says he would not trust the city to do it right. Two faces back on the road, because of you.
  • Look at the posts. An owl on every one. The night watch says it is like having company. Dagny says hers has bigger eyes. It does not. Well. A little.
  • Tick read me version four last night. The true one. He read it slowly, the way Brindle lets him read the slate. Then he said he wants to be like you. I did not know what to say. I still do not.
  • What can I do for you?
    • Choice: What are you carving?
    • Choice: Tell me about Tick.
    • Choice: Who comes up the road these days?
    • Choice: Nothing. Goodbye.
  • Foxes, hares, goats. Owls. I worked wood on Workshops Row before the Watch, carrying beams for the rooftop bridges. The work dried up. The habit did not.
  • The owls go to Dagny. I tell her she is the bravest of us. She laughs and thinks it is a joke. It is not a joke. Brindle is still looking for the right words. I decided owls would do in the meantime.
  • My boy. Ten years old and he salutes the cat. His mother had a loud laugh; he remembers that, or thinks he does. He grew up between the guards' boots, here.
  • He wants to be an adventurer, like Hatch. I want him to be a joiner. A baker. A fiddler. Anything with a roof. We have this argument at supper. I am losing it. I know I am losing it.
  • He will go out that gate one day. I know it now. I have stopped arguing at supper; it was only making us both tired.
  • If he must go, I want him taught by the right people. Hatch. Shade. You, Player. Do not tell him I said so. He will salute me, and I will not be able to bear it.
  • Carters. Peddlers. Hunters. The cider men. The egg woman. A fellow who brings nothing but bad jokes, every month, and I laugh every month. I know them all by face.
  • When one stops coming, I notice first. I am noticing more of that every season. What I fear is the evening a regular face does not come up the road, and Tick is the one who goes looking.
  • Come back the same way, Player. I will be counting.

docs.title: Korrin
docs.text:
Chieftain's Son

Town Midbarium Where Midbarium Story Korrin in the lore Services Quests

Bet I can climb higher than you.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "I tied my boots like Bekk. See?"
  • "I'm not climbing. I'm just standing on the wall."
  • "Kesh! Kesh, over here!"
  • "When I'm on the trail watch, I'll go first."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• The Second Stick (completes)
  • The Boys' Lookout (gives)
  • The Tallest Ledge (gives)
Dialogue
  • Psst. Do you climb? I've been up every terrace in town, and some of the walls, and Grandfather Ulm's chimney once, but don't say.
  • You went up the highest ledge on the North Ridge! Was it windy? Bekk goes up there. I tied my boots like him today. See?
  • Kesh told you about the stick. And the bridge. We weren't supposed to have a lookout, so we couldn't tell anyone. Was it bad, what we saw?
  • You kept our lookout secret. Even from Father. When I'm on the trail watch, you can walk patrol with me, Player.
  • What?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What do you want to be?
    • Choice: Who's Kesh?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Korrin. My father's chieftain of the Kragvar, so everyone says I should be a mason. I'm nine. I have the scabbiest knees on the terraces.
  • Trail watch! With the Uskari, like Bekk. My family thinks that's funny. Grandfather Ulm says the Kragvar who stayed under the World Tree were the best watchers of all, so it's practically the same thing.
  • Kesh is my best friend. We met hiding under the same cistern lid when we were little. Mother found us both and was very cross. Kesh talks more than me. A lot more.
  • Don't tell anyone where I climb!

docs.title: Kragvar Mason
docs.text:
Town Midbarium Where Midbarium

Watch the scaffold. Dorrek's up there somewhere.

docs.title: Says

docs.text:
Adventurer

Town Goa Harbour Where Goa Harbour Story Lachlan in the lore Services Boss: The Inkmother, Quests

Player! Just the person. I've a plan. It's a good one.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "The first true map of the sea caves. My name on it. Soon."
  • "Gwenna said no again. That's progress. Last time she said it louder."
  • "Round's on me! Well. The next round's on me."
  • "Low water at dusk. Perfect for the Mouths."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Before the Still Pool (gives)
  • Ronan at the Mouth (gives)
  • The A Mark (gives)
  • The First True Map (gives)
  • The Inkmother (gives)
Dialogue
  • There it is, Player. The first true map of the Sounding Caves. My name, and yours beside it. Grandfather would have laughed. The real laugh, this time.
  • I told you about the water. I've told nobody else. Let's finish it, you and me.
  • An A, by a tide mark. That far in, and he never said. Not once.
  • You found Ronan before I did. With my rope! I owe you. And he owes me a rope.
  • Gwenna's map! Well, a map, and a lecture. I've read the map three times. The lecture once. Mostly.
  • So? Caves, coves or a drink? Any order.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: The sea caves?
    • Choice: Ronan?
    • Choice: Take me to the Sounding Caves.
    • Choice: Take me to the Still Pool.
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Lachlan, adventurer, coves-born. My grandfather Alasdair raised me. He'd been everywhere on this coast in a little boat and had a story for every rock.
  • I've his old oilskin and his tide-reckoner, and I use both. He went a little way into the sea caves once, as a young man, and came out faster than he went in. He laughed about it. I never quite believed the laugh.
  • The sea caves under the cliffs. The mouths open at low water and the sea booms in and out. Nobody's mapped them. I've marked every mouth from the Inlet Quay to the far cove, with the tide to go in by.
  • A few dozen yards in, most of them. A bit further in two. Every trip I go deeper. First I need Gwenna's old maps. She keeps saying no.
  • The Sounding Caves, I'm calling them, for the noise. The Mouths first, then down past Gwenna's Drop. Every trip a bit deeper. You're coming, of course.
  • You know about the moving water now. The only one who does. I'm not turning back again. Not with you there.
  • Mapped, end to end, Still Pool and all. Next I'll map something nobody has even heard of. Give me a week.
  • The little magpie from the coves. I let him carry my rope to the quay once and he's never let me forget it. He wants to come to the caves. "When you are bigger," I tell him. I've started to worry he won't wait.
  • I still tell him "when you are bigger". After that day I said it differently, and he heard it. I think he'll wait now. I hope he will.
  • Off you go. Mind the tide. It doesn't mind you.
  • Low water, the Fishers' Coves, the third mouth along. Follow me and mind your head.
  • Past the Long Echo. Listen. You can hear it breathing from here.

  • The trouble is, nobody knows how a street juggler gets invited. I asked Clement the herald. He was very kind and promised nothing.

docs.text:
• A Relic for the Stage (gives)
  • An Ending by Friday (gives)

Dialogue
  • Ah. An audience. Lavinia, Mistress of the Gilded Stage. You may admire me, Player, and then you may buy a ticket.
    • Choice: Tell me about yourself.
    • Choice: Tell me about the Gilded Stage.
    • Choice: What is the new play?
    • Choice: How is the play?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • I walked through that stage door at fifteen and asked for anything at all. I swept the boards for a season. Then an actress fell ill, I went on in her place, and I never came off again.
  • Thirty-five years of every great part in this house. The old manager left it to me. I have been married to it ever since, and it has been far more expensive than any husband.
  • Gilt, crimson, a cheap gallery under the roof and a box for the palace that no one from the palace has sat in for years. One night the queen will sit there. Mark me.
  • Crispin's Balrog War. All of it, the largest thing the Row has ever attempted. I have bet the theatre's savings, a loan on the building and my own name on it.
  • He has four acts and no fifth, my two leads will not share a stage, and the audiences go home earlier every month. One last triumph, Player. That is all I ask of the world.
  • Exit stage left, darling. Always leave them wanting more.
  • The fourth act has its wonder, darling. Amber in the lamplight. Now if only Crispin would give me a fifth.

Keeper of the Low Door

Town Urbanograd Where The Great Hall Story Leland in the lore Services Boss: The Warmstone Colossus, Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Hear that? Water, under the flagstones. Always has been."
  • "Mind the rope. Mind the step. Mind everything, down there."
  • "Sixty years of wells, and never a door like this one."
  • "A little more chalk on the map every day."
  • "The stone down there is warm. I keep coming back to that."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Low Grad Rounds (gives)
  • The Floodwells (gives)
  • The Undercroft (gives)
  • The Warm Quarry (gives)
Dialogue
  • Leland. Well-digger, or I was, until my knees retired before I did. You will be wondering why an old man stands in a kitchen passage staring at a door. Everybody does. Mags has stopped asking and started bringing me stew.
  • The Table said yes, I hear. Opened in one night, they say upstairs, and nobody can believe it. Well, the door has not heard. Hex will have to tell it. I am going to stand right here while that happens.
  • Keeper of the Low Door. They gave me the title, a lamp, and a coil of new rope from Rivet. I gave myself the chalk. Going down, Player?
  • Undercroft, Floodwells, Deep Roads, Warm Quarry. All four on the wall in chalk, thanks to you. Mapped, not understood. Still: mapped. Going down again?
  • What can an old well-digger tell you?
    • Choice: What is behind that door?
    • Choice: Tell me about digging wells.
    • Choice: What is under the city?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Down, or a word first?
    • Choice: Take me down into Low Grad.
    • Choice: Open the way to the Warmstone Colossus.
    • Choice: Show me your chalk map.
    • Choice: What is under the city?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Nobody knows. The Walkers found it locked when they patched this hall, and they had roofs to mend and plays to put on, so they left it. A hundred years, everyone has walked past it to get to the stew.
  • I have put my ear to it. I hear air moving, and water, a long way down. That is all I will say about what I hear. A well-digger who guesses out loud ends up digging in the wrong place.
  • Sixty years of them, all over the city. Yards, cellars, under a bakery once; the baker brought me a loaf a day until I struck water. You learn to read stone by the sound your pick makes. Dull is earth. Bright is rock. Hollow is trouble.
  • Under this city, the pick rings hollow more often than you would like. There are rooms down there nobody has lived in since the Aristocrats left. I have broken into two by accident. I bricked them up and said nothing. I am saying something now.
  • Old Grad was a fortress before it was a city. A fortress digs: cellars for its stores, cisterns for its water, tunnels so its soldiers could get in and out without the gate. The Walkers built their city on top of all that and painted it bright.
  • The bright part is real. So is the part underneath. I have always thought somebody ought to know both. It seems that somebody is me.
  • Rope's tied. Lamp low. Mind the third step; it is not a step. I will be right here at the top.
  • Not yet. I have seen what crawls along those shelves, and you are not ready for it. Come back when you have a few more scars from the Outworks, around level 20. I mean that kindly.
  • To the Warm Quarry's heart, then. Potions. Mind the glowing floor. And come back up.
  • Here, on the kitchen wall: Mags allows it as long as I do not chalk over the soup list. Top to bottom, as far as anyone has gone. Every stair, every walkway, every place the floor is not a floor.
  • Where I have not been, I draw a question mark. There are fewer question marks every week. There are still a lot of them.
  • Go well. Up here or down there.

Dialogue
  • Two maps, one line. Gervase and I agree, and neither of us is happy about it. Thank you for walking it, Player.
  • Hm? Oh, hello. Mind the ink, it is still wet. I am Leofric. Were you looking for the queen, or for a road?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What is this map?
    • Choice: What worries you?
    • Choice: Sorry to disturb you.
  • The queen's consort, though I was a road surveyor first. I spent seven years walking the royal roads with Gervase, measuring every mile.
  • Then a young woman in the Scholars' Quarter told me my road was in the wrong place. I proved it was not, at some length. We were married before the year was out.
  • Every royal road on Veligor: every town, ford, bridge and milestone. It took me years.
  • The red marks are newer. Edric sends me the patrol reports each week, and I mark every place the patrols met monsters, with the date beside it.
  • The pattern. The marks used to sit in a few wild places. Now they creep along the roads, a little nearer the towns each season.
  • I am a surveyor, Player. I know a line when I see one, and this is starting to look like something with a direction.
  • Yes, yes, of course. Do mind the... ah. Never mind. It was only Kaldemor.
