Dialogue
  • Boots. Off. Or at least wipe them; I just swept. Are you hurt? No? Then sit there and don't bleed on anything.
  • Cliff gnawers. Their teeth carry dirt from their nests deep into a wound, which is why the bites fester. Now that I know what I'm treating, I can treat it properly.
  • Fresh rimwort from the far slopes. I can stop rationing. I've been counting bites all year, and every count was higher than the last.
  • Iron boar armour makes splints that hold a bone the way a Kragvar wall holds a terrace. Brakka came by just to look at them. Then she tracked mud all over my floor.
  • Well? Hurt, buying, or visiting?
    • Choice: Show me your remedies.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What about all these bites?

  • Salves, tonics, and a draught for the worst breaks. Use them properly, and wipe your feet on the way out.
  • Lessa, bonesetter. Odda and Thrun's daughter, Neffa's mother. I set my first bone at fifteen. I keep my mother's book of forest herbs by my bed, and I visit Mabbu every few days to argue about her knees.
  • More monster bites this year than in my first ten years of healing put together, and they fester. I clean them with rimwort, a grey bitter herb from the far slopes, and the Uskari have stopped bringing it back. I'm rationing what's left.
  • Gnawers on the bridge, boars on the slopes, goats that bite their own herders. I keep a tally of every bite, and the tally is finally going down. Slowly.
  • Feet! Wipe them!

Town Guide

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Story Lia in the lore Services Quests

Morning, Player!

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Need a hand with anything? Just ask!"
  • "Press Space near someone to talk to them."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Welcome Home (gives)
Dialogue
  • Hi, Player! What can I do for you? Nobody knows Kaldemor better than me.
    • Choice: Where am I?
    • Choice: What is there to do here?
    • Choice: Anything new in town?
    • Choice: Am I ready for the fields?
    • Choice: How do I...?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Of course! What would you like to know?
    • Choice: ...move and fight?
    • Choice: ...see how strong I am?
    • Choice: ...learn and use skills?
    • Choice: ...carry and wear things?
    • Choice: ...keep track of my quests?
    • Choice: Never mind.
  • Walk with the arrow keys and jump with Alt. Up takes a portal or climbs a ladder, and Down with Alt drops through a ledge.
  • Swing with Ctrl, pick up what monsters leave behind with Z, and talk to people with Space or a click. Every key can be changed with the backslash key.
  • Press S to open your stat window: your level, HP and MP, and the strength, dexterity and the rest that decide how hard you hit.
  • Every level gives you ability points to spend there. A warrior puts most of them into STR.
  • Press K for your skills. Each level from the second one gives you skill points, and a click on the + puts one into a skill.
  • A skill has a key of its own, and costs MP each time you use it. Blue potions bring the MP back.
  • Press I for your inventory: four tabs, one for what you wear, drink, collect and sit on. Double-click a potion to drink it.
  • Press E for what you wear: double-click a piece of equipment to put it on, and a worn one to take it off.
  • Press Q for your quest log: what you can take up, what you are doing, and what you have done. Pick a quest to read its story and its rewards.
  • The quests you follow are listed on the right of the screen with how far you are. Click one to open it in the log.
  • This is the town square of Kaldemor. The big treehouse behind us is the oldest building in town.
  • The people here are friendly. Say hello to everyone: press Space near someone, or click them!
  • Visit the Market to the east for potions and gear. When you feel strong, the fields beyond the town are full of monsters to practice on.
  • People with a light bulb over their head have a job for you. Helping them is a good way to learn your way around!
  • Oh, yes! The clock tower in the park has stopped. Nobody can say when it will tick again.
  • Old Ewan, the clockkeeper, has been up there for days. Maybe he would like some company.
  • You carry (how many you carry) Red Potions - good. Snails nibble, and a potion mends it. Drink one with its key before it gets serious!
  • I would take some Red Potions along first: you carry (how many you carry). Bram sells them in the market, east of here.
  • Have fun, Player!

  • Mum shouted. Dad didn't say much. Gran called me a fool to the whole market and then sewed me a kit bag. Double seams.
  • I want to crew the race boat more than anything. Quenna picks the crew herself.
  • Old Thaddeus keeps shouting advice at me from his bench. I go the long way round to avoid him. Sometimes I try the advice, though. It's annoyingly good.
  • See you, Player!

docs.title: Lucan

Bargemaster

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:

Dialogue

  • Eleven before me. Their names are scratched into the oldest beam of the lamp store, at the foot of the first tower. Lionel Callow's is the last. I carried his oil for years before I carried his ladder.
  • There is room on the beam under his name. I scratched mine there with a nail and then sat on the floor for a while. Twelfth. It is a long line to stand at the end of.
  • Something does. Only the lanterns facing the wilds, only on the outward side of the walls, and never two nights in a row. The frames are bent and the glass is everywhere.

  • Lampbats, and something bigger that leads them, roosting under the outer towers. I would rather know than wonder. Knowing is still not the same as the lanterns being safe.

  • The farmer? He has fallen off the hanging course eleven times. I passed it first try.
  • He is all right, though. He never gives up. And whatever he says about me and the fountain, it was a very warm day.
  • Further than I let on. I scout the edge of the woods for Hale when he is busy. That is all I am saying, Player.
  • See you out there, Player. Try to keep up.

Dialogue
  • The two envoys sit side by side at supper now and quarrel only about the soup. Progress, Player.
  • Welcome to the Envoys' Hall, Player. I am Melisende. Sit, if you like; nobody here will take offence, and one or two will take it as a compliment.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What is the Envoys' Hall?
    • Choice: What worries you?
    • Choice: Good day.
  • I was born in an envoy's house by the plaza and carried trays through rooms where every town's manners met. I learned them the way other children learn songs.
  • Now I host the envoys every town keeps at the palace. When two towns quarrel, the queen asks me what each side actually wants. It is rarely what they say.
  • A long wing of the palace: a dining room, a garden court, and a set of rooms for every town, each furnished the way that town likes it.
  • A harbour captain who interrupts you is agreeing with you. A Fairy Forest guest who falls silent is thinking, not bored. Remember that, and you will do well in here.
  • The quarrels have grown smaller. Towns that argued over the price of wool now argue over who guards the carts, and then agree to share the cost.
  • That is good, and it is also a sign. What troubles me are the empty chairs: envoys late back because the roads are slow, and letters arriving with their seals cracked.
  • Good day, Player. Come to supper one evening; I seat travellers next to the people they ought to meet.

Caravan Master

Town Selsior Where The Gate Inn Story Merrick in the lore Services Quests

  • "HAMON! Is my supper on?"

    • Choice: What do you carry?
    • Choice: Do you hire guards?

  • I deliver on the day I say I will. That name is worth more than any cargo I ever carried, and I guard it harder.
  • Always! Any town, any blade that can hold a road. I judge a fighter in one look: how you stand, and whether you watch the wagons or the trees.
  • I pay well because I have to. Danger's priced like salt now: by the weight, by the distance, and by how much worse it got since last season.
  • You I'd hire on sight, Player. The terraces are on the bill at double now, and the wagons still roll. One more run than the roads can stop. That's the game.
  • Knew him when he was a dreadful child throwing stones at the horses! His father and I shared many a fire. Now we argue over who should guard whom. Truth is, there aren't swords enough for either.
  • Off you go! And if you can swing that thing, come and find me.

  • Player! Have you seen Kenna? Is she practising? She's practising, isn't she.

  • Want to know the first line on my door? It isn't a tree. It's a race, when I was nine, against Kenna. Raft landing to the end of the point and back.
  • I came back over the rocks and won by a stride. She's called it cheating ever since. You're the first I've told it's at the top of my door, Player. Don't tell her.
  • I want a crew of my own. Haldor says I'll get one. Then he says something else, but I've usually stopped listening by then.
  • Out there past the edge there are trees as tall as masts. Tamsin would give anything for one. Whoever brought one out would have a crew by morning, I reckon. I'm only saying.
  • Not ready, he says. I kept the cleanest edge on the shore. I don't know what ready looks like, Player. Osric watches the deep woods all day, and Haldor watches Osric, and nobody tells me anything.
  • Haldor walked us all along Osric's black marks this morning. Me first. Everybody saw. I'm not stupid, Player, I know who that was for.
  • I'll not go past them. Not without asking. I said that out loud, so now I have to.
  • Kenna's one of Torva's now, so she stands at the edge of the trees all day watching my crew work. Best and worst thing that ever happened to either of us. She still says I cheated. Nobody made any rules.
  • The rematch is on. Sand both ways, Bethoc holds the line. We'll pick a day when Haldor and Torva can spare us both, which at this rate is never. I'll still win.
  • Off you go. I've a tree to beat.

docs.title: Mhairi

Fiddler

    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Mhairi, fiddler of the Gap Inn and the race send-off. My da made my first fiddle from a mast offcut when I was seven. It squeaked on every note. It's on my wall still.
  • Cormac taught me the old tunes when I could barely hold the bow. He said a tune is a story you can dance to. Now I play them faster than he can sing them, to make him laugh.
  • A verse for the gap at dawn, one for Iska at the tiller, one for Tamsin hammering on the slip all winter, and a rowdy one for Jory that he keeps asking me to make longer.
  • No last verse. The last verse is the finish, and I won't write the Gap Runner losing. So Goa has to win. I've told the whole inn. The crew love me for it. Some days.
  • Sometimes Cormac starts that old gap verse and stops after one line, and his face goes still. I don't like it. I play something quick after, and he laughs, and that's better.
  • Off you go! Feet first.

  • This year I write the road notices in shorter, plainer words. Plain words frighten people less.
  • Thirty years in office, and he still takes the treehouse stairs two at a time. I would like him to keep doing that for a good while yet.
  • Good day, Player. Do keep out of trouble. It is so hard to spell.

  • I would still rather be out on the wild coast with Torva's hunters. Ask Ruan. Actually, do not ask Ruan.
  • Three winters back I was on watch when the first one came up the face. I ran for the iron bar at the head of the Long Stair and rang it till my arms went.
  • Torva came, her and two of hers, and they drove it over the edge. I saw what it did to her jaw. That is all. I do not tell it much.
  • The Long Stair goes from the Inlet Quay all the way to the clifftop. I do it two at a time, then come down and do it again.
  • The Long Stair, the Inlet Quay to the clifftop, two at a time. And the Gullwalk is quieter since you thinned it. The way down to the Saltface starts there, so I like it quiet.
  • Kestra races me some evenings. She usually wins. I usually let her.
  • They are coming more often. Always the darkest nights. And they are getting better at finding the bits the lanterns do not reach. I told Ruan. He nodded and wrote it down. His face said he already knew.
  • You have seen the dark stretches for yourself now. Ruan wants lanterns on all of them. Gunna wants time. I want to be first down when the bar rings.
  • Off you go. Two at a time!

Item Price Highland Jumper 3,200 mesos Sea-Mittens 3,000 mesos Cove Fisher's Hat 1,200 mesos White Undershirt 20 mesos Dialogue
  • Teague says you'll do for brave company. I told him I'd be the judge of that. I've judged. You'll do. Now eat something.

Sailor of the Saltlark

Town Bain Harbour Where The Docks Story Morwenna in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Moth
docs.text:
Keeper of the Night Market Stalls

Town Urbanograd Where The Night Market Story Moth in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "First name, first pick. No exceptions. Several exceptions. No exceptions."
  • "Pepper and coals: Ladle. Spiced tea: Saucer. Dusty paper: Dog-Ear. I could do this asleep."
  • "Sunrise is the city's only real mistake."
  • "Counted the hat again. Do not ask what number."
  • "Glim's lanterns, end of the row. Not that I am biased. I am completely biased."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Counting Names (gives)
  • Empty Corners (gives)
Dialogue
  • Evening. Is it evening? It had better be. Name for the hat? No? Just looking? Fine, look. Everything here moves after dark, including me.
  • A crate of glass, through my market, at this hour? Through the busiest row in the city? Of course. Tinsel's panes for the outer lanterns. Stay behind me and keep it level.
  • Two new names in the hat, Player, and a wool carter who still looks over one shoulder. The hat is a little fatter. I can feel it.
  • The Table is arguing my question. Slowly. Bastian has done both sides; the stall-holders are doing a third side nobody expected. Whatever they decide, it will be decided properly. The hat approves. I asked it.
  • What do you want to know? Quickly. The draw starts at dusk.
    • Choice: How does the draw work?
    • Choice: Tell me about the Night Market.
    • Choice: Why are corners empty?
    • Choice: Glim is your daughter?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Every stall-holder's name goes in this hat. At dusk I draw them out one by one: first name, first pick of the corners. Nobody owns the best spot for long, and a newcomer has the same chance as someone who has traded here forty years.
  • The first traders started it, in the Walkers' early years, after they quarrelled over corners so badly somebody nearly lost an ear. This is the third hat anyone remembers. It is held together by habit. Mostly mine.
  • Sixteen years I have kept the stalls, since old Bramble handed me the hat. He taught me the rules, which are few, and the exceptions, which are many: who cannot go next to whom, which stall needs water, whose smoke goes where when the wind turns.
  • I can walk it with my eyes shut. Ladle's pepper, Saucer's tea, Crow's odd sharp smells, Dog-Ear's dust, and at the very end, warm wax: Glim. This market feeds half the city through the winter. It matters.
  • The roads. Salt sellers, wool carters, spice peddlers who came every month: some nights none of them get through. I count the names before each draw now. That never used to be necessary.
  • An empty corner in a night market is a hole in a winter. I worry about the winter. I worry in the afternoons, mostly, which is when I wake up.
  • She is. Her name goes in the hat like everyone else's. I have never fixed a draw for her, and she has never once asked me to. We are both proud of that. Unbearably.
  • She is saving for a cart. She wants to take her lanterns to other towns, when the roads are safe. I am proud of that, and terrified of it, and I have not yet found a way to say both at once.
  • Go on. And if anyone asks, I was awake before noon. Nobody will believe them.

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Story Mott in the lore Services Quests

  • Out of the gates of Selsior in a basket, and all the way here. That is the most important fact about this city, and don't let anyone at the Table tell you otherwise. The Charter's all very well. My mother was in a basket.

  • Player! Look at the guild master's nose in the old cartoon. Proper red again, the exact red the Walkers used. The wall looks thrilled. I'm sure of it.
  • Player. Have you seen Figgy's wall? Under the Fiddler's Crossing? It rained on Tuesday. She stood under the bridge and watched it all run down and declared it finished. I nearly cried. I did cry.

Dialogue
  • Come in, sit. The Brenna host every choosing, Player, and I have hosted two, so I am very good at telling people to sit. Tea?
  • The Edgewood is quieter, and my letters can go east. I have written to the same friend in Fairy Forest every spring since my envoy days. Neither of us has missed a year.
  • Corwell will send my letter with the next caravan east. It will be slow; caravans are slow now. My friend will forgive it. We are both old enough to know that letters arrive when they arrive.
  • Rimwort from the far slopes again. Lessa nearly smiled. I keep the old forest-herb lore, but this herb is ours: grey, bitter, and good for what bites.
  • I told Ahvi to sing it. The bites, the goats, the gnawers, the dry springs, Imre's dates: all of it in front of me, and a verse that says the beasts grew wild before the Burning. What it means, the families must decide together. That is what a gathering is for.
  • Now. What can I do for you?
    • Choice: Who are you?

    • Choice: How do you keep four families at peace?

  • Odda, chieftain of the Brenna these twenty years. Healer's mother, drummer's wife, keeper of a great many stories. When I was young I walked to the forests as an envoy, as the Brenna once did, and I kept a friend there.
  • I hosted the choosing that named him, after Varra died. A long night: argument, drumming, song. Hask said almost nothing, and that is why the families chose him. I advise him. Sometimes he even listens.
  • Four families, each proud as a mountain. I settle their quarrels with stories: I find one where both chieftains were right, and let them hear it together. It works more often than you'd think.
  • Go gently, Player. And come back for tea.

Dialogue
  • Sit, Player. I have had a long morning of chieftains telling me that everything is well. You have walked our roads. I would like to hear it from someone with no family pride to guard.
  • You walk the ridges with Skarra's people now. Good. Tell me what you see out there, not what you think the Old One wants to hear. That is all I ask of you.
  • The ridges hold, and they hold because you walked them. The Uskari cannot keep that up alone; I knew it, and now I have heard it said aloud. The far slopes are next, Player.
  • The drum sounds whole again, and every family heard it. Now the springs fail beyond the slopes. I need your eyes in the Withered Reach as much as I needed them on the ridges.
  • The council said it aloud at last: the patrols are thin, and all four families will share the watch. I have closed many councils. That is the first one I will remember. You told the truth when it was asked of you, Player.
  • What is on your mind?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Why ask me, and not one of the families?
    • Choice: How is the town?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • I am Hask, born an Uskari. I led my family nine years before the four families chose me Old One, the night after Old One Varra was mourned. I gave up the Uskari that same night, as custom asks.
  • Old One is a title, not an age; Ahvi likes to remind me I am one of the youngest the songs name. I try to listen more than I talk, and when I do talk, to say it once.
  • Because you belong to none of the four families, and you are no stranger to this kingdom either. A Kragvar will tell me the walls are fine. An Uskari will tell me the patrols are enough. You have no family's pride to protect.
  • Every season the red dots on Skarra's map creep closer, and every season the families say in council that all is in hand. Pride is a fine thing in a hunter. In a council it can get people killed.
  • Kragvar masons walk the bridge with Uskari bows beside them, and Tolmach herders tell the watch where the goats stray. It is not easy for proud people to ask each other for help. They are learning.
  • Walk carefully, Player. And come back and tell me.

  • Three falls and a breath of quiet. I have rebuilt the whole first act around them. The words stay the same, of course. The words always stay the same.
  • The Old Barracks Troupe, Player. Juna's play, on a cart, every Walkout Day, the way it was first done. What do you want? Quickly. Everything is quickly.
    • Choice: Tell me about Juna's play.

  • So every Walkout Day we play it on a cart, as it was first played. Quint reads the Charter in the square first, slowly, on purpose, and I time our first entrance to his very last word.
  • I joined at nineteen, pushing the cart. Hambone showed me how. Then I played Juna for nine years, and when Bellamy Stroud died, the troupe looked at me, and I looked back, and that was that. Thirteen years ago.
  • My father carried me on his shoulders to my first Walkout Day play. I have been giving notes ever since. Yours: stop slouching.
  • Dex, the grandee, fifteen years in the hat. Rue, our new Juna, who froze in the wings and then owned the stage. Pip, who writes when she thinks I am not looking. Piper, who writes far too many songs. Hambone and the cart, Thimble and the costumes, and Sprout, who knows every part by accident.

  • When I meet someone I would trust with all of them, I shall know. I have not yet. Do not look so hopeful; it takes rather more than a pleasant face.

  • A woodsman. My father's trade. For thirty years I walked the deep forest ahead of the crews and marked what they'd cut.
  • Now I mark at the edge, and I watch. Haldor says I'm still the best he has. Haldor's kind.
  • See the twist of rowan over my door? My father laughed at it. I hang a fresh one every spring.
  • Hang one over your own door, Player. It costs nothing, and you've nothing to lose by it. That's the whole of my wisdom.
  • Never whistle under the big trees. Never sleep with your back to the deep wood. Be out of the forest before the sun is. Knock twice on a stump before you sit. The young ones call it old men's nonsense, and I'm still here.
  • I'll not go in, and I'll not talk about it. Don't ask me what's in there. People have.
  • What I will say is this. Merrin looks at the tall trees out there the way I used to look at them. I'd like her not to.
  • The black marks are up, all along the edge, and Haldor walked the crews along them, Merrin first. Whatever is in there, it's past the marks. Let it stay past them.
  • Go on. And be home before dark.

  • Patch. I keep the herb house by the gate, which means I see the road's damage first. Mind your head on the bundles. Everybody hits that one.
  • You again. The one who can tell yarrow from hemlock. Come in. Do not touch the jars.
  • The lamp-hangers come in bitten and go out clean now, thanks to your peppery weed. They still look at me like I am the dangerous one. I am.
  • I have silent root drying in the rafters for the first time in four years. Every time I walk under it I think of the birds. Sit. Have a sweet. You earned three.
  • Well? I have patients.
    • Choice: What herbs do you need?
    • Choice: What is in Dagny's drink?
    • Choice: Who comes through your door?
    • Choice: Nothing. Goodbye.
  • My mother sold herbs. Every summer morning she took me out past the gate and made me learn them: yarrow from hemlock, feverfew from chamomile, which roots in spring and which in autumn. Forty years I gathered my own.
  • Now my knees are slow, the fields are risky, and Brindle has told me to stop going out alone, first politely and then not. The carts bring less. And the herbs I need most grow where nobody sensible walks any more.
  • Willow bark, mostly. And something else. No, I will not tell you. If I told Dagny she would stop believing in it, and then it would stop working. She walks me home after, with both lamps. Unnecessary. Do not tell her I like it.
  • It used to be carters with barrels dropped on their feet and peddlers with blisters. Now it is bites, gashes, claw marks. In the middle of the night. Carried. More every season.
  • Ivo on the square sees them after me; we send them back and forth. I scold, he soothes, and between us we cover most kinds of person. What I am afraid of is the one I cannot help, and the morning after, when the jar I needed was empty.
  • Go on. And if you get bitten, walk here. Do not run.

Dialogue
  • Some of the dusk routes fly again, Player. Not all. On a few roads east the birds still turn back at dusk, and I still write them down. But the list is shorter than it was. I never thought I would see it shrink.
  • The routes over the Highbeacon are open. Greyfeather's daughter flew one at noon yesterday, and again at dusk. I watched her the whole way.
  • Stormcrest sleeps at noon on the Highbeacon. Whenever you are ready, I will tell you the wind.
  • My list, Player. You are on it now, in a way. In the margin, beside the route you walked.
  • The loft is quiet just now. Sit, if you like. What would you like to know?
    • Choice: Tell me about the pigeons.
    • Choice: Which routes do the birds refuse?
    • Choice: Why is there a cat in a pigeon loft?

    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • The birds carry messages to the other towns; the runners carry them inside the city. I learned the loft from Isolde Spurr, who kept it before me, and I have kept it since I was twenty. Fifty-one years on the Crooked Tower.
  • I understand birds better than people. I admit it freely. Birds never ask me what I meant.
  • It began a few years ago with old Greyfeather, who would not take the road east at dusk. Then others would not. Some routes are refused only at dusk. A few at any hour. I keep a careful list.
  • The all-hours routes fly again, since Stormcrest. The dusk ones are different. Some have opened, some have not, and the birds will not tell me why. I keep the list as carefully as ever.
  • Starling brings up the flicker dates and we lay them side by side. Some match. Some do not. Neither of us knows what that means. We drink the tea anyway.
  • Pounce arrived one wet autumn, years ago, and decided the loft was his. The pigeons have accepted him with deep reluctance. He sleeps beside the little iron cat Ferro made for us last Walkout Day. I think he believes it is his sister.
  • The wind is from the west today; it will push you toward the tower's edge, so keep your back to the beacon cup. Go at noon, Player, while it sleeps. And come back.
  • Mind the stair on the way down. The birds will see you off.

  • Farewell! Did you see the cloak? I did not mean to swirl it. It simply happens.

  • Something you want? I warn you, I am quick with a comeback and slow with everything else.

  • She lived to eighty-eight and never once introduced me as a Marrow. Everybody else does. I miss her.
  • Everybody expects me to write one as good as Juna's. So I have written three and burned two, which is a very Marrow thing to do, apparently. Dina has been my teacher since I was small. She has never asked to read them. That is how I know she wants to.
  • Nix is making a new Juna mask for the play, and the old pictures of Juna all disagree, so Nix asked me to sit for it. Rue will wear my face on Walkout Day. That is not strange at all.
  • Off you go. Do not look at the notebook on your way out.

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Forty Lights (gives)

Dialogue
  • I am Prism! I paint pictures with lights, here at the gate, for whoever comes up the road. Did you see the cart? The little lit one, with people waving? That was the Walkers. I learned it from Nana Gristle. She says I got the basket wrong.
  • Lux promised! I still cannot believe it. I practise every night now. Fifty-three, last night, for nearly three breaths. Then I sat down very suddenly.
  • The frame is half woven! Every reed holds a light that does not tire. Two hundred, almost. Lux comes down from the towers to watch and does not say anything, which means it is good.
  • Ask me something! Or I will ask you something. I have so many.
    • Choice: What do you paint?
    • Choice: What is the Walkout Day show?
    • Choice: Where are you from?
    • Choice: Nothing. Goodbye.
  • The city's own stories! The Walkers' cart. The line of people with bundles. The first lanterns going up between the towers. Herons, because I like herons. I asked everyone in Urbanograd to tell me their stories. It has taken a year and I am not finished.
  • I only paint inside the walls, never toward the road. The Watch were worried lights in the dusk could be mistaken for other things. They were right to worry. Tick salutes my herons, though.
  • After the play, when the square is full, the whole Long Walk across the sky above Lantern Square, in light! Hundreds of lights. I have done forty. Once. I am a little frightened of standing in front of everybody and making three small sparks.
  • It is going to work. I think. The frame holds the lights, Lux dims the lanterns, and I only have to remember to breathe. On Walkout Day, stand in the middle of the square and look up!
  • Fairy Forest! My family weave baskets there. My gift is small: only little lights, a few breaths each. The Grove School taught me all the things it cannot do. No great workings, nothing a scholar would want.
  • But I wanted to make pictures with it, just because they are lovely, and I heard of a city where nobody needs a reason. So I walked out with the glass-carters two springs ago. The letters from home are mostly cheerful. Mostly.
  • Goodbye! Look up at the gate tonight. I will paint you something.

  • Player. Come in; the queen's door is open to anyone who climbs these steps. What is on your mind?
    • Choice: Who are you, Your Majesty?

    • Choice: Nothing, Your Majesty.
  • Aveline, crowned under the Great Bell sixteen years ago. The Bell has not rung since, and I am in no hurry to hear it again.
  • My husband Leofric keeps the map of the roads, my son Alaric keeps beetles, and my daughter Elinor keeps me guessing. I keep all three.
  • The crown's task is to keep the kingdom together, not to command it. I will not tell Midbarium how to choose its chieftains, or Bain Harbour how to run its docks.
  • I settle quarrels, keep the royal roads open and answer every letter: every message from our friends at Cavelor, and every argument from Urbanograd. Those I enjoy.
  • The roads. Every week the patrols meet more monsters, and every week the red marks on my husband's map creep nearer the towns.
  • The towns will never turn on one another; I know that. I fear the danger growing faster than our patience. If you walk the roads, Player, tell Edric what you see.
  • Go well, Player. The kingdom is the people in it, and that includes you.

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Reading Slowly (gives)

Dialogue
  • Ah, a visitor! Come in, come in. Ask me about anything you like: the weather, the bread, Bastian's bridge, my knees. All very funny. Ask me about the Charter and I shall put on my serious face, which I keep for the purpose.
  • The cart moves on the silence. I think of it every morning now. I have been practising my pauses. Dina will be furious. I am delighted.
  • Peace and laws, Player. I said it to the Table and the Table listened, which it does about once a decade. A door nobody watched is now a door somebody keeps. That is the Charter working, in a very small and dusty way.
  • Smell that? Moss-bark. The case smells like a forest after rain now, and the scroll sleeps dry. I check it every morning anyway. Old habits are the only kind I have.
  • What shall we talk about?
    • Choice: What is the Open Charter?
    • Choice: Tell me about Walkout Day.
    • Choice: How long have you known Ozzie?
    • Choice: Who will keep the scroll after you?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • When the Walkers came here, some in Selsior wanted them sent home. The question went to the royal court. And the court said the founding treaty's promise protects not only the four peoples who signed it, but any people who choose to live differently, so long as they keep the kingdom's peace and laws.
  • That is the Open Charter. The kingdom could have sent us home, and it chose to welcome us. Every young hothead who stands up at the Table and says Urbanograd answers to nobody: I remind them gently. We answer to a promise. It is a good one.
  • Our rebellion has always been about how we live, never about tearing down the realm that let us. There. Serious face off. Would you like a biscuit?
  • Every Walkout Day morning I carry the scroll out to the square and read the whole Charter aloud, beginning to end. The square is noisy right up until I start. Then it is silent. Then the play.
  • Dina says I read too slowly. I do. On purpose. A ruling that let a whole city exist deserves to be heard at the speed of a person thinking about it.
  • Since we were boys stealing apples on the same rooftops. He says I was the worse thief. I was the better thief: I was never caught. He was caught every time, because he stopped to tell the owner a story about apples.
  • Supper most weeks, still. I am the only person in the city who can find his spectacles. They are always on his head. I have never told him how I do it.
  • Ah. You found the one question I do not joke about either. Mercy Oakes chose me because I handled paper as though it might bruise. Twenty-six years. I am seventy-seven.
  • I have not found the next one yet. When I do, I shall know them by their hands. Until then the scroll has me, and I have the scroll, and we are both doing very well, thank you.
  • Off you go. Keep the peace. Keep the laws. Live however you like.

  • Eighty bouts, the spring I was nineteen, one every evening after drill, against an Uskari of Midbarium named Tavi. Forty-one to Tavi, thirty-nine to me.
  • No one ever pushed me harder. Three years ago we tried one more bout in this yard, and the drill bell rang before either of us won. It is still unfinished.
  • Not yet, Player. Courage you have; the arm needs time. Come back at level 30, and we shall see whether you are ready for the Guard's trial.

  • Level one hundred and twenty, Player. Speak to me again and I will set you the Grand Swordmaster's trial, the one I passed myself.

  • Level one hundred and sixty, Player. Speak to me again and I will set you the old test, the Sword Saint's. I tell you honestly: it is older than I am.

  • Ropes, a hand-winch, a platform and a counterweight of old fortress stones, all bolted to the old granary at the end of the Row. Built it three years ago. I was nineteen. Everyone said it wouldn't hold.
  • My mother hauled crates up the rooftop stairs for twenty years till her back gave out. Hedda. Porters work the winch now and nobody's back gives out. That's why it's there. Not to sparkle.
  • Near the Old Barracks, over the public stair. Theatre folk haul scenery up to the roofs every Walkout Day by hand. But it's a public stair, so the Table has to agree. I've stood up twice. Bastian's covered bridge talked over me both times. Loud man. Nice man. Loud.
  • Margo builds things that go bang and might work. I build things that work and don't go bang. We argue every day. She's wrong about springs.
  • Last winter a crate of Tinsel's glass jammed halfway up and Margo climbed the ropes with a spanner in her teeth. I rehung her door the last time she blew it off. That's how it goes. Don't tell her I said any of that.
  • Mind the rope. It's working.

docs.title: Rook
docs.text:
Caller of the Open Table

Town Urbanograd Where The Great Hall Story Rook in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "I make candles. Whatever anyone tells you, I make candles."
  • "The back benches have something to say. They always do."
  • "Bastian, sit down. No, the other kind of sitting down."
  • "A Caller rules nobody. Some days I wish I could rule the stew queue."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• A Way In (completes)
  • Letters to the Queen (gives)
  • The Quiet Ones (gives)
  • The Table Argues (gives)
  • Dates and Lists (completes)
Dialogue
  • Evening, Player. If you have come to ask the leader of Urbanograd for something, I am afraid there is no such person. There is a chandler who chairs the arguments. Will that do?
  • Player, the letter-carrier! The queen answered, you know. Four pages. She says I am wrong about the guilds and right about the patrols, and she wants the recipe for Mags's stew. I will not be sending it; Mags would never forgive either of us.
  • Listen to that. Bastian has been on his feet for an hour and has so far argued both sides of the door twice. Go and hear him, then Quint, and then come and find me. I will be here. I am always here on Table nights.
  • The Table agreed in a single night. I am still not over it. Dimity has checked the shelves, and she says it is the fastest yes in forty years. Now we wait on Hex and a very old lock.
  • The iron door is open and Leland stands by it like he was born there. Keeper of the Low Door: the Table chose him before I had finished saying his name. Second fast decision this year. People will start to talk.
  • Leland's chalk map is pinned up beside my chair now, all four levels of it. I read his tallies out at the Table: who went down, what they put back down. Your name comes up a lot, Player. Bastian has started cheering it.
  • Perch sent a pigeon to say you would be bringing me something from the Rooftops. Starling's dates and Perch's list, both? Good. I want them in my hand before I write a word to the capital.
  • The dates and the list went east with my last letter, every line of them. No answer yet. The queen answers everything, eventually, usually with an argument. This time I am hoping for an answer instead.
  • What can a candle-maker do for you?
    • Choice: What does a Caller do?
    • Choice: Tell me about the Open Table.
    • Choice: You write to the queen?
    • Choice: What worries the Table these days?
    • Choice: What became of the door under the hall?
    • Choice: What will the queen make of Starling's dates?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Convene the Table. Keep order, which mostly means keeping Bastian to under an hour. And make sure the quiet ones get a turn, because the loud ones will take every turn there is if nobody stops them.
  • It does not mean ruling anybody. People ask me to rule on things every day, and every day I say no and hand them a candle. This is my first year as Caller and I have said loudly that it will be my last. Nobody believes me.
  • Anyone who lives in Urbanograd may stand up at the Open Table and speak. Anyone. A hundred years of it: lamp-oil taxes, roof repairs, whether a goat may attend. The goat may, by the way. Carried.
  • It is loud and slow and it runs till dawn, and Mags feeds everybody, and Dimity writes it all down, jokes included. I sat under those benches as a child and thought it was better than any play. I still do.
  • Every fortnight for nine years. I wrote her an angry letter once, about the Guard's patrols stopping short of our road. I expected nothing. She wrote back herself, three pages, agreeing with half and arguing with the rest. The patrols were extended the next year.
  • We argue about everything now: guilds, theatre, whether a kingdom needs a crown. She concedes a point the moment it is fairly made, which nobody at the Table has ever done except Bastian, and he does it by accident.
  • Fewer food carts every season. Brindle asking for volunteers because the monsters come closer to the walls than they used to. Moth counting the names in the hat. Mags's pot fed from rooftop tubs.
  • And the Table was built to be slow. Slow is good for most things. I am afraid of the day something will not wait for us to finish arguing.
  • Still shut. The Table said yes; the lock has not yet heard. Hex is the one to talk to, on Workshops Row. Bring patience. Bring a riddle, if you have one; Hex likes to trade.
  • Open, and Leland keeps it, with a rope and a lamp and a map in chalk on the kitchen wall. If you want to go down, ask him. If you come back up with stories, tell me. I will read them at the Table.
  • Honestly? I do not know. Starling's flickers, Perch's refused routes, some dates matching and some not. I laid them side by side on my table for a whole night and could make nothing of them that I would put my name to.
  • So I sent them as they are, with no theory attached. The queen has better eyes and more of them. Some of the dusk routes are open again, Perch tells me. Not all of them. I am grateful for some.
  • Mind the stew queue on the way out. And come to the Table some night. Sit at the back. I will make sure you get a turn.

  • A line and a half as a maid with a letter. I made them applaud the letter. She has never forgiven me, and she has given me the best parts in the house ever since.
  • My husband is Crispin. He never finishes a sentence unless I wait for it. I read every draft he writes aloud, in every voice.

  • Exit gracefully, darling. Like this. See?
  • None. Whoever wrote it wanted a quarrel, and got a truce instead. Percival loops his y's, you know. I had never noticed.

docs.text:
Captain of the Cliff Watch

docs.title: Says

  • "Lanterns up before dark. Always."

docs.text:

Dialogue
  • Player. The hollow is empty. Climbers still come. Fewer, and slower about it. I will take that.
  • Player. Iska has all of it now. Should have put it in front of her sooner.
  • Player. Lanterns on the high landings. Still dark between them. Better than it was.
  • Player. Stand a minute, if you like. Not long. Dark comes early on the cliff.
  • Cliff Watch. What do you need?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Tell me about the watch.
    • Choice: Anything troubling you?
    • Choice: Nothing. Keep safe.
  • Ruan. Captain of the Cliff Watch, ten years. Grew up above the Long Stair. Joined at eighteen, when the watch was old men and boys.
  • Now it is a dozen guards and not enough nights. That is the job.
  • You asked before. Here is the rest. Three winters back the first one came up the face, not down the paths. Moira rang the bar. Torva and two of hers drove it over the edge.
  • I held the lantern while Elspeth stitched Torva's jaw. Have not told that to many. You have steady hands. Keep them.
  • We stand the high landings, where the forest paths reach the top. Walk the stairs at night with lanterns. Ring the iron bar at the head of the Long Stair when something comes.
  • Same work. The high landings, the stairs at night, the bar at the head of the Long Stair. Difference is Gunna's lanterns on the landings now. They burn steady in any wind.
  • I test every rope on the cliffs once a month. Hang my whole weight off it. Kestra's I test twice. She hates that. Rope still holds.
  • The roads in from Gorse Downs and the Saltwood are quieter since you walked them. Less coming down to the stairs from that side. Good. One side fewer.
  • They come up the face now. At night. Always where it is darkest. I want a lantern on every high landing. Gunna says a good lantern cannot be hurried.
  • Tarran says brighter, sooner. I have not said no. Things coming down from the forest I understand. Things coming up from the sea are something else.
  • Lanterns help. The climbers find the stretches between them. Moira saw that first. Or she thinks she did.
  • People have brought me things they told no one else. I want to be sure before it goes to Iska. I am afraid sure will come too late.
  • Iska listened. Did not waste a word. Neither did I, for once. My reports are still short. She still has not asked for longer.
  • Mind the stairs after dark.

  • Sit on the fiddler's other knee if you like, Ferro won't mind. Don't ask for anything slow. I don't do slow.
  • Player! The Outer Wall's finished. Number ten! I played it last night and two lanterns blew out. I'm choosing to take that as a compliment.

docs.title: Sennu
docs.text:
Chieftain of the Tolmach

Town Midbarium Where Midbarium Story Sennu in the lore Services Quests

Two hundred and twelve. Twice. Good. Hello, Player.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "The near pastures are grazed to the root."
  • "Count the heads twice. Always twice."
  • "Grass decides where the Tolmach go. Not pride."
  • "Ennek's whistling again. Must be a good day."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Tell Your Mother (completes)
  • The High Pasture (gives)
  • A Safe Pasture (gives)
  • The Herds Go Out (gives)
  • A Word for Tavi (gives)
Dialogue
  • Two hundred and twelve. Two hundred and twelve. Forgive me, Player, I count heads twice. The herds are closer to town this year than they have ever been, and the near pastures are grazed to the root.
  • Tavi got my word, then, and sent one back. Good. Neither of us will be the first to walk to the other's fire, but the trails are shared whether we like it or not.
  • My mother on a high pasture again, after five years. She scolded the grass for being short and the wind for being cold. I have not seen her so happy since my father was alive.
  • The herds went out past the Boar Runs side and came home with every head counted. Twice. Thank you.
  • The Greywater. It ran through the driest year my mother can remember, and now it is dust. Ennek carried that alone for a summer. I always feared this day. I did not think it would come so quietly.
  • It runs again, thin as a thread, but it runs. My mother walked all the way to the cleft to see it, knees or no knees. Some days a chieftain only has to stand back and watch.
  • Say what you need. I'm listening, and counting.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: What about the Uskari chieftain?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Sennu, chieftain of the Tolmach these thirteen years, since old Bekku died. I lead from a hide tent like any herder, and I move the camps when the grass says so. Mabbu is my mother, Harra my sister, Ennek my son.
  • Tavi and I share the trails and not much else. Tavi wants the herds kept close; I need them on the high pastures. Neither of us will walk to the other's fire first. That is pride, and I know it, and I still won't.
  • Tavi walks the worst stretch personally, I will say that. If the high pasture is safe, Tavi's people and you made it so. I may even say it to Tavi's face. At the next gathering. Possibly.
  • Count your steps on the ledges, Player.

Dialogue
  • Shade. I bring travelers in over the last stretch of road. Never lost one. Don't plan to start.
  • She asked who sent you. Said you were just passing. Good.
  • Brought a salt caravan in by the high side last week. All of them. Your route.
  • Walked the old hill path yesterday. No big tracks. Boar running from me instead of at me. I might take people that way again. Might.
  • Well?
    • Choice: Which roads are still safe?
    • Choice: Who taught you?
    • Choice: Where did you grow up?
    • Choice: Nothing. Goodbye.
  • Fewer than there were. A ford where something waits at dusk. A cutting in the woods where the birds went quiet. A hill path with tracks the size of a cartwheel. Hatch walked all three before me. I'm looking for new ones. Longer. Stranger.
  • The hill path's coming back. The ford, still no good at dusk. The cutting, still quiet. One out of three. Better than none.
  • Hatch. Four seasons, spring to winter, when I was twenty. Tracks, weather, sleeping light. How to tell a hungry animal from something worse.
  • He says I'm the best he ever taught. He talks too much after the second cup. I come by every few days to listen to him do it.
  • Rooftops. My parents played music in the streets. They died within a year of each other, when I was twelve. The roof folk fed me after. They still feed strays.
  • By sixteen I could cross the city without touching a street. Useful. The knives are Ferro's. They have names. I won't tell you them.
  • Keep to the high side.

  • Simkin, cobbler of this lane for fifty years. My wife Winifred tells the stories on the step. I mend the shoes and correct her.

  • Captain Skarra, trail watch. If you're walking the trails, you're walking them on my watch, so walk them properly. Patrols leave at first light.
  • Windworn Hill and the Long Ridge, both checked. I put a fresh date by each dot. The marks are closer than last season. They always are.
  • You measured them yourself. Wide as a cooking pot and as deep as my wrist. I'll say it once and not again: those tracks frighten me.
  • Out of arrows, cornered by hogs, and not a scratch on him. I could have wrung his neck. I held him so long instead that he complained. Thank you, Player.
  • A Trail Watch post at the Old War Camp, in the middle of the Reach. If you'd told me a year ago we'd keep a fire lit out there, I'd have laughed. Dryly.

  • I mark every sighting on a hide map in my tent: a red dot and a date. You don't need to see it. Nobody does, except Tavi.
  • Tavi said to show you, so you've seen it. Dots on the high pastures, on the south path, at the far end of the bridge, on the canyon stretch below the rim. Every season they creep closer to town.
  • My son is the fastest climber on the rim, and he knows it. He wants to track whatever raids the high pastures. Not alone. His father tracked a great horned beast alone, thirteen years ago, and did not come home.
  • He came home. He'll go out again, I know that. But he'll go with someone at his back now, and he knows why.
  • Eyes open. Back before dark.

docs.text:

  • The Children (gives)
Dialogue
  • There's my child-minder! Sit, sit. Eilidh's been civil to me for three whole days. I don't know what you said to her.
  • Player! Brodie's smoking my catch for nothing all summer. Now I've nothing to shout at him about. It's been very hard.
  • Ah, my boar-hunter. The shingle's been quiet since. Quiet enough to gut on, anyway.
  • Well? Out with it. The tide won't wait, and neither will I.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: How is the fishing?
    • Choice: Tell me about your father.
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Sorcha. Agna's girl, Calder's wife, mother of two little terrors. That's the Sea Thrift on the shingle there, my father's boat. More patches than planks, my mother says, and she patched most of them.
  • Calder and I bring in the best catch in the coves. I find the fish, he mends whatever broke finding them. It works. Don't ask me how.
  • Rougher than it was. The weather past the point turns on you in an hour now, and it never used to. My mother's had nets back torn to rags.
  • So I go out past the point alone, or with Calder. The children stay inshore. Eilidh hates me for it. She'll live.
  • Still rough past the point. But I can beach the Thrift on the Strandwood shingle again and gut there while the tide turns, and that's thanks to you. The children still stay inshore.
  • Eilidh's been keeping a tide slate. Of course she has. My mother looked at it and went quiet, and my mother is never quiet. I keep the children inshore, and I'll keep them there.
  • Donal. Big slow man, hands like oars. He put me in the Thrift before I could swim and told me the sea would teach me the rest. It did.
  • He'd have liked you. He liked anyone who did a job without being asked twice.
  • Off you go. And if you see a small boy up to his knees in a tide pool, send him home!

  • My mum was Lark. She sang in the chorus. I do not remember her, but I know her songs. On her day, me and Dad go up on the Rooftops and watch the lanterns come on and sing one. Dad forgets the middle bits. I do not.
  • AHEM. I am a GRANDEE of SELSIOR and I BAN... fun! And... music! And... cheese! HUZZAH for JUNA! Oh no, I am falling off the cart! ...That was the fall. I land on Hambone's sacks, usually.

docs.title: Starling

Rooftop Stargazer

Town Urbanograd Where Urbanograd Story Starling in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• A Flicker Night (gives)
  • Dates and Lists (gives)
  • The Lower Beacon (gives)
  • The Walker Stars (gives)
  • The Newest Lens (completes)
Dialogue
  • The dates went to Rook, and Rook's letter has gone to the Queen. I keep looking east anyway. Some nights it still flickers, and I still do not know why. I am getting very good at not knowing.
  • Far beyond the downs, further east than they reach. That is what you saw from the Beacon Line, and it is in the margin now, in very small letters.
  • You saw one, Player. A real flicker, from my roof. Now there are two of us who have seen it and do not know what it is. Three, with Perch. It is becoming a club.
  • The Lost Bow is inked in. Every night I find it first, before the Fiddle. It would feel rude not to.
  • Mind the telescope. It is very old and held together with hope. What can I tell you?
    • Choice: What are you mapping?
    • Choice: Tell me about the telescope.
    • Choice: What is the flicker?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Every star over Urbanograd, one day. A whole chart. My parents left me an old one from the city's first years, with the Walkers' names: the Cart, the Fiddle, the Open Door.
  • I use the old names. The Walkers patched these roofs and then lay on them looking up. It seems only fair to call the stars what they did.
  • A long brass tube, three eyepieces, and a finder made from the bottom of a bottle. Every lens is one of Tinsel's spares, the ones with a bubble or a ripple. Flawed glass, perfect sky.
  • I do not know. That is the honest answer. Some nights, toward the middle of the island, the horizon wavers for a few breaths, like the air over a stove. Then it stops. Never on a schedule I can find, and never from below the Rooftops.

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:

Dialogue
  • Ha! Player! Come, stand by the great drum. Mind the patch. She mutters now, ever since the hide split at the first feast this spring.
  • Vosk says the stand is sound, bless him. The drum is not. A hide from a great horned beast of the plateau, that is what she needs, and no hunter alive should be asked to go and get one.
  • Did you hear her? The first beat on the new hide rolled down every terrace and out over the canyons! I wept, Player. I am not ashamed of it.
  • I drummed the four families in, and they came, every one. Ahvi sang, Hask spoke, and you told the truth. Finest night of drumming since the choosing. Maybe finer. Don't tell Hask.
  • What can an old drummer do for you?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Tell me about the great drum.
    • Choice: What are the gatherings like?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Thrun, drummer of the gatherings, forty-five years at it. Husband of Odda, father of Lessa, grandfather to the most serious girl in the highlands. I laugh from the belly and I drum the same way.
  • Kragvar timber, bound with rope, taller than a man. The hide was taken in my grandfather's day from a great horned plateau beast. Few are seen now, and those that are have gone wild. So I patch, and she mutters.
  • The new hide came off the Ash Mesa. Vosk and I fitted it together, two old men arguing over every lashing. She speaks clean now, and deeper than the old one, I think.
  • Every choosing, every feast, the drum calls the families and they come. Food, contests, stories, and drumming till the stars go pale. I drummed the whole night Hask was chosen, and I will fight anyone who says it wasn't the best.
  • Off you go! And if you hear a drum, come running.

docs.text:

Dialogue
  • I am Tick! Gate messenger. I run messages from the gate to everywhere else, by stairs and alleys. Da is Knox, the big one on the gate. I am going to be an adventurer. Da says I am going to be a joiner. We will see.
  • I read your check out to Hatch. "Water ran the right way. Octopi plenty, and cross." He said that is the most honest line in the whole notebook. I nearly fell over.
  • Kite is in capitals on the list now. Underlined. I ran the alley route twice this morning. Still slower. Still going to do it.
  • A buried city! Under our feet! Because of page fifty-two! I have started a new volume just for Low Grad. It is called Volume Four: Underneath.
  • Brindle read page fifty-two and went very still, and then took it to the Table! And Brindle saluted me. Properly. I am never washing this hand. That is not how saluting works, but still.
  • Version four is my favourite page in all the books. Da asked me to read it to him twice. He went very quiet after. Good quiet, I think.
  • Do you want to hear something from the notebook? Or ask me something? I know everything at this gate.
    • Choice: What is in your notebook?
    • Choice: Kite's record?
    • Choice: Why Hatch?
    • Choice: Nothing. Goodbye.
  • Every strange story a traveler tells me, with their name and the date. A talking crow on the road from Kaldemor. A ford that ran backwards for an evening. A stag with antlers like a burnt tree. Lights moving in a wood where nobody lives.
  • I do not judge them. Some are nonsense. Some are not, and those are coming more often. Zip's arm is in there three times. Three versions. All told by Zip.
  • And page fifty-two, the wanderer and the warm stone. Velvet still has it at her stall. She will not say what she thinks it is. I asked. She told me a different story instead. I wrote that one down too.
  • Kite holds the record from the Gate Walk to the Great Hall, over the roofs. I am going to beat it by the streets. Everybody says it is impossible. I write their names down so I know who to tell. The list is long. It is good motivation.
  • Thirty years on the roads! He can smell rain a day early. He can tell a hungry animal from something worse. He pretends I annoy him, and then he answers every single question.
  • One day I want to walk out of that gate with his blessing. Da does not like it. I am winning the argument at supper. I do not know why winning makes Da look so tired.
  • Salute! Bye! Running!

    • Choice: You know the roads well?
    • Choice: Ever had trouble out there?

  • Drive a road once with your eyes open and you never need ask the way again. The Royal Road to Kaldemor? Every bend, every ford, and the puddle that never dries.
  • Last autumn, past the Greenwood at dusk, Thistle stopped dead. Ears flat. Something big went through the trees beside us and never once showed itself.
  • Then he walked on like nothing happened. I don't drive that stretch at dusk any more. I tell passengers Thistle likes his supper. He does, too.
  • Mind the road!

Dialogue
  • Come to see a woman swallow the sun, have you? Show's at dusk. (Off-stage, quietly:) Sorry. Hello. Have you seen my bucket? Oh. There it is. Good.
  • Player! The new oil burns like a dream. Clean flame, no black smoke, no cough. Ivo says my throat thanks you. I say the crowd does.
  • (Tinder glances at the water bucket. It is full. Tinder checks it anyway, once, then stops, and smiles a little.) Hello, Player.
  • Player! The whole square, end to end, and not one burnt finger! Ivo got the first coins, Jinx kept the crowd back, and I didn't move my pitch once all night.
  • What'll it be, friend?
    • Choice: Where did you learn to eat fire?
    • Choice: Why the bucket?
    • Choice: Why do you move when the storytellers start?
    • Choice: Nothing. Good luck tonight.
  • Brightwater's travelling show. Painted wagons, acrobats, and a dancing goat called Duchess who hated everyone. My parents tumbled in it. I was born in a wagon somewhere between two towns.
  • Cassius, the show's fire-eater, taught me from eleven. He died the winter before the show reached Urbanograd. When the wagons left, I stayed. Nobody here told me to stop. The show never came back.
  • Cassius's rule. Check the bucket three times. Once for the fire, once for the crowd, once for yourself. On stage I'm all swagger. Off stage I'm a coward with a bucket. Both are true. The bucket's why I still have eyebrows.
  • The old stories of the Burning? Bad luck. Cassius said it's bad luck to play with fire while the fire is listening. When someone starts telling those, I pick up my torches and move to the other end of the square. Laugh if you like. I still have all my fingers.
  • Stand well back at dusk, friend. Well back.

Dialogue
  • Come in, come in, mind the pipe. It is hotter than it looks. Most things here are.
  • Player. Lux says the outer walls are glowing again. I went out to the Gate Walk last night to see. Amber, mostly. It was the right fog for it.
  • Starling sent down a note: the new lens is perfect, and the sky is enormous. Both of those were true before, but it is nice to hear.
  • Player. The little dark chip on my sill is still warm. Every morning I put my hand on it before the furnace is lit. Every morning, warm.
  • The furnace is drawing nicely. What did you want to look at?
    • Choice: How do you make the lantern colours?
    • Choice: What are those on the windowsill?
    • Choice: Is glass getting harder to make?
    • Choice: Nothing. I will let you work.
  • A pinch of this and that in the melt. Gold dust for rose, if you can believe it, though only a whisper. Copper for sea-green. The amber is iron and patience. Old Ignatius Fenn taught me at this furnace when I was small enough to sit on the sand bin.
  • Lux says amber carries furthest in fog. I say it depends on the fog. We have been saying it for years. Neither of us wants to win.
  • My failures. I am trying to make a glass that glows on its own, with no flame behind it. Powdered shells, rare sands, river stones, a powder from the apothecary, once some of Margo's spark-powder. That last one was loud.
  • None of them glow. They make very pretty paperweights, though. Hold one up to the window. There. You see why I keep trying.
  • Paperweights, all failures, all pretty. And at the end, the chip you brought up from under the city. It does not glow. It does not cool, either. I do not know what to make of that, so I have made nothing of it yet.
  • Good sand comes from outside the walls, on carts, and fewer carts come. So I melt down broken glass now. Old bottles, cracked panes, a whole crate that once got stuck halfway up Rivet's lift last winter.
  • It works. It is a little cloudy. I do not like it. But a cloudy lantern is better than a dark one, Lux says, and Lux is usually right about lanterns.
  • Go on. Look up at the lanterns on your way. Some of that light is mine.

  • Ah, Player! Lia told you about the clock tower, did she? Old Ewan has been fretting about it for days.
  • Welcome to Kaldemor, the greenest town this side of the old forest. What can I do for you?
    • Choice: Tell me about Kaldemor.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Guess how many people live here.
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • Kaldemor grew up around the great treehouse behind me. The mushroom houses came later - the soil here grows them big enough to live in!
  • West of the square is the Park, with the clock tower and the old windmill farm. East is the Market: potions, weapons, bread, all of it.
  • Walk through the glowing portals with the up arrow to go between them.
  • I'm Tobin, mayor of this town for thirty years now. Would you like to hear how Kaldemor began?
  • Long ago a traveller planted a single seed in this meadow and slept under it for a night. In the morning it was a tree taller than a tower.
  • People came to see it, and some never left. That traveller's name is lost, but we still say: every great town starts with one seed.
  • Another time, then. Old men always have time for stories.
  • A guess, is it? Go on: how many people live in Kaldemor, would you say?
  • N, you say? Not bad, Player! There are just under three hundred of us - not counting the snails.
  • Take care out there, Player. Come back any time!

Dialogue
  • Player. You did the board's work along the crews' edge. The cutters noticed. So did I.
  • Player. Caddoc told me what you saw by his cage. He's not slept since. Neither have I, much.
  • Player. A cub in the cage and the old one somewhere under the roots. Kenna wants to go now. We go when I say.
  • Player. Caddoc says his traps work now. He's furious about it. That's him happy.
  • Player. I've stopped touching the scar when I think nobody's looking. Mostly.

    • Choice: What's coming out of the forest?
    • Choice: Your scar.
    • Choice: Take me to Brushtail's Earth.

  • Nobody chose me to lead. The others just started waiting for me before they went out, and after a while it was true.

  • A creature. It climbed. Elspeth stitched it. That's the story, whatever they tell you at the Gap Inn.
  • You want to know what frightens me? Not the thing that did this.
  • Elspeth. She scolds me every time she stitches me, then she tucks me in, and I do exactly what she says. Don't tell her I said so. She'd be unbearable.

  • Under the fallen pine. Stay where I can see you, and watch the dust.
  • Behind the Wrack Ledges. I know the way in the dark. I have done it in the dark.

Dialogue
  • Torvi Brask. From the high slopes, from the goats. Came down to see the city for a week, six years ago. Ha! The music was good. Still is.
  • You! The one who cleared the boardwalks. Did you eat the cheese? Outside? Good. In the highlands we would call you cousin for that.
  • Five hand-spans. I dream about those tracks. In the dream I am on the right side of the stream for once.
  • HA! There is the one who went down into the Wallow! I would hug you, but you would not survive it. City ribs.
  • She stood at the wall all afternoon and did not go. Ha. I have never been so proud of someone for doing nothing.

    • Choice: How is Zip doing?
    • Choice: How are the roads?

  • The Brask homestead. A stone shelter and goat pens on the far slopes, a long walk from anywhere. My grandmother Hulda put this axe in my hands. She split wood with it, cleared scrub, and once drove off a hill cat while holding a full pail of milk. Did not spill a drop. Ha!
  • In the highlands, anyone who comes to your fire in peace gets water, food and a bed. Here, I learned, you do not invite strangers in off the street, you queue for skewers, and you do not settle arguments by wrestling. Strange people. Good music.
  • Fast. She learns everything fast. Footwork in a month, guard in two. Everything except running. That one she fights like it owes her money. One day she will stand when she should run, and I will be too far away. I think about that.
  • She is learning the second day now. Walk away, come back when it is yours. It is the hardest thing I know, and she is learning it. Do not tell her I said she is good. She will dare me to something.
  • I guard caravans to Kaldemor, Selsior, the harbours. I charge fair and I never promise a safe road when there is not one. Fewer traders every year. A city that cannot trade stops dancing first. I came here for the dancing.
  • Ha! Go well. Come to the square tonight; Drum is playing.

  • Did. My father hunted them from a narrow boat called the Patience, and I did after him, alone, from eighteen until the deep water changed.
  • She lies on the beach below the Waterfront now, under a sailcloth. I stand at the Heron's bow instead.
  • Twice.
  • I missed once.
  • Mm.

docs.title: Tully
docs.text:
Dockworker

Town Bain Harbour Where The Docks Story Tully in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Everything looks smaller after lunch."
  • "Tea chest, iron, leaky barrel. I get all the good ones."
  • "Someday. My own boat. Someday."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Hooks for Merriwether (gives)
  • Pelts for the Tanner (gives)
  • The Boat Under the Sailcloth (gives)
Dialogue
  • Need something carried? I carry things.
    • Choice: Do you like the work?
    • Choice: What would you do with a boat of your own?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • I like it fine. I came to the docks at twelve and Garrow took me on. Heavy stuff is my job, the tea chests and the iron and the barrels that leak.
  • Hobart never checks my count. He says I can't count. I say I can carry, which is better.
  • Fish the bay in the mornings. Carry small cargoes up the coast in the afternoons. Be my own foreman.
  • Six years I've been saving. Got about two thirds of the price of a plain little boat from Dunstan's yard. Dunstan's too busy this summer anyway.
  • Fair winds, Player.

docs.title: Ulm
docs.text:
Keeper of the Council Fire

Town Midbarium Where The Great Hall Story Ulm in the lore Services Quests

Mind the fire. Stand there, where the smoke won't find you.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "There, now. Burn steady. That's it."
  • "Forty years, and not once has this fire burned low."
  • "Gorra's jug of water should be along about now."
  • "Does anyone beneath the Tree still sing our names?"

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• By the Fire (gives)
  • Wood for the Fire (gives)
Dialogue
  • Hm. Forty years I have kept this fire, and it has never once burned low. It will not start because a visitor stands too close. Well. Since you are here, sit.
  • That bark you brought burns slow and steady. The fire likes it. So do I, though I will not say so twice.
  • You carried my words to the Old One. Good. Some things a keeper cannot say in council. The fire hears them, and now Hask has too.
  • The fire is listening. So am I, more or less.
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Tell me a Kragvar song.
    • Choice: How was the council?
    • Choice: Goodbye.
  • Ulm, keeper of the council fire. I was a mason once, with stone dust in my beard instead of ash. When the family looked to me for chieftain, I said no: the keeper does not leave the fire. My brother Baruk took it instead.
  • The songs say the best of the Kragvar did not come home from the war. They stayed beneath the World Tree to keep watch. My grandson Korrin sits on the woodpile and listens to every word.
  • Sometimes I wonder whether anyone down there still sings our names back. Nobody comes up the road to tell me. So I keep the fire, and I keep singing.
  • Loud, as always. Four families, four kinds of pride. The Old One sits with me late after, and we say to the fire what nobody said to each other.
  • Go on. The fire and I have things to talk over.

docs.title: Ulric
docs.text:
Stonecarver

Town Goa Harbour Where Goa Harbour Story Ulric in the lore Services Quests

Ah. Player. Mind the step. Look at it, as you pass.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Slowly. The stone is listening."
  • "A step is cut for the hundredth foot. Not the first."
  • "There is a hare on this one. Do you see it?"
  • "Gorm's mallet. Too high on the haft. Again."
  • "The Anvil does not hurry. Nor do I."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Edges for the Anvil (gives)
  • The Hardest Step (gives)
Dialogue
  • Player. The seal on the far cove stair. It has been walked on twice today. Good. That is what it is for.
  • Player. The stone Gorm sent me. Claws, and from below. I have not stopped thinking of it. Sit a while.
  • Player. The chisels are keen again. Thank you. The Anvil thanks you less.
  • Player. There is room on the bench. There always is.
  • Hm. What is it, Player?
    • Choice: Who are you?
    • Choice: Tell me about the animals.
    • Choice: What are you working on?
    • Choice: Nothing. I'll let you work.
  • Ulric. I carve the stone. My father kept goats on the clifftop. I learned these cliffs climbing after them.
  • I was Master of the Stairs once. Twenty-seven years. Then I gave it to Gorm. He argues with crews better than I do. I cut the hard steps now.
  • Old Struan took me on at fourteen. He made me sweep stone dust for a year before he let me hold a chisel. He said a stair belongs to the cliff. It only borrows the town.
  • He carved small things too, now and then. A shell. A knot. I took the habit from him. You are the first in a long while to ask where it came from.
  • A little animal on every step I cut. No bigger than a palm. A crab. A hare. A gull. A seal. Most people walk over them and never look down.
  • Fionn runs his shortcuts and skips half of them. I tell him he reads with the pages torn out. He laughs. Look at them as you pass, Player. That is all I ask.
  • The Anvil. The flight of Gorm's far cove stair that cracked in the frost. Hard rock, and broken. By daylight only, a little at a time. Gorm cuts the new seaward edges sharper. I have not asked him why. He will tell me. He always does, in the end.
  • Gorm told me, in the end. Now I cut the seaward edges sharper too. Stone can be taught to say no.
  • The Anvil is cut. Now I sit, and think about the last step of the Long Stair. The one at the bottom, by the quay. It has nothing on it. Not yet.
  • Go slowly. The steps will still be there.

docs.text:
Carts for Hire

Town Urbanograd Where Urbanograd Services Taxi

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Carts to any town with a stand. You have to have walked there once."
  • "The Walkers walked. You don't have to."
  • "Mind the scaffolds on the Gate Meadows. The carts go round them."
Dialogue
  • Evening, Player. The Gate Walk carts run from here, by the gate, to any town with a stand you have already walked to.
    • Choice: How do the carts work?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • A fixed fare, straight to a town's stand, never into the wilds. And only to a town you have walked to before: the carters will not drive anyone to a place they have never seen for themselves. Old Walker rule.
  • Safe roads!

docs.title: Uskari Scout
docs.text:
Town Midbarium Where Midbarium

Rim's quiet today. That's when you watch hardest.

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Red dots on Skarra's map again. Closer this time."
  • "Tavi walked the worst stretch again last night."
  • "If you're headed for the ridges, go in pairs. Or go armed."

docs.title: Vane
docs.text:
Rooftop Bridge-Builder

Town Urbanograd Where Urbanograd Story Vane in the lore Services Quests

docs.title: Says
docs.text:
• "Every plank gets jumped on before anybody walks on it."
  • "The Wobbler does not wobble. I named it as a warning to the others."
  • "West wind. Good bridge weather."
  • "Scrap! Stairs exist! ...She is not listening."
  • "The Kiss is short. That is the whole joke."

docs.title: Quests
docs.text:
• Scrap and the Roads (gives)
  • Short of Timber (gives)
Dialogue
  • Scrap fell off the Kiss yesterday. On purpose. Rolled, stood up, grinned at me. I did not shout. I want that written down somewhere, Player.
  • The Gutter Queen took your bark like a new coat. I jumped on her this morning. Not a creak.
  • More than two hundred bridges up here, Player, and I know every one by name. What do you need?
    • Choice: Tell me about the bridges.
    • Choice: Who is Scrap?
    • Choice: Will there be a bridge over Lantern Square?
    • Choice: Nothing, thanks.
  • I learned from old Corbett and took over his planks at twenty-four. The Long Lean, Grandmother's Step, the Fiddler's Crossing over the square, the Wobbler, the Kiss, the Gutter Queen, Old Copper. Each one has a temper.
  • Sometimes I find paintings under them. Herons, giants, a moon dropping a coin down a chimney. I know whose they are. I say nothing. A bridge is a good place for a secret.
  • My daughter. Nine years old, and she has never once used the stairs. She collects lost things and names them, and she sneaks up on everybody. I am raising her as well as I can, and I worry about the day she wants the roads.
  • Bastian's covered bridge? I have told him: it would take more timber than reaches the city in a year. He nodded, and then made a speech about it anyway.
  • I have measured the gap, mind. Quietly. Twice. A builder cannot help it.
  • Test every plank, Player. Twice if it has a name.
